World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Trump administration again boycotts UN human rights review
World.content:
The United States ⁠⁠has again boycotted a United Nations examination of its human rights record, drawing criticism from rights groups who say violations under President Donald Trump are surging to levels not seen in decades.

US representatives on Tuesday failed to show up at the UN in Geneva for the review, which all 193 UN member states undergo every four to five years.

“The delegation of the United States is not present in the room,” UN Human Rights Council President Sidharto Reza Suryodipuro, of Indonesia, announced as the session was set to begin.

The US refusal to participate prompted the UN body to delay examining the US human rights record until January. This is the second year in a row that Washington has skipped its own review.

The US withdrew from the council in February 2025 shortly after Trump began his second presidential term, claiming it was biased against Israel.

The Trump administration has been a fierce critic of the UN, withdrawing Washington from key agencies, slashing its funding and bypassing the body in launching the war on Iran.

A US State Department spokesperson said participation would imply endorsement of the council’s work.

“[We] give no credibility to the agency,” the spokesperson said.

“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the official added, without responding to allegations about the US record.

The 47-member council has not directly criticised Washington’s rights record. However, experts have expressed alarm over issues such as migrant deportations, which Washington maintains are carried out in accordance with US immigration law.



UN documents show countries had planned to raise issues such as abortion access and the death penalty.

US and international non-governmental organisations also sent nearly 200 UN submissions covering ⁠⁠topics from migration to racial discrimination.

“Enough is enough,” Jamil Dakwar, of the American Civil Liberties Union, told ⁠⁠reporters in Geneva.

“We’ve seen attacks on fundamental human rights and civil liberties unprecedented in generations,” he added.

Fourteen countries are due to take part in ⁠⁠the review process in Geneva this month. During Trump’s first term in office, the US submitted its UN Universal Periodic Review (UPR) report.

Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council’s first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council’s review system.

“If the predominant global power, which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms, doesn’t show up and doesn’t even justify why, then you are in big trouble,” he said.

World.title: Spain braces for nationwide strike as anger over housing, costs boils over
World.content:
The 24-hour protest, called by Spain’s two biggest unions, is due to start on Wednesday.

Share Spain braces for nationwide walkout as anger over housing, costs boils over on social media

Spain is bracing for a nationwide general strike over soaring rents and the cost of living, as a deepening housing crisis fuels social unrest weeks before a crucial election.

The 24-hour walkout due to begin at midnight on Wednesday was called by Spain’s two biggest unions – the Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) and Union General de Trabajadores (UGT) – under their slogan: wages, housing, prices. The last time the pair called a general strike was in 2012 when the country was engulfed in an austerity crisis.

The protest will disrupt transport, schools, healthcare and other public services across Spain. Flight cancellations and delays are also expected, while public transport in major cities will operate at reduced capacity.

Schools, hospitals, shops and other services could also face closures or reduced staffing, although minimum services will be maintained in essential sectors.

The action follows the September eviction of an 87-year-old, who has since passed away, from her home in Madrid, after her corporate landlord increased the rent. Images of Maricarmen Abascal being forcibly removed on a stretcher struck a nerve. The moment led to nationwide demonstrations and encampments in a wave of protests that also fuelled a political crisis, prompting the government to call the November 29 snap elections.

Wednesday’s strike could help the government bring the housing crisis back to the centre of the political debate, said Luke Stobart, a political analyst who writes about social movements and politics in Spain.



“(Socialist Prime Minister Pedro) Sanchez has been famous for taking risks in the past, and he’s often been quite successful when he’s taken them. And he knows that if you have a general strike before elections, that will force everyone to talk about housing. And that is happening – it is helping to keep housing at the centre of the debate in the run-up to the elections,” Stobart said.

The country has 750,000 fewer homes than it needs, according to the Bank of Spain, which estimates that the gap could exceed one million by 2028.

Rents have rocketed to an average of 1,176 euros ($1,318) per month, and the average salary of a young person is 1,190 euros ($1,333), according to data collated by the Spanish Youth Council.

Many struggling to make ends meet are forced to live in overcrowded shared flats or stay with their parents.

Spain is not alone, as other European nations witness weekly mass protests over costs and living conditions.

While Sanchez has not explicitly endorsed the strike, he praised collective action as the driving force behind the country’s social gains.

“Your eight-hour working day. Your pension. Your public healthcare. None of this fell from the sky. They were collective achievements. We will not let anyone take them away from us,” the prime minister said in a video message on Monday.

He believes his government has more to offer on social policies than political opponents.

But his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) has lost support in recent months over its handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta. It is also plagued by a series of corruption scandals involving Sanchez’s inner circle and family members.

Recently, a deadly train crash in early November gave the opposition, the conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox, an opportunity to shift the national debate towards transport safety and what they described as government incompetence.

The crash, which occurred on the same railway line as another deadly accident less than a year earlier, killed 69 people. Transport Minister Oscar Puente, a senior PSOE figure and close ally of Sanchez, resigned.

The PP is ahead in opinion polls and could form a government with Vox, a prospect that would bring a far-right party into Spain’s national government for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s 1939-1975 dictatorship.



Both opposition parties have dismissed the strike as politically motivated, accusing unions of targeting the opposition ahead of the election. They have also criticised its timing, coming a day after the state funeral for the victims of the train accident.

Stobart said the strike has multiple layers, with different left-leaning groups putting forward a different narrative.

Some are critical of the government. These include Basque unions ELA and LAB, Galicia’s CIG, and Spain’s CGT, which have accused the regional and national governments of failing to tackle housing speculation.

“It’s not clear whether the big trade union leaders and the government are going to be able to control the narrative,” Stobart said, warning that the protests could develop into a broader wave of social unrest, as seen in France and Italy, potentially backfiring on the government.

World.title: Myanmar summons German envoy over controversial video
World.content:
Mathias Licharz calls for the ‘unconditional’ release of ousted politicians, including former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has summoned the head of mission at the German embassy in the country over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians such as former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

The ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that Mathias Licharz in the video “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest”.

Licharz met Deputy Foreign Minister Ko Ko Kyaw, was “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire, the ministry said.

“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” the ministry said.

Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the figurehead president of Aung San Suu Kyi‘s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.

The German diplomat said in his message, marking Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.

In the video, he called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained, including Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi” – using the affectionate term by which Aung San Suu Kyi‘s supporters refer to her.



Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not immediately comment.

Win Myint’s downfall

Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 military coup, ending Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.

Since then, pro-democracy rebels rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority rebellions challenging central rule boiled over.

Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions – charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.

However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.

“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet, and he’s not allowed to communicate independently,” he added, using a male honorific.

The military leadership behind the coup organised elections, installing a nominally civilian government this year, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.

“Should the Charge d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” the Foreign Ministry statement said on Tuesday.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyidaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

World.title: Photos: Crowds greet Pope Leo in Argentina after 40-year wait
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has urged Argentinians to follow the “holy example” of the country’s saints and build a more “fraternal and caring nation”, as an estimated 650,000 people packed the central city of Cordoba for Mass.

The 71-year-old pontiff, on a 12‑day Latin America tour less than a month after lung cancer surgery, on Tuesday celebrated the liturgy on the esplanade of a military aircraft factory.

The Vatican said it was attended by 650,000 pilgrims, following Monday’s Mass in Buenos Aires, where about 2.5 million worshippers gathered – the largest of his pontificate so far.

In Cordoba, Leo listed Argentinian saints and blessed figures as examples of a unity “between passion for the Gospel and commitment to building a fraternal and caring nation”, urging citizens to evangelise “at school and in the square, in the family and with friends, in the countryside and in the city, at the dairy farm and in the office”.

Faithful travelled from across the country after nearly 40 years without a papal visit. “It was quite a journey,” said Erika Vinales, who travelled 2,000km (1,242 miles) from Patagonia with fellow teacher Elena Llanquenao.

Throughout his three days in Argentina, Leo has repeatedly challenged President Javier Milei’s right-wing government to make the economy more inclusive, protect trade unions and reverse funding cuts that hurt the poor and people with disabilities.

World.title: US petrol prices are down, but elevated inflation continues
World.content:
Inflation remained high, despite some easing in fuel prices caused by the US war on Iran.

Consumer prices in the United States increased in October more than expected, even as petrol prices fell to a four-month low after some easing of concerns about the long-term impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets.

In its latest report released on Tuesday, the US Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for all items rose by 0.4 percent in October, continuing an inflationary trend since July. The average cost of shelter, as well as food, also rose in October, according to the agency.

The Labor Department’s report was higher than the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, which had forecast the CPI to increase by 0.2 percent, and economists polled by FactSet, who had predicted an increase of 0.3 percent, despite the lowering pressure on energy prices.

On Monday, US President Donald Trump said that future military action against Tehran was unlikely. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”

The average price of a gallon of petrol fell below $4 ($1.06 per litre) for the first time since July, according to the American Automobile Association. But the average price, currently $3.98, is still significantly higher than the $3.07 mark it was at a year ago. The average price of a gallon of petrol was $2.98 ($0.78 per litre) on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

The economy and cost-of-living concerns were leading concerns for voters in midterm elections that were held on November 3, which saw Republicans lose control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on the eve of the elections found that 78 percent of voters said cost-of-living was very important or the most important issue for them when considering how they would vote. Democrats, the poll found, were favoured by 43 percent of voters, compared with 32 percent who preferred Republicans to handle it.



How voters view Trump himself has also turned largely negative since the war and its impact on the economy. Only 32 percent of voters approved of his job performance, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll, just one point above his record low of 31 percent last month.

Trump’s Republican Party was dealt major losses in the midterm elections, losing typically Republican seats in Congress in states like Texas and Kansas.

Trump himself, as well as key members of his administration like Vice President JD Vance, have acknowledged that the war on Iran played a part in those electoral losses.

World.title: Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb
World.content:
Iran says it is committed to non-proliferation treaty, but hardliners may be pushing for a change in nuclear policy.

Tehran, Iran – Iran says it has not suspended its commitments under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), but as mediated talks to end the war with the United States continue, broad international inspections of Iranian sites remain far off.

Following US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s main nuclear facilities in and assassinations of senior leaders, Iranian authorities have increasingly discussed the possibility of abandoning the international treaty and building a nuclear bomb.

US President Donald Trump’s threats to attack the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near the Natanz nuclear facility and other sensitive sites have only emboldened hardliners in Tehran to demand a shift in the country’s nuclear doctrine – under assassinated Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, nuclear weapons were officially forbidden.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei emphasised to reporters during a news conference in Tehran on Monday that the Islamic Republic remains committed to the NPT, despite restricting cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog.

“Other parties have imposed conditions, namely the attacks by the US and Zionist regime against our nuclear facilities which have caused issues concerning implementation of safeguards commitments,” he said, in reference to Israel.

“As long as this situation continues, we cannot act like normal circumstances in our cooperation with the agency,” Baghaei said about the IAEA, while also renewing Tehran’s criticism of its director, Rafael Grossi.



But the spokesman confirmed that new IAEA inspections were conducted days earlier at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.

The electricity generation plant, built in cooperation with Russia and under development for new phases, is the only facility still accessible to the agency, as it was not directly bombed during the war. US warplanes did, however, attack the perimeter of the plant several times and caused damage, prompting partial evacuation of Russian personnel, who have yet to fully return.

IAEA chief Grossi told the UN Security Council in late October that the body was unable to verify Iran’s nuclear material because Tehran “has not provided the requested information and access”.

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the International Crisis Group, said Tehran is keeping one foot inside the NPT and the other near the exit.

“Allowing inspections at Bushehr is a low-cost gesture designed to keep diplomacy alive and hardliners at bay, while preserving leverage over the underground nuclear sites that matter most,” he told Al Jazeera.

Those sensitive sites include the Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan facilities, among others.

Seyed Hossein Mousavian, a visiting researcher at Princeton University and a former Iranian nuclear negotiator, said Iran’s position “reflects a distinction between honouring its NPT commitments and permitting inspections of facilities that have been bombed”.

Mousavian said the IAEA had no established inspection protocol for nuclear facilities damaged by military attacks, and pointed out that the Iranians fear that IAEA access to sensitive sites would lead to information being shared with the US and Israel that could then be used in future attacks.

“Tehran views restrictions on broader inspections as a security concern rather than necessarily a rejection of its NPT obligations,” he said.

Nuclear commitments and benefits

Iran has had one of the most scrutinised nuclear programmes in history, and its international obligations are governed by several treaties and UN resolutions.

The NPT establishes the fundamental rules against nuclear proliferation, while recognising the right to peaceful nuclear energy. A separate safeguards agreement with the IAEA sets out how the agency monitors Iran’s nuclear activities to make sure it isn’t moving towards weapons development. Subsidiary arrangements, UN Security Council resolutions and nuclear agreements have fulfilled additional requirements.

As a party to the NPT, Iran’s peaceful nuclear-use rights are recognised, and it is allowed to undertake peaceful exchanges and receive assistance with nuclear development.



In exchange, the country commits not to receive, manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons, and to accept safeguards and information sharing in its territory.

Withdrawal requires a notice after a decision has been made that “extraordinary events” have “jeopardised the supreme interests” of the country.

However, the treaty does not protect from conventional military attack, and this gap between promised peaceful-use benefits and actual vulnerability has been at the centre of the appeal by domestic hardliners to leave the NPT.

But such considerations have not been limited to a handful of hawkish figures.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has publicly deliberated the possibility of abandoning the treaty on multiple occasions. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said earlier this week that the organisation “will create the necessary preparations” if the Islamic Republic goes through with the decision to change its nuclear doctrine.

Negotiations ongoing

Regional mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to relay messages between Iran and the US to prevent another all-out war, although analysts have warned that escalation is likely over the coming months.

Tehran has maintained that it will not allow its highly enriched uranium to be taken out of the country, but remains open to downblending it under international supervision inside Iran. It has also said it will not abandon enrichment altogether, but can accept a limit on enrichment as it did with the 2015 nuclear deal that US President Donald Trump unilaterally abandoned in 2018, during his first term in office.

Arriving at a deal that thoroughly addresses Iran’s nuclear programme would also require a resolution to hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and beyond, something that is unlikely to materialise in the foreseeable future.

“Tehran might be willing to open the door a crack in exchange for tangible American concessions, but it is unlikely to surrender its most valuable nuclear bargaining chips upfront,” the Crisis Group’s Vaez said.

The expert added that a preliminary deal could potentially unlock limited, phased inspections based on the 2025 Cairo agreement between Iran and the IAEA.

The agreement came several months after the US and Israel bombed Iran’s nuclear facilities during the 12-day war of June 2025. It envisaged restored access for agency inspectors to all Iranian facilities, if case-by-case permission is granted by the country’s Supreme National Security Council.

But it was never enforced, and was followed by tensions that led to the US and Israel attacking Iran again on February 28.

“Restoring meaningful transparency over Iran’s nuclear programme will require a larger bargain on enrichment, stockpiles and sanctions relief,” Vaez said.

But Mousavian said Tehran would want more than just a preliminary agreement like the Cairo deal.

“Such cooperation would require a comprehensive agreement that addresses the overall security and nuclear issues; without it, inspections of the bombed sites are unlikely,” he said.

World.title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion valuation in massive stock market debut
World.content:
The maker of Claude is looking to raise up to $64.4bn in one of the largest IPOs in history next week.

Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion for its upcoming IPO, with the company looking to raise as much as $64.4bn in what would be one of the largest stock market debuts in history.

The company, which makes the Claude AI chatbot, launched its investor roadshow on Tuesday, with reported plans to go public next week.

According to its filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Tuesday, Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78, giving it a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion when potential shares are included.

It has also secured $26bn in a separate private placement backed by some of the world’s largest tech companies, including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and AMD.

The listing is being closely watched as a major test for how much investors are still willing to bet on AI companies, which have driven huge gains in tech stocks and the broader US market.

The $1.4 trillion valuation is lower than earlier estimates, which had suggested Anthropic could be valued between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, as concerns grow about the company’s enormous infrastructure spending and recent swings in AI stock prices.

Those concerns extend beyond Anthropic, with investors increasingly questioning whether AI companies can make enough money to justify their soaring valuations and sustain the boom.

Despite the uncertainty, Anthropic’s growth has been explosive.

The company reported revenues of $17bn in their third quarter, up from $1.4bn a year earlier, as its net losses narrowed. On Tuesday, Anthropic said it was on pace to generate about $81bn in annual revenue, $10bn higher than its estimate a month earlier.



The company credits its growth to the demand for Claude, including from industries like healthcare, financial services and legal services.

But to keep up with that demand, Anthropic has committed almost $900bn to computing costs with partners including Amazon and Google, a massive financial bet on continued demand for its product.

The IPO also lands in an uncertain political climate, with Democrats having just won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections last week. The new Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate have raised the prospect of more regulation of AI companies and new restrictions on the construction of data centres that power the technology.

AI stocks slid after the midterms, with the Nasdaq falling 5.5 percent on Thursday, its biggest one-day drop in more than a year. The selloff, also driven by declines at Nvidia, whose CEO was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy, wiped out trillions of dollars from the market.

Markets have since recovered some of those losses, though the Nasdaq dipped slightly below 1 percent on Tuesday. Some analysts argued the sell-off was an overreaction and that the election was unlikely to derail the expansion of data centres.

World.title: Israeli president warns against repeat election in new Knesset session
World.content:
Herzog calls for an inquiry into the October 7 attacks during a Knesset session amid political gridlock following elections.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged lawmakers to “leave no stone unturned” and launch an investigation into the October 7 attacks by Hamas in a speech opening the new parliamentary session, after the election left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc short of a majority.

Herzog called on party leaders to “make concessions” and do “everything possible to avoid a repeat election” at the swearing-in of newly elected members in the 26th Knesset on Tuesday.

The Israeli president tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government on Sunday, starting the clock for him to cobble together a coalition within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.

While also short of a parliamentary majority, Eisenkot and his allies hope to use their newfound legislative power to move rapidly to establish an independent inquiry into the October 7 attacks.

“I am committed in this complex situation to form a national emergency government as quickly as possible,” Eisenkot said, ahead of the Knesset session.

Netanyahu has previously refused to form a commission to investigate the attacks, arguing that a panel appointed by the Israeli Supreme Court would be biased against the government.

On Iran, Herzog said in his speech that Tehran “does not stop even for a moment in its plots and threats, whether directly or through its partners”, repeating the notion from his speech officially delegating Eisenkot to form the new government.

The president said Israel “must fortify the alliance” with the United States amid increasing disapproval of Israel among the US public due to the genocidal war on Gaza and the US-Israel war on Iran.



“Alongside the stubborn and determined war against those who seek to harm us, we must build a stable political horizon in the region with our neighbours,” he said, adding that Israel must “strengthen and even add to the peace agreements with Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain”.

Political gridlock

The speaker of the Knesset, a member of Netanyahu’s Likud Party, will remain in the caretaker position until a new vote is held.

“Yashar, Eisenkot’s party, has already submitted 61 signatures of new parliamentarians demanding that the vote take place as soon as possible,” said Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu and his bloc continue to protest the result of the October 27 elections, claiming foreign interference after Palestinian-Israeli parties secured a 19-seat bloc.

“Those protests have gone unanswered because the results have been certified and every relevant authority has dismissed the allegations that there were widespread violations,” Odeh said.

Eisenkot has yet to strike deals with parties that could bring him to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government. If neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu forms a coalition, another round of elections could follow.

World.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks constructive, Zelensky says
World.content:
The first of two days of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.

While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions, President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved "constructive and quite substantive".

Speaking from Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said the meeting had been "very productive".

Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.

Zelensky also said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges had been discussed.

At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".

Kushner had said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

He and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.

Until now European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.

The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".

However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.

Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.

Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.

A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".

However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe â which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

World.title: Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
World.content:
Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.

There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.

Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.

The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.

Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (Â£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.

Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.

World.title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
World.content:
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.

Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.

Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.

Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.

"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.

He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".

Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.

"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.

One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.

The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.

World.title: Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods 'insufficent'
World.content:
In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.

The Board added that delays in approving the entry of supplies "exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge" and delayed the start of decommissioning weapons and transferring Hamas authority to a transitional government.

It also said Hamas's failure to disarm and transfer power had compounded the difficulties facing Gaza's civilians.

The UN's humanitarian agency OCHA said more than 150,000 tents were outside Gaza ready to go in, but aid efforts were constrained "by Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and equipment and funding shortfalls".

UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said on Monday that stocks of essential shelter and winter items inside Gaza had been exhausted.

"Israeli authorities must immediately lift all restrictions on entry of the supplies," he said, adding "we have run out of time".

Israel's foreign ministry spokeswoman Michal Maayan on Monday said Israel had in recent months put in place a winter plan in coordination with the Board of Peace and international charities.

That plan has brought in more than 91,000 tents and 8,200-plus trucks with tarpaulins, blankets, winter clothing, and other equipment, according to Cogat, the Israeli military body responsible for aid.

Cogat said it would not allow in equipment that could be used for military purposes.

Maayon accused Hamas of hoarding aid, saying: "Hamas is responsible for the delays in making more progress in the Strip, and winter-related hardships are a consequence of Hamas's action and policy."

In response to the Board of Peace, Hamas said in a statement published on Palestinian media that its comment "presents a distorted account of the causes of the disaster". The group denied it was responsible for ceasefire delays, pointing to a statement in August , externalfrom Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators that accused Israel of violations.

Hamas said Israeli restrictions prevent the entry of materials necessary for shelter and recovery - and added the Board as the ceasefire implementor should look at its own "serious shortcoming".

Under the deal to end the two-year-long war in October 2025, Hamas agreed to give up governance and its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza it still occupied. Israel, however, has insisted Hamas must fully disarm before withdrawal.

The dispute has left the next stages of the peace plan stalled, with both sides blaming each other.

The war in Gaza began after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 when around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

The Israeli military campaign in response has killed 74,645 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the ceasefire in October last year.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza since then.

World.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
World.content:
A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."

The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."

Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.

It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.

Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.

Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.

The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.

Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".

Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.

"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."

Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

World.title: French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104
World.content:
One of France's last Resistance heroes from World War Two has died at the age of 104. Solange Alexandre was also a rare woman who, with her future husband, created and commanded her own unit of anti-German fighters.

After serving as a Resistance courier from 1941, three years later she founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network near the town of RuillÃ©-sur-Loir.

With some 30 men under her orders, she organised sabotage operations, sheltered Allied airmen and, after the Allied landings in Normandy on D-Day in 1944, joined the fight against the occupying German forces.

President Emmanuel Macron was among many to pay tribute to Alexandre, after her death was announced at a nursing home in Le Mans.

"She said she only ever did her duty. But her duty was our freedom. France will never forget. Thank you," Macron posted on social media.

Born in 1922 in the Sarthe department of western France, Solange Alexandre, nÃ©e Dubuisson, grew up in a patriotic family that had suffered in World War One.

"My mother lost her first husband in the war, and my father was wounded in 1917. The words homeland and honour were very important to us. They were in my blood," she recalled in her memoirs.

In June 1940 she heard on the radio the appeal from General Charles de Gaulle in London, calling on the French not to give up the struggle against Germany. She had never heard of him, but that did not matter.

"From that moment I knew I had to join up," she wrote.

Some months later she was recruited by a friend of her father's â a Tunisian-born French army veteran called SaÃ¯d Belhaffaf, who had joined the Resistance.

Using the code-name Corlay, she criss-crossed the region around Le Mans by bicycle, gathering information and passing on messages.

"There were no mobile phones back then, and no private cars either because of the lack of petrol. The bicycle was king," she said in an interview two years ago.

In 1943 she met her first husband Guy DÃ©liot, who had deserted from the French gendarmerie after refusing to arrest some Jews.

The following April, with the Allied invasion approaching, they decided to take to the maquis, in other words live clandestinely in the forested hills, supplied with food by local farmers.

Their group consisted of deserters from German forced labour programmes, as well as survivors from another Resistance outfit that had been destroyed by the enemy. There were also two airmen, one American and one Canadian.

"Twice the Gestapo came for me, and twice I slipped through their hands," she later recalled.

After taking part in the liberation of Tours in September 1944, she ended the war with the rank of sub-lieutenant in the French Interior Forces (FFI).

Later she worked as a teacher and followed her husband on his many postings as an officer of the gendarmerie in French overseas territories. He was killed in 1960 in Martinique, and in 1981 she remarried.

Twice Solange Alexandre turned down the LÃ©gion d'Honneur, saying that she had only done her duty and that others were more worthy.

Finally in 2024 she relented.

On receiving the award she said: "It is a great pleasure and a great honour. I am very proud â even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die."

World.title: Twelve dead after motorway pile-ups in Bulgaria fog
World.content:
Twelve people have been killed after dozens of cars and lorries were involved in two pile-ups on the Trakia motorway in south-eastern Bulgaria, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.

Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 11 people died at the scene on Tuesday, near the town of Zimnitsa, while another person later died in hospital. About 50 others were taken to hospital with injuries.

Sliven regional governor Mihail Kasherov told journalists that more than 70 vehicles were involved in the incident, Bulgarian state news agency BTA reported.

Officials have said dense fog reduced visibility and was the likely cause of the first crash, which occurred on the eastbound carriageway.

Radev declared Wednesday a day of national mourning following the incident.

World.title: US federal authorities could have prevented Epstein crimes, report finds
World.content:
Regarding Epstein's death in a New York prison, investigators concluded this was a result of "a series of institutional failures at the facility," which included staffing shortages, overworked employees, poor recordkeeping, and lax security practices.

Testimony the panel solicited was "unable to definitively dispel certain theories" surrounding Epstein's death, the report states, including accounting for a lapse in surveillance footage.

It found the justice department (DoJ) failed to communicate about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive personal information.

Earlier this year, the DoJ had to remove thousands of documents related to Epstein from its website after victims said their identities had been compromised.

The report also alleges that financial institutions like American Express enabled human trafficking and immigration fraud, by allowing Epstein to use decoy flights and dummy itineraries to transport foreign workers across borders. The BBC has contacted American Express for comment.

The investigative panel recommended that Congress should pass legislation to prevent the weaponisation of non-disclosure agreements, which they said Epstein used to silence survivors.

"Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims," said James Comer, the Republican chairman of the committee.

He called upon the DoJ to "interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records.

The report accuses Democrats of being "obsessed" with trying to implicate US President Donald Trump and that an "unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors".

Trump has previously said he was friendly with Epstein before they fell out in 2004. The president's name has appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files but there is no suggestion that appearing in the documents implies any wrongdoing.

The committee's review of documents did not identify any that would implicate Trump, the report concluded.

In a statement, Rep Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, alleged his Republican colleagues "released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein".

Garcia accused the justice department of withholding "over 2.5 million pages of documents".

"We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation," said Garcia, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January following the recent midterm elections.

World.title: Adeleke speaks on Osun’s debt profile, amid reported $26.56m borrowing increase
World.content:
Osun State Governor, Ademola Adeleke, on Tuesday, denied taking any foreign loan since taking office in November 2022, following a Debt Management Office (DMO) update revealing a rise in the state’s debt profile.

Mr Adeleke attributed the increase in the state’s external debt to repayments and obligations arising from loans obtained by his predecessor.

The governor’s denial followed a DMO report showing that Osun’s external debt stock increased from $75.14 million as of December 2024 to $101.70 million as of 30 June 2026.

The figures represent an increase of approximately $26.56 million or 35.3 per cent increase within 18 months.

In a statement issued on Tuesday by his spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, Mr Adeleke blamed the increase on a $25.8 million loan obtained by the previous administration led by Gboyega Oyetola, for the Rural Access and Agricultural Marketing Project (RAAMP).

“The loan repayment process had matured by December 2025, hence its inclusion by DMO in its report,” the statement read.

According to the governor, four other external loans obtained by the previous administration have also matured for repayment and may soon be reflected in the state’s external debt stock.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It noted that breakdown of the DMO figures cited by the governor’s office shows that Osun’s multilateral debt rose from approximately $67.60 million in December 2024 to $94.15 million in June 2026.

“Its bilateral debt also recorded a marginal increase, moving from approximately $7.54 million to $7.55 million within the same period.”

Mr Adeleke, however, maintained that his administration had not taken any external loans since assuming office, describing allegations that it secretly borrowed foreign funds as false.

“The above clarification is necessary to set the records straight. If at all, our administration is to take loans for any reason, it will be open to the public with utmost transparency and compliance with due process,” the governor said.

World.title: What emerging artistes need to succeed in Afrobeats — Puffy Tee, Krizbeatz, Andre Vibez
World.content:
In the last decade, Afrobeats has evolved from a predominantly African sound into a global musical movement, attracting international audiences, collaborations and commercial opportunities.

Top artistes like Burna Boy, Wizkid, Davido, Tiwa Savage, Tems and Ayra Starr have pushed the ‘Afrobeats to the world’ movement to several continents.

But its growing popularity has also brought renewed conversations about the genre’s identity, the diversity of sounds it accommodates and the challenges facing emerging artistes seeking to establish themselves in an increasingly competitive industry.

As the genre expands, questions about originality, financial investment, artistic expression, and the future of African music have become increasingly important.

Against this backdrop, MTN’s Next Afrobeats Star, a music reality competition designed to discover and develop emerging Nigerian talents, is providing a platform for aspiring musicians to showcase their abilities and receive guidance from established industry professionals.

Speaking to PREMIUM TIMES during the trials of the competition’s second season, three of the show’s judges, music producers Puffy Tee, Krizbeatz and Andre Vibez, shared their perspectives on the state of Afrobeats.

Talent not enough to succeed in music

Music producer Puffy Tee said emerging artistes need financial resources, not just talent, to succeed in Nigeria’s increasingly competitive music industry, arguing that ability alone may not sustain a career.

According to him, artistes must understand the financial demands of building a successful music career, including production, promotion, distribution and other investments required to reach a wider audience.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“What I would say to any artiste who wants to stand out with all this competition is: have money and have talent. Talent without money is toluntu. Have talent and have a lot of money, a lot of it. That will help you propel your goals forward,” the ‘Yahooze’ producer said.

Asked what distinguishes an artiste with potential from one prepared for the demands of the industry, Tee again emphasised financial capacity, arguing that emerging musicians must recognise music as a business.

He clarified, however, that he was not suggesting money should take precedence over talent, but that both were necessary.

Using the example of a pastor seeking to establish a church, he explained that having a message alone would not be sufficient without the resources to secure a place of worship, equipment and personnel.

Afrobeats as an umbrella

The ‘Eleko’ producer also defended using Afrobeats as an umbrella term for contemporary African music, dismissing concerns that the genre’s growing international popularity could overshadow the continent’s diverse musical traditions.

He argued that Afrobeats accommodates different sounds and influences, including reggae, dancehall and R&B, while allowing artistes to incorporate their cultural identities and indigenous musical styles.

“Afro means Africa. So when you say African music, it’s also Afrobeats. Now, what we define as Afrobeats can be reggae, can be dancehall, can be R&B, can be all of it. Afrobeats, this genre, is actually a magnet that puts all kinds of genres together,” he said.

Evolving African sound

Mr Puffy Tee maintained that traditional Nigerian sounds such as Fuji and Juju should retain their distinct identities rather than be renamed Afrobeats. However, artistes could incorporate them into contemporary Afrobeats productions.

The next Afrobeats judge also argued that the genre had created room for musicians across Africa to express themselves through their languages, traditions and cultural experiences.

His comments come amid wider conversations about how African music is categorised and represented internationally, particularly as the genre continues to attract global attention.

The producer expressed concern, however, about what he described as declining lyrical quality in some contemporary Afrobeats releases, saying the trend risked weakening the genre’s artistic value.

Christian music, creative freedom

Another judge, music producer Krizbeatz, discussed the relationship between music, culture and Christianity, arguing that Christian music should not be restricted to particular sounds or musical arrangements.

He said people’s understanding and appreciation of music were often shaped by their cultural environments, adding that African Christians should not automatically associate indigenous or contemporary African sounds with secular or ungodly influences.

According to him, “music is influenced by geographical and cultural experiences, just as clothing and other forms of expression differ across societies.”

The ‘Pana’ producer explained that the perception that slow, classical-sounding songs are more appropriate for worship than contemporary African rhythms was largely shaped by religious and cultural conditioning.

Krizbeatz also argued “that musical arrangements could create spiritual experiences,” noting that melodies, instruments and lyrics could work together to communicate a particular message.

The producer said the right combination of instrumentation, melody and lyrics could produce music that inspires listeners, regardless of the performer’s background.

Although he acknowledged producing songs with lyrics he would no longer accept, he said his approach had changed over time.

“If you want to produce a song and the lyrics are not good, that song will never come out. It will just be in my studio alone,” he said.

The producer explained that rather than dismissing an artiste’s creative direction outright, he would suggest alternative lyrics that could communicate the intended message without compromising his convictions.

Originality, identity, longevity

Meanwhile, music producer Andre Vibez urged emerging artistes to prioritise originality over imitating established musicians or rushing to adopt sounds simply because they were trending.

The ‘Rush’ producer said one common mistake among upcoming artistes was reproducing successful formulas without developing a distinct musical identity.

“Emerging artistes like to copy a formula that has worked for maybe another artiste. When they see something trending, something popping, they jump on it, and they tend not to have their own identity.

“That doesn’t take you so far. You might have one or two viral moments, but at the end of the day, if you really want to go far, you need to create your own path,” he said.

The ‘Calm Down’ producer also identified talent, consistency and longevity as essential qualities for a sustainable music career.

According to him, talent matters, but artistes must stay consistent and patient because success may not come immediately.

“Those three things, if you have all three put together, you are guaranteed to succeed. You have talent, you stay consistent, and you are bound to succeed,” he said.

Vibez also explained that producers had a responsibility to help artistes discover and develop their individual sounds rather than force them into particular musical styles.

The music producer said his approach involved creating instrumentals that complemented an artiste’s natural vocal abilities and directing them towards performances that brought out their strengths.

“You don’t want to change how an artiste sounds. That’s their uniqueness, right? How they sing is how they sing,” he said.

He added that producers should understand an artiste’s vocal range and musical preferences before developing beats that suit their abilities.

Next Afrobeats Star

The second season of MTN Next Afrobeats Star is designed to discover and develop emerging Nigerian music talents through auditions, mentorship, music production and performance challenges.

The competition brings together established music producers who assess contestants and guide them through the programme’s different stages.

Ayo Benzi won the inaugural edition, held in 2025, and received a ₦150 million recording deal.

The ongoing second season offers an expanded prize package, with the winner expected to receive a ₦225 million recording deal, alongside additional benefits.

World.title: 2027: In Plateau, Obi pledges to unite Nigeria, tackle insecurity, poverty
World.content:
The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has pledged to unite Nigeria, end insecurity and lift millions of citizens out of poverty if elected in 2027.

Mr Obi made the pledge on Tuesday during a town hall meeting with supporters in Jos, Plateau State, where he outlined his agenda for the country, identifying national unity, security, economic productivity and accountable leadership as the priorities of his administration.

The former Anambra State Governor said Nigeria had become increasingly divided along ethnic and religious lines, insisting that restoring national cohesion would be central to addressing the country’s political, economic and security challenges.

“Our number one commitment is to unite the Federal Republic of Nigeria because today we have no unity. We are divided along tribal and religious lines. That should not be. We are Nigerians,” he said.

Mr Obi identified insecurity as another major challenge requiring urgent intervention, promising to ensure that Nigerians could live and conduct their businesses without fear of attacks, kidnapping and other violent crimes.

“I assure you that no mother will continue to cry over the loss of her children. No woman should experience the pain of losing her husband, and no father should suffer the agony of losing his wife,” he said.

He also pledged to prioritise the return of internally displaced persons (IDPs) to their ancestral communities, arguing that the continued displacement of Nigerians reflected the failure of government to guarantee their safety.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“If any Nigerian remains in an IDP camp, we have failed. Once one Nigerian is in an IDP camp, the entire Nigeria is in an IDP camp. People must return to their homes,” he said.

The NDC candidate vowed to strengthen the country’s security architecture and ensure that kidnappers and other criminal elements were pursued and brought to justice.

“Nobody will kidnap two children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you,” he declared.

Mr Obi said his decision to engage communities through town hall meetings before the formal commencement of campaigns was informed by the need to understand citizens’ concerns and develop policies based on their actual needs.

“When you want to serve, you must listen to the people. When we come for campaigns, we only talk, and we don’t listen to the people. We have decided that leadership must be demand-driven,” he said.

He recalled his visits to Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Mangu and other violence-affected communities in Plateau State, describing the security situation as unacceptable.

The former governor said his presidential ambition was driven by the need to address the suffering of victims of insecurity, particularly displaced families and households that had lost loved ones to violence.

“If I have one person in an IDP camp, it means we are all in an IDP camp. I am competing because I want to know how we talk to that mother whose child was killed, that husband who lost a wife and that woman who lost a husband. Who is going to listen to their cries?”

On the 2027 general election, Mr Obi urged Nigerians to take responsibility for protecting their votes, insisting that electoral accountability should not be left entirely to electoral institutions.

He called on voters to remain at polling units after casting their ballots to monitor the counting, recording and transmission of results.

“In the next election, every voter is an agent. Don’t vote and go home. Take that day as the one day you are giving to Nigeria as a patriotic Nigerian,” he said.

“Your vote must be counted, recorded and transmitted. Nobody should give you any excuse. It is your vote, and we want this election to be about the future of Nigeria,” he added.

On the economy, Mr Obi said his administration would seek to transform Nigeria from a consumption-driven economy into a production-based one, arguing that increased local production would stimulate employment, strengthen businesses and reduce poverty.

He said insecurity had prevented farmers from accessing their farmlands and contributed to the collapse of businesses, including companies operating in Plateau State.

“Our determination is to unite Nigeria, secure Nigeria and pull people out of poverty. That is why we said we are going to move Nigeria from consumption to production,” he said.

“By increasing production, we will increase employment. Today, farmers cannot go to their farms because of insecurity. Companies operating in Plateau State have collapsed because of insecurity. When we unite Nigeria and secure it, we will create opportunities.”

Mr Obi also promised to improve access to funding for small and medium-sized businesses, saying his experience in the financial sector has given him an understanding of the difficulties entrepreneurs face when seeking credit.

He said his administration would work to ensure that a portion of credit available in the banking sector was directed towards small businesses to support their growth and capacity to create jobs.

“I know what it means to access funding. I have been a director and chairman of a financial institution, and I understand how banks operate,” he said.

On corruption, the presidential candidate promised to strengthen accountability in public finance and ensure that government resources were deployed for the benefit of citizens.

“I have managed public money, so when I say I am going to fight corruption, I know what I am talking about. I will fight corruption. Public money must be used for public good. Today, public money is wrongly being used, and that must change,” he said.

The NDC candidate also promised increased investment in education, expressing concern over the estimated 18 million Nigerian children who are out of school.

He said his administration would construct additional classrooms, recruit teachers and improve the quality of public education to ensure that more children had access to functional schools.

“We want our children to go back to school. We want our schools to work. The more educated you are as a nation, the more developed you become,” he said.

On healthcare, Mr Obi called for stronger investment in primary healthcare centres, saying inadequate medical facilities in many communities had contributed to preventable deaths, particularly among pregnant women and children.

He lamented that many Nigerians lacked access to functional hospitals and were sometimes compelled to seek help from religious institutions when they fell ill.

“The foundation of access to healthcare is primary healthcare. We must strengthen our primary healthcare centres and ensure that every community has access to quality medical services,” he said.

He also expressed concern over poverty, infant mortality and the growing number of out-of-school children, arguing that Nigeria has the resources to address these challenges through strategic investment in education, healthcare and agriculture.

Mr Obi further stressed that government must demonstrate compassion by prioritising vulnerable citizens, including poor people, elderly Nigerians and persons living with disabilities.
