World.title: Ramaphosa announces salary hikes for judges, MP's and Cabinet
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Judges and other public officials are set to receive a pay hike.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has announced salary increases of between 3.5% and 4% for the 2026/2027 financial year, effective 1 April 2026.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Presidency said the 3.5% increase applies to members of the national executive, members of the National Assembly, permanent delegates to the national council of provinces, premiers, members of provincial executive councils, and members of provincial legislatures.

World.title: NCC recalls more than 23,000 Cherry and Omoda vehicles
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Over 20,600 Chery and Omoda vehicles are being recalled across the country over potential safety defects.

The National Consumer Commission says the recall affects the Chery Tiggo 4, Omoda C5 and Cherry Tiggo 8 Pro Max 2.0 vehicles.

The defects could pose serious safety risks.

The Tiggo 4 sold between October 2023 and March 2024 and Omoda C5 models sold between February 2023 and July 2026 may have faulty welding on the rear axle.

This could cause the axle to dislodge and the rear suspension to collapse.

The Tiggo 8 Pro Max manufactured from May 2026 faces a different risk.

READ | Hyundai recalls 253 Tucson vehicles

Its front brake pipe could wear against the turbocharger, potentially causing brake-fluid leaks and reduced braking performance.

Owners are urged to contact authorised Chery dealerships for inspections and repairs.

All remedial work will be done free of charge.

The NCC says it is also investigating Chery over allegations of previous recalls that were not reported to the Commission.

World.title: Why President Ruto shouldn't put his hopes on Oburu's Linda Ground
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto and ODM leader Oburu Oginga at a past event. [File, Standard]

Raila Odinga worked with friends and foes. He treated his voting blocs with respect, and they paid him back. For the last five elections, Luhyas ranked number one in voting for Raila. The Kamba did the same, election after election, in great numbers. Then came 2022. Raila was on the ballot a fifth time. ODM held governors, senators, MPs, MCAs — everything. And still, 700,000 Luo Nyanza voters stayed home. Stations were half-empty by midday. If Nyanza would not wake up for its own, why would it wake up for William Ruto because Oburu Oginga, Gladys Wanga, John Mbadi or Opiyo Wandayi said so?

A year since Raila’s death, the ODM map has shrunk. And recently, it exploded in Homa Bay. Violence rocked its bedrock and brought back memories of the worst post-election bloodshed 20 years ago. When leaders turn to intolerant rhetoric that fuels violence, they mutilate the former ODM leader’s legacy.

This is the same week we marked Raila’s first anniversary. Tremors are now hitting the ODM orbit harder than ever. It remains to be seen where the Odinga family will align. Winnie Odinga of East African Legislative assembly appears to favour Edwin Sifuna, who tops favourability because he carries the Odinga spirit. If the family defies Oburu’s Linda Ground, Ruto gets a double puncture in Luoland.

President Ruto handed lucrative dockets, including Finance, to Raila’s largely Luoland wing of ODM, now led by Raila’s brother Oburu under the Linda Ground camp, to lure Luo Nyanza for 2027.

Was this a flawed bet? Look at the driver. Linda Ground is presented as Raila’s successor, but Oburu is indisposed and aged. Unlike his brother, a tactician who turned a funeral into a rally, Oburu speaks but lacks the ruthless instinct that made his brother a colossus. Ruto has less than a year to the election and is hunting numbers. That is why Linda Ground tempts him. On paper, it promises Luo Nyanza votes, but the numbers say the opposite. Luos are loud in campaigns but absent at the ballot. Some of the leaders sounding loyal to Ruto are transactional, chasing appointments, tenders or harambees. They trade loyalty for gain. Not votes. They failed Raila. They will fail Ruto.

If I were Ruto, I would treat them with a pinch of salt. Relying on them without taming polarising politics will cost him victory. Under the guise of backing Ruto, some Luo leaders prove loyalty through intimidation. Yet Babu Owino, Edwin Sifuna, George Natembeya and Carol Omondi have every right to traverse Kenya undeterred.

The recent attack on former Vice President Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka during his Ukombozi Alliance tour in Luo Nyanza augurs badly and paints the region as intolerant. It alienates the region from the rest of Kenya. The Kamba voted for Raila in great numbers. The least the region can show Kalonzo is tolerance and respect. But now, some Luo leaders are treating the rest of Raila’s followers, who hold a different opinion, as traitors, abusing them to make Ruto happy. Foul language dominates their pronouncements.

In Parliament, an ODM MP once argued that the Standard Media Group should be banned, even though his mentor, Raila, always advocated for a free press.

Fallout is already visible. In Gusiiland, voters who once loved ODM see no reason to follow Oburu. Richard Onyonka, Okong’o Omogeni and Anthony Kibagendi tilted to Fred Matiang’i and Linda Mwananchi. In Luhyaland and Nairobi, the ground shifted to Sifuna, Orengo, Natembeya and Babu. On the Coast, Aisha Jumwa and Mohamed Ali emerged as the strongest voices of loyal opposition. Oburu’s ODM has lost Luhyaland, Nairobi, Kisii and Coast, Turkana, Maasailand and North Eastern.

Expelling Sifuna and Godfrey Osotsi alienated Luhyas. An intact ODM would have been Ruto’s muscle; Sifuna, the ideal running mate. They forgot optics before kicking him out. How will leaders from Luo Nyanza, alleged to be behind the attacks on Linda Mwananchi and the Ukombozi coalition, campaign for Ruto in Luhyaland and Ukambani, where Sifuna and Kalonzo hold sway?

These are Raila orphans now in a queer street, claiming Raila left them in broad-based. In Nyanza, Western, Nairobi, Turkana, Narok, North Eastern and Coast, association with Raila alone won elections.

If Joho, Wycliffe Oparanya and Simba Arati could not deliver the presidency for Raila, how will they deliver for Ruto?

Mr Nyaringo is a Kenyan public affairs commentator based in Washington, USA

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Family identifies two security officers involved in Abshir Abdi abduction
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

LSK president Charles Kanjama leads members in a protest over the disappearance of lawyer Abshir Abdi. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

The family of Nairobi lawyer Abshir Ahmedsadak Abdi has identified two security officers alleged to have taken part in their kin's abduction, even as his colleagues threatened mass protests to push for his release.

The Law Society of Kenya (LSK) said the two names have been forwarded to the police to aid in investigations and demanded that the office of the Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, speed up the probe into the abduction.

"One is named Siad and the other is Hussein, and we want them released for investigation, arrest, prosecution, conviction, sentencing and imprisonment," said LSK.

The revelation came during a demonstration led by (LSK outside the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Police and other towns yesterday .

Abshir was forcibly taken on November 1 along Muchai Road, his vehicle was pursued and intercepted by armed individuals in two vehicles before he was seized.

While state security agencies have denied holding him in custody, court filings and colleagues suggest his abduction may be connected to his professional work representing clients in high-profile cases involving senior police officers.

Furthermore, the LSK presented additional names of security personnel linked to the incident, demanding immediate legal action against Chief Inspector Vitalis Kibet, Inspector Kennedy Kimani Karanja, Siad Mohammed, Abdurahman of the Anti-Terrorism Police Unit (ATPU), and KDF officer Ali Hussein.

The leadership voiced their frustration over the state's inaction and the alarming pattern of extrajudicial actions targeting officers of the court. Representatives insisted that lawyers must be allowed to execute their duties without fear of intimidation, torture, or abduction.

"We demand that the officers involved be handed over, arrested, prosecuted, and convicted. We will stand in the courts, in the streets, and in the boardrooms until abductions come to an end," they said in a statement.

The LSK has issued a stern ultimatum to the police command, including the president, DIG Gilbert Masengeli, Inspector General Douglas Kanja, and senior commanders. If Abshir is not released safely and the identified suspects are not formally charged in court by Monday, the LSK warned it will initiate private prosecutions itself.

Furthermore, the society threatened to bring activities to a complete shutdown and demand the immediate resignation of Kanja, Masingeli and Minister for Security Kipchumba Murkomen, carrying their demonstrations to Parliament and State House if necessary.

As court proceedings continue under a habeas corpus application at the Milimani High Court, the legal fraternity remains resolute: the protest at Jogoo House is merely the beginning of an unyielding campaign for justice and the rule of law.

In Nakuru, lawyers protested within the Law Courts, calling for his production.

“It is shocking that one of our colleagues was picked and today we do not know where he is. Unless we voice our concern, there will be complete lawlessness in the country,” said LSK member Ekaterina Handa. “Our lives matter and silencing lawyers is silencing justice. we will not relent until we get justice.”

Rift Valley LSK Chair Wangari Mwangi said it was shocking that the alleged abduction was captured on CCTV.

She rubbished the narrative that the missing lawyer was involved in a crime syndicate, maintaining that he should have been arrested and charged in court. [Additional reporting by Daniel Chege]

World.title: Goon financiers should be cursed and sent to hell, Chief Justice Koome says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Chief Justice Martha Koome said goonism falls under serious organised crimes that goes against the Rome Statute and humanity. [Phares Mutembei, Standard]

Chief Justice Martha Koome now says those mobilising and financing goons should be cursed and thrown to hell.

Koome on Thursday said goonism falls under organised serious crimes that go against the Rome Statute and humanity.

She spoke at Kieganguru, Maara constituency, where she presided over the opening of the Maara law courts.

While calling on police to focus more on arresting the mobilisers and financiers, Koome said a time has come for the country to plead with God to protect the country and rescue the youth who are being misused and misled into organised gangs and goonism.

“Nobody gives birth to a child to be called a goon. Those organisers will go to hell, we curse them,” Koome said, adding, “If they will not go to hell they will meet God's justice. These are our children, and we reclaim them in the name of our Lord Jesus.”

According to her, the last time she checked, people are charged at the International Criminal Court with Organised crime.

She maintained that the best solution to the current goonism that wreaked havoc, especially in political meetings, is to arrest the organisers.

Koome said the courts cannot hold arrested goons without bail, yet the constitution grants them the right to bail or bond.

“When we arrest small people with petty crimes of causing disorder, the law allows us to release them on bail and bond, but when you bring the organisers, we will charge them under the Serious Crimes Act,” she said.

Koome said currently, the judiciary has gazetted a serious crimes division at the High Court to support Magistrates handling the cases.

“Let us look at the root cause of goonism across the country and rehabilitate those involved by getting them gainful employment,” she said.

Her sentiments, however, differ from those of Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, who on Wednesday told the National Assembly that the judiciary was the weakest link in the fight against the menace.

Tharaka Nithi Governor Muthomi Njuki, in his remarks, supported Koome’s view of arresting the planners.

Njuki, who doubles up as the Council of Governors Chairperson, said politicians have had their time and organising goons against their opponents should not be condoned.

Using the analogy of a dog, Njuki said ‘every barking dog has an owner ’, and it is time serious action was taken against such characters at whatever level they are.

The county boss said CoG will work closely with county security teams to arrest the fast-rising menace and report all cases.

Security agencies have been under scrutiny regarding goons, with calls for their arrest and prosecution.

Earlier on, Koome and DCI boss Mohammed Amin differed on how to handle the goons during a National Council for Administrative Justice meeting as with the DCI boss also accusing the Judiciary of laxity and granting minor bail to arrested goons.

But Koome maintained the issue must be addressed lest it becomes a thorn in the flesh ahead of the 2027 elections.

World.title: IEBC warns UDA SG Hassan Omar over remarks on deceased voters
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

UDA Secretary General Hassan Omar meets Village Elders and Mabalozi wa Nyumba Kumi from Jomvu Sub-County’ on September 10, 2026. [Nehemiah Okwemba, Standard]

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has issued a stern warning to Senator Hassan Omar after finding him in breach of the Electoral Code of Conduct over remarks he made at a political rally in Mombasa, cautioning that any repeat offence could attract tougher sanctions.

In a determination released on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the Electoral Code of Conduct Enforcement Committee (ECCEC) found Omar guilty of breaching paragraphs 6(k)(i) and 6(l) of the Electoral Code of Conduct.

The committee consequently issued the senator with a formal and strict warning and severe caution, directing him to comply with the electoral regulations for the remainder of the applicable election period.

Omar was further instructed to refrain from language or conduct that could reasonably be understood as encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice or undermining public confidence in the integrity of the ballot.

The decision follows investigations into remarks the senator allegedly made during a public rally in Mombasa on September 11, 2026, which raised concerns over the possibility of encouraging electoral malpractice.

According to the commission, Omar was summoned to appear before the committee on October 21, 2026, to respond to the allegations. He honoured the summons and appeared in person, accompanied by his lawyer, where he was given an opportunity to explain his remarks and present his defence.

In reaching its determination, the committee considered the context in which the statements were made, Omar's explanation that his words were intended figuratively to encourage voter registration and participation, his subsequent clarification and the absence of evidence linking the remarks to an actual electoral incident.

However, the committee maintained that the language used could not be excused by the explanation offered.

It observed that the impugned words, considered in their original Kiswahili form and ordinary meaning, invoked the use of biometric identification details belonging to a deceased person to facilitate voting in that individual's name.

The committee consequently found the remarks inconsistent with the obligation under paragraph 6(l) of the Electoral Code to reassure voters about the integrity of the ballot.

The warning places Omar on clear notice that any recurrence of similar conduct could attract more severe sanctions under the Electoral Code of Conduct and applicable laws.

“The determination places Hon. Hassan Omar on clear and unequivocal notice that the warning issued by the Committee is intended to mark a firm boundary against any recurrence of similar conduct,” IEBC stated.

The commission further emphasised that political leaders and other electoral stakeholders have a constitutional right to campaign, criticise, debate, persuade and participate in political discourse.

However, it cautioned that political expression must be exercised responsibly, warning that statements perceived as advocating, encouraging or normalising electoral malpractice could undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

“As Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election, the Commission calls upon all political leaders, candidates, political parties, supporters and other electoral stakeholders to exercise responsibility, restraint and vigilance in their public utterances and conduct,” the commission said.

The determination comes as political activities gradually intensify ahead of the 2027 General Election, with the electoral body seeking to strengthen compliance with regulations governing political campaigns and public conduct.

IEBC maintained that enforcement of the Electoral Code should not be interpreted as an attempt to suppress legitimate political competition or freedom of expression.

Instead, it said the measures were intended to safeguard democratic participation and ensure that every Kenyan could exercise their right to vote without intimidation, manipulation or interference.

The commission reiterated its commitment to protecting the sanctity of the ballot, assuring Kenyans that every vote must be protected and counted in accordance with the law.

It warned that it would continue enforcing electoral regulations firmly, fairly and without fear or favour, as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum.

World.title: Death rumours made me stronger, says ODM leader Oburu
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi when they paid a visit to ODM leader Oburu Oginga at his Nairobi residence on November 4, 2026. [Speaker’s Press Unit]

ODM leader and Siaya Senator Oburu Oginga has said rumours about his death while he was admitted to hospital only strengthened his determination to overcome his illness.

Dr Oburu who is recovering after being discharged from hospital, assured his supporters that he was making remarkable improvement and would return to active politics soon.

Speaking at his Nairobi residence on Wednesday when Speakers Moses Wetang’ula and Amason Kingi paid him a visit, the ODM leader said the rumours only strengthened his resolve to come out of the hospital bed.

“Those who wrote me off while I was in hospital by declaring me dead only made me stronger and more determined to fight my sickness. Here I am, recovering and growing stronger by the day,” he said.

He said that his recovery was a testimony to God's protection, saying those who had spread the false reports had been put to shame.

Oburu admitted that the illness had slowed down him down but he was looking forward to returning to the political arena.

“The sickness slowed my political activities. Very soon, I will be back roaring in the best way I know how,” he said.

The senator thanked the National Assembly Speaker Wetang’ula, his Senate counterpart Kingi and other legislators for taking time to visit him following his discharge from hospital.

He said the visit had lifted his spirit and revealed that he missed participating in parliamentary debates and engaging in national political affairs.

“I have no words to explain my feelings after the Speakers of both Houses and fellow legislators created time to come and check on me,” he said.

“I miss being on the floor of the House debating and roaring in the political arena. I urge my supporters to pray for me and be patient because soon I will be back,” he added.

Despite his recent health challenges, Oburu kept his visitors entertained with his trademark humour while expressing confidence that he would soon resume his political duties.

The two Speakers condemned the spread of false information on social media, particularly rumours that the senator had died while undergoing treatment.

Wetang’ula said they were encouraged by the senator's recovery and wished him a full and speedy return to good health.

He, however, cautioned Oburu against rushing back into politics before fully recovering, urging him to give his health priority.

“Prioritise your health and avoid rushing back into political engagements before making a full recovery,” he said.

The National Assembly Speaker also praised the senator for his courage and determination in facing his health challenges.

Kingi said the Senate missed Dr Oburu's contribution to debates, parliamentary proceedings and national politics.

“As the Senate, we miss your contributions to proceedings and debates as well as your guidance in national politics. We pray that you get better and resume your political duties as soon as possible,” he said.

Those who accompanied the two Speakers included Senate Chief Whip David Wakoli, Senate Minority Leader Stewart Madzayo, Senators William Kisang and Daniel Maanzo.

Others were National Assembly Minority Whip Millie Odhiambo, Parliamentary Commissioner Mishi Mboko and MP Eve Obara.

World.title: Ukraine peace talks restart after 9 months. What makes them different this time?
World.content:
A fresh round of peace talks between the US, Ukraine and Russia is underway in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, as the Trump administration renews its drive to end the nearly five-year conflict even after it announced significant concessions to Moscow.

Russia has made clear it wants the negotiations – the first of their kind since February – to be strictly trilateral, though national security advisers from several European nations, as well as officials from NATO and the European Union, are also in the UAE capital for separate meetings.

“The hope today is not only to discuss the bilateral issues between the countries, and how do we end the war and bring some good humanitarian relief, but it’s also how do we create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe,” US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner said at the outset of Tuesday’s talks.

However, many – particularly in Europe – have cast doubt on Moscow’s intentions. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Monday she saw little sign that Russia was willing to negotiate in good faith.

Meanwhile, the US official also said that it would be up to Trump to decide whether to offer a US security guarantee as part of peace talks.

Who is leading the negotiations?

The US is represented by Kushner and Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff, while Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief and top negotiator Rustem Umerov is leading the Ukrainian delegation.

US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff following talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv in September. Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images

Russia has sent deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin as delegates, according to Russian state news agency TASS, as well as Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and member of general staff Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Representatives from the E4 group – the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Italy – as well as NATO and the European Commission are also in Abu Dhabi, and met with the Ukrainian and American delegations before Tuesday’s trilateral talks.

Asked about the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Europe has its own channels of communication with Kyiv and Washington, while reaffirming that the talks are “a trilateral negotiation – involving Russia and Ukraine – with the United States acting as a mediator.”

What makes these talks different?

Notably, these talks come amid a renewed push by European nations for a more active role in negotiations over Ukraine’s future, and the security of the bloc at large, after Trump touted a new security deal for Ukraine that “might involve all of Europe.”

“We are working hand in hand with the Ukrainians, and our objective is to assert a fundamental principle: the pursuit of peace in Ukraine and security in Europe are inextricably linked,” the Elysée Palace in Paris said Tuesday before the talks started.

Europe has long been wary of any US-brokered peace deal negotiated without its involvement, with Umerov saying Monday that Ukraine was “doing everything we can to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process.”

While the main talks will remain trilateral, Witkoff said Tuesday he and Kushner met with Ukrainian and European partners to continue the “close coordination on efforts to end the war in Ukraine and establish the conditions for a durable peace, including support for robust security guarantees as part of any settlement.”

“The participants reaffirmed their shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture and arrangements, and were clear that a strong NATO will remain central to Euro-Atlantic collective defense,” Witkoff posted on X.

How likely is a breakthrough?

This will be the fourth round of trilateral talks. All have ended without significant breakthrough.

Earlier this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that trilateral talks in Geneva, Switzerland, in February fell short of Ukraine’s goals, saying “sensitive political matters, issues of possible compromises and the necessary meeting of leaders have not yet been sufficiently worked through.”

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels on October 16. Omar Havana/AP

The US later postponed a round of trilateral talks that were expected to take place in March due to the war in Iran.

Putin is still making maximalist demands previously rejected by Kyiv, including Russian control over Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, a reduction in the size of Ukraine’s military and the abandonment of Kyiv’s ambitions to join NATO.

John Herbst, senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center and a former US ambassador to Ukraine, said any expectations for the Abu Dhabi talks should be “very modest.”

“They are only taking place because Putin wants to give Trump a reason to continue to distance himself from Ukraine,” Herbst wrote last week.

What is the situation on the ground in Ukraine?

With Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year and gains on the battlefield remaining difficult to come by, Moscow has escalated its aerial attacks – with deadly results for Ukrainians.

At least 55 people were killed last Monday when Russia dropped several bombs on a school building used as a shelter and aid center in Zaporizhzhia, marking one of the deadliest single incidents of the war to date. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are at their highest point since the start of the war, with more than 2,700 killed in Russian strikes so far this year, according to ACLED, a global conflict monitor.

Smoke rises over an underground shelter at a compound of a local school, following Russian strikes in the frontline town of Komyshuvakha, Ukraine, on November 2. Press Service of the National Police of Ukraine in Zaporizhzhia Region/Reuters

And continuing a pattern seen in previous years, Russian drones and missiles are already hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, but harder and earlier than in other winters, analysts say. Russian attacks on the power grid left more than 600,000 people in the Dnipropetrovsk region without electricity overnight into Sunday, Zelensky said, as temperatures plummet and winter draws in.

Over the past few months, Russia has deployed faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, which are harder to shoot down. At the same time, more missiles are slipping through Ukraine’s air defenses as Kyiv grapples with a chronic shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors that are one of the few defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.

Where does the US stand on the war – and could the midterms change that?

Where the Biden administration positioned the US as Ukraine’s biggest single donor and most powerful ally, the Trump administration’s relationship with Kyiv has been decidedly more complicated. It halted financial aid to Ukraine at the beginning of 2025, while the intelligence and technology support it still provides has come under strain in recent weeks too.

Last month, Zelensky accused his Western allies of not providing intelligence warnings before multiple ballistic missile attacks, a claim that the Trump administration denied.

In October too, Ukraine’s ability to use Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service that is critical to its military operations, was hampered when speed limits were imposed on the satellite terminals. Trump denied approving that decision, while Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a social media post.

Undergirding all this recent tension has been Trump’s sensitivity to rising gas prices, which skyrocketed due to the Iran war and contributed to the Republicans’ landslide defeat in last week’s midterms.

He has shown a willingness to strike business deals with Moscow, including one to supply markets with Russia’s diesel, in a sharp break from the sanctions aimed at punishing and isolating the Russian economy, and pressured Zelensky to accept a short-lived “energy ceasefire.”

So, as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress, Zelensky has publicly said he hopes the “blue wave” can bolster US support for Ukraine since the party “speaks very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine.”

It remains unclear whether the midterms will substantively change US policy toward Kyiv, however. In a “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, Trump refused to say whether he trusted Zelensky or Putin more and suggested Ukraine may have to cede some of its territory.

“They’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine,” he said, outlining a scenario that Zelensky has repeatedly rejected.

World.title: US evacuates aircraft from British military base after threat from Iran, WSJ reports
World.content:
The United States has evacuated American military aircraft from a military base in England on Monday following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited sources familiar with the matter.

The exact threat to the base, Royal Air Force base Mildenhall, remains under discussion by US officials, The WSJ reported.

Flight tracking data analyzed by CNN shows that 10 US refueling aircraft were relocated away from RAF Mildenhall on Monday. Four of those KC-135 Stratotankers went to Germany’s Spangdahlem Air Base, one to Germany’s Ramstein Air Base, four to Spain’s Morón Air Base and one to Scotland’s Glasgow Prestwick airport.

CNN has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

The United States also upgraded the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and another airbase RAF Lakenheath to “FPCON Charlie,” according to The WSJ and the defense industry publication The War Zone, citing a US official on Monday. That threat level – the second-highest level in the Pentagon’s force protection system – indicates that some form of terrorist action or targeting action is likely.

A US KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft taxis for take-off on the airfield at RAF Mildenhall in England on July 14, 2026. Ben Birchall/PA/File

A UK Ministry of Defense spokesperson said that they “do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.” The spokesperson added that “aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”

The movement of the planes comes after another Iran-linked threat last month to another military base in England, RAF Fairford.

RAF Fairford had been used by US B-1 bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five men were arrested outside the base in the early hours of September 27.

British prosecutors charged two British nationals under the National Security Act in relation to the incident outside RAF Fairford airbase, with police saying the two were suspected of assisting Iran.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

World.title: Big Tech has a spy problem
World.content:
The PC revolution was upon us, and American tech companies were running circles around Compagnie des Machines Bull, the legendary but struggling French computer company.

France was determined to find out how and why. Between 1987 and 1989, the Direction Générale de la Sécurité Extérieure, France’s equivalent of the CIA, planted moles inside the offices of Bull’s biggest American competitors, IBM and Texas Instruments, where the spies passed trade secrets back to the French company. The FBI and CIA ultimately uncovered the scheme and the employees were fired.

Four decades later, the global Big Tech corporate espionage problem has grown – and so have the stakes.

US-based Nvidia, the world’s largest and most important AI chipmaker, is investigating reports that it was a victim of a foreign surveillance effort. CEO Jensen Huang also acknowledged he had an extramarital affair. Although Huang and Nvidia haven’t provided details or connected those two revelations, The New York Times reported last week that the US State Department developed significant scrutiny of Huang’s relationship with an executive from Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote speech at Computex 2026 in Taipei on June 1, 2026. I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images

Silicon Valley is particularly vulnerable to corporate espionage: The cutting-edge technologies it develops have grown vital to the global economy, and OpenAI, Google, Apple and many other high-profile tech companies in recent weeks and months have reported foreign and domestic spying attempts at their companies.

“Corporate espionage has always been a big challenge, but today it’s especially so in areas where US firms are building technologies that are foundational to economic, military and other forms of power,” said Matthew Waxman, cybersecurity law professor at Columbia University.

But Big Tech’s spy problem is almost certainly a lot bigger than anyone realizes.

Man on the inside

As IT exploded in economic import over the past several decades, information has become one of the world’s most valuable commodities. That has turned Big Tech’s secrets into the gold sitting in the underground vault – and made it rife for theft.

AI has significantly intensified the battle for trade secrets.

Cyberattacks and digital intrusions aren’t going anywhere. But the higher stakes of acquiring trade secrets have placed a renewed emphasis on human espionage inside corporations, said Greg Pollock, director of research and insights at risk management company UpGuard.

“It’s true that huge amounts of data have been compromised through hacking, but the most important information is still what’s said in private,” Pollock said.

While cyberattacks can help countries and companies steal information, a human source can help advise what secrets matter and what decisions will be made about them. Tek Image/Science Photo Library/Getty Images

The most sophisticated actors don’t choose only one path to gain access to trade secrets: Cyberattacks can help countries and companies steal information, but a human source can help advise what secrets matter and what decisions will be made about them, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.

Adversaries looking to obtain trade secrets through old-fashioned in-person espionage tend to accomplish that in one of two ways: hiring away employees who are willing to spill the beans or plant moles who befriend people.

Having a human on the inside gives companies a potentially much longer timeframe to obtain information than via cyberattack alone – which tend to trip alarm bells after a while. Humans, by contrast, may be able to access key documents that could be related to their everyday tasks – or at least appear to be, noted Madhu Shashanka, cofounder of security firm Concentric AI.

And, unlike computers, humans can gain the trust of employees, many of whom hold keys to crucial information. That makes anyone a target.

“It’s not just the CEOs who are targeted, and it doesn’t all look like a James Bond movie,” said Krauthamer. “The average Silicon Valley employee knows to be on the lookout for phishing scams. But humans trust other humans. That’s just a growing risk.”

Tip of the iceberg

That risk long predates the computer era.

Corporate espionage dates back to at least 1700, when French Jesuit priest François Xavier d’Entrecolles was sent on a mission to Jingdezhen, China – but not the kind of mission you’re probably thinking of.

Imported Chinese porcelain was flooding the dining rooms of Europe’s elite in the early 18th century, and d’Entrecolles was sent to Jingdezhen, home of the country’s porcelain factories, to determine the manufacturing process that had stumped European porcelain makers. D’Entrecolles, who spoke Chinese, spent the next two decades touring factories and interviewing families to determine the secret behind Chinese porcelain. In 1712, he wrote his first letter to the treasurer of the Jesuits’ China missions with a details of the materials used, as well as the process for purifying, molding and firing the porcelain.

Security experts agree that the corporate espionage problem has grown significantly over the past several hundred years – and particularly in the past decade. But how much it’s expanding can’t be fully known.

US federal courts saw a record 1,500 trade secret cases filed last year. And high-profile cases have been a constant in the news lately. A month before the revelations of Huang’s affair, OpenAI said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” in one of its US offices planted by a Saudi employee who had used an internal productivity tool to determine when and where high-profile executives were meeting. (The former employee pleaded not guilty to the charges.) And in February, the US Justice Department indicted three former Google employees who were spying for foreign countries, including Iran.

The OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco on September 16, 2026. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images

But the cases we know about are just scratching the surface of a potentially much more prevalent concern, said Elizabeth Rowe, a University of Virginia law professor specializing in trade secrets and intellectual property.

“It’s a bigger problem than we are aware of,” said Rowe. “The ways these cases come to our attention tend to undercount how pervasive it is.”

The most recent federal statute that criminalizes this espionage, passed in the late 1990s, relies heavily on companies self-reporting. Companies can also take civil action against adversaries, but that still relies on corporations speaking out.

The problem: Businesses have many incentives not to talk about the problem of corporate espionage.

Companies that go to court signal to investors that they lost potentially crucial information. Civil suits – particularly those dealing with complex trade-secret lawsuits – can be incredibly expensive.

The biggest barrier: Filing a complaint exposes the trade secrets and makes them vulnerable to being lost through the lawsuit or the press.

“All this suggests when you see a case that makes headlines, there are many, many more that never made it to the public,” said Rowe.

World.title: Built for heat and humidity, Thailand’s beauty brands might be the next big thing
World.content:
When Jan Angelo Ong traveled to Bangkok three years ago, he expected temples, street food and the familiar rush of traffic and heat. He did not expect to return home with a bag full of Thai sunscreens and skin care products.

The Filipino skincare enthusiast noticed their lightweight, matte finishes stayed on his face under the hot, humid Southeast Asian climate.

Sunscreens made elsewhere can also be lightweight, Ong said, “but if it blends onto your skin a bit shiny, a lot of Filipinos will still consider it as a bit greasy … And I imagine it’s the same with a lot of Southeast Asians, like Singaporeans, Thais, Indonesians, because we experience the same weather,” he said.

Ong is among a growing number of consumers looking beyond the beauty powerhouses of South Korea and Japan, turning their attention to Thai brands. Designed for a demanding climate, Thai beauty products are gaining a reputation for comfort and the longevity to withstand tropical conditions.

It’s not just sunscreens; Thai cosmetics from serums to face lotions are finding favor in the region because their formulas are made to stay on your face, no matter how hot or sweaty it gets.

Laura Tjahjadi, an analyst from market research company Euromonitor International, said that many Thai brands focus on solving the practical problems of living in a tropical climate.

“Thai brands benefit from operating in one of the world’s most demanding beauty environments. Year-round heat, humidity, and high UV exposure mean products must perform under conditions that are also highly relevant across Southeast Asia,” Tjahjadi said. “This has encouraged brands to develop products that prioritize comfort and wearability rather than just technical claims.”

The Thai beauty sector achieved record retail sales of roughly $3.2 billion in 2025, marking a 7% increase over the previous year, according to estimates by Euromonitor.

Redefining Thai beauty

Thailand has a long history of using herbs and oils in wellness treatments and traditional massage. But a new generation of founders is developing products that are rooted in tradition and engineered for tropical life.

Chayadhorn “Ing” Kitiyadisai, better known online as Ing, has built a following of more than 443,000 people on Instagram while touting Thailand as a testing ground for skin care products. The 29-year-old began making his own beauty products about four years ago, drawing on his family’s business experience in cosmetic sourcing and manufacturing.

“There’s a huge underrepresentation of skin care made by people in the region for people in the region,” Kitiyadisai told CNN, referring to Southeast Asia.

INGU Skin now gets orders from around the world. Courtesy Keeratad Kitiyadisai

His brand, INGU Skin, has gained a devoted following through social media and in-person pop-up events. Some of the company’s best-selling products incorporate Thai green tea extract and local black rice.

International orders mainly come from Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines, Kitiyadisai said, while he regularly gets inquiries from consumers and retailers in the US and UK. INGU Skin has partnered with e-commerce retailer YesStyle which makes its products available to 155 countries.

Kitiyadisai said climate change is also expanding the potential market for products designed for heat, humidity and intense sun exposure.

Other brands have drawn from earlier waves of beauty innovation in South Korea and Japan and modified them to create products that better suit Thai people’s needs.

Nui Waritta Suebphanwong, CEO of Thai skincare brand MizuMi, said she began with Japanese formulation technologies for sunscreens when building her brand in 2015, because they were popular at the time.

“We used a lot of their raw materials (and) UV protection technology. But we did do a lot of adaptation in terms of texture to fit Thailand’s climate,” Suebphanwong said.

A selection of MizuMi products. Mizuhada Group Company Limited

More than a decade on, Suebphanwong has been asked many times what the “secret sauce” for Thai product formulation really is.

“I would say that I don’t think any single brand has any mysterious ingredients or anything, but for Thai beauty brands, when we develop products, we always keep in mind what Thai people would love to wear over the day,” Suebphanwong said.

While South Korea and Japan had a head start in the beauty market, Southeast Asian brands are luring in customers with products at a cheaper price point.

“There are really good Korean brands too, but they are a bit more expensive usually. The Thai ones are more affordable, and I think the Thai ones are just as good,” Suebphanwong said.

Singapore-based content creator Amelia Alexander, who has almost 80,000 followers, said her videos on TikTok about her favorite Thai beauty products, ranging from sunscreens to hydrating face masks and serums, are some of her most viewed posts on the platform.

“I didn’t expect that, because usually I only do Korean, K-beauty (content), but apparently there is a lot of interest in Thai beauty, so I can see that it might actually be as popular as K-beauty in the near future.”

World.title: Irrigation Minister: Government to support Italian-Egyptian water technology schools
World.content:
Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Hani Sewilam said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, the ministry would provide all necessary support to ensure the success of the Egyptian-Italian Agro Schools for Water Technology, describing them as a leading model for specialized technical education.

During a meeting with the ministry’s officials, Sewilam reviewed the operation of the schools in five governorates, stressing coordination with the Education Ministry to ensure effective teaching, practical training and qualified graduates.

He said students would receive hands-on training at pumping stations, barrages and irrigation facilities, under the supervision of ministry engineers and technicians.

The program covers water resources management, infrastructure, mechanical and electrical equipment maintenance, and water treatment and desalination, helping prepare skilled technicians to meet labor market needs.

World.title: Local Development Minister reviews Greater Cairo Air Pollution project
World.content:
Local Development and Environment Minister Manal Awad discussed on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, with a World Bank delegation, led by Regional Director for Egypt, Yemen and Djibouti Alwaleed Al-Atbani, progress on the Greater Cairo Air Pollution and Climate Change Management Project, implemented in cooperation with the bank.

The meeting, held at the ministry’s headquarters in the New Capital, was attended by Environment Affairs Agency Chief Sherif Abdel Rahim, National Project Coordinator Mohamed Hassan, and World Bank officials and environmental experts.

Awad welcomed the addition of 20 new electric buses to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system under the project’s vehicle emissions reduction component.

Supported by nearly $7 million in World Bank Group funding, the buses mark an important step toward more sustainable and efficient urban transport and wider adoption of clean transport technologies to reduce air pollution and climate-related emissions, particularly in densely populated urban areas.

The minister and the delegation reviewed preparations for operating the integrated waste management facility in 10th of Ramadan City.

Covering 1,228 feddans and costing $16 million, the facility is expected to be one of the largest of its kind in the Middle East and Egypt’s first fully integrated facility.

It is designed to process 15,000 tons of waste daily, equivalent to around 50 percent of the waste generated in Greater Cairo, and serve the region for more than 30 years under a public-private partnership.

They also reviewed implementation progress and the facility’s expected environmental and economic benefits, including a 30 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, a 10 percent decrease in waste-related fires, support for local manufacturing industries and greater private-sector participation, as well as the creation of more than 3,500 direct and indirect jobs.

The meeting also addressed plans to close the Abu Zaabal dumpsite and eliminate its accumulated waste.

A simulation of the site after closure was presented, highlighting expected reductions in fires in Qalyubia Governorate and greenhouse gas emissions in Greater Cairo, as well as improvements in environmental conditions, quality of life and the economic value of nearby residential areas.

The delegation reviewed an environmental development plan for the industrial zone in Al-Akrasha, Qalyubia, which faces challenges due to the overlap of industrial and residential activities.

Proposed measures include establishing a green belt, separating residential and industrial areas, and addressing untreated domestic and industrial wastewater through a proposed drainage system.

Discussions also covered the development of the Amiriyah bus depot to accommodate 100 electric buses.

It is set to become Egypt’s first electric bus depot and one of the largest in the Middle East.

Its operation and maintenance will be managed through a public-private partnership, creating more than 1,100 jobs and supporting research, development and the adoption of best practices.

Awad also reviewed progress on Component 6 of the project, which aims to reduce unintentional releases of persistent organic pollutants by improving the management of electronic and healthcare waste.

Plans include comprehensive guidelines for healthcare waste management, Egypt’s first unified training materials in this field, and a pilot project to collect and recycle 40 tons of electronic waste.

The component also involves assessing waste management practices, providing technical support to formal recycling facilities and the informal sector, evaluating startup capabilities, and developing an integrated digital management information system (MIS) to improve monitoring and update electronic waste data.

Awad called for accelerating all projects and programs under the initiative, stressing their importance to the government and their direct impact on citizens’ lives in the targeted governorates.

For their part, the World Bank delegation reaffirmed its continued cooperation with the ministry to achieve the project’s objectives, monitor performance indicators and implementation rates, address challenges and complete the project on schedule, supporting Egypt’s goals for sustainable development, green transition and protecting citizens’ health and safety in the targeted governorates.

World.title: PM witnesses signing of LE14B billion partnership to develop hotel portfolio
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, witnessed the signing of a partnership agreement between PRE-Group and global hospitality company Hilton to develop and manage an integrated hotel portfolio in Egypt, with investments estimated at LE14 billion.

The agreement is expected to add around 2,000 hotel rooms and branded residential units to Egypt’s hospitality sector. The signing ceremony took place at the government headquarters in the New Capital, in the presence of Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathi.

The agreement was signed by PRE-Group Founder and CEO Walid Zaki and Hilton Middle East and Africa President Guy Hutchinson.

Zaki said the partnership covers 10 projects, comprising six hotels and four branded residential developments, which will operate under five of Hilton’s leading brands: Canopy, Tapestry Collection by Hilton, Hilton Hotels & Resorts, DoubleTree by Hilton and Hilton Garden Inn.

The projects will be developed at key destinations within PRE-Group’s portfolio, including Telal Ain Sokhna, Jebal Ain Sokhna, Telal Alamein and Eivor East.

Zaki said the partnership reflects the conviction that Egypt’s unique natural resources and tourism assets, including its extensive coastlines and climatic and cultural diversity, require world-class infrastructure and hospitality facilities to unlock the sector’s full potential.

He noted that tourism is a labor-intensive sector with strong links to numerous supporting industries, adding that the projects are expected to generate thousands of direct and indirect jobs once fully operational, while contributing to sustainable foreign currency inflows and tax revenues.

He added that PRE-Group’s expansion into the hospitality sector through its partnership with Hilton builds on the company’s legacy and experience in the Egyptian market and reflects its vision of developing an integrated hotel portfolio in line with international standards.

The selection of Hilton’s brands, he explained, was tailored to the nature and location of each project and the needs of different customer segments, ensuring an appropriate hospitality experience for each destination.

Zaki also highlighted the role of the government’s substantial investments in infrastructure, transport networks and airports in creating a favorable environment for private-sector expansion in hotel and tourism-related investments.

He said the new projects would help deliver distinctive hospitality experiences and enhance the competitiveness of Egyptian tourist destinations.

He added that the partnership forms part of PRE-Group’s strategy to integrate hospitality facilities into its residential developments, bringing together hotels, services and amenities with residential components to provide comprehensive experiences for residents and visitors throughout the year.

For his part, Hilton Chief Development Officer for the Middle East and Africa Carlos Khneisser said the company began operating in Egypt more than 65 years ago and continues to see significant growth opportunities across the country.

He said Hilton shares PRE-Group’s confidence in the future of Egyptian tourism, adding that the partnership would allow the two companies to select brands and hospitality experiences suited to each destination and its growth potential.

World.title: Egypt, China discuss establishing Egyptian-Chinese hospital
World.content:
Minister of Health and Population Khaled Abdel Ghaffar held on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, talks with Zheng Zhe, Deputy Minister of China’s National Health Commission (NHC), on ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation in localizing medical industries, manufacturing medicines and vaccines, digital transformation, exchanging expertise and medical training.

During the meeting, the minister also reviewed a proposal to establish a 350-bed Egyptian-Chinese hospital, with the participation of former health minister Hatem el Gabaly.

Spokesman for the Health Ministry Hossam Abdel Ghaffar said the minister reaffirmed Egypt’s appreciation of its longstanding strategic relations with China and its aspiration to expand cooperation in pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing, localize the production of medical equipment and supplies, and benefit from Chinese expertise and technologies to strengthen Egypt’s healthcare system.

The meeting explored opportunities for cooperation in developing ambulance services through the exchange of expertise between the Egyptian Ambulance Authority and the Chinese side, as well as the provision of equipment and technologies used in ambulances.

Discussions also covered the potential localization of mobile X-ray equipment manufacturing in Egypt.

The minister noted that negotiations were underway with several Chinese companies to facilitate technology transfer and local production.

The minister called for increased Chinese investment in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, particularly in the manufacturing of medical equipment and supplies, which would create opportunities to expand into regional markets.

The two sides also discussed potential partnerships to equip hospitals currently being prepared for integration into the Universal Health Insurance System.

The minister expressed his aspiration to increase the number of short-term educational grants offered by China to train Egyptian physicians at Chinese medical institutions across various specialties, including digital transformation.

Regarding the proposed Egyptian-Chinese hospital, Gabaly outlined the project, which aims to establish a fully integrated 350-bed hospital through joint Egyptian-Chinese investment. The facility would rely on Chinese medical equipment, technology and expertise, while allocating part of its services to treatments based on traditional Chinese medicine.

The minister said the project represented a promising model of partnership that would go beyond providing medical services to encompass technology transfer and support for investment in Egypt’s healthcare sector.

For his part, Zheng expressed his country’s appreciation of Egypt’s standing, reaffirming China’s interest in strengthening bilateral cooperation and implementing existing agreements between the two countries.

He stressed the importance of continued coordination to identify priority areas and establish practical mechanisms for partnerships in medical manufacturing, ambulance services, digital transformation and medical training.

World.title: A US$1.54 Billion Budget, but Lawmakers’ Fuel Costs More Than the Nation’s Medicines
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s government is preparing to spend more money than at any time in its history. The draft national budget for fiscal year 2027, prepared by the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, totals US$1,538,916,274. That is US$236 million, or 18.1 percent, more than the US$1.30 billion approved for 2026.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The government calls it “A Growing Budget for Bigger Impact.” The timing helps. On 14 September 2026, domestic revenue collection passed US$1 billion in a single year for the first time. Officials credit a mining boom, a stronger Liberian dollar and a planned switch from a sales tax (GST) to value-added tax (VAT).



But a line-by-line review of the 845-page document by FrontPageAfrica shows that much of the new money goes to creditors, the security services, the Legislature and the Monrovia area. Farmers, the poorest households and much of rural Liberia get far less.

WHERE THE MONEY GOES

The largest single block, US$419.6 million or 27.3 percent of the budget, sits in a new category called “General Obligations and Programs.” About US$275.5 million of it is debt service, up from US$232 million this year.

The biggest payments go to Liberians’ own banks and the central bank. Commercial banks receive US$103.3 million, mostly Treasury bond repayments. The Central Bank of Liberia receives US$65 million, including US$22.4 million in interest alone. External creditors, led by the World Bank, receive US$78.8 million.

Debt service now takes about one dollar in every five of core domestic revenue. It is twice the entire health budget and fifteen times what the government will spend on agriculture.

Public sector pay is the next big draw. Compensation rises to US$369.4 million, nearly a quarter of the budget. The government says about 17,065 workers will benefit from new hires, the conversion of volunteers into paid staff, and salary top-ups. Teachers are the main winners: new minimum monthly salaries of US$650 for teachers with a master’s degree, US$400 for a bachelor’s degree and US$200 for a C-Certificate. Pay will be equal across Ministry of Education and Monrovia Consolidated School System schools. About 1,934 police officers will get raises tied to rank, and 616 Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency staff will get 15 percent.

THE WINNERS

Security. The security and rule-of-law sector rises 21.5 percent to US$198.4 million. The budget promises to recruit 600 police officers and between 800 and 1,200 soldiers; the document gives both figures. The National Security Agency receives US$30.25 million, with no capital projects. Its 2026 budget was US$24.7 million, but by 30 September it had already spent US$30.2 million, 22 percent over budget with a quarter of the year still to go.

Spending on “intelligence services” across government rises from US$21.1 million to US$28.9 million. The NSA’s share rises to US$13.7 million and the Ministry of Justice’s to nearly US$8 million. Neither the budget nor its annexes explain what these lines pay for.

The Legislature. Liberia’s 103 lawmakers and their staff are allocated US$58.2 million. That is more than three times the entire agriculture sector (US$18.4 million) and more than four times the Ministry of Agriculture alone (US$13.1 million).

The 2026 figures show how far the Legislature already exceeds its budget. By 30 September it had spent US$64.3 million against an approved US$57.2 million:

• Constituency visits: US$1.12 million budgeted, more than US$6.2 million spent.

• Legislative committee hearings: US$1.4 million budgeted, US$6.5 million spent.

• Transfers to the Public Accounts Committee: US$738,000 budgeted, US$3.6 million paid.

For 2027 the constituency-visit line more than triples to US$3.8 million. The Legislature’s vehicle fuel allowance rises by US$1 million to US$5.47 million. That is more than the Ministry of Health’s entire budget for drugs and medical consumables, which stays at US$4.23 million. Health spent less than half of that drug money by September. The Legislature also keeps US$2.66 million for “entertainment and representation,” almost 77 percent of all entertainment spending in government. Its cleaning budget rises from US$130,000 to US$954,677.

The Presidency and Vice Presidency. The Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs rises 32.6 percent to US$21.9 million. Domestic travel jumps from US$35,000 to US$535,000, vehicle repairs from US$120,000 to US$520,000, and “special operations” to US$1.79 million. A US$1.3 million line for “Special Presidential Projects” is not explained. The Office of the Vice President’s allowance for domestic travel subsistence rises from US$220,000 to US$770,000.

Monrovia, sport and motorcyclists. The Monrovia City Corporation’s budget rises 74 percent to US$8.46 million, partly for a US$4 million “smart sanitation and city beautification” programme. Paynesville gets a 60 percent increase. The Ministry of Youth and Sports nearly doubles to US$18.2 million, including about US$3.9 million in transfers to football; the government says US$3 million is for the Lone Star national team. A new US$2 million “Motorcyclist Empowerment Program” sits alongside a US$2.5 million small-business initiative. Government purchases of vehicles double, from US$4.7 million to US$9.5 million, in the same budget that allows agencies to buy second-hand cars.

THE LOSERS

Farmers. Agriculture and fisheries produce 27.4 percent of Liberia’s economic output and employ much of its rural population. The sector receives 1.2 percent of the budget. African Union governments pledged under the Maputo and Malabo declarations to spend 10 percent. The whole Ministry of Agriculture allocation for seeds, tools and other farm inputs is US$997,080, less than half what the Legislature will spend on entertainment. Of the US$5.5 million approved for agriculture capital projects in 2026, nothing had been spent by September.

Health and education. Health gets 8.8 percent of the budget, against the 15 percent African governments pledged in the 2001 Abuja Declaration. Education gets 10.6 percent, below the 15 to 20 percent recommended internationally. Health also struggled to spend what it was given in 2026: none of its US$7.15 million capital budget or its US$1.62 million for laboratory supplies had been spent by September.

The poorest households. The flagship Social Protection Safety Net receives US$1.05 million. The same budget sets aside US$2.23 million in benefits for former elected officials and those who have “elected and served.”

The environment. Environmental sustainability, which includes forestry, the Environmental Protection Agency and disaster management, gets 0.7 percent. Most of Liberia’s climate work is left to donors. Energy spending falls 5 percent, with the Liberia Electricity Corporation’s allocation cut from US$50 million to US$40 million.

Rural counties. Most spending is not linked to any county: about 89 percent of agency spending is booked as “nationwide.” Of the US$124.5 million that is, Montserrado, the county that includes Monrovia, takes US$52 million. Rivercess receives US$837,710, the least of any county. Lofa University’s allocation rises 73 percent to US$3.5 million. Nimba University’s vote, by contrast, falls from US$2 million to US$386,200. Its US$2.04 million subsidy appears instead under the budget of Grand Bassa University.

UNUSUAL ALLOCATIONS

Several lines raise questions the Finance Ministry will need to answer.

• Payments to mining companies. The Ministry of Local Government’s budget includes three new transfers totalling US$7.1 million. US$3.3 million goes to “Cavalla Resource Liberia Inc.,” US$2.38 million to “China Union Mining Company” and US$1.43 million to “Hummingbird Resource Liberia Inc.” Elsewhere, county social development funds from ArcelorMittal and Firestone are listed under the counties that receive them. These three are written as transfers to the companies themselves.

• Unexplained transfers. A “Transfer to Vendor Share” of US$14 million and a US$2.95 million “Deficit Pool Fund” have no explanation.

• A laboratory under Defence. The Ministry of National Defense will pay US$1.3 million to the National Reference Laboratory, which is normally a health function.

• Foreign travel jumps. Foreign air travel at the Ministry of Local Government rises from US$17,690 to US$780,357. At the Judiciary it rises from US$55,000 to US$455,000, and at the Ministry of Information from US$35,000 to US$295,000.

THE REVENUE GAMBLE

The budget counts on tax revenue rising to about US$1.07 billion, an increase of more than 26 percent on this year’s estimate, driven mainly by the move to VAT. One-off “sign-on bonuses” from new concessions fall from US$228 million in 2026 to US$40 million. That money is expected to come from two port operators, APM Terminals (US$25 million) and Marsa Maroc (US$15 million), and is “contingent”: US$40 million of spending will happen only if the money arrives. Mining royalties are projected to fall from US$287.6 million to US$119.4 million.

Of the US$92 million in outside money that goes directly into the budget, US$72 million is borrowed from the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the IMF. Only US$20 million is a grant, from the European Union.

Seventeen of Liberia’s 20 state-owned enterprises missed the deadline to submit their 2027 financial plans. The figures shown for them were estimated by the ministry from past trends.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Liberia’s revenue is growing and its economy is expanding faster than the regional average, with growth projected at 5.1 percent in 2027. The question the Legislature must now answer, as it reviews the draft, is whether the extra money will reach the farms, clinics and rural communities the ARREST Agenda promises to serve, or stay with the institutions that already overspend.
