World.title: Georgia Tech issues apology to fans who were allegedly ejected from home game for standing and cheering
World.content:
Standing up to support the Georgia Tech football team during a game being played at Georgia Tech can, apparently, result in you being told to leave the stadium.

Georgia Tech was blown out by Louisville this past Saturday, 44-17, in what was the Yellow Jackets' fourth straight loss, and to make the situation even more embarrassing, a video showing two Tech fans being ejected from the game has gone viral on social media.

The video of the fans being escorted out by stadium security gained so much traction that Georgia Tech issued a public apology over what transpired. The apology came two days after the incident unfolded.

TEXAS BANS FAN WHO WAS CAUGHT FLIPPING OFF FLORIDA PLAYERS IN POSTGAME VIDEO FOLLOWING GATORS' UPSET

"Georgia Tech athletics was made aware of the situation and immediately began gathering information to better understand the circumstances," the statement from Georgia Tech athletics read, in part. "On Sunday, a senior member of Georgia Tech athletics’ staff personally contacted the individuals who had been ejected to apologize for their experience.

"The fan experience is a top priority for Georgia Tech athletics, and we regret that these fans had a negative experience as a result of the misapplication of our processes for addressing in-stadium complaints."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The video of the incident was originally shared on X during Saturday's contest against Louisville.

The person filming the video can be heard asking an officer if the fans were being ejected from the game "because they were standing." The officer confirmed that to be the case, explaining that the fans had been asked to sit down.

According to the man filming the video, the people who were asked to leave are alumni of the university.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

While the entire scene and exchange with security is bizarre, perhaps the most egregious aspect of it all is that the fans who were asked to leave appeared to have been sitting on the last row of their section, meaning there was nobody seated directly behind them who would have had their sightline to the field obstructed.

With Georgia Tech sitting at 2-7 on the year and occupying the basement of the ACC standings, which consist of seven more teams with losing records this season overall, allegedly ejecting fans for simply standing up in support is about as bad a look as possible.

World.title: Duke vs Michigan State headlines a loaded college basketball slate that deserves attention before March
World.content:
Most sports fans don't start paying attention to college basketball until February or March, and that's unfortunate. One thing the sport does really well is pack the early-season slate with massive matchups, thanks to events like the Champions Classic and the ACC/SEC Challenge.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Tuesday night slate features three Top 25 matchups, including a showdown between No. 5 Michigan State and No. 2 Duke at the United Center in Chicago as part of the State Farm Champions Classic.

Let's dive into a fantastic early-season slate of college hoops.

CBB WITH DANNY Z: KANSAS, TENNESSEE AND USC LEAD ANOTHER HUMAN POLLS VS. ANALYTICS ARGUMENT

No 5 Michigan State (2-0) vs No 2 Duke (2-0)

Spread: Duke -7.5, Total: 145.5

7:00 p.m. ET, ESPN

Tom Izzo has been doing this long enough that it's easy to take him for granted. I don't. For my money, he's the best coach in history at getting the most out of his teams. This season, he also has one of the best point guards in the country, which certainly makes the job easier.

Michigan State went 27-8 and reached the Sweet 16 last season, and the Spartans bring back Jeremy Fears Jr., who averaged 15.2 points and led the nation with 9.4 assists per game. Forward Coen Carr also returns after averaging 12 points and 5.4 rebounds. The concern is up front, where Izzo has to replace starting big men Jaxon Kohler and Carson Cooper.

Duke, meanwhile, went 35-3 last season before its run ended in the Elite Eight on a miracle buzzer-beater by UConn's Braylon Mullins. The Blue Devils lost their two leading scorers, Cameron Boozer and Isaiah Evans, to the NBA. Normally, that would qualify as a pretty serious problem. At Duke, it mostly means somebody else gets to become a household name.

Jon Scheyer brings back four of his top six scorers: Patrick Ngongba II, Caleb Foster, Dame Sarr and Cameron's twin brother, Cayden Boozer. He also added Wisconsin transfer John Blackwell to the backcourt. Ngongba just scored 28 points against Coastal Carolina, while Cayden Boozer handed out 12 assists.

The analytics love Duke, as usual. Both TeamRankings and KenPom's Nov. 1 preseason ratings placed Duke first. But don't sleep on Sparty; TeamRankings and KenPom rated Michigan State eighth entering the season.

TOM IZZO, DAN HURLEY CONTINUE TO DEMAND ACCOUNTABILITY WHILE AMERICA GETS SOFTER

The key to this matchup is whether Fears can consistently create good shots against Duke's strong defense and whether Michigan State's rebuilt frontcourt can handle Duke's size. The Spartans have an experienced floor general who should keep them organized, but this is a considerable jump from opening the season against Quinnipiac and Toledo.

One inconvenient detail for my Izzo appreciation speech: he's 3-15 against Duke. Apparently, the Blue Devils aren't nearly as impressed with him as I am.

No 3 Illinois (2-0) at No 16 Texas Tech (2-0)

Spread: Illinois -2.5, Total: 166.5

8:00 p.m. ET, Peacock

I'm a huge fan of Texas Tech head coach Grant McCasland, and I think he's the most underrated coach in the country. He's taken the Red Raiders to the NCAA Tournament in each of his first three seasons, including an Elite Eight appearance in 2025. He took over in 2023 after a 16-16 season under Mark Adams and immediately got the Red Raiders back into the NCAA Tournament.

Last season ended at 23-11 with a second-round loss to Alabama, but Tech played the tournament without star forward JT Toppin after he tore his ACL in February. Toppin is back on the roster this season, although he's still recovering and has said he's targeting a return by the end of December. The Red Raiders also lost point guard Christian Anderson to the NBA after he averaged 18.5 points and 7.4 assists. That's a lot of offense to replace while waiting for your best big man to get healthy.

Fortunately, McCasland has other options. Sharpshooter Donovan Atwell returns after making 130 three-pointers last season, and Darrion Williams is back after spending a year at NC State. Yes, he left Texas Tech and then returned to Texas Tech. College basketball in the transfer portal and NIL era is weird like that.

The new backcourt features Cruz Davis and Dra Gibbs-Lawhorn, who both averaged more than 20 points last season at Hofstra and UNLV, respectively. Gibbs-Lawhorn also spent his first two college seasons at Illinois, so there should be some familiar faces on the other bench.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

And that other bench has plenty of talent. Illinois went 28-9 and reached its first Final Four since 2005 last season, with a roster that gave Brad Underwood good reason to keep recruiting overseas. As I wrote last March, European recruiting helped Underwood build that Final Four roster.

"This is the most fun I've ever had coaching a team," Underwood told OutKick's Dan Dakich last year. "We don't have bad practices because the truly great thing is they are competitive as heck. They show up, they love ball, they love to work, [and] they love to compete."

Several of those players are back, including David Mirkovic and the Ivisic brothers, Tomislav and Zvonimir. Andrej Stojakovic also returns, giving Illinois a substantial amount of experience from that tournament run. The departures of guards Keaton Wagler and Kylan Boswell leave important roles to fill, but Providence transfer Stefan Vaaks and freshman Quentin Coleman give Underwood new backcourt scoring options.

As we covered in last week's rankings comparison, both analytics models placed Illinois fourth. The expectations are justified, although Mirkovic is sidelined following foot surgery and an appendectomy, and forward Jake Davis is also out with a shoulder injury. So, neither team is bringing its full roster to this one.

Illinois has scored 232 points in its first two games. That's not a typo, although FDU and Penn probably wish it were. Now the Illini take that offense into Lubbock, where Texas Tech has won 48 consecutive nonconference home games.

No 24 Kentucky (2-0) vs No 15 Kansas (2-0)

Spread: Kansas -4.5, Total: 158.5

9:30 p.m. ET, ESPN

This is the matchup that brings us back to last week's humans-versus-computers discussion. Kansas opened at No. 17 in the AP Poll, fifth in KenPom and sixth at TeamRankings. Usually, a program with "Jayhawks" across the front of its jerseys doesn't need much help getting attention. This year, the computers were considerably more enthusiastic than the voters.

Neither program had the March it wanted last season. Kansas finished 24-11 and Kentucky went 22-14, with both exiting in the second round of the NCAA Tournament. For blue bloods like the Jayhawks and Wildcats, that's nothing short of incredibly disappointing.

Kansas lost Darryn Peterson to the NBA and big man Flory Bidunga to Louisville, but Bill Self has another highly touted freshman in Tyran Stokes, the nation's top recruit. Returning wing Tre White provides experience and scoring, while Purdue transfer Trey Kaufman-Renn gives the Jayhawks a proven interior option after averaging 14.2 points and 8.3 rebounds last season.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

There's also a major new problem: returning guard Melvin Council Jr. broke his foot in practice Monday and is out. Council averaged 12.7 points and 5.1 assists last season, so Kansas is losing an experienced playmaker right before its first major test. Freshman Taylen Kinney and Toledo transfer Leroy Blyden Jr. figure to take on more responsibility. Nothing like stepping into the spotlight against Kentucky inside a 20,000-seat United Center on national television.

The Wildcats have done plenty of rebuilding themselves. Otega Oweh and Denzel Aberdeen are gone, while center Malachi Moreno and wing Kam Williams are among the returnees. Mark Pope added Washington guard Zoom Diallo and Furman's Alex Wilkins, but the name casual fans should learn is Milan Momcilovic.

The Iowa State transfer made 136 three-pointers and shot 48.7% from deep last season. Read that again. The kid made nearly half his three-point attempts playing in the Big 12 last year. And he introduced himself to Kentucky fans by hitting six threes and scoring 24 points in the opener against Manhattan.

Kentucky's ability to spread the floor gives it a real opportunity here, especially against a Kansas team adjusting to Council's absence. The concern is whether the Wildcats can get enough stops after allowing James Madison to score 80 points Friday. Stokes and Kaufman-Renn present a different set of problems, and Kansas should have opportunities to attack inside.

For me, the interesting part is how Kansas handles possessions without its veteran guard and how Kentucky handles a team that can punish it in the paint.

And if you're one of those fans waiting until March to start watching college basketball, you're going to miss a pretty good Tuesday night.

World.title: Amazon’s Ring debuts security robots including a drone
World.content:
Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where a fixed camera cannot reach.

The $250 Ring Drone Camera offers exactly what the product’s name implies — the technology to capture moving images from a lens affixed to a small quadcopter drone, according to the company.

Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff said his customers have been asking for an expansion of the company’s popular doorbell cameras without having to install more cameras around the house.

Ring Rover Cam is a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously. Amazon

“For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one,” Siminoff said in a statement released by the company Tuesday.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be. That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time. But we kept at it until we got it right—and that’s Ring Robotics. It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.”

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot and navigate autonomously.

The drone provides “wall-to-wall coverage,” according to Ring, with 148-degree peripheral vision and the ability to rotate 360 degrees to quickly spot potential threats.

LED lights also equip it to work in “low-light environments” so that homeowners can “always get clear, crisp video,” the company said.

Ring also rolled out its $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, tailored for businesses.

The tool could be used to “investigate a disturbance” or be set to do “regular sweeps” of the property.

“Get a closer look wherever and whenever you need it without the cost and complexity of wiring up every corner of every room,” the company said.

Both pieces of equipment require a subscription fee of $5 per month or $60 annually, a customer service rep told NBC News.

World.title: Man charged with murder on cruise says he ‘snapped’ and choked woman, complaint says
World.content:
A man seen on video being escorted off a cruise ship in Texas after a woman’s body was found in a cabin room told authorities that he repeatedly struck and choked her after they got into an argument, according to a criminal complaint.

Jason Leon Watford, 48, was charged with murder in connection with the investigation involving the MSC Seascape, according to the complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas.

Jail records show he was in the Galveston County Jail on a federal hold Monday evening. He is set to appear in court for an initial hearing Tuesday afternoon.

The victim has not been identified, and it’s unclear whether Watford has retained an attorney. The Galveston medical examiner’s office said Monday that the deceased was a female and that an autopsy is scheduled for Tuesday.

Jason Leon Watford is led by police Monday in Galveston, Texas. KPRC

Authorities believe the woman was killed Sunday night. She was found lying on the floor of the room and had “multiple facial injuries,” the complaint says.

Watford told the FBI in an interview that he and the woman got into an argument while eating dinner at a restaurant on the ship, according to the complaint. He alleged that they continued to argue after they returned to their room, causing him to “snap” and hit her multiple times, the complaint says.

According to the complaint, Watford said at one point he choked the woman and wrapped his arm around her neck while she was lying down. He said that he applied pressure to her neck for about four to five minutes and “released his hold only after becoming exhausted,” the complaint says.

The complaint states that a security camera showed Watford returning to the room at 7:46 p.m. ET and the woman arriving at 8:11 p.m. ET. No one else was seen entering the room.

Watford said the woman was lying motionless on the floor for about 10 minutes before a housekeeper knocked on the door, the complaint says.

The complaint says the footage showed the housekeeper knocking at 9:02 p.m. ET to provide towels. Watford opened the door and briefly spoke to the housekeeper, the complaint says.

After the housekeeper left, Watford exited the room wearing different clothes, sat on the hallway floor and scrolled on his phone, the complaint says.

Employees of the ship later responded to the room after the housekeeper reported seeing blood on Watford’s hands and pants and “a motionless female lying face down on the floor,” the complaint states. He was detained by ship security, and authorities were called.

The FBI said that during a search of the room, they found bloodstained clothing on the floor.

Jail records show that Watford was arrested in 2024 on a charge of assault causing bodily injury to a family member. He was sentenced to 15 months of probation and 30 hours of community service.

The 1,060-foot cruise ship left Galveston on Sunday but was instructed to turn around after what the ship company described in a statement as a “guest incident aboard our ship.”

The ship was scheduled to travel to Costa Maya, the Roatan Islands and Cozumel before returning to Texas on Nov. 15.

Passenger Becsei György told NBC News that late Sunday night, an announcement said, “Mike Echo at level 10.” On Monday morning, he awoke to find that the ship had returned to Galveston.

World.title: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing of Sandra Birchmore, unborn child
World.content:
A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child. The verdict was read in federal court in South Boston Tuesday afternoon.

Farwell was charged with killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. He pleaded not guilty. The jury had previously said in a note on Monday that it was "in a deadlock."

There were gasps from Birchmore's family as the verdict was read aloud in court.

Jurors heard from 50 witnesses over four weeks of testimony. If convicted, Farwell faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. The Department of Justice could have pursued the death penalty against Farwell, but decided last year it would not.

To convict Farwell on the charge of killing a witness or victim, jurors had to find find that he not only killed Birchmore, but that he did so to prevent her from reporting his crimes to federal authorities.

Farwell and Birchmore met when she was a 13-year-old cadet in the Stoughton Police Department's youth explorers program. Prosecutors say Farwell began a sexual relationship with her when she was just 15.

The 23-year-old Birchmore was found dead in her Canton apartment with a strap hanging around her neck in February 2021. Her death was initially ruled a suicide. But more than three years later, Farwell was arrested and the medical examiner changed Birchmore's manner of death to "undetermined."

Prosecutors made the case that Farwell strangled Birchmore, who was pregnant with what she believed was his child, and then staged her death to look like a suicide in order to cover up their years-long affair. The defense says Birchmore had a history of mental health problems and committed suicide because Farwell told her he was not the father and the relationship was over.

This is a breaking news story that will be updated as more information is available.

World.title: Hotter-than-expected October CPI raises chances of Fed rate hike
World.content:
Consumer prices rose more than economists expected in October on a monthly basis, offering little relief to Americans grappling with high living costs.

The Consumer Price Index, which tracks changes in prices over time, rose at a monthly pace of 0.4%, the Labor Department reported on Tuesday.

The Labor Department did not report a year-over-year inflation rate for October 2026 because the 2025 government shutdown left it without October 2025 consumer price data for comparison.

By the numbers

October's monthly inflation increase cooled from September, when headline inflation rose 0.6% on a monthly basis.

However, the figure was hotter than expected, with economists polled by FactSet predicting October prices would rise 0.3% month-over-month.

The October inflation data is one of the first snapshots of the economy following the midterm elections, which underscored Americans' frustration with high prices.

"Today's CPI report suggests underlying inflation remains more persistent than the Fed would like," Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust, said in an email. "While headline inflation moderated from September, core prices rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month, indicating that underlying price pressures have yet to meaningfully ease."

While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, October's data shows that costs for other types of goods and products are also rising. Shelter costs, which rose 0.3% in October, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly all-items increase, the Labor Department said.

Food prices also accelerated, rising at a monthly pace of 0.5% last month after remaining flat in September, the data shows.

Energy prices

Energy costs, which have surged due to the Iran war, contributed less to the monthly rise in inflation than in past reports. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, compared to 5.2% in September.

Gas prices have been falling for weeks as stations switch to cheaper winter blend and people pull back from summer travel.

Global oil costs, the main factor in setting prices at the pump, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.

On Tuesday, the national average prices for gasoline sank below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months, according to AAA.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, rose 0.3% in October, in line with September but slightly above economists' forecasts.

Josh Hirt, senior U.S. economist for Vanguard, said in an email that elevated energy prices have led to a "longer-lasting shock pass-through" to core inflation, prompting the investment company to raise its year-end 2026 core inflation forecast to 3.2%.

What this means for interest rates

Wall Street analysts predicted that firmer inflation last month will spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when it meets in December.

"This is the last look at CPI inflation the Fed will get before its December meeting, and it most likely seals the deal on a rate hike to close the year," James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in an email. The bigger question, he added, is whether the central bank will raise its benchmark rate by a quarter or half of a percentage point.

After the latest inflation data, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed an 85% chance the Fed would raise rates by 0.25 percentage points in December and a 15% chance of a 0.50 percentage-point hike.

The central bank stayed on the sidelines at its October meeting, although two Federal Open Market Committee members voted in favor of a rate hike.

During a conference in London on Tuesday, Christopher Waller, a member of the Fed's Board of Governors, said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase when the central bank meets on Dec. 8-9.

"Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," he said.

World.title: Gas prices slip below $4 a gallon for first time since July
World.content:
Gasoline prices in the U.S. are below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months.

According to AAA, the national average for a gallon of gasoline was $3.98 on Tuesday, down from $4.56 a gallon earlier this year.

"We're heading in the right direction in terms of what drivers want to see," AAA spokesperson Aixa Diaz told CBS News. "They don't want to be paying more than $4 a gallon at this time of year.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at tracking firm GasBuddy, predicts that fuel prices will continue to ease into the Thanksgiving holidays.

Diesel costs have also fallen, with the national average now running at $6.16 a gallon, down from $6.53 in late September.

Far from normal

Although lower gas prices offer relief to motorists, prices are still historically high for this time of year, AAA's Diaz said. The record high for average U.S. prices at the pump around the Thanksgiving holiday was $3.58 a gallon in 2022, data from the motor club shows.

"We're still a ways away from even being close to normal for this time of year," Diaz said.

The average price of regular gas has jumped $1 per gallon since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Consumer prices rose at a monthly rate of 0.5% in October, new government data shows.

October's CPI data, released Tuesday, suggests high fuel costs may be spilling over into other categories, such as food, which rose at a monthly rate of 0.5% in October after remaining flat in September.

Why are prices down?

Gas prices have fallen in recent weeks as filling stations switch from summer-blend fuels to cheaper winter blends. Federal rules require gas stations to sell a summer blend, designed to guard against evaporation, from June 1 to Sept. 15. Outside that period, stations are allowed to use a winter blend, which is cheaper to produce, explaining why prices often fade in the fall.

The winter blend switch coincides with a drop in fuel demand, as people take fewer road trips and vacations later in the year. According to AAA, gas prices typically fall by around 10 to 30 cents per gallon during the winter months.

Global oil costs, the main factor affecting gas prices, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.

"Some optimism about what could happen over in the Middle East and along the Strait of Hormuz certainly plays a role here," Diaz said, while also acknowledging the impact of lower winter fuel costs.

On Tuesday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at around $91 per barrel.

In an interview with CBS News "60 Minutes" on Sunday, President Trump said he is "not looking" to escalate the war in Iran.

"I don't think there's any reason to," he told "60 Minutes" correspondent Ross Douthat.

The timeline for reaching a resolution, however, remains unclear. Gregory Brew, senior analyst for Iran and energy for the political risk consultancy Eurasia Group, said Monday that the prospect for a deal remains "unlikely."

"Despite ongoing mediation, neither the U.S. nor Iran has shifted its negotiating position," he said in a research note Monday.

World.title: First snow of the season is coming to Northeast
World.content:
The first snowfall of the season is expected in parts of the Northeast later this week, although there is uncertainty over how much snow will fall and which parts of the region will be hit hardest.

Temperatures are also forecast to drop well below average for this time of year in that region and other parts of the eastern U.S., impacting a large swath of the country.

Cold snap to spread over eastern U.S. this week

A large dip in the jet stream will cause cold air to spread across the eastern half of the U.S. starting Wednesday through the end of the week, reaching from the Canadian border to the Gulf Coast. Temperatures are expected to drop between 20 and 25 degrees below average for this time of year.

CBS News

Overnight feels-like temperatures are forecast to be near or below freezing in major cities, including Chicago and Atlanta. Daytime highs will only reach the mid-30s and 40s from Thursday through the upcoming weekend.

Snowfall potential

A separate storm system developing over the Midwest on Wednesday will strengthen and head to the Northeast before the end of the week, potentially helping usher in the first snowfall of the season.

Some of the moisture associated with the storm will fall as cold rain, which is expected in cities like Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Washington, D.C., even though the I-95 corridor will likely see warmer temperatures this weekend.

CBS News

But places at higher elevations and those in the interior Northeast, like upstate New York, New Hampshire and Vermont, could see their first snowfall.

CBS News

The storm is expected to move away from land once it reaches the Mid-Atlantic region. A second, smaller storm could potentially form off of that system and impact coastal areas from the Mid-Atlantic up to New England. The path of the second, smaller storm will determine how much snow or rain may fall in those areas, and exactly which locations could be affected.

World.title: France says Iran behind costly grocery store refrigeration hacks
World.content:
French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, the Paris prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks. On Tuesday, France's foreign minister said the country "rules nothing out" in its response to what he called "a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country."

The Oct. 11 hacking attack struck major supermarket chains, hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.

The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by similar hacks affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden. A separate cyberattack targeted several blood banks in France, but the products and samples were not damaged.

In August, refrigeration outages at six U.S. military bases sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News. Hamilton told CBS News this week that the division's Cyber Field Office was working with French law enforcement to understand the refrigeration outages in Europe.

There has been no assertion yet by officials in France, the U.S. or the other European nations hit by the hacks that all of the incidents were connected.

In its statement Monday, the Paris public prosecutor's office said its cybercrime division had opened a judicial investigation on charges including "fraudulent interference with an automated data-processing system and causing damage by means dangerous to persons — both committed as part of an organized group."

View of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, Oct. 12, 2026. Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

It said the alleged offenses were "further aggravated by the fact that they were carried out to serve a foreign power — in this case, Iran — in addition to participation in a criminal conspiracy to prepare for the commission of a serious crime (felony)."

According to the allegations, the investigation is targeting the leader of an Iranian group known as "Shahid Kaveh," which the prosecutor's office described as "a cyber-offensive unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC-ECC) — as well as his two deputies and any other individuals who may be identified."

"The attackers gained remote control of the equipment via web interfaces, initiating indefinite, abnormal defrost cycles while simultaneously disabling safety alerts — alerts designed to trigger when temperatures exceeded specific thresholds," the prosecutor's office said, adding that the probe had "uncovered an attack methodology characteristic of this [Iranian] unit, including the use of the Persian (Farsi) language and IP addresses that trace back to devices located in Iran."

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Tuesday that the country "rules nothing out" in terms of its response to the cyberattack.

"This is a terrorist organization that has committed an attack of unprecedented scale and aggression against our country," Barrot told French broadcaster Franceinfo.

"We are going to summon the [Iranian] ambassador and will call for European sanctions," he said, adding that "we will not stop at merely" those measures in response.

Barrot called the cyberattack "a major threat to the security of the French people" and said the government was "taking every measure to deter any further attacks."

Later Tuesday, the foreign ministry reitterated most of Barrot's remarks, and said in a statement that the hack was "unprecedented in its scale and level of aggressiveness and has been the first offensive cyber campaign carried out purely for the purposes of sabotage on French soil."

In a statement shared on social media last week, the FBI's cybercrime branch said that, along with its partners, it was "seeing malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world," noting that "security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings, potentially causing inventory loss and equipment damage."

The FBI urged all organizations that rely on such systems to take their controllers "off the public internet" and to keep access to the systems behind a firewall, in addition to other security measures.

There was no immediate response from Iranian authorities to the allegations by the French prosecutor on Monday, but the regime has threatened for months to expand its retaliation for the war launched by the U.S., and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of its ports, using unspecified, asymmetrical means.

CBS News' Karine Barzegar contributed to this report.

World.title: What types of debt payments can you negotiate?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Understanding which balances are most likely to be settled is an important part of the debt negotiation process. Years/Getty Images

The amount you owe on a credit card, personal loan or medical bill may seem set in stone. After all, your statements show exactly what you're expected to pay, and creditors generally aren't eager to accept anything less. But when financial circumstances change and keeping up with those obligations becomes difficult, the amount listed on your statement isn't necessarily the only amount a creditor will consider accepting.

That's an important distinction for borrowers who are already struggling to make progress on their balances. According to a recent survey from Achieve, 34% of respondents said they were unable to make the full monthly payments on all their debts. And with everyday expenses continuing to compete for room in household budgets, finding a way to reduce what you owe may be just as important as finding a more manageable payment schedule.

Not every creditor approaches these situations the same way, though, and the options available to you can vary considerably depending on what you owe, how far behind you are and who's responsible for collecting the balance. Understanding those differences can help you identify where negotiations might be worthwhile — and where another form of debt relief could make more sense.

Find out how Achieve can set you on a path to becoming debt-free today.

What types of debt payments can you negotiate?

Debt settlement is one option that a significant share of borrowers are willing to explore. In fact, 44% of Achieve's survey respondents say they would consider working with a debt relief company to negotiate settlements on their behalf. But while creditors may be willing to lower your interest rate, temporarily reduce your payments or extend your repayment term if you're experiencing financial hardship, negotiating a reduction in the actual balance is a different matter.

That's because debt settlement requires a creditor to accept less than the full amount owed as payment in full, and some debts are considerably easier to settle than others. Here are five types of debts you can typically negotiate:

Credit card debt

Credit card debt is generally one of the easiest types of consumer debt to negotiate because it's typically unsecured, meaning the lender doesn't have collateral it can seize if you stop paying the bills. If an account becomes seriously delinquent, the card issuer must decide whether it's more likely to recover the full balance through collections or to accept a smaller lump-sum payment now to close the account.

In many cases, accepting a settlement can make financial sense for the creditor, especially after an account has been charged off or sent to collections. That's why credit card companies and collection agencies are often willing to negotiate, particularly if you can make a lump-sum payment after an agreement has been reached. Keep in mind, though, that waiting until an account reaches this stage can significantly damage your credit.

Explore the debt relief options Achieve can offer you now.

Medical debt

Medical debt is also frequently negotiable because healthcare providers often have more discretion than traditional lenders in collecting unpaid balances. Hospitals and physician groups would generally prefer to recover part of what's owed than spend months or years pursuing collections for the full amount.

If your medical bill has already been sent to a collection agency, settlement may become even more likely. Before negotiating, however, ask whether you qualify for financial assistance or charity care, as those programs can reduce your balance without the potential credit implications of settling a debt if you qualify.

Collection accounts

Once a debt reaches collections, negotiations often become easier because the economics change. Collection agencies frequently purchase delinquent debts for pennies on the dollar or work on commission for the original creditor. That means accepting less than the full balance can still be profitable for them.

For borrowers, this often represents an opportunity to negotiate a dramatically lower payoff amount. If you take this route, though, just be sure to obtain any settlement agreement in writing before sending payment and confirm that the agreed-upon amount satisfies the debt in full.

Private student loans

Private student loans are typically less negotiable because lenders generally expect borrowers to repay according to the terms of the loan agreement. As long as the loan payments remain current, the lender has little incentive to reduce the balance.

If the loan goes into default, however, the situation changes. At that point, some lenders or collection agencies may determine that accepting a partial payment is preferable to the cost and uncertainty of continued collection efforts. That said, while these settlement opportunities exist, it's worth noting that they're much less common than they are with credit card debt.

Auto loans and mortgages

Auto loans and mortgages are among the hardest debts to settle because they're secured by collateral. If you stop making payments, the lender has the legal right to repossess the vehicle or foreclose on the home, giving it another avenue to recover its losses.

Because lenders have that protection, they're generally less willing to forgive part of the balance. Settlement usually occurs only after the collateral has been sold and a remaining deficiency balance still exists, or in situations like a negotiated short sale.

The bottom line

If your goal is to pay less than the full amount you owe, credit card debt, medical debt and collection accounts generally offer the greatest opportunity for successful negotiations. Secured loans and private student loans, meanwhile, are much less flexible and typically offer structured hardship programs rather than settlement opportunities.

Before attempting to settle any debt, though, make sure to understand the potential tradeoffs. Debt settlement can negatively affect your credit score, and forgiven debt may have tax implications in some situations. If negotiating with creditors on your own feels overwhelming, a reputable debt relief company may be able to negotiate settlements on your behalf and help you determine whether debt settlement is the right strategy for your financial situation.

World.title: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
World.content:
U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running

toggle caption i Lian Yi/Xinhua via Getty Images

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Sponsor Message

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Sponsor Message

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

World.title: Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says
World.content:
Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says

toggle caption i LM Otero/AP

How much money would it take for you to feel financially secure? Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Mona Chalabi spent five years following 10 Americans, from those living paycheck to paycheck to those earning hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, in an effort to answer that question. Her new book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, explores why financial security can feel so elusive.

"It's called 10 Lives because I specifically didn't just want to focus on the 1%," Chalabi says. "Instead I wanted to talk about how the 99% of us aren't all in it together, and the kind of power differentials between us."

Sponsor Message

Chalabi says almost everyone she profiled in the book was deeply worried about their financial future, even those who earn plenty of money.

"Across the board, everyone just seemed to be expressing this feeling of panic that I think is really, really particular to U.S. capitalism, which is an incredibly precarious and cruel system where you are one crisis away from experiencing a real economic shock," she says.

Chalabi also noticed that many of the people she profiled considered themselves middle class, regardless of what their actual income was. She says that disconnect between actual wealth and a sense of class has consequences — not just for how we see ourselves, but also in how we judge everybody else.

"To be poor in this country is to encounter an enormous, enormous array of obstacles, including assumptions about your intelligence [and] your educational level," she says. "And so it's actually quite rational sometimes for people to try to present themselves as middle class, maybe even to try and signal wealth with the clothes that they buy or the cars that they drive. I don't think it's simply aspirational. I also think it is them trying to avoid the discrimination that they might face if their real income level were disclosed."

Sponsor Message

Interview highlights

Penguin Random House

On the importance of parents when it comes to financial security

If you really want to understand somebody's economic security, you need to understand who they can turn to when times get hard, and obviously a household is an imperfect measure of that. People sometimes even live with spouses that they can't necessarily lean on. ... But one of the things that came out time and time and time again from the book is how much money your parents have is so profound in shaping your economic security. …

Class is about more than the number that is printed on your pay slip or the number that's in your bank balance. Our class identities are very often tied to our households that we were in growing up. They're tied to the professions that our parents had. ... Most people who are born in poverty in this country do not make it out.

On younger generations choosing partners for economic compatibility

Who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.





There was this TikTok trend that I saw a while ago with people talking about how they were looking for a partner who was 6'5", blue eyes and working in finance, which has never been any partner of mine. I grew up with a particular model of feminism that was about being able to support yourself, not relying on a man. But I also think that for my generation, there was this ... understanding of romance that it's somehow supposed to be post-materialist, that you're not really supposed to talk about wanting a partner from a particular set of economic circumstances. …

[There] was a study that was published by the National Bureau for Economic Research. And they compared 1960 to 2005 and what they found was that it's not necessarily that people are seeking out partners in the same income bracket, but people very often seek out partners with a similar educational background, and education has a huge impact on income. So they actually found that over that period from 1960 to 2005, the trend has gotten even stronger. So we are much more likely now to date someone with a similar educational backgrounds to ours. And the reason why this is important to scrutinize is because I would say who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.

Sponsor Message

On being transparent about her own finances, including her large book advance

I felt the people that I was speaking to had a right to understand my economic privilege, my vantage point as I'm asking them these deeply personal questions. And as you know, as journalists, we typically do not pay people for their time for interviewing them. … But that's a very different kind of equation when you are asking people to share these vulnerable parts of their lives, and especially when I am profiting from those stories.

At the start of every interview with everybody that I spoke to, I told them a number of things. I said, one, I will be paying you $40 per hour for your time. If that feels uncomfortable for you, let's talk about it. I said that anything that I asked them as a journalist, they had the right to ask me back. So if I asked them how much money they made, they had the right to ask me that exact same question.

On making judgments about her class from her accent

The accent thing is huge. ... When I'm back in the U.K., people can get a pretty good read, honestly, on my class by my voice. And what's fascinating is that as an immigrant, Americans don't really understand these nuances in the British accent. And so I'm just read as posh here. And I think that has conferred me, actually, these huge class benefits. I think that my accent in the U.S. has been really powerful in counterbalancing some of the obstacles I might have faced because of my race and gender. Because with this voice, it is assumed that I am educated, that I'm cultured. Not sure how true any of these things are, but there's just this assumption that I think is very beneficial in a corporate environment.

Sponsor Message

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high
World.content:
Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Inflation-scarred consumers are finding a bit of relief these days at an unlikely place: the gas pump.

The average price of gasoline dipped below $4 a gallon Tuesday for the first time in three months, according to AAA. The price of regular gas has fallen by 38 cents in the last month to a national average of $3.98.

The overall cost of living, however, remains stubbornly high. Consumer prices in October were up 0.4% from the previous month, according to a report Tuesday from the Labor Department. That's a bigger monthly increase than forecasters had expected.

Rising housing costs accounted for about a third of the monthly increase. Grocery prices were also up sharply during the month.

Sponsor Message

Why gas prices are falling

The drop in gasoline prices in recent weeks is thanks to a combination of falling crude oil prices, refineries' switch to a cheaper blend of winter fuel, and the typical seasonal drop in demand for gas.

"Temperatures are getting colder," says Patrick De Haan, petroleum analyst for GasBuddy. "People who have boats and RVs are probably done for the year. I would say, by Thanksgiving, so long as we don't get any wild cards geopolitically, the national average could be $3.75 a gallon."

Gas prices are still at a record high for this time of year, however — about a dollar a gallon higher than when the U.S. went to war with Iran. Even with the recent drop in prices, this year's drive to grandma's for Thanksgiving could be the most expensive ever.

Diesel prices have also fallen, but more slowly than gas prices. AAA says the average price of diesel fuel is $6.15 a gallon, down about 13 cents from a month ago.

The high cost of diesel fuel is another byproduct of the war — not only the U.S. war with Iran but also Russia's war with Ukraine. Russia is ordinarily a big exporter of diesel fuel, but that supply has largely dried up because of damage to Russia's refineries.

Sponsor Message

"When a country like Russia isn't exporting diesel, that is very impactful for the global market. So diesel prices – they will come down but they will still remain very elevated," De Haan says.

Heating oil prices are also high

Rising diesel prices are also driving up the cost of heating oil in the northeast, because heating oil is a close cousin of diesel.

Mild fall weather has kept heating costs in check so far, but De Haan says a blast of cold air could push heating oil prices even higher.

Higher diesel prices also affect the cost of other goods that have to be moved by truck or train or cargo ship.

"You're starting to see higher freight costs get passed through," says economist Mike Reid of RBC Capital Markets. "We've seen it show up notably in goods that are heavily imported — apparel, recreation goods, IT equipment."

In a speech Tuesday before the inflation release, Federal Reserve Chris Waller suggested that energy shocks could have more lasting effects on inflation that previously though. Waller suggested the central bank may need to raise interest rates more aggressively to curb price hikes than markets had previously expected.

No annual comparison for inflation this time

While Tuesday's inflation report shows how much prices rose in the last month, it does not include the typical reading on how prices have changed over the last year. That's a casualty of last year's government shutdown, which idled hundreds of government price-checkers so prices from October 2025 were never recorded for comparison.

The Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank estimated before Tuesday's release that consumer prices in October were up 3.7% from a year ago. That would outstrip average wage gains of just 3.1% during the year, so the typical worker is losing buying power. That's a big reason for the heavy turnout in last week's mid-term elections. 49.1% of eligible voters took part in the election, the second highest total for any midterm in more than a century.

World.title: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
World.content:
'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent

toggle caption i 朝鮮通信社/KCNA via KNS via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.

Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family's fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.

"My husband and I didn't want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom," said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.

Sponsor Message

North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.

This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.

Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she's being groomed as her father's heir.

The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.

North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.

To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country's previous power successions, as well as several experts.

Sponsor Message

Most defectors believe the girl is Kim's heir

Not much is known about Kim's daughter except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.

Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.

South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.

"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.

toggle caption i Lee Jin-man/AP

Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea's economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.

Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.

Doubts remain about a woman becoming North Korea's leader

Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.

Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.

Sponsor Message

"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.

Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family "are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter."

Kim's push for hereditary power transfer faces little resistance at home

Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea's spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.

North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with," said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.

During North Korea's first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.

The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.

"A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system," said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul's Korea Institute for National Unification. "North Korea's ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens."

Sponsor Message

Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them "nonsense."

Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.

Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.

"Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. "They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger."

World.title: Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
World.content:
Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility

toggle caption i Dita Alangkara/AP

JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.

Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.

It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.

Sponsor Message

As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.

"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."

The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.

Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.

The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.

The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.

The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.

Sponsor Message

Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

World.title: The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000
World.content:
The average cost for a new vehicle in the U.S. hits a record high: over $51,000

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

The average transaction cost for a new vehicle has reached a record high: $51,109. That's according to a report out today from the Kelley Blue Book, which is part of the analytics firm Cox Automotive.

That's about $500 above the last record, set in December 2025.

Car prices have been stubbornly high for years, especially since the pandemic, mainly driven by supply chain issues. And they've gotten higher recently, in part thanks to tariffs and to buyers flocking to, and car companies making, larger, fancier vehicles.

Sponsor Message

Yet there's a little good news: Cars are getting more expensive … more slowly.

While that $51,109 figure is an all-time high, that's only up 2.1% in the past year.

"A 2.1% year-over-year increase is actually below inflation," said Erin Keating, an executive analyst at Cox Automotive who co-authored the report. Between 2012 and 2021, cars got 3.4% more expensive a year on average, she continued.

The Kelley Blue Book's transaction cost is based on what people wound up paying for a new vehicle — that means whatever's on the sticker price, plus add-ons for fancier features, and minus any incentives, such as dealer discounts.

It also doesn't include one other expense that adds to the cost of owning a car: interest on auto loans. The cost of borrowing has risen over the past several years as the Federal Reserve has kept interest rates high in an effort to drive down inflation. Auto loan rates are now about 11% for used vehicles and over 7% for new ones, according to Edmunds, a car analytics company.

Keating says all of this can add up to some sticker shock for buyers — partly because people don't buy cars all that often and can be surprised by how expensive they've gotten, and partly because of interest rates.

Sponsor Message

"I mean, we are seeing a true shift in the percentage of your monthly payment that's going towards interest versus towards principal," she said.

Used cars are not a steal

The Kelley Blue Book's average includes all kinds of vehicles — SUVs, pickup trucks, electric vehicles — from all kinds of auto companies, including Toyota, Subaru, Tesla and Mercedes-Benz.

It doesn't, however, include used car sales, which normally make up about two-thirds of total sales. Ivan Drury, director of industry insights at Edmunds, crunched those numbers too and found the same trend. "No matter what you're looking at, the price is up," he said.

The average used car now costs close to $27,000, 6% higher than last year, according to Cox Automotive. Vehicles that cost less than that are a "sliver" of the industry, Drury said.

Supply chain challenges, including a semiconductor shortage, during the COVID pandemic meant fewer cars got made. Carmakers had to pick and choose which vehicles to prioritize making — they picked their most profitable models. As a result, fewer used vehicles entered car lots in the early 2020s. So today there's less inventory to choose from.

That's good for people who already own a car, Drury said. It means people can upgrade to a new car without much additional money up front.

But, he continued, "The consumer that I sympathize with the absolute most? The first-time car buyer." Those buyers face a steep down payment, with nothing to trade in.

No matter whether buyers are choosing new or used, data from Edmunds shows that in 2026, they have been financing with lower down payments and longer auto term lengths. "We've just seen those explode," Drury said.

A report from Edmunds found that car buyers financed more than ever, taking out loans worth an average of $44,664 in the past quarter. They also found that more than a quarter of car buyers financed using loans with 84-month-long terms — or longer.

Sponsor Message

The combination of a small down payment — sometimes in the range of $500 or $1,000 — and a lengthy loan term can get really expensive for buyers in the long term, Drury said, especially with high interest rates.

"So people just say, 'Oh, forget it,' you know. 'I'll just, I'll just choose the longer term length and put less money down. I've got other bills that are pulling at me,'" Drury said.

Why are new cars so expensive?

In part, vehicles cost more because the cost of making them has gone up for automakers. There are now more tariffs on steel and aluminum, as well as on goods imported from Canada. That matters for American automakers who assemble vehicles on both sides of the border. The cost of computer chips (used in sensors and electronics) and copper (used for automotive wiring) has also risen thanks to competing demand from data centers.

But vehicles also cost more because Americans like bigger cars, SUVs and trucks, which tend to come with a higher price tag. The average sticker price for a full-size pickup truck is nearly $72,000, according to the Kelley Blue Book.

American carmakers have largely shifted their gears away from compact sedans. In earnings calls with investors, they've often cited American demand for bigger vehicles.

Plus, as analyst Mike Wall at Mobility Global points out, smaller vehicles offer lower margins for carmakers. "They were sort of that loss leader. It gets the eyeballs in the door," he said.

For the carmakers, they're not making as much money as they would compared to their bigger vehicles with pricier features.

Drury notes, people appreciate those features. They've gotten used to driving with 360-degree cameras, heated seats and parking assist systems. All of these drive up the cost of buying. "No one wants entry-level anymore," he said. "Everybody goes mid-to-upper trim levels."

Sponsor Message

"People love walking up to their car that already has the air conditioner going when it's 110 degrees outside, and think, 'You know what? I don't have to get in here and potentially burn my hands,'" Drury continued. "So as we get accustomed to more features, more options, we naturally kind of pile on, too. And automakers, they're very aware of that."

A challenging time for automakers

Over the past few years, "automakers have been under incredible stress," Keating said. Yes, there are tariffs and other rising production costs. Many also poured money into developing electric vehicle technology, but EVs still only make up a small slice of the U.S. car market. About 6% of new cars sold are electric, according to Edmunds.

And the market for car buyers is smaller. About 16 million people buy new cars every year — about 1 million fewer since the pandemic.

Notably, fewer people in their late 30s and early 40s are buying cars. "They're just simply holding onto their cars longer," Keating said. Her hypothesis? "That age group and that cohort is simply just dealing with different household pressures for their money and are making the choice to stay in the vehicles that they have."

For the most part, the people buying new cars tend to be older and wealthier. Keating said that might be because older drivers are staying on the road longer. " We have seen this interesting shift towards individuals keeping their licenses longer and therefore more 65 and up, 75 and up individuals are purchasing vehicles than ever before," she said.

For automakers, a drop in car buyers means they have to compete more with each other for sales.

"At the end of the day, each of these competitors are sharing, trying to go after a pie that isn't necessarily growing," Keating said. So instead, " they're stealing share from their competitors as opposed to counting on more consumers entering the picture."

World.title: Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
World.content:
Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling

toggle caption i AFP/via Getty Images

"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.

On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.

"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."

Sponsor Message

For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."

During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.

"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.

There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.

Sponsor Message

"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."

For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.

"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."

A worldwide worry

Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.

So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO . While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan , hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.

Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.

"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.

The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people . The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.

Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement

The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.

Sponsor Message

Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.

"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.

In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.

"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.

NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.

Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.

A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.

"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.

An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.

Sponsor Message

"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.

Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray , says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."

Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.

"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."
