For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
World.content:
Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you

toggle caption i Bruce Glikas/Getty Images

What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.

The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).

School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.

Sponsor Message

"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.

Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!

Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.

Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.

School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.

Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.

After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."

toggle caption i Bruce Glikas/Getty Images

A perspective on colorism

Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.

Sponsor Message

Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."

While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.

"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."

The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.

"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.

Audience reaction

School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.

"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.

Sponsor Message

For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.

"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Stellantis auto plant closure in Brampton, Ont., a 'betrayal' to all Canadians, Carney says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said automaker Stellantis shuttering its plant in Brampton, Ont., is a betrayal to the country and all Canadians.

"The situation in the Brampton plant is unacceptable," Carney said in Montreal on Tuesday.

"It violates the obligations that Stellantis has under several agreements, but to be more fundamental, it's a betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada and by extension to all Canadians."

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre blames the Liberal government for failing to prevent the closure and called on Carney to fire Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for her handling of the file.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre speaks during a news conference on Tuesday near the Stellantis assembly plant. (Arlyn McAdorey/The Canadian Press)

"The Liberal strategy has failed to save jobs from Stellantis to Stelco," Poilievre said outside the idled auto assembly plant in Brampton earlier on Tuesday. "In both cases the Liberals promised they would get the jobs back."

"Today the Official Opposition is calling for the Liberal prime minister to fire his failed, costly, job-killing Liberal industry minister."

Stelco is owned by Cleveland-Cliffs, the U.S. company that said in September it plans to lay off hundreds of Ontario steelworkers despite promising to keep the number of unionized workers at 2024 levels for three more years.

WATCH | Poilievre calls for Joly to be fired: Poilievre calls for Joly to be fired: 'She's done nothing' | Duration closed caption 0:38 Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is calling for Industry Minister Mélanie Joly to be fired, calling out her handling of Ontario's hard-hit steel and automotive sectors, and saying the Liberal strategy has failed to save jobs.

Standing next to Joly, Carney said his industry minister is doing "an exceptional job in very difficult circumstances," and she will continue to "fight for these workers."

"The issue is not the exceptional work of Minister of Industry Joly and her colleagues, it is the behaviour of the company versus those workers," Carney said.

Joly said that her office has been engaging with Stellantis and Unifor, the private-sector union representing the workers at the Brampton plant, for more than a year to try and come to a solution to no avail.

"Stallantis has decided to go ahead and violate its contract and so that is why we will … use the full force of the law to make sure that we protect jobs but also bring back justice to these workers," she said.

WATCH | Carney calls planned Stellantis sale a 'betrayal': Carney calls planned Stellantis sale a 'betrayal' of workers, defends Joly's work | Duration closed caption 1:11 Prime Minister Mark Carney said the situation at Stellantis is 'unacceptable' as the assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., is set to be purchased by a Canadian armoured vehicle maker. 'We will fully enforce our rights,' in the protection of workers and Canadian funds, he said, without offering specifics.

In a deal announced by the Trudeau government in 2022, Ottawa said it would inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them retool to increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

The contract barred Stellantis from closing its assembly plant in Brampton before 2035 unless it was subject to circumstances beyond the automaker’s "reasonable control" that made the facility "commercially unviable."

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023 to refit the facility to produce the Jeep Compass.

But Stellantis paused the retooling plan in early 2025, announcing in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.

The plant's future in Brampton had been left in limbo until Monday, when Stellantis announced it was selling the facility to Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel Inc. in a deal that could see Stellantis lease some of the property back.

Feds gave $222M to Stellantis

In an interview with CP24, Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov said his company plans to convert the Brampton plant into "a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing," but won't commit to bringing back Stellantis workers.

"Brampton is an amazing place to develop and to create a competitive business, but a competitive business cannot work by taking obligations of other companies and we are not going to even consider taking any responsibilities of anyone from previous engagements," Shimonov told CP24.

The prime minister said his government intends to "fully enforce our rights in protection of those workers and protection of Canadian funds."

Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown told CBC News that he wants to see a unified Team Canada challenge to U.S. President Donald Trump's attempts to destroy Canada's auto sector.

"If we allow Stellantis to leave easily and ignore their legal obligations, this will not be the last auto plant that falls in Canada," Brown said. "Really this is ground zero of protecting auto jobs."

Joly will host a meeting of all stakeholders in Toronto on Thursday in an attempt to find a way forward for the laid off Stellantis workers.

WATCH | Industry minister says Stellantis violated its contract: Stellantis has decided to 'violate its contract,' industry minister says | Duration closed caption 0:47 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she will bring together stakeholders to talk about Stellantis, which plans to sell an idled assembly plant to an armoured vehicle company. Joly, who Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wants to see fired, pledged to protect workers, saying 'patience has its limits.'

Last December, CBC News confirmed that the federal government had given $222 million to the Canadian arm of Stellantis between 2023 and 2025. CBC News asked the federal government for the most recent total but has yet to receive a response.

Stellantis issued a statement on Tuesday saying it would voluntarily pay the subsidies back.

"We recognize that Canadians expect accountability for public funding, and that is why Stellantis has offered to voluntarily return the government support received for Brampton Assembly's original retooling plan," the company said.

It added that "confidentiality provisions" prevent it from disclosing further details.

No Ontario money went to Brampton: Ford

That 2022 deal also saw Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government pledge to support the plants with an investment of up to $513 million.

CBC News confirmed on Tuesday that Ontario has not provided the company with any funding for its Brampton retooling initiative because it didn't meet conditions related to job creation and project milestones.

The company did, however, get $55 million for the Windsor plant from the Ford government.

World.title: 4 grizzly bears found responsible for killing mother and daughter in B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with an attack near Bella Coola that left a mother and daughter dead.

Forensic testing confirmed a sow and three cubs were actively involved in the attack that killed Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20.

In an update Tuesday, BCCOS Insp. Jeff Tyre said the attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which is considered "very rare."

"We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, as well as these findings, bring some measure of closure," he said.

"Our thoughts remain with everyone affected."

The four bears captured over the weekend were not involved in the 2025 attack on a group of students and teachers, Tyre added.

More to come.

World.title: Defiant Hegseth calls Republican's impeachment resolution a 'farce'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the articles of impeachment introduced against him a farce and a stunt at a news conference Tuesday morning. Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment against him on Monday, largely focusing on the war in Iran.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth condemned a resolution in the House of Representatives calling for his impeachment, describing it as a "farce" from a "disgruntled congressman" who is leaving office.

Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, who won't be in Congress when the new session begins in January, filed a privileged motion on the House floor on Monday to introduce eight articles of impeachment.

Impeachment resolutions can carry over to the next session, which begins on Jan. 3 with Democrats holding the House and Senate majority. If the House were to impeach and a Senate trial were to occur, the threshold for a conviction and removal from office requires two-thirds of senators voting in favour.

Hegseth said any such proceedings would be a "show trial against the president and the secretary of war" and he characterized the articles of impeachment as "policy disagreements" that don't meet the impeachment standard of high crimes and misdemeanours.

"The proper remedy for a policy disagreement, it's legislation, it's debate, it's the next presidential election," said Hegseth, holding his first press briefing from the Pentagon since May.

WATCH | Massie says he's taking a stand, not 'disgruntled': U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth | Duration 2:27 Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, largely focusing on the war in Iran and his role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela. A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping midterm election losses.

U.S. President Donald Trump gave an enthusiastic response on social media to Hegseth's pushback. Trump has said he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached.

Under the rules of Massie's motion, a vote is supposed to be held within two legislative days unless a majority supports a countering motion to kill the effort. Massie introduced a similar measure in September, but the House legislators were sent home before a vote could occur.

A vote in the House could come by mid-week, but the next steps are highly uncertain.

'They will fail again'

The articles of impeachment in Massie's motion lead with the lack of congressional authorization for the war in Iran. The articles also reference Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, and the deadly strikes on boats allegedly transporting drugs in waters near South America.

"I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said on Tuesday.

He said "thousands of American lives" were saved with every boat strike — even as human rights organizations and international bodies have said they possibly constitute crimes against humanity. Hegseth also said that former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro was "not kidnapped, he was brought to justice by America's best."

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky speaks Monday outside the Capitol about articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

The articles also refer to attempts to prosecute Congress members Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin after they recorded a video advising service members they were not obliged to follow illegal orders.

Massie, who was defeated earlier this year by a Trump-backed Republican opponent in a primary, pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership, with outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson saying it would be "a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see."

The last House impeachment was of former Homeland Security chief Alejandro Mayorkas in Joe Biden's administration in 2024, for breach of public trust and willful refusal to comply with the law. The Republican-led House cited the surge of migrants at the southern border in just the second ever impeachment of a cabinet secretary, but the Democratic-led Senate then never took up the measure.

Trump was twice impeached in the House, in 2019 and 2021, but acquitted at Senate trials. In the second impeachment, many Republicans argued that Trump's actions leading up to the 2021 Capitol riot were best dealt with in the courts, but Trump completed a remarkable political comeback before criminal indictments he faced were resolved legally.

Hegseth called those Trump impeachments failures and predicted that the current efforts "will fail again."

Razor-thin confirmation

What constitutes "high crimes and misdemeanours" is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide.

Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, Johnson's potential successor as the next Speaker, recently said he is a"hard yes" for impeaching Hegseth. Several other Democrats took to social media on Tuesday to say they were in favour.

A vote will put pressure on Republicans, many of whom blamed their midterm election wipeout on the Iran war.

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of Hegseth, told reporters on Tuesday he wasn't a fan of the impeachment articles in their present form. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska has highlighted other concerns not contained in the articles, including Hegseth's firing of dozens of senior military leaders, but he also questioned Massie's motives.

"If we were allowed to amend it, I'd maybe feel a lot of differently," said Bacon.

Republican Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio said, "blaming Hegseth for a duty Congress shirked and the president made is wrong."

"This isn't about Iran, this about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon," said Vice-President JD Vance.

Vance broke a tie in the Senate to enable Hegseth's confirmation in early 2025. Republicans Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell — each set to leave Congress — voted against his confirmation, as did Republican Lisa Murkowski and all of the Senate Democrats.

Thom Tillis, a Republican also leaving the Senate, has expressed regret for his vote to confirm Hegseth, saying in part in September that the secretary "retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defence."

LISTEN | David Smith, Washington reporter for the Guardian, on Hegseth's influence (March 16): Front Burner 30:05 Pete Hegseth: the Iran war’s chief promoter

Democrats and a handful of Republicans questioned Hegseth's fitness for the job nearly two years ago. Hegseth admitted paying a settlement to a woman who alleged he sexually assaulted her, in order to prevent a costly and drawn-out process.

His confirmation hearings also included allegations of excessive drinking and financial mismanagement at two veterans' organizations he previously led.

During Trump's first term, Hegseth was an on-air Fox News contributor who lobbied the president on behalf of three service members who faced accusations of war crimes in military tribunals, arguing they were being treated unfairly.

Trump ultimately granted clemency to two of the men, and elevated a third in rank.

Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon has been unconventional, and that was on display on Tuesday. Defence secretaries typically stay away from partisan political statements, but Hegseth laid out criticisms of predecessor Lloyd Austin and disparaged the military recruitment and retention efforts of Biden's administration.

He also told the U.S. troops to "stay the course" while evoking his Christianity, even as he has been sued for imposing his religion on federal workers.

World.title: 'The editor's here!': CBC journalist stars in viral video with American stand-up Josh Johnson
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Listen to this article

A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday.

American comedian Josh Johnson, a stand-up and occasional host of The Daily Show, was cracking jokes about CBC's coverage of a bodega cat getting evicted due to health concerns, during his show at the Vogue Theatre in Vancouver last month.

"I want so badly to meet the editor," Johnson quipped.

A voice from the audience shouted out: "He's here!"

A befuddled Johnson replied: "The cat's here?"

Nope.

"The editor's here!" shouted the crowd.

Enter Jon Azpiri.

Wearing a dark grey hoodie, coincidentally mirroring Johnson's signature light grey hoodie, Azpiri walked onstage for a 10-minute back-and-forth filled with jokes about cats, disappearing islands and journalism.

Johnson started to ask Azpiri about the bodega cat situation before Azpiri interrupted.

"We do a lot of stories about cats. So I need to know the specific cat."

Azpiri, a copy editor and reporter, answered Johnson's various questions about how a newsroom chooses what to cover.

"We're a public broadcaster," Azpiri said. "So we have a thing called Journalistic Standards and Practices."

"There's really no need to brag," Johnson replied.

As of 9:30 a.m. PT, Johnson's video shared on Instagram has more than 1.2 million views.

Johnson ended the exchange, and the two shook hands.

As Azpiri left, he reminded Johnson the province was set to have an election the next day.

"That's a real editor right there, too," Johnson said. "Even as he's leaving, [he's like] 'We do have an election tomorrow.'"

CBC News has reached out to Johnson.

World.title: Connor Hellebuyck tells media online death threats, family played roles in trade demand
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Connor Hellebuyck spoke to Winnipeg media Tuesday afternoon for the first time since his trade out of the city, saying online death threats and his family were major factors in the move.

"Some things happened to my family that, for me, crossed the line … and made that decision very certain," he said.

"I needed to be a good husband and good father and do what's best for my family."

There was more to the decision, but "I won’t go deeper than that," Hellebuyck said, then added there was also some uncertainty with his career, "and I felt that a change in scenery is what was best."

Hellebuyck wouldn't say if the threats were actually from anyone in Winnipeg.

The Michigan-born goalie led Team U.S.A. to Olympic gold over Team Canada in February. Hellebuyck and several teammates then visited the White House, where U.S. President Donald Trump gave Hellebuyck the Presidential Medal of Freedom while anti-American sentiment was soaring in Canada due to tariffs and Trump's references to making Canada the 51st state.

The Jets management previously said the harassment Hellebuyck faced had escalated to the point where team security and local police were involved, with increased monitoring around Hellebuyck's Winnipeg residence.

"I’ve loved my time here but there are a few moments that I don’t want to see happen again,” Hellebuyck said Tuesday.

"There is more that made me and my family uncomfortable. I’m, please, going to ask you to respect my family's privacy."

Read the previous story below:

Connor Hellebuyck will face the media — but not his former teammates or Jets fans — when he returns to Winnipeg for the first time since his trade to the New Jersey Devils.

Hellebuyck, 33, has said he plans to explain his reasons for leaving Winnipeg when he speaks to reporters Tuesday following the Devils' morning skate.

CBC News will livestream his news conference here and on CBC Gem and YouTube.

The skate takes place at 11:30 a.m., so the livestream is scheduled to begin around 12:15 p.m., though it's not clear yet when Hellebuyck will start speaking.

New Jersey general manager Sunny Mehta announced Sunday, after Hellebuyck and his team posted a 4-0 shutout win over Toronto, that the star goaltender would not play in his first return to the city where he spent 11 NHL seasons.

"P laying in this game would potentially give us a reduction in our expected win probability," Mehta's statement said, despite Hellebuyck being undefeated so far in five games with the Devils.

In his post-game interview on Sunday, Hellebuyck said he wanted to face his former team but understands the Devils' decision and " it's out of my hands."

At Hellebuyck's request, the team has co-ordinated a media availability after the morning skate at Canada Life Centre, Mehta's statement said.

Backup goalies typically skate in the pre-game warmup, which might be the only chance for Jets fans to see him.

There’s no room for backup goalies on the visiting team’s bench in Canada Life Centre, so Hellebuyck won’t be exposed to greetings from the crowd during the game.

Hellebuyck's trade out of Winnipeg followed a prolonged and strained end to his career as a Jet and has left many fans bitter.

He made his trade request at the end of last season, just two years after committing to a seven-year contract extension and declaring, "I’m ready to be a Jet for life and bring a Cup to this city, because I truly believe we can get it done here."

When the requested trade hadn't been made before training camp started in fall, Hellebuyck failed to show up, so the Jets suspended him.

He was traded the day that suspension was set to end.

Following the trade on Oct. 23, fans circled Nov. 10 on their calendars. It's the only visit by the Devils this season, though the teams meet up again Nov. 28 when the Jets play in New Jersey.

Tickets for Tuesday's game sold out quickly and prices tripled in some cases.

Jets fans and head coach Scott Arniel expressed disappointment that Hellebuyck is not suiting up for the game.

The Jets want closure for the organization and its fans, but now the issue is pushed down the road, Arniel said on Monday.

World.title: Descendants say reviving Japanese Canadian veterans' Legion rights historical wrong
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After internment forced its closure, a Legion that served Japanese Canadian veterans of the First World War is being resurrected.

As Remembrance Day approaches, members of Royal Canadian Legion-British Columbia Japanese Canadian Branch No. 9 — many of whom are descendants of the Japanese Canadian veterans it served — say joining the long-lost Legion is a way to honour their relatives' memory.

The attack on Pearl Harbor prompted Canada to label its residents of Japanese heritage as "enemy aliens," and thousands were forced into internment camps, while their possessions were seized and sold without consent.

Members of Branch No. 9 seek to spread the word about the Legion to right a historical wrong while educating the public about the veterans' contributions.

"I think he would be very happy about it," said new Branch No. 9 president David Mitsui, reflecting on his grandfather.

He is the grandson of Masumi Mitsui, a decorated veteran of Vimy Ridge and Hill 70 who headed the branch before it closed.

Community historian Debbie Jiang is pictured in Richmond, B.C., on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Jiang spearheaded the creation of the lost Legion branch. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

Uncovering the past

The revival of Branch No. 9 was spearheaded by Richmond community historian Debbie Jiang.

Digging through archival files, Jiang discovered an old newspaper clipping from the Vancouver Daily Province.

"There was a headline that said 'Japanese charter voted down,'" she said. "I thought that was a very strange headline and thought, 'What are they talking about here?'"

A newspaper clipping from the Vancouver Daily Province shows that the Japanese Canadian legion branch was voted down, despite the promise that it would be reinstated after the Second World War. (Submitted by Debbie Jiang)

Jiang, a former project co-ordinator with Library and Archives Canada, dug a little further.

She said that by going through historical files, she found that in 1942, the president of Branch No. 9, Masumi Mitsui, had surrendered its charter.

"When I found that letter of surrender, it did say that this suspension is only until the end of the war against Japan," Jiang said.

But the Legion denied its reinstatement after the Second World War, she said.

After rediscovering the clipping, Jiang worked to connect with descendants of Branch No. 9 members and uncovered archival documents that convinced the Legion to reopen this forgotten branch.

"We are proud to support the reopening of Japanese Canadian Legion #9 and making right a historical wrong," Bob Underhill, president of the Legion's B.C./Yukon Command, wrote to CBC News.

So far, the branch plans to hold gatherings online as most descendants are scattered across the country, Jiang said. An official reinstatement ceremony is slated for February next year at the Vancouver Japanese Language School.

Dozens have joined and the hope is to continue to grow the membership.

Sgt. Masumi Mitsui, centre, was leader of what was then known as Japanese Branch No. 9, The Canadian Legion, British Empire Service League before it was shut down due to internment in the Second World War. His grandson, David Mitsui, is the branch's new president. (Submitted by David Mitsui)

Descendants of members speak out

Mitsui said it was hard for his grandfather to deal with internment and the closure of the Legion.

"I think all of them felt betrayed after they tried to do an honourable thing," he said. "Then they were, literally, you know, spat upon and denied the opportunity to continue their involvement with the Legion."

He recalled Masumi never attended a public Remembrance Day ceremony after the Second World War, but he would still dress in his uniform, wear his Legion beret, shine his medals and honour his fallen comrades at home.

Yoshihiro Kamachi, whose uncle served in the First World War, is pictured in Vancouver, B.C., on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

"I've joined because of Otoji," said Yoshihiro Kamachi, who served in the military as a dentist.

His sais his uncle, Otoji Kamachi, was a veteran of battles such as Vimy Ridge, and he was wounded five times.

About 200 Japanese Canadians from B.C. travelled to Alberta to enlist and fight in the First World War, he said.

"Then in the Second World War, they weren't treated very well," said Kamachi. "Most of them were treated as enemy aliens, and then they were sent to internment camps like everybody else."

Because Otoji was a veteran, authorities asked him to spy on the Japanese Canadians he was interned with, which added to the sense of betrayal, he said.

Bunkichi Hamade, a veteran of the First World War. His descendant, Britt Moberg, says that joining the newly revived Branch No. 9 is a way to heal from the injustices of the past. (Submitted by Britt Moberg)

Kamachi said he hopes the re–establishment of this Legion can help bring some awareness to their story.

The Legion seeks to reconnect with other descendants and grow its membership, which is available to all members of the public. Details can be found by contacting them by email.

"They fought valiantly for Canada and it should be known in history that they did serve well," Kamachi said.

World.title: Amid sky-high oilpatch profits, Alberta's premier wants to offer oil companies a new subsidy. Here's why
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Alberta government is preparing to unveil new subsidies later this month for oil companies to ramp up production in order to help fill the province's proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast.

The incentives would come as the largest oil producers are posting billions of dollars in profits in their latest financial results and the industry as a whole is experiencing one of its most lucrative years over the last decade.

Suncor Energy, Cenovus Energy, Canadian Natural Resources and Imperial Oil posted combined profits of more than $12.5 billion in recent quarterly earnings reports. The Canadian oil and gas industry is forecast to post revenues of more than $200 billion in 2026, according to Studio Energy, after oil prices climbed above $100 US per barrel several times this year amid the U.S.-Iran war.

That's why some industry experts question why new subsidies are needed.

"What kind of incentives does the oil and gas sector really need?" said Janet Annesley, a former executive with Husky Energy and Shell Canada, on CBC Radio's Alberta at Noon.

"They've got money, they're buying back shares, they're flowing lots of dividends to shareholders. So what really more do we Albertans have to do to get them to make investments here and have more projects?"

Premier Danielle Smith, Annesley said, will have to "prosecute the case with Albertans about why we should be giving more incentives to oil companies."

WATCH | How oilsands executives could be gauging investor interest in possible growth: Why oilsands investors may be reluctant to support big expansion projects | Duration closed caption 3:18 Former Suncor chief executive Mark Little explains why shareholders of oilsands companies may have little incentive to support spending tens of billion of dollars on new production facilities. Currently, the Alberta government is developing an incentive program to encourage companies to increase production.

Oil production is already at record levels, but with several new and expanded pipeline projects in development, there is uncertainty whether the industry will pump out enough crude to justify beginning construction on the Pacific Link — for which Smith wants construction to begin in fall 2027.

The province is seeking to create an "alternative enhanced royalty structure," according to Smith, to incentivize companies to commit to growing oil production.

"We hope that once that is on the table and they know all of the factors that would go into it, I suspect that you're going to see a lot of interest in being able to fill that pipeline," Smith told journalists in Fort McMurray, Alta., in September.

More oil wanted

The new subsidy is expected to be aimed at the oilsands sector, since that is the source of most oil production in the province and new projects are often large enough to noticeably increase overall production levels.

The Alberta government already provides a financial incentive to oilsands companies to build new projects, since they pay much lower levels of royalties to the government during the first few years of operation.

A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

Already, some companies are hinting at potentially moving quicker to build new projects.

Imperial Oil was considering a decision to proceed with its Aspen oilsands project by the end of the decade, but chief executive John Whelan said that could occur sooner.

"We are looking at do we want to bring it forward," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Oct. 30, while acknowledging the company is encouraged by steps taken by the provincial and federal governments to support the sector.

Suncor executives are looking at their growth plans over the next several years and contemplating how they could potentially move faster, if they decide to, said chief executive Rich Kruger.

"We're asking ourselves and doing some preliminary work," he said, during a conference call with analysts on Nov. 4.

"We're all anxiously waiting to hear more from the province on royalties and incentives there. The parties are all sleeves rolled up, meeting endlessly, working hard together."

The Oil Sands Alliance would not comment on the proposed Alberta incentives until an actual announcement is made.

Introducing a deadline

Some oil companies could be hinting at possible growth plans as a way to alert investors and gauge their interest. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits for shareholders, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.

Many investors are enjoying the robust profits and are reluctant to give up the cash they collect, says Mark Little, the former chief executive of Suncor.

The company leaders are "testing investors' appetite for expansion," said Little, to hear if they will support growth plans or if they warn not to do it.

"To me, the biggest uncertainty on growth isn't the [federal government], it's not the province, it's not money," said Little, "It's whether the investor will support it."

LISTEN | Digging into the Pacific Link pipeline: West of Centre 32:08 Pacific Link: A pipeline in whose interest?

The last large oilsands project to be constructed was nearly a decade ago, which is why Little says it's important for the industry to make investments to ensure the sector's long-term future.

"I almost call it the 'liquidation phase' because all we've been doing is basically producing, spending as little as possible, and handing the cash back to the shareholders," he said.

An aerial view of an oilsands mine north of Fort McMurray, Alta. Oil production continues to increase as companies expand and improve existing facilities. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

The Alberta government's move to introduce a new incentive is "mystifying," said Little, since the current royalty system is already sophisticated, flexible and works well. However, he could see merit in the provincial government introducing a deadline for companies to develop the properties they own.

Production from the oilsands continues to increase as companies invest in expansion projects and find ways to improve existing operations.

Lennie Kaplan, who previously served as a senior manager with the Treasury Board, estimates that some level of incentives are necessary for companies to spend billions of dollars to build new large-scale oilsands projects.

"These projects are very capital intensive," he said, about the level of investment required.

For the Alberta government to reach its goal of doubling oil production, Kaplan's calculations estimate the government would need to provide $115 billion of incentives between 2027 and 2050, which includes $95 billion of royalty relief and $18 billion of additional construction subsidies. Under that scenario of normal oil prices, as forecast by Alberta Energy, the government would collect an additional $250 billion in royalties.

However, in a scenario with low oil prices, the government would need to provide $240 billion of incentives and yet experience a net fiscal loss of $80 billion.

Kaplan's modelling does account for other considerations, including a rising industrial carbon tax, which he said is important considering the Alberta government still pledges to be net-zero by 2050.

World.title: David Walliams, U.K. comedian and author, accused of preying on teenage girls
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British comedian and author David Walliams has been accused by multiple women of using his celebrity status to prey on them at a young age, often for sex, according to a three-year investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

Walliams has also been accused of inappropriate behaviour in the workplace during his time on the show Britain’s Got Talent, where he was a judge for 10 years, and at his former publisher HarperCollins, which has since dropped him.

Walliams has denied the allegations. Earlier this year, his lawyers took a case to the U.K.'s High Court in an effort to stop the Guardian and ITV News from publishing the claims and naming him in their reporting.

A judge rejected his injunction request last week, but protected his identity until late Monday.

That case was dismissed last week, meaning those claims could be shared. Walliams's legal team claimed that if those allegations were made public, he'd take his own life, according to a story by the BBC.

Women accuse Walliams of grooming

While most women say they were over the age of 18 during their interactions with Walliams, two say they were 15 when they first met him.

One woman told the Guardian and ITV News she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event, when she was 15 and he was 32. He was starring in the hit BBC comedy series Little Britain at the time, and she hoped to one day be a comedy writer.

Matt Lucas, left, and Walliams, right — dressed as their characters Lou Todd and Andy Pipkin — signed copies of their comedy CD in January 2004. It was at such a fan event where one of Walliams' accusers says she first met him. (Steve Finn/Getty Images)

At the event, she says he called her "a very attractive lady" and wouldn't stop staring at her. She gave Walliams some scripts she'd written and her contact information, and after that, she says, he called her at home.

She claims he told her the scripts were very funny, and said they should stay in touch. During the call, she says her age was discussed several times.

As time went on, and communication continued, she says the conversation turned sexual, and Walliams asked for pictures of her naked. At the age of 17, she says her and Walliams had consensual sex.

Walliams told the Guardian and ITV News that he doesn't remember asking for such pictures, and that he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex.

Walliams won a Pride of Britain Award in 2006 as the Most Influential Public Figure, after raising money for the charity campaign Sports Relief by swimming across the English Channel. (Ian Walton/Getty Images)

Another woman also claims to have met Walliams when she was 15, after the two connected on the social network MySpace in 2007. She says they arranged a meet-up when she was in London where they kissed in an alleyway; she said he later touched her sexually at his house and then suggested they connect again when she turned 16.

Walliams denies having sexual contact with the second woman, and says he's never engaged in the grooming of young women.

Other women have also levelled claims that Walliams tried to take advantage of them at a vulnerable age.

Alleged harassment at HarperCollins and Britain's Got Talent

Walliams, who has sold more than 26 million children's books in the U.K. such as Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy, was dropped by his publishing company HarperCollins in 2025. The company has since announced it will also no longer publish his back catalogue of books.

According to information obtained by the Guardian and ITV News, that action was taken because of concerns raised over the years, including allegations of an inappropriate sexual relationship with a young female employee.

David Walliams has sold millions of copies of children's books through the publisher HarperCollins, which has since dropped him. (Ben Pruchnie/Getty Images)

Walliams also made a name for himself as one of the judges for Britain's Got Talent from 2012 to 2022. There he was accused of inviting teenage girls to the show as guests, as well as harassing young women who worked on the show.

In November of 2022, Walliams was recorded saying disparaging and sexual comments toward contestants. He has since left the show.

All the while, Walliams and his alleged proclivity to date younger women was the butt of jokes among comedians in the U.K.

'I am not a sexual predator'

Walliams denies any wrongdoing. In a letter to journalists with the Guardian and ITV news who were working on the story, he wrote: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

"I realize I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

Walliams had the opportunity to appeal the High Court's decision allowing the Guardian and ITV News to publish their findings, but Walliams and his legal team didn't file an appeal or request for more time to do so.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Sunrise Movement Co-Founder Elected to Congress on Anti-Data Center Platform
World.content:
By Democracy Now

HAVANA TIMES – Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

“I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’”

Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

Transcript

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan Gonzalez.

In Michigan, progressive candidate Will Lawrence has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence is the co-founder of the youth-led climate group the Sunrise Movement. He ran a grassroots campaign focused on lowering the cost of housing and healthcare, opposing the war in Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

One of the central issues of Lawrence’s campaign was opposition to artificial intelligence, AI, data centers. He called for a pause on the construction of new centers, joining residents’ concerns about their impact on Michigan’s water, electricity bills, quality of life, including noise pollution. Three hyperscale data centers have been proposed in different parts of the district. Lawrence also campaigned against Flock surveillance cameras and called for tighter restrictions on AI overall.

The race was one of the most expensive House contests in the country, $66 million spent on political advertising.

But Will Lawrence is now in Washington, D.C. The congressmember-elect is there for orientation.

Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence, welcome to Democracy Now! If you can start off by —

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN: — talking about what you’re planning to bring to Congress, and then respond to what’s happening? The House leader race is underway. There’s going to be an internal vote, I think, next week, with Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries as the House speaker. But there are those who are questioning that leadership. I’m wondering if you can talk about that, as well.

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Thank you, Amy. It’s a real honor to be here. Longtime fan of the show.

You know, I’m just thrilled to be here to offer independent-minded representation for my district. People voted to get Big Money out of politics, to hold Big Tech accountable, to stop these endless wars around the world and to bring our money home to invest in first things first, good jobs and education, housing and healthcare, so that we can all look forward to the future again. And I just couldn’t be more honored to represent the people of my district.

And, you know, I’ve been getting the correspondence from my constituents over the last number of days, you know, expressing concern about who the next speaker is going to be. And I do want to make clear that I’ve said since July that I will support Hakeem for speaker. I’m a man of my word, and I intend to keep that word. But the correspondence is very important, not just in my district, but I’m hearing from all my other incoming freshmen here that they’re also hearing the same thing. And it reflects the anxiety that people feel that this election, which was clearly about change and a repudiation of the status quo, could result in more of the same. And they’re hungry to know that it’s going to be different and the Democratic Party is truly going to fight for real reform in our economy and our democracy. And people doubt that that will happen because of leadership’s well-documented ties to Big Money, including weapons manufacturers and health insurance CEOs and AIPAC and many others.

And so, I’m going to push Leader Jeffries publicly, and I will push him privately, to hear those concerns and commit to giving voice to the American people by putting votes on the floor that reflect the issues that I and people across the country campaigned on. We need to have a vote to block the bombs to Israel. We need to have a vote to guarantee healthcare to every person in my district. And we need to have a vote to get Big Money out of politics and ban super PACs, because people deserve to know that their representatives actually represent them rather than the wealthy elite. And as long as we have this Big Money in politics, they will never be able to be confident in that knowledge. So, regardless of the speaker’s own positions on those issues, he can give voice to the American people by putting those votes on the floor and letting us have those votes, regardless of where he personally comes down on the issue. And I’m going to be pushing hard to ensure that that happens.

JUAN GONZALEZ: Well, Will Lawrence, one of the big planks of your campaign was your opposition to these data centers and AI regulation, Flock cameras. Now that you are — will be in Congress, and I expect, if history is any lesson at all, the tech industry will start shifting more money to Democrats, hoping to peel people off and be able to neutralize any major legislation, what are your red lines, and what are you expecting to be able to accomplish when it comes to AI regulation, these data centers and Flock cameras?

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Well, what I hear from residents across my district is that this is out of control, it’s moving too fast, and we need to slow it down. And they’re fighting on a playing field that is fundamentally rigged to the benefit of these billion-, soon to be trillion-dollar corporations in Silicon Valley and leaves local communities behind.

So, I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development. I mean, these developers come into small towns, and they say, you know, “We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.” I mean, what are we talking about? What are we talking about? Why have we allowed these clearly reckless individuals, who do not share the values and aspirations of my constituents in Michigan, to determine the future of our entire economy?

You know, I believe that AI could be used for the benefit of humanity, but right now it’s on track to make the already rich and powerful even richer and more powerful. And that’s why there is such a bottom-up grassroots rebellion happening, not just in my district, but around the country. And it’s uniting Democrats and Republicans from the bottom up who do not trust Big Tech to write the future of our communities and our entire economy.

JUAN GONZALEZ: And could you comment about what made it possible, despite all this money poured into the — into your district to defeat you, that you were able to emerge victorious?

REP.-ELECT WILL LAWRENCE: Well, we had an unprecedented ground game. You know, I’m an organizer by trade. I was a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement. I’ve been an organizer fighting alongside renters and tenants to assert our rights and prevent homelessness in my area. And we built a ground game that knocked on 350,000 doors between the primary and the general election. And when there were so many negative ads on TV, so many lies and so many smears, it was those face-to-face conversations, eye contact, a handshake, a real human being coming to you and talking about the values that we share and the future we can build together, that cut through all the noise. And that’s what allowed us to win this election. And I’m just tremendously proud of all the volunteers, the whole team, everybody who poured into the movement. It was a true team effort, and I couldn’t be more honored to be representing that movement here in Congress.

AMY GOODMAN: Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence of Michigan, thank you so much for being with us as you stand there in Washington at orientation for new congressmembers. He defeated incumbent Republican Congressmember Tom Barrett in one of the most competitive swing House races these midterms, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement.

Read more interviews here on Havana Times.
