World.title: Ladies in White Leader Released After Two Days in Detention
World.content:
Berta Soler was injured in her right foot as a result of violence during her arrest. / Facebook/Ángel Moya

Berta Soler was subjected to violence during her arrest, confined to a dark cell, and interrogated by State Security.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Berta Soler, leader of the Ladies in White, was released on Monday after being held by State Security for 46 hours, during which her whereabouts were unknown. Her husband, Angel Moya, announced the news on social media: “Released bearing the marks of violent repression.”

Moya reported that Berta Soler was released at around 10 a.m. “on a public street, near the headquarters of the Ladies in White,” in the Havana neighborhood of Lawton. In his post, Moya provided details about an injury the activist sustained to her right foot as a result of the violence during her arrest.

Soler was taken to the Aguilera police station in Diez de Octubre and later transferred to the Cotorro police station, where, according to the activist, she received medical attention before being confined to a dark cell.

According to Moya, before her release, Soler was interrogated by an officer from the State Security Investigation Department at Villa Marista. The officer questioned her about what had happened during the peaceful protest at which she was arrested, reminded her that she was under a precautionary measure of house arrest and that the measure could be revoked, and warned her that she would soon be summoned for questioning.

The post included photographs of the injury Berta Soler sustained to her foot during her arrest. Hours earlier, Moya had denounced her detention, saying he had overheard police officers mention that they had seen his wife “walking with a painful limp.”

According to activist Blanca Reyes, Moya went that same day to the Revolutionary National Police (PNR) station on Aguilera Street, in Lawton, in Havana’s Diez de Octubre municipality, to find out where the opposition leader was being held, “since she was beaten and no one knows whether she is at a police station or in a hospital.” Reyes stated: “Our sister’s situation is worrying.”

According to Moya’s account, on Saturday, two days after Soler had been arrested for several hours alongside fellow Lady in White Mara Cristina Labrada — the same Thursday that Yoani Sanchez, director of 14ymedio, was also arbitrarily detained — Berta Soler joined a “public and peaceful protest” with about 20 women from Lawton who were suffering from a lack of water.

The water shortage, Moya claims, is “intentional,” caused by the state-run company Aguas de La Habana to harm the Ladies in White headquarters and the area “within a 50-meter radius.”

Shortly after 10 a.m. that day, “several high-ranking State Security repressors” arrived at the scene and spoke with the protesting women, while the security operation was reinforced over the following hours.

“At noon, representatives of the state-run company Aguas de La Habana arrived and offered an explanation that also failed to convince the protesting women,” Moya recounted. His impression was that the authorities “had no intention of resolving the underlying cause of the problem, which is the deliberate manipulation of the water supply valve.”

With no satisfactory response, half an hour later the demonstrators blocked traffic on Porvenir Avenue, “using their own bodies as barriers.”

Moya said he did not witness the end of the protest because he had already been arrested by the political police and taken to the Aguilera station, where he overheard that his wife was walking in pain and that she had subsequently “been taken in a patrol car to another location,” which was not identified.

After an eight-hour interrogation, Moya was released, but his wife was not. The activist also clarified that “with the exception of Berta Soler, none of the women participating in the protest belong to organizations opposed to the Cuban communist regime. They are working women.”

The regime has intensified its persecution of activists and journalists on the island in recent weeks. Also on Saturday, dozens of residents took to the streets in El Cobre, Santiago de Cuba, to demand the release of Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano, a young activist known for his community work who had been detained hours earlier by State Security in an operation involving armed agents.

As for independent journalists, before Yoani Sanchez’s detention, Adelth Bonne Gamboa and Camila Acosta, both contributors to CubaNet, had also been arrested during the same week.

Meanwhile, Rolando Pérez Lora, an evangelical pastor known as the Preacher of Christ, was forcibly transferred from Havana to Las Tunas, where he was released on Monday, with a pending police summons.

According to reports from the Cuban Observatory for Human Rights and the Alliance of Christians of Cuba, Perez Lora had been detained while providing pastoral support to a young Christian member of the religious organization, who was also arrested.

In mid-September, State Security also detained Henry Constantin, director of La Hora de Cuba. In his case, rather than being released like the other journalists mentioned above, he was transferred to Kilo 7 prison in Camagüey, where he remains in pretrial detention on a charge of disobedience.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times,

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Serbia’s Student Movement: From Protest to Power
World.content:
By Andrew Firmin (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – On the night of 25 October, tens of thousands filled the streets of Belgrade and other cities, as they’d so often done in protest over the past two years. But this time they came out to celebrate. In that day’s National Assembly election, Student List, a slate of political newcomers, defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), in power since 2012. The student-led movement behind the protests, which rose up against corruption, has given Serbia the opportunity for a democratic reset.



From grief to protest

Serbia became steadily more autocratic under Vučić. Public institutions served ruling-party interests amid a web of corruption, patronage, coercion and impunity. Public media became a ruling party mouthpiece.



Civic freedoms deteriorated dramatically. In 2018, the CIVICUS Monitor rated Serbia’s civic space as narrowed, meaning that fundamental rights were broadly respected. By the end of Vučić’s rule, the rating had collapsed to repressed, meaning that criticizing those in power carried severe risks. The state used violence against protests and treated civil society as a security threat, targeting it with spyware and subjecting organizations to raids and police investigations.



The seismic shift began in November 2024 with the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city. Sixteen people died. The government insisted it was a tragic accident, but the station had only recently been renovated and, with construction contracts shrouded in secrecy, many suspected corners had been cut. For protesters, this was a lethal symbol of the costs of corruption, negligence and impunity. No one has been held accountable.



Students held vigils and mass protests on a scale unseen since 2000, when demonstrations ousted Slobodan Milošević, the infamous authoritarian leader and accused war criminal. This time, their most effective tactic was a months-long education strike in which they blockaded and occupied universities.



As the protest movement grew it connected with existing groups, including environmental and legal aid organizations, independent media and, crucially, academics, university administrators and education unions, who took solidarity strike action. This built wider public support, backed by a ‘students in every village’ campaign that saw students meet with rural communities to ask about what mattered most to them.



State attempts to suppress the movement failed, including mass arrests, violence by security forces and gangs of ruling-party supporters and an extensive campaign of disinformation and smears. Vučić vilified protesters as agents of foreign powers bent on subversion and the government fired education sector employees for taking part in strikes.



Change on the cards



Ultimately, the protests forced Vučić’s hand. Constitutionally barred from seeking a third term as president, he announced an early parliamentary election in June and stood down as president in September, making clear his intention to hold onto power as prime minister. He presumably gambled that a skewed playing field, characterized by intimidation and biased coverage, would let him win again and unleash an even fiercer crackdown.



The gamble failed because of the movement’s discipline and the smart choices it made. Throughout, students resisted opposition parties’ attempts to co-opt them, insisting that deeper change was needed to re-establish the rule of law, free public institutions from political capture and tackle corruption. From its early days, the movement practiced internal democracy, taking decisions in university plenums, open assemblies where people debated, learned and decided together. When it decided to field a slate of candidates, it used the same method to select them. Students didn’t put themselves forward, choosing instead public figures untainted by association with established politics and likely to command broad support. Those who’ve won seats include academics, actors, former sports stars and medical professionals.



The result surpassed all predictions. According to projections based on the preliminary count, Student List has around 53 per cent of the vote, which would give it a clear majority of 141 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats. The SNS-led bloc trails on around 39 per cent. The margin was such that Vučić had to concede quickly.



Challenges of power



After the euphoria comes the challenge of moving from protest to power. A movement that has refused to have formal leaders must now unite behind a prime minister. Once the National Assembly convenes, Student List will have 90 days to form a government. Its deliberately broad campaign focused on major questions of national renewal but offered little detail. This strategy papered over political differences among representatives who range from nationalist to more liberal, which can be expected to surface if the incoming government succeeds in restoring the space for normal political debate. There’s also the question of how those elected will relate to the student movement.



As in Hungary, where long-term autocratic leader Viktor Orbán finally fell to electoral defeat in April, the new government will face the difficult task of reorienting state institutions that have bent to the former ruling party’s interests. An early sign of change came when the public broadcaster apologised to viewers for its bias towards the SNS, something that also happened in Hungary. The government will need to repay voters’ faith by rooting out corruption, which will mean overhauling institutions including the judiciary and police. All this will unfold alongside a presidential election that’s due by the end of the year.



Challenges lie ahead, but a population that has rediscovered the power of collective action can face them with confidence. Serbia also offers a vital source of international inspiration. Together with Hungary’s example, it shows there’s nothing permanent about autocratic rule. The world’s many Gen Z-led movements that have self-organised to demand a fairer distribution of economic and political power, and civil society more broadly, can take heart. Serbia has shown that organising and protesting works, and change is possible.



Andrew Firmin is CIVICUS Editor-in-Chief, co-director and writer for CIVICUS Lens and co-author of the State of Civil Society Report.

Read more feature articles here on Havana Times.

World.title: Hamburg hearing opens as Argentina seeks to halt Sea Lion and the UK disputes jurisdiction
World.content:
Hamburg hearing opens as Argentina seeks to halt Sea Lion and the UK disputes jurisdiction

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 15:31 UTC Full article

Because the United Kingdom chose the International Court of Justice for such disputes and Argentina opted for the Hamburg tribunal, the merits of the case must be settled by an arbitral tribunal

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea began hearing Argentina and the United Kingdom in Hamburg on Tuesday over Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands. Argentina argued that the resources of a disputed continental shelf cannot be exploited unilaterally, while the United Kingdom rejects the tribunal’s competence to rule on what it considers a question of sovereignty.

“The islanders cannot appropriate the resources of the disputed continental shelf,” said Argentina’s agent, Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal, presenting his country’s four requests: that the UK prevent the start or continuation of exploitation at Sea Lion, refrain from granting new permits, preserve information obtained during exploration and protect the marine environment. Oyarzábal cited the islands’ 2021 census, with 3,142 usual residents, of whom 1,625 hold the residence status granted by the Governor, and said those resources “belong to the Argentine people”.

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, an adviser to the delegation, said Argentina refers to sovereignty only to show that its claim to the continental shelf is plausible. “The land dominates the sea. That is why, and only why, we refer here to Argentine sovereignty,” he said, arguing that it is enough that the United Nations recognises the existence of the dispute. Argentina relies on UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 of 1965 and 31/49 of 1976, which call on the parties to avoid unilateral decisions, and warns that oil once extracted could not be restored by a later ruling. Dutch jurist Nico Schrijver, an expert on sovereignty over natural resources, also addressed the tribunal.

The United Kingdom is presenting its position in the afternoon session. Ahead of the hearing, Attorney General Ellie Reeves, who leads the British delegation, told The Times that the UK respects international law and the tribunal “but we don’t believe they have jurisdiction to hear a claim around sovereignty”. “We are absolutely clear that this is sovereign British territory,” she said. A spokesman for Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted that “the hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands” and that the islanders “have the right to develop their natural resources”, according to DPA.

Because the United Kingdom chose the International Court of Justice for such disputes and Argentina opted for the Hamburg tribunal, the merits of the case must be settled by an arbitral tribunal. Hamburg can only order provisional measures while that tribunal is being constituted, if it finds that the arbitral tribunal would have prima facie jurisdiction, that there is urgency and that the right invoked is plausible. Argentina’s Frida María Armas Pfirter, the tribunal’s vice-president, recused herself from the case, so Argentina appointed Raúl Vinuesa as judge ad hoc; the UK chose Vaughan Lowe. Both were sworn in on Monday.

The hearing concludes on Wednesday with a second round from each side. According to an expert consulted by Infobae, the decision could come around Friday, November 13. Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration about 200 kilometres north of the archipelago, is expected to begin drilling in January 2027.

The hearing coincides with Princess Anne’s arrival in the islands on Monday and comes ahead of the debate on Argentina’s sovereignty defence bill in the Chamber of Deputies, scheduled for Thursday. The British government announced in October that it will introduce legislation to protect companies from possible Argentine sanctions.

World.title: Venezuela signs a memorandum with ExxonMobil for the oil major’s return after leaving in 2007
World.content:
Venezuela signs a memorandum with ExxonMobil for the oil major’s return after leaving in 2007

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 14:52 UTC Full article

The signing took place in Caracas in the presence of acting President Delcy Rodríguez and ExxonMobil Upstream President Dan Ammann

Venezuela on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding with US oil company ExxonMobil with a view to its return to the country, which it left in 2007 after the nationalisation of the last privately held oilfields under Hugo Chávez’s government. The document is not a contract, and no investment figures or timelines have been disclosed.º

The signing took place in Caracas in the presence of acting President Delcy Rodríguez and ExxonMobil Upstream President Dan Ammann. Rodríguez called it a “very important signing”, reached after “months of negotiations for an effective return” of the Houston-based company. She said the memorandum covers “brownfield and greenfield” fields, that is, those already producing and those yet to be developed, with “billions of barrels of reserves”, and said ExxonMobil has “the capacity, technology and investment needed”. She also expressed hope that it would “very soon translate into concrete agreements”.

Ammann said the memorandum is “an important first step” in a process he hopes will lead to the company’s return. “We believe our unique capabilities, combined with this country’s extraordinary resources and Venezuela’s long history in oil and gas production, will bring significant benefits to all parties involved,” he said.

The rapprochement contrasts with Rodríguez’s position a little over a year ago. In March 2025, when she was Nicolás Maduro’s vice president, she accused ExxonMobil of “conspiring against Venezuela for more than a decade” to undermine its territorial integrity and take its resources.

Since Maduro’s removal from power following the US military operation on January 3, President Donald Trump has urged US energy companies to invest in Venezuela. In April, Rodríguez reported meetings with ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, among other companies, after a reform of the hydrocarbons law opened the sector to private and foreign investment.

World.title: Nicaragua: Ortega reappears after 68 days as the government gives no word on his health
World.content:
Nicaragua: Ortega reappears after 68 days as the government gives no word on his health

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 13:35 UTC Full article

Ortega walked slowly and looked frail, and the official broadcast avoided close-ups

Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega reappeared in public on Monday night, 68 days after his last appearance, at a tribute in Managua to Carlos Fonseca, founder of the ruling Sandinista National Liberation Front. It was his longest absence since returning to power in 2007. The government has never reported on his health or explained his absences.

Ortega, who turns 81 on Wednesday, attended the event at the old Plaza of the Revolution accompanied by his wife, co-president Rosario Murillo, who announced it on Sunday, members of the Sandinista Youth and relatives. He did not give a speech. “Carlos, here are the young people, those who will never forget you, who will never betray you, who will always be loyal to you, until death,” he said in brief remarks. According to international press reports, he walked slowly and looked frail, and the official broadcast avoided close-ups.

His last appearance had been on September 2, at an event marking the anniversary of the Army. His absence broke the 61-day record set in 2024. According to a count by the newspaper Confidencial, Ortega had appeared only 11 times so far in 2026, compared with an average of 26 between January and October in each year from 2018 to 2025. In September, the ceremony to receive the Central American independence torch was held without him or Murillo, and their children Maurice and Camila Ortega Murillo attended instead.

During his absence, the National Assembly approved a constitutional reform that abolished the vice presidency and created “presidential designees”, twenty months after the reform that created the co-presidency. Opposition analysts interpreted it as an attempt to secure the continuity of power within the presidential family. Also in that period, Nicaragua refused to receive Natasha Franceschi, the ambassador designated by US President Donald Trump, and Washington recalled its top representative in Managua, Elias Baumann, for consultations, according to El País. Neither Ortega nor Murillo has offered public explanations.

World.title: Princess Anne and Sports VIPs present at official opening of Falkland Islands Sport Complex
World.content:
Princess Anne and Sports VIPs present at official opening of Falkland Islands Sport Complex

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

HRH The Princess Royal and Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence will be present at the opening this Tuesday

The Falkland Islands Government and National Sports Council are proud to announce the official opening of the Falkland Islands’ new National Sports Complex, this Tuesday 10 November, in the presence of HRH The Princess Royal and Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence.

Attending VIPs from the world of sport include Katie Sadlier, CEO of Commonwealth Sport, and Andrew Inkster, Chair of the Island Games Association.

Other international sporting VIPs have offered their congratulations to the Falklands and the Sports Council on this long-awaited boost to provision for the Islands’ sporting community.

Lord Moynihan, Olympic rowing silver medalist and Chair of the British Olympic Association for London 2012, said “nothing could give me greater pleasure than learning of the new national sports facility there. What’s particularly impressive is it’s going to cover so many sports – and there’s already so much sporting activity in the Falklands. So this is a very special occasion for me, it’s a special occasion for the BOA, and I congratulate you all.”

Asanka Gurusinha, Sri Lankan World Cup-winning cricketer in 1996, expressed how impressed he was “that you have built a cricket pitch as well. Infrastructure plays a major part in the development of sport, and this investment will support all athletes to perform better and to have a dream to achieve their goals. I hope one day I can visit this beautiful place and see it for myself.”

Baroness Davies of Devonport, Olympic silver medalist and Commonwealth Games champion swimmer, offered her “many congratulations on your fantastic new sports complex in the Falkland Islands. What a brilliant thing that you’ve done. Young people need sport more than ever, we need to look after ourselves, we need to have fun, we need to get off our mobile phones. I wish you all the best.”

Sophie Kurzman, emerging Jackaroo with Australian bowls, competed alongside the Falklands earlier this year in Australia: “Opening up facilities like this and supporting their athletes is one of the most fundamental things a country can do for its athletes and itself. So a huge, heartfelt congratulations.”

Brigadier Charlie Harmer, Commander British Forces South Atlantic Islands, said he had “had the privilege of playing sport in lots of places, but to be able to play here, at the National Sports Complex, is a huge privilege for me, and indeed for the rest of my forces, be they Army, Navy or Royal Air Force. For us to have a chance to be a part of this community and continue to support the development of Falkland Islands sport is very, very important to us.

Numerous young Falkland Islanders competing overseas and at the national level have also sent messages of congratulation back to Stanley.

The National Sports Complex is a joint project between FIG, the National Sports Council, and private sponsors. Five and a half years in the making, it represents the first major investment in Falklands sporting facilities since the construction of the Stanley Leisure Centre and Swimming Pool some 30 years ago, with the long-term strategies of ensuring sport for all, achieving sporting excellence, and safeguarding and strengthening sport.

Chair of the National Sports Council, Mike Summers OBE, said “the creation of the National Sports Complex has already enabled additional developments like the cricket pitch and the archery Gold Centre. The 3G floodlit pitch already delivers significant enhancements in junior football participation, overall skill levels and the introduction of touch rugby. We look forward with huge anticipation to the use of the new sports hall to provide opportunities in a wide range of existing and new sporting activities, and providing a key focus for community development. Whilst enhancements to sports assets and outcomes has been our primary driver, this development also offers significant opportunities to those who manage the health of the Falklands population, with exercise tailored to all ages and abilities, and to all sectors of society. This is a major investment in sport, but most important of all it is an investment in our community.”

Steve Dent, FIG’s Director of Development and Commercial Services, said he was “absolutely delighted to see the National Sports Complex opening its doors. This is a hugely positive development for the Falkland Islands and, most importantly, for the next generation of young athletes. It will provide an expanded range of opportunities for young people to discover new sports, develop their skills, challenge themselves and reach their full potential. I am excited to see the breadth of opportunities this facility will create and the positive impact it will have on sport and physical activity in our community for many years to come.”

Marcus Morrison, Stanley Leisure Centre Manager, said “it is incredibly exciting to see the National Sports Complex completed and ready to open its doors to the community. As Manager, it is a proud moment to see a facility that will create new opportunities for people across the Falkland Islands and help meet the growing demand for sport and physical activity, complementing the already popular Stanley Leisure Centre. What excites me most is the potential to welcome teams and athletes from around the world, showcasing both our sporting ambitions and the unique community spirit of the Falkland Islands.”

The facilities now on offer will contribute to health and wellbeing in the Islands, and the huge support we get through the Falklands’ engagement with international competitions like the Island Games and Commonwealth Games.

The complex encompasses a floodlit all-weather football/rugby pitch; an indoor centre for archery, bowls, and cricket nets; and a new 50x52m sports hall to cater for existing and new sports, including (Gl)ice-hockey, indoor football, basketball, netball, volleyball, tennis, table tennis, weightlifting, and climbing. Exercise studios will also facilitate yoga, Pilates, dance exercise and ballet, as well as spin classes.

The sports hall additionally incorporates changing rooms, office and storage areas, a mezzanine viewing area, and a potential café area; and the all-weather pitch is equipped with spectator stands and toilets.

All of these works, other than specialist installation supervision, have been delivered by local contractors and suppliers.

The facility as a whole is already reaping considerable rewards, including burgeoning youth attendance, new women’s and girls’ teams in several sports, and fresh qualifications and training in various disciplines.

MLA Roger Spink, portfolio holder for Development and Commercial Services, said “the new sports facility and all-weather pitch funded by the Falkland Islands Government, as well as considerable contributions from the private sector which enhanced its facilities, together with the Falklands companies involved in its construction, shows what can be achieved by teamwork. The construction led by the NSC Chair and his team will provide a range of first-class facilities for a wide range of sport in our community, improving physical health, mental resilience, and social connection. I’m sure I echo the thoughts of the entire community in saying how delighted we are to be able to welcome Her Royal Highness and Sir Tim back to the Islands for this official opening.”

The National Sports Complex will go a long way to giving our sportsmen and -women the proper conditions in which to enjoy a wide range of sports and exercise programs, and better prepare for international events.

World.title: UK Defense minister admits Special Forces under mounting pressure and legal scrutiny
World.content:
UK Defense minister admits Special Forces under mounting pressure and legal scrutiny

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 10:48 UTC Full article

Mr Streeting spoke to BFBS Forces News at his first Remembrance Sunday service as defense secretary. Picture: BFBS

Britain’s Defense Secretary Wes Streeting has acknowledged the mounting pressures facing UK Special Forces (UKSF) amid ongoing legal scrutiny, as he attended his first Remembrance Sunday service since taking up the role.

Asked by BFBS Forces News what he promises service personnel to meet the challenges ahead, Mr Streeting pointed to members of UKSF whose service often goes “unseen and unsung.”

“Today, they live under a cloud, worrying about whether they are going to be persecuted rather than thanked for their service,” he said. “Those are things I need to put right – there's going to be a process; it's not simple.”

“But on days like today [Remembrance Sunday], they galvanize me, and they galvanize the entire government around our responsibility and our duty to stand by our armed forces, by our veterans and their families.”

Acknowledging there was “much more to do”, the defense secretary said he was looking forward to working closely with the Armed Forces community to “make good on the commitment that we owe them”.

Mr Streeting's words echo the growing unrest and anxiety among UKSF members, following escalating waves of retroactive legal security. Central to this is the Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan.

Chaired by Lord Justice Sir Charles Haddon-Cave, the public inquiry is examining operations carried out by the Special Air Service (SAS) between mid-2010 and mid-2013.

It is investigating allegations that SAS members executed men and children during detention raids, that unlawful conduct was concealed, and that military police subsequently failed to investigate properly.

The inquiry could lead to further criminal investigations into the alleged killings and any cover-up. It can establish facts and recommend further action, but any prosecution would be separate. (BFBS)

World.title: UK with eyes from space: launches its second military satellite, Titania
World.content:
UK with eyes from space: launches its second military satellite, Titania

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 10:44 UTC Full article

UK launches Titania, giving the Armed Forces improved observation from space, along with new trial network of ground sensors to monitor threats to UK satellites.

Britain has a new pair of eyes in space, with the successful launch of British-built military satellite Titania. The launch – completed last month from California on an Space X rocket– will further help the Armed Forces coordinate their efforts on and above Earth, by improving their ability to observe military activity on Earth from space.

Titania is the second satellite in the UK’s growing constellation of military satellites in orbit, following the successful launch of Tyche in October and will be operated by UK Space Command as part of the ISTARI program.

Like Tyche, Titania weighs around 100kg – about the size of a washing machine – and orbits the Earth every ninety minutes, travelling at twenty-seven thousand kilometers per hour.

The successful launch comes as the Ministry of Defense (MOD) also stands up Project Inaros, a new trial of an advanced network of sensors designed to monitor space from three sites around the world.

Secretary of State for Defense Wes Streeting MP said: “The new space age is here. Space underpins everything from weather forecasts and financial transactions to sat-navs and mobile phone connections, and it is critical for our national security and military operations.

“Having Titania now in orbit and Project Inaros stepping up how we watch over our satellites means we can see threats sooner, making the UK safer.

“Titania and Inaros are British-built and British-designed, backed by more than £3 billion of investment in space capabilities. That means highly skilled jobs across the UK, a stronger industrial base, and a more secure United Kingdom”.

Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, the Chief of the Air Staff, said: “The ability to observe the Earth from space is critical to both national resilience and military advantage. This will be demonstrated by Tyche and Titania, alongside Juno and Oberon in the years ahead.

“We will monitor these vital satellites using state-of-the-art technology around the world, including our Inaros sensors – to ensure our Armed Forces can fight and win wherever they are.

“Under the ISTARI program, MOD is delivering satellites and supporting ground systems to expand space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, giving British troops around the world an operational advantage.

“Titania was designed and built in Hampshire by the partnership of Defense Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl) and BAE Systems as part of a £9.5 million contract, and will be followed by satellites Juno, with SSTL, and Oberon, with Airbus Defense and Space.

Andrea Thompson, Managing Director, BAE Systems Digital Intelligence & Land, said: “This program highlights the strength of the UK’s sovereign space capability and the critical role it plays in protecting the nation. Building on our established heritage in space, we are proud to be investing in advanced technologies, strengthening specialist skills and supporting highly skilled jobs across the UK.

“As a trusted partner to Government, we remain committed to delivering innovative space solutions that enhance the nation’s resilience, security and prosperity for the long term”.

Dr. Paul Hollinshead, Chief Executive Officer, Dstl, said: “Dstl has been at the heart of Titania, from the original concept, through Science and Technology investment, technical development, program delivery, and successful launch.

“The achievement reflects the expertise, resilience, and dedication of the Dstl team and showcases the value of long-term Defense Science and Technology investment, delivering mission success for our armed forces.

“Project Inaros will trial three ground-based neuromorphic sensors, developed by British Australian company Optera in partnership with the National Security Strategic Investment Fund, to monitor movements in space from sites in the UK, Australia, and British facilities on the island of Cyprus.

“This cutting-edge technology, which mimics biological processes by detecting changes in light, could be developed to be an early warning system to spot unusual or threatening activity near UK satellites. Information gathered by Inaros will help UK Space Command units, like No. 1 Space Operations Squadron, No. 2 Space Warning Squadron, and the new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron, to safeguard the UK satellites which guide British ships, connect mobile phones and warn of missile attacks”.

Titania and Inaros will help deliver on the recognition in the Strategic Defense Review that space is increasingly vital to the UK’s national security and daily life. The work is part of the £3bn committed by the Defense Investment Plan for space-based capabilities to protect UK assets in space and strengthen deterrence on Earth. The DIP has committed £298 billion of spending over the next four years.

World.title: Falklands Sports Complex, the joint effort of Government and private sector companies
World.content:
Falklands Sports Complex, the joint effort of Government and private sector companies

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 10:38 UTC Full article

The National Sports Council, NSC, has delivered this project as a community service at no fee; the Falklands Government has provided the funding for design, procurement and construction

The opening of the new multi-sports Falkland Islands National Sports Complex makes the Islands’ community reflect on the joint effort that brought this to fruition.

The National Sports Council, NSC, has delivered this project as a community service at no fee; the Falklands Government has provided the funding for design, procurement and construction, supplemented by major donations from private sector companies. Access, parking and services has been provided by FIG under a separate contract.

Local design company Ajax Ltd. were retained to provide design and engineering services, and have themselves sub-contracted architectural services, design and project assistance to Arch Henderson Ltd from Aberdeen.

The Complex is estimated to have cost in the range of £5 million.

The NSC has one paid part-time employee to provide project management services, and the NSC Project Board oversaw the project, interfacing as required with the FIG Joint Supervisory Committee. Local company SG Accounts provides project accountancy services. All of the works, other than specialist installation supervision, have been delivered by local contractors and suppliers.

World.title: Princess Anne arrives in the Falklands and will open the new National Sports Complex
World.content:
Princess Anne arrives in the Falklands and will open the new National Sports Complex

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 03:26 UTC Full article

Buckingham Palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit, although it coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, arrived in the Falklands on Monday with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, at the start of a visit that will later take her to South Georgia, and among other engagements will formally open the new National Sports Complex in Stanley.

“It’s wonderful to have Her Royal Highness back in the Falklands,” Members of the Legislative Assembly said in a welcome statement. “We are delighted they will get a chance to see the progress made in the Islands since their last visit in 2022.” During her stay, the Princess will meet members of the community and visit Cape Pembroke Lighthouse and Tussac House, as well as attend a reception at Government House.

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, which works to protect the heritage and environment of South Georgia, where she will commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton.

Buckingham Palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit, although it coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is holding hearings in Hamburg on Tuesday and Wednesday on Argentina’s request to halt the Sea Lion oil project, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies plans to debate the sovereignty defence bill on Thursday. Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

World.title: ‘We need to recover respect for the apparently non-living’: Yameli Guadalupe Aguilar Duarte on geodiversity
World.content:
Geodiversity might be biodiversity’s lesser-known sibling, but bringing attention to its importance has become a priority for Dr. Yameli Guadalupe Aguilar Duarte. A scientist at the National Institute for Forestry, Agriculture and Livestock Research (Inifap), she is currently working on a project studying karren formations in the Yucatán Peninsula.

Mexico News Daily spoke with Duarte about why geodiversity matters, its biocultural significance for Indigenous communities, why we need to recognize and protect these valuable rock formations, and how to rediscover a sense of wonder for the ground we walk on — and which sustains us.

There is a lot of talk about Mexico’s rich biodiversity, but much less about what sustains it. Why is it so important to pay attention to geodiversity too?

We talk a lot about Mexico’s biodiversity: its extraordinary variety of animals, plants and fungi. But less about that biological diversity that exists because there is also a diversity of physical environments that support it. The two go hand in hand.

We cannot protect, conserve or properly manage biodiversity without considering the conditions that make it possible. Different types of rocks, soils, bodies of water and landforms create different environments in which life can develop.

That is why we need to bring geodiversity into the conversation.

“Protecting an animal or a plant is not enough if we destroy the soil, contaminate the water or transform the landscape on which it depends.”

Another important factor to consider when talking about geodiversity is time. Some of these elements are described as renewable resources, but their recovery may not be possible within a human lifetime. When we lose soils or geological formations, we cannot simply replace them. We need to recognize the consequences of damaging something that took much longer to form than we have to restore it.

While preparing for this interview, I realized that although I consider myself fairly well informed about biodiversity, I knew very little about geodiversity. How would you explain it to someone encountering the subject for the first time?

Geodiversity refers to the variety of components of the physical environment that we generally consider nonliving, or abiotic. These include rocks, minerals, soils, fossils, landforms and different bodies of water.

Think of rivers, lakes, lagoons, aquifers and coastal environments. Or the differences between mountains, depressions and rocky outcrops. These are some of the elements that help create the conditions in which biological diversity develops.

“We tend to pay more attention to what is visibly alive, but these apparently nonliving elements are fundamental. Without them, life as we know it on Earth could not exist.”

When you talk about ‘non-living’ elements, I feel those words deserve quotation marks: a rock may appear motionless or inert, but that does not mean nothing is happening within it. How do you understand that distinction, given your scientific training and your relationship with Indigenous peoples?

My training as a biologist taught me to distinguish between biotic and abiotic components. But my training as a geographer and my experience working with Indigenous peoples changed how I relate to those categories.

Rocks, landforms, soils and bodies of water are not static. They undergo processes of transformation. Rocks can also harbor microorganisms, and soils contain an enormous diversity of life that remains little understood.

For me, that invites a broader way of thinking about the apparently non-living. It is not only a question of scientific classification; it is also about how we understand and relate to our surroundings.

Maya communities in the Yucatán Peninsula have ways of understanding the environment that encourage respect for its different elements. We need to take seriously the scientific, empirical and intergenerational knowledge that contributes to caring for those environments.

In the socioecological crisis we are experiencing, we need to recover respect for water, soils, mountains, cenotes and forests, including what we in modern societies do not ordinarily recognize as alive.

As I listen to you, I think of geodiversity as the home that makes our lives possible, even though we often do not notice it. When do you think we lost that respect for water, soil and rocks?

I do not think it happened at a single moment. There have been different turning points throughout history.

One was colonization, which brought the imposition of other beliefs and political systems, alongside the extraction of gold and the appropriation of land. Those processes also displaced knowledge and ways of relating to the environment.

“I am not saying that Indigenous societies had no internal conflicts. But colonization marked an important rupture in how their knowledge, beliefs and relationships with the environment were valued.”

Another factor is how we teach and study nature. From my perspective, biology education in Mexico has placed considerable emphasis on genes, populations and species, while more integrated approaches linking biological processes with those of the physical environment have received less attention.

Today, we also need to question models of development that treat landscapes primarily as sources of materials or spaces to build on or transform. When we discuss extraction or urban expansion, we should ask: development for whom? Who benefits, and who bears the environmental costs?

When I started researching, I saw rocks with very organic shapes, as though water had gradually sculpted them. What exactly are karren formations, and how do they differ from the karst system they belong to?

To understand karren formations, we first need to understand karst. Karst systems develop in rocks that can dissolve and also reform through interaction with various factors, particularly water. That process produces different formations, both underground and at the surface.

Karren are features produced by that dissolution at the rock’s surface. They can include small channels, grooves, pits and various types of hollows, and can even extend across large areas of exposed rock. They are also known as lapiés.

It is important to distinguish these formations from the system as a whole. A karst system is an integrated concept that includes rocks, soils, water, biota, and surface and underground formations through which water flows. Karren, or lapiés, are part of that broader system, but occur at and just below the surface, with some degree of interconnection with the underground environment.

In the Yucatán Peninsula, some karren formations are small hollows that hold water and have their own Maya names, such as haltunes. Other examples are known as xúuches: these are also hollows or natural shafts that channel water into the aquifer.

Although other landforms, such as cenotes and caves, are better known and more widely studied, karren formations such as haltunes and xúuches are also important and deserve to be studied.

I was struck by the fact that these small hollows not only have their own Maya names, but also specific uses and ways of being cared for. How do they relate to agriculture and the knowledge communities have developed about their surroundings?

Their biocultural importance is connected to the knowledge people have developed through observing and using their surroundings.

Some hollows collect water that has been used to support agricultural work or provide drinking water for domestic animals. Others accumulate organic matter. Leaves and small organisms fall into them; moisture encourages decomposition, and a dark, nutrient-rich material forms.

Farmers have collected that material and mixed it into the red soils of their plots. It is a very particular way of understanding the landscape: recognizing that a hollow in a rock can contribute to agricultural production.

One of our research questions is how much of that knowledge remains, how much has changed and how much is being lost.

During our first field visits, an older woman from a community near Valladolid took us to several haltunes. At one site, she explained that the water helped them irrigate the milpa. At another, she told us that those hollows were not to be disturbed because bees came there to drink.

That stayed with me: “These haltunes are for the bees.”

“It demonstrates a very nuanced understanding of the environment. She distinguished between sites according to their functions and cared for them accordingly. That is what biocultural knowledge expresses: a relationship between people, their practices and the particular characteristics of the place where they live.”

The story of the woman who reserved certain haltunes for bees made me think about everything we might overlook when we see a simple ‘puddle.’ Beyond their biocultural importance, what functions do they serve for wildlife, water and the environment?

They create small habitats and water sources for wildlife. A formation that may look like an ordinary puddle to someone passing by can be important to the animals that use it.

Some are also connected to the subsurface and provide pathways through which rainwater infiltrates the ground. Studying them helps us understand the relationship between the surface and the karst system as a whole.

In cities, we are losing many of those natural functions by covering the ground with streets, buildings and concrete. When people pave their entire yards, they remove spaces through which rainwater could enter the soil and rock.

Spaces that retain vegetation, soils and natural rock formations can also provide wildlife refuges and help moderate urban heat. These are not empty or unused spaces. They perform functions that we easily overlook when we think only about what we can build there.

I imagined these formations in remote places, far from cities, but you have explained their connection to urbanization: they disappear when land is cleared or leveled, or when rock is extracted. What are the main threats to them and to the karst system, including oil and gas extraction?

Two major pressures are urbanization and the extraction of stone for construction.

When land is cleared and leveled for development, vegetation, soils and rock formations can disappear together. The damage begins before the buildings go up. Sometimes even cenotes and karren formations are filled or sealed.

Limestone extraction also removes the formations and transforms the surrounding environment. Large artificial excavations can alter underground water flows and expose groundwater at the surface, making it more vulnerable to contamination and evaporation.

Beyond the direct destruction of karren formations, the karst system faces pressures from activities that demand large quantities of water and generate waste. In the peninsula, these include intensive agriculture, livestock production, mass tourism and urban growth.

The oil and gas industry is another concern. Our project also studies a mountainous karst region in San Luis Potosí, where Indigenous peoples have opposed fracking. The concern is how drilling and extraction can transform these environments and affect the springs and other bodies of water on which communities and their traditional activities depend.

That is why we need to study these formations as parts of an interconnected system, rather than as isolated rocks. Their loss affects more than the visible landscape: it can also affect water, habitats and the communities whose lives and practices depend on them.

We are accustomed to admiring a cenote with blue water, but perhaps not to stopping in front of a rock, a patch of soil or a small hollow. How can we rediscover that sense of wonder?

In my experience, one of the most effective ways is to go into the field.

A photograph, video or documentary can awaken curiosity, but being in a place, observing it and experiencing it directly creates a different connection. Even in a city, we can help people discover the spaces that still retain natural soils and rock formations.

Visiting a geopark and following one of its geological trails is another way to experience that connection. One place I recommend is the Mixteca Alta Geopark in Oaxaca. I have taken two of its routes, and I was fascinated. The trails introduce you to the diversity of soils and landforms, but also to the region’s history, agriculture and the ways people use local materials, such as clay.

What makes those experiences valuable is the connection between the landscape and the communities who participate in its interpretation and management. You are not simply looking at scenery: you begin to understand how the place formed, how people relate to it and why it matters. That direct encounter can awaken a sense of wonder at something you might previously have considered just a rock or a little soil.

We also need other ways of connecting, such as art. I collect rocks and soils, and when I take samples to public talks, people begin to recognize differences in their colors, textures and forms.

With a colleague, I have also made watercolors using soils. We talk about soil diversity, then invite people to paint a postcard with a message about caring for it. Someone who is not immediately interested in scientific terminology may connect through that creative experience.

The idea is not that everyone must become a specialist. It is to recognize the diversity of the elements we walk over every day — and to understand how they connect to water, vegetation, food production and our own lives.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Sargassum season is officially over, a month later than last year and with nearly double the seaweed
World.content:
Sargassum season in the Mexican Caribbean has officially ended.

The conclusion date came a month later than in 2025, but finally, autumn’s cold fronts are bringing a drop in sea temperature and a consequent reduction in seaweed arrivals.

Figures from Quintana Roo’s state Ministry of Ecology and Environment (SEMA) indicate a record collection of 156,631 tonnes of seaweed throughout the year — nearly double the 85,000 tonnes reported in 2025. The Mexican Navy was responsible for the removal of 72,000 metric tonnes of that amount, representing a fourfold increase in its sargassum missions over last year.

The navy used drones and satellite images to anticipate sargassum’s movement at sea. Still, it’s estimated that only about 16.4% (25,751 tonnes) was collected from the open ocean.

According to local media, approximately 4.3 billion pesos (US $231 million) was allocated to clean-up, a combined effort by hoteliers and all three levels of government.

Sargassum levels at the source in Northwest Africa — of which 1-5% reaches Mexico — rose by 10% to 15% compared with 2025 (from about 900,000 tonnes to 1 million), according to Esteban Amaro, director of the Sargassum Monitoring Center in Quintana Roo.

Agencies predict that 2027 could bring even more sargassum to the region, depending on several factors. The “Super El Niño,” one of the strongest climate events of its kind in modern records, as well as changes in the Atlantic Ocean’s hydrodynamics, could determine when the next season begins and how much seaweed the tides will bring.

The Quintana Roo state government is aiming to install a large ocean barrier, known as GO 60 by 60, between Cozumel Island and Tulum to reduce the quantity of seaweed reaching the region’s main tourist destinations.

The structure would be placed 60 km offshore at a 60-degree northeast orientation, where it can take advantage of ocean currents to divert the seaweed.

The project is expected to comprise six 10 km sections, arranged in a staggered pattern, allowing ships to traverse the waters if approved. However, the extremely strong currents in the Cozumel Channel, between the island and the beach town of Playa del Carmen, pose a significant technical challenge for construction.

In addition, concerns about the structure’s potential impact on marine life mean that further analysis must be conducted before it can proceed.

With reports from La Jornada and N+

World.title: Authorities rescue Río Bravo mayor in Coahuila a day after armed highway abduction
World.content:
The mayor of the northern border municipality of Río Bravo, Tamaulipas, was found safe and sound in the state of Coahuila on Sunday, one day after armed men allegedly stole his vehicle and abducted him on a highway that links the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí.

Miguel Ángel Almaraz Maldonado, mayor of Río Bravo since 2024, was “rescued” at a state police checkpoint near Coahuila’s border with Zacatecas, according to the government of Coahuila.

*BAJO RESGUARDO DE AUTORIDADES DE COAHUILA, ALCALDE DE RÍO BRAVO.* • Fue rescatado en un filtro de la Policía Estatal en los límites con Zacatecas. Saltillo, Coahuila de Zaragoza; 8 de noviembre de 2026.— El Gobierno del Estado de Coahuila y la Fiscalía General del Estado https://t.co/nRyonPUGH0 — Gobierno de Coahuila (@GobDeCoahuila) November 8, 2026

Almaraz told reporters that he escaped from his captors after being held in a field for an unspecified period of time.

“[I was held] in a field but suddenly they left,” he said, referring to his captors.

“We jumped the fence, ran an hour without stopping and then wandered the whole night, 80 kilometers, until we arrived here,” Almaraz said, referring to the police checkpoint in Coahuila.

While he spoke in the first-person plural, the mayor didn’t say who was with him during his escape, according to the newspaper El Universal. At some stage, the mayor and an unidentified companion boarded a bus that took them to the police checkpoint in Coahuila.

Almaraz described his ordeal as a “bad experience” and said he suffered a “terrible fright.”

However, he said he felt “well,” telling reporters that he wasn’t beaten and didn’t sustain any injuries.

Almaraz didn’t specify the location of the field where he said he was held, and didn’t provide detailed information about the men who allegedly kidnapped him.

Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that Almaraz had been located just before noon on Sunday.

“He was located by the Security Cabinet of the government of Mexico in coordination with the authorities of the governments of Zacatecas, Coahuila, San Luis Potosí and Tamaulipas,” he wrote on X.

García Harfuch noted that Almaraz had been missing, but didn’t make any reference to the mayor’s alleged kidnapping.

The abduction

Almaraz, a National Action Party (PAN) mayor, was traveling to Real de Catorce, a pueblo mágico (magical town) in San Luis Potosí, when armed men allegedly intercepted his vehicle on the highway between San Tirbucio, a small town in Zacatecas, and Vanegas, a town in San Luis Potosí. The mayor was traveling with at least one colleague and members of his family when his car was allegedly intercepted on Saturday night. Alleged criminals hijacked other vehicles near the border between San Luis Potosí and Zacatecas on Saturday, according to the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office.

According to the Tamaulipas Attorney General’s Office, Almaraz and his travel companions were abducted. However, the alleged kidnappers later released their victims, with the exception of the mayor. Those released were left on the side of the highway and subsequently sought assistance from authorities in the town of Cedral, San Luis Potosí, according to state authorities, who cited the testimony of an unidentified victim.

The motive for the alleged abduction of the mayor was unclear.

With reports from El Universal, El Financiero, La Jornada and El País

World.title: Mexico’s inflation rate rises for third straight month, hitting 3.75%
World.content:
Inflation is showing no sign of letting up and, led by green tomatoes, consumer prices rose more than expected in October, marking three consecutive months of increases.

According to data released on Monday by the national statistics agency INEGI, the annual inflation rate reached 3.75%, up from 3.57% in October 2025.

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) exceeded the 23 estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists, which yielded a median prediction of 3.65% and was 0.65% more than the 3.45% recorded in September of this year.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, accelerated to 3.80% year-on-year and rose 0.34% month-on-month, while non-core inflation reached 3.59% year-on-year.

Within the core inflation index, goods increased by 0.22% and services by 0.44%.

On a monthly basis, the non-core price index rose 1.75%, with fruit and vegetable prices climbing 2.35%. Energy and government-regulated prices rose 2.13%, which was largely due to the end of the summer electricity tariff subsidy in 18 cities

The six products that increased the most were:

Green tomatoes: 35.58%.

Air transport: 26.36%.

Pumpkins: 23.22%.

Electricity: 18.51%.

Professional services: 9.88%.

Red tomatoes: 9.68%

The six products that decreased the most were:

Limes: -16.53%.

Serrano chilis: -8.98%.

Oranges: -8.90.

Avocados: -7.20%.

Potatoes and other tubers: -6.29%.

Bananas: -4.83%.

Just last week, the central bank cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%, a decision that reignited debate over whether policymakers are easing the economy too quickly before inflation has sustainably returned to the bank’s target of 3%.

The bank also revised its forward guidance, indicating that the new rate is likely to remain unchanged for an extended period. In a statement, it argued that keeping borrowing costs at current levels would help inflation converge toward the target, while acknowledging that risks to the outlook remain tilted to the upside.

And even as economic activity continues to rebound — GDP expanded by 3.2% year-on-year in the third quarter — the bank maintains that the economy is still operating below its potential, limiting demand-driven inflation.

However, if the economy demonstrates sustained growth, the bank’s position might be difficult to sustain.

With reports from El Financiero, El Economista and LopezDoriga.com

World.title: Belgian artist Carsten Höller unveils towering ‘Mexico City Slides’ at Polanco-area mall
World.content:
Four giant, intertwining spiral slides — the tallest reaching 38.5 meters, or about 126 feet — have been installed at Mexico City’s upscale Antara shopping center by Carsten Höller, a Belgian-born sculptor known for his interactive works.

Touted as a permanent feature, “Mexico City Slides” is part of a big expansion at the 20-year-old Polanco-adjacent shopping center located in Colonia Granada.

Made of steel and polycarbonate, the slides range from about 12 to 38.5 meters tall, with slide lengths of about 32 to 91 meters.

Each slide carries an individual rider, allowing four people to descend simultaneously from different starting points before reaching a common landing area.

According to ARTnews, riders will enter the slides from a restaurant area, Google’s offices, the future Rosewood hotel and a new exhibition space for Arte Abierto. Rosewood lists 2028 for the hotel’s planned opening in the tower of Antara’s expansion.

Right now, the slides are available to view, but Arte Abierto — a contemporary art nonprofit with sites in Cabo San Lucas and elsewhere — has not specified on its website when visitors can begin riding them. It advises checking Instagram for updates.

Arte Abierto and developer SOMA commissioned the installation in collaboration with the architecture firm Sordo Madaleno, according to the online magazine Designboom. The firm also designed the recently opened St. Regis Costa Mujeres resort in Quintana Roo.

The slides accompany an expansion of Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site. The open-air mall’s current lineup includes stores such as Carolina Herrera, Hugo Boss, Apple and Zara.

Höller, born in Brussels to German parents, trained as a scientist before becoming a full-time artist in 1993. He earned a doctorate in agricultural science at the University of Kiel in 1988 and worked as an insect researcher, according to a biography by the international art gallery Gagosian.

He began his slide series at the 1998 Berlin Biennale. Later installations included five slides inside London’s Tate Modern in 2006 and projects in New York, Florence and Copenhagen.

Arte Abierto calls the Mexico City version Höller’s largest slide installation to date.

“Sliding is a way of thinking through the body,” Höller, 64, says on Instagram. “It is a controlled fall that opens a space between fear and pleasure, where the mind momentarily reorganizes itself.”

With reports from Designboom, Radio Fórmula, ARTnews.com and Lado.mx

World.title: CJNG operator ‘R2’ and 19 others arrested following shootout with Mexican Navy in Guadalajara
World.content:
Listen to this article

The alleged leader of a criminal cell linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and 19 other people were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday after a shootout with members of the special operations unit of the Mexican Navy.

Rafael Álvarez Ayala — a man known as “R2” who federal authorities say is the leader of the “Los Rs” cell of the CJNG and linked to the 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo — was shot before he was arrested and taken to a hospital in Guadalajara. He reportedly underwent surgery after being shot in his abdomen, leg and arm.

The clash between the alleged criminals and navy personnel occurred at the Sabea restaurant and hookah lounge, where Álvarez reportedly arrived 20 hours before he was shot and arrested on Sunday afternoon. Authorities said that his arrest occurred at a restaurant in Zapopan, but Sabea is actually in Guadalajara’s Vallarta Norte neighborhood, near the state capital’s municipal boundary with Zapopan.

According to the navy and the federal Security Ministry (SSPC), the alleged criminals began shooting first and navy personnel returned fire.

A member of the navy was also shot during the gun battle, but the injury doesn’t pose a risk to his life, according to the SSPC.

R2 is the brother of R1, the alleged mastermind of Carlos Manzo’s assassination

Rafael Álvarez Ayala is the brother of Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, identified as the mastermind behind the Nov. 1, 2025, assassination of Carlos Manzo. Ramón Ángel, a “Los Rs” leader known as R1, was arrested in Jalisco in July. Both he and his brother were previously arrested in 2012 and spent a decade in prison before their release in 2022.

The Navy Ministry (SEMAR) and federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported the arrest of R2 and 19 other people in social media posts on Sunday afternoon. In a statement, the SSPC described the 19 additional suspects as “alleged lawbreakers” and said they were turned over to the “appropriate authorities.”

García Harfuch said that authorities located Álvarez thanks to intelligence work carried out by the National Intelligence Center (CNI) and information shared by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The Michoacán Attorney General’s Office also provided information, according to the SSPC.

García Harfuch said that a judge in Michoacán had issued an arrest warrant for R2 on a homicide charge. García Harfuch also said that Álvarez was subject to an arrest warrant for the purpose of extradition to the United States.

In his social media post, the security minister also wrote that “Los Rs” are “mainly” involved in “extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, unlawful deprivation of liberty, kidnapping and attacks against authorities.”

The criminal cell’s “extortion victims” include business owners and avocado producers, he added.

The SSPC called Álvarez “one of the main generators of violence in the region.” The ministry was referring to Jalisco and the neighboring state of Michoacán.

R1, R2 and another brother, Jesús Santiago, known as “R3,” used to take direct orders from former CJNG leader Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, according to a Reforma newspaper report that cited information from Mexico’s Defense Ministry. Oseguera was fatally wounded in a Mexican military operation in Jalisco in February.

DEA commends Mexican authorities for arrest of R2

The DEA acknowledged the arrest of R2 in a social media post. The agency called Álvarez “a senior leader of the CJNG terrorist organization responsible for drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping, and deadly violence across Mexico.”

Mexican authorities have arrested Rafael Álvarez Ayala, alias “R2,” a senior leader of the CJNG terrorist organization responsible for drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping, and deadly violence across Mexico. Intelligence shared by DEA helped Mexican authorities locate R2, who is also wanted in the United States on federal drug trafficking and firearms charges. World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra at Degollado Theater, a vermouth festival and airport updates
World.content:
As Guadalajara eases into the year-end holiday season, the events calendar is heating up. This week, we preview the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra’s upcoming performances at Degollado Theater and the second annual Guadalajara Vermouth Festival.

But first, we have some news regarding expanding international air service at Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo Airport and an update on road work happening on the Chapala Highway.

Guadalajara gains another nonstop connection to Seattle this winter

Those plotting an escape from Seattle’s notoriously gray and rainy winter months will soon have another option to consider.

According to Simple Flying, Alaska Airlines is set to begin nonstop service from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport to Guadalajara on March 18, 2027. The airline expects to fly the route year-round, up to three times weekly, using Boeing 737-800 aircraft. While the exact days and times have not yet been announced, the planned flight would give Seattle travelers their third nonstop route to Guadalajara.

Mexican carriers Volaris and Aeroméxico are already offering nonstop flights between Seattle and Guadalajara. Volaris began offering the route 10 years ago, while Aeroméxico launched its service between the two cities last year.

According to the Port of Seattle, outbound travel from SEA to Mexico in 2024 was double its 2019 levels.

New project on the Chapala Highway is slowing traffic and fraying nerves

Municipal workers kicked off paving work on the southbound lanes of the Chapala Highway on Nov. 1. The project is causing new headaches for motorists headed to and from the airport and those traveling between the city and Lake Chapala.

Workers are reportedly occupying the center lanes in both directions, so motorists are being diverted to outer lanes, which is causing bottlenecks about 700 meters from the entrance to Guadalajara International Airport.

On top of the congestion, motorists complained that signage didn’t make it clear which lanes pass by the airport and which ones lead to it.

As one female driver told El Informador, “It’s a mess … they don’t warn you. I was going to take the horseshoe to avoid taking the road to Chapala … but it turns out it’s closed and they diverted me to the airport.”

The current project is part of the comprehensive renovation of the Chapala Highway that began last year. The latest phase aims to modernize the road surface and prevent structural damage from the thousands of heavy trucks that ply the highway daily.

While local officials have not announced a target completion date for the paving work, it’s likely to run through most of November. For anyone planning to fly out of Guadalajara airport in the coming weeks or during the Thanksgiving holiday, it’s best to build extra time into your schedule.

When construction work wraps up, traffic flows, road safety and access to the airport should all materially improve.

The Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra performs at Degollado Theater this month

The Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra (known locally as Orquesta Filarmónica de Jalisco, or OFJ) returns for its final season of 2026 with a handful of concerts at the venerable Degollado Theater throughout the month.

The season’s performances will bring together works by Beethoven, Mahler, Stravinsky, Sibelius, Tchaikovsky, Dvořák and several Mexican composers. It will also feature the world premiere of a work commissioned by the OFJ itself.

The concerts will be led by artistic director José Luis Castillo, along with guest conductors and soloists such as David Cohen, Rodolfo Ritter, Dieter Hennings and Cristian Coliver.

Looking ahead to the upcoming performances on Nov. 12 and 15 to be conducted by José María Moreno, the program features works by Florence Price, Carlos Chávez, Mozart Camargo Guarnieri and Joaquín Turina.

Later in the month, Rodrigo Sierra Moncayo takes the helm as guest conductor, accompanied by Carlos Gutiérrez on piano, with a program that includes Ludwig van Beethoven’s Violin Concerto (piano version) and Johannes Brahms’ Symphony No. 3.

Wrapping up the series on Nov. 23 and 29 are two special concerts featuring the world premiere of “Ruiseñor de la sombra” (“Nightingale of the Shadow”), a work commissioned by the OFJ from the Guadalajara-born composer Ricardo Zohn-Muldoon.

The concerts are performed each Thursday evening at 8:30 p.m., as well as on Sundays at 12:30 p.m. To view the full schedule and buy tickets, visit the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra website or the Teatro Degollado box office in person.

The Guadalajara Vermouth Festival returns to Colonia Americana mid-month

In just its second edition, the Guadalajara Vermouth Festival returns to the city on Nov. 14.

Long a popular apéritif in Southern Europe, vermouth is beginning to find a receptive audience here in Mexico. Made from a base of neutral wine, the drink is fortified with a distilled spirit and infused with a wide variety of botanicals (herbs, spices and florals). Vermouth can be dry or sweet, white or red.

Guests at this year’s event will have the opportunity to learn about how this drink is made and sample a wide variety of vermouths made in Europe and Mexico. For those interested in taking things a step further, there will also be hands-on vermouth-making workshops where participants can craft their own recipe.

Live music and bar snacks are also in the works, to keep the buena onda flowing.

Tickets to the festival are available online and from a handful of Guadalajara bars partnering with the event, including Metódico Café, Lito Aperitivo Social, Ocio en Plural and Vermutería Don Ajenjo.

Each ticket grants the holder a commemorative glass and one complimentary tasting. For more details, check out the festival website.

Date: Nov. 14 from 6 p.m. to midnight

Nov. 14 from 6 p.m. to midnight Location: Patio Paraíso at Loba Cervecería, Gregorio Dávila 86 in Colonia Americana

Patio Paraíso at Loba Cervecería, Gregorio Dávila 86 in Colonia Americana Cost: 350 pesos, not including fees

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico’s National Energy Commission approves 6 solar energy permits worth US $750M
World.content:
Mexico’s National Energy Commission has approved six photovoltaic power generation permits with investments totaling US $750 million that will add 649 megawatts (MW) of net capacity to the National Power System (SEN), through projects that will begin operations in 2028 and 2029.

The commission (CNE) granted the six permits, dated Nov. 5, to subsidiaries of Cox, Invex Controladora and Viva El Sol for private projects with an estimated investment of US $750 million.

According to information reported by Bloomberg Línea, Green Park Energy, a subsidiary of Cox, obtained three permits; Invex Controladora’s Ammper Generación received two, while Viva El Sol obtained one.

In a statement announcing the approval, the CNE said the permits are part of the Second Call for Proposals (Privados II) for priority processing of generation and interconnection permit applications to the SEN, in accordance with the binding planning issued by the Energy Ministry.

The Second Call received 57 applications, of which 31 met the basic requirements to obtain an electricity generation permit. However, only the six approved projects met all the criteria established.

The permits granted will operate under the Wholesale Electricity Market generation model and will provide greater operational flexibility while also strengthening the stability and reliability of Mexico’s grid.

Although the six projects represent a net capacity of 649 MW, they represent a combined installed capacity of 751 MW alternating current (MWac) and an estimated annual generation of 1,881 gigawatt-hours (GWh).

They also feature battery storage systems for 204 MW and approximately 628 MWh, which will serve to strengthen the stability and reliability of the electrical grid.

More than one-third of the capacity will become operational in 2028 and the remaining 63% in 2029.

Cox’s plants will be built in the states of Aguascalientes, Jalisco and Guanajuato, while the Invex subsidiary Ammper will locate its two in Tlaxcala and Morelos, and Viva El Sol’s project will be located in Coahuila.

Strategic Energy published details of the six projects, reporting that Ammper Generación’s Antares project to be built in Tlaxcala will be the largest single power plant among the six authorized, and is the development with the highest planned production within Privados II.

As such, the Western Region will add 350 MW, the Eastern Region 289 MW and the Northeastern Region 10 MW.

With reports from El Financiero and Bloomberg Línea

World.title: Argentine Province Moves Vote to February
World.content:
ARGENTINA · ELECTIONS

Neuquén, a key Argentine province for Vaca Muerta, the country’s shale oil and gas field, will vote on Sunday, 14 February 2027. Governor Rolando Figueroa set the date by decree 1860/2026 on Monday, 9 November.

That is about eight months before the national presidential vote, which El Economista, an Argentine business outlet, calls the first big test of the year for President Javier Milei’s camp. It gives US investors in Vaca Muerta and President Javier Milei an early read on local politics.

Voters will choose a governor and vice governor, plus 35 lawmakers for the provincial Legislature and 18 alternates. Mayors, councillors and local commissions are also on the ballot in dozens of towns.

In the capital, also called Neuquén, residents elect a new mayor and 20 councillors. They also answer yes or no on a change to the city charter that would set a maximum of 20 councillors.

Milei’s Stake in the Vote

El Economista says the vote is the first test for Milei’s camp. His party, La Libertad Avanza (LLA), must decide whether to run its own ticket or ally with local forces, it added.

Nadia Márquez, an LLA national senator from the province, publicly questioned the early date, both outlets reported. See our guide to the 2027 presidential race.

It is not known who will run for governor, whether LLA will field its own ticket, or what happens to the PASO primaries. Diario Neuquino reports that the electronic ballot will be used.

Investors in Vaca Muerta will get a provincial verdict on Figueroa, who governs the province. Our report on the province’s credit rating upgrade shows how much the region matters.

When does Neuquén vote?

On Sunday, 14 February 2027, about eight months before Argentina’s national presidential vote in October 2027.

What is on the ballot?

The governor and vice governor, 35 provincial lawmakers with 18 alternates, and local posts in dozens of towns. The capital also elects a mayor.

His party, La Libertad Avanza, has not said whether it will run alone or ally with the governor’s camp. The result will be an early read on his support.
