World.title: Central America – Where Soccer Is Stuck in Time
World.content:
Bryan Oliva, 12, runs across a field of yellowing, overgrown grass in a densely populated neighborhood of San Salvador. He dreams of becoming a professional soccer player, but talent alone is not enough to make that happen in a Central America where the sport is moving backward.

Eleven-year-old Darixon Rivas of Honduras shares that dream. Every afternoon, he trains on a muddy field, but first he must work on his family’s ranch in La Abisinia, a remote village in the northern department of Colón. “You make a lot of money as a soccer player, but I don’t feel like it’s possible for me,” Bryan admits in Zacamil, a neighborhood of apartment buildings in the Salvadoran capital.

Hoping to help his family financially, he believes it is “really difficult” for young people from poor communities like his to get noticed by scouts, since the few opportunities available tend to reach more privileged areas. Poverty touches almost everything in Central America, where roughly half the population lives in those conditions. But soccer’s problems go further: with few exceptions, investment in infrastructure and player development is scarce.

“We have a long way to go,” Salvadoran Soccer Federation President Yamil Bukele recently acknowledged. He is promoting a plan to strengthen the youth divisions.

Moving Backward

The consequences are plain to see: only Panama and Guatemala qualified for the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, which begin Thursday. In fact, Panama was the only Central American team at the recent World Cup in North America, where Caribbean nations Curaçao and Haiti also represented Concacaf.

El Salvador last appeared at a World Cup 44 years ago, during the rise of striker Jorge “Mágico” González, considered Central America’s best player of the 20th century. More than 40 coaches have led the team since then. The job is currently held by Colombia’s Hernán Darío Gómez, who has coached at the World Cup.

Honduras, led by Spain’s José Francisco Molina, has also spent years living on memories. Its last World Cup appearance was in Brazil in 2014. That tournament was also where time stood still for Costa Rica, which has never again fielded a team like the one that stunned the soccer world by reaching the quarterfinals. Guatemala, Nicaragua and Belize have never played at a World Cup.

“There has been a regression,” Argentine coach Diego Vázquez, who led Honduras from 2022 to 2023, tells AFP. “Youth leagues need to be organized, and governments need to invest too,” he adds. Former Panama international Víctor René Mendieta says El Salvador, Honduras and Costa Rica “neglected” the development of new talent.

Costa Ricans and Hondurans in particular “think the coaches are to blame, when the reality is that their talent pool (…) has been drying up, and they can’t compete with the emerging forces in the Caribbean,” Salvadoran journalist Bruno Porzio said.

No One Taking Responsibility

With nearly 50 million inhabitants, Central America has around 4,400 professional soccer players, most of them spread across 68 teams, according to FIFA figures from 2024. Yet domestic competitions, lacking stars or prominent coaches, are of a modest standard, and only a handful of players earn more than $5,000 a month.

Most teams lack youth affiliates and training centers. Many clubs also play in small stadiums with artificial turf. “In El Salvador, major business owners stopped taking an interest in soccer,” and club officials have no interest in “leaving a legacy,” Porzio says. In Honduras, meanwhile, executives “want to stay for life,” Honduran coach Reynaldo Tilguath tells AFP.

Central America also lacks players in major leagues who could raise the standard of its national teams, unlike Haiti, Suriname and Curaçao, whose squads are filled with players developed in Europe. Panama is “doing a better job” of developing players, while “the rest of us are falling behind,” Tilguath says.

Meanwhile, high in the mountains of La Abisinia, Darixon and his friends share their field with horses and cows, trying to score in goals made from rusty metal posts. One wears a Lionel Messi jersey, while another sports clothing covered in images of Cristiano Ronaldo.

“Honduran soccer is broken (…). Look at the state of this little field. Our fathers used to come and play here too,” Darixon says.

World.title: DEA Traced Costa Rica’s First Female Extradition Case to a 2-Ton Jungle Lab
World.content:
A U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration investigation that reached a jungle cocaine lab in Colombia and a fishing boat anchored off Peru lies behind the case of Shirley Yesenia Gómez Parra, the first Costa Rican woman approved for extradition to the United States on drug charges.

Gómez Parra, 39, and her partner, Viveros Viveros, 50, a Colombian-born naturalized Costa Rican, are among six people named in a single indictment returned by a federal grand jury in Arizona on Oct. 1, 2025, according to the federal court docket in United States v. Arredondo et al. The indictment carries one count and a forfeiture allegation.

Investigators allege the pair acted as local leaders of a network that moved cocaine from Colombia through Panama, Costa Rica and Mexico to the U.S. market. Neither has been convicted, and the allegations have not been tested at trial. According to case records reported in Costa Rica, a confidential DEA informant met in Bogotá on July 31, 2024, with Edgar Santiago Barbosa Andrade, who investigators say acted as an emissary for Colombian supplier Jorge Sánchez Gamboa. The meeting was recorded.

On Oct. 3, 2024, the informant met Francisco Mantilla Angulo, known as “Frank,” and a second man known as “Primo” in Cali, investigators allege. The informant was then taken about an hour and a half to a jungle complex that could hold up to 2 metric tons (about 4,400 pounds) of cocaine and was watched by roughly six lookouts.

During that visit, according to the allegations, the suppliers set a price of 5.8 million Colombian pesos per kilogram, or about $1,350. On Oct. 18, 2024, an emissary handed over 7 kilograms (15.4 pounds) of cocaine for $10,000 in cash at a shopping center in Cali. DEA laboratory tests later confirmed it was high-purity cocaine hydrochloride.

In December 2024, investigators allege, the group’s leaders offered a fishing vessel anchored in Peru to move drugs across the Pacific. The DEA also recorded Gómez Parra on video negotiating a 100-kilogram (220-pound) cocaine shipment to Arizona, investigators allege. U.S. authorities further link the network to biweekly flights from Colombia, a set of safe houses and the seizure of 273 kilograms (602 pounds) of cocaine from two vehicles in August 2024.

Colombian investigators, working with the it’s navy and a military anti-kidnapping unit, located Sánchez Gamboa, Barbosa Andrade and Mantilla Angulo in Bogotá, Cali and Buenaventura and served them with the U.S. request, Colombia’s Attorney General’s Office said in March.

In Panama, authorities detained Oscar Enrique Virula Arredondo, a Guatemalan national who prosecutors allege offered safe houses and transport routes in Costa Rica. He is listed as the first defendant in the Arizona case. Gómez Parra was detained in Ciudad Neily and Viveros Viveros in La Sabana, both on March 13, 2026. She is held at the Vilma Curling Rivera women’s prison, and he is in the maximum-security module at La Reforma.

The San José Criminal Court approved the extradition of both on Sept. 14. Their defense appealed within three days, arguing that the alleged acts date to July 2024, before the constitutional reform that allowed Costa Rica to extradite its own citizens took effect. The defense also argued that DEA agents made covert purchases without a formal cooperation agreement endorsed by Costa Rica’s Foreign Ministry.

The trial judge rejected the retroactivity argument, finding that drug trafficking is a continuing offense and that the alleged conduct ran until Oct. 1, 2025. The judge also ruled that the validity of the DEA’s evidence is a matter for the courts in Arizona, not for an extradition hearing.

The appeal is pending, and neither defendant can be handed over until it is resolved. The case adds to a widening set of U.S. drug investigations that run through Costa Rica. If the appeal fails, Gómez Parra and Viveros Viveros would follow former Public Security Minister Celso Gamboa, who was extradited to Texas in March, among the Costa Ricans sent to face trial in U.S. courts since the reform.

World.title: Strong Winds Up to 75 km/h and Rain Forecast for Costa Rica
World.content:
Hold on to your hat if you’re in northern Guanacaste today. Trade winds pick up across Costa Rica on Tuesday, Nov. 10, and gusts could reach 75 kilometers per hour (47 mph) in the country’s northwest corner, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). In the Central Valley, the North Pacific and the mountain ranges, expect gusts of 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph). That’s strong enough to bring down weak branches, rattle loose roofing and signs, and push motorcycles and high-sided vehicles around on open stretches of road.

The wind isn’t the only thing to watch. On the Central and South Pacific coasts the day starts mostly clear, but sea breezes will build clouds through the morning. By afternoon you can expect isolated showers and downpours, some with thunderstorms. In the Central Valley, skies will be partly cloudy with moderate morning winds and only light, scattered rain in the afternoon. San José should range from 19°C (66°F) to 28.5°C (83°F).

Guanacaste will be the windiest and hottest part of the country. Skies stay mostly clear, with the strongest gusts over high ground in the morning and moderate winds into the afternoon. Liberia is forecast to hit 35°C (95°F). Along the Central Pacific, clouds thicken through the morning, and showers and possible storms form over the mountains in the afternoon. Quepos tops out near 31.5°C (89°F), and coastal showers are possible after dark.

The South Pacific follows the same pattern. Isolated downpours with possible thunderstorms develop in the afternoon, followed by showers along the coast at night. Golfito expects a high of about 30°C (86°F). On the Caribbean side, moisture coming off the sea brings partly cloudy skies and scattered rain in the morning. In the afternoon the rain stays close to the mountains, and Limón and Guápiles both top out around 29°C (84°F).

The Northern Zone gets a similar mix, with scattered morning rain and possible afternoon showers in the mountains. Ciudad Quesada ranges from 17°C (63°F) to 28°C (82°F). If you’re driving in northern Guanacaste, keep both hands on the wheel and give trucks and motorcycles extra room. Gusts hit hardest on open roads and ridgelines, where nothing breaks the wind. Bring in or tie down anything loose on balconies, patios and rooftops.

If you’re headed to a Pacific beach, plan to be off the sand and out of the water by early afternoon, when storms are most likely to form. Lightning is the main danger, and it can strike before the rain arrives. Looking ahead, IMN expects the trade winds to stay strong through Wednesday, ease for a short time midweek, and pick up again Saturday and Sunday. That weekend push comes from a weak cold front system to the north that speeds up the winds over the Caribbean. Rain should decrease nationwide over the week.

This is the usual pattern of the shift from the rainy season to the dry season. Sunny days, occasional showers and bursts of strong wind take turns until the dry months settle in. IMN has also forecast warmer-than-normal temperatures from November through January.

World.title: Protest Caravan to Santa Ana Could Slow Traffic West of San José
World.content:
Drivers who carry tourists, students and workers around Costa Rica plan to drive a protest caravan from San José to Santa Ana this morning. If you’re heading west of the capital, expect delays as the convoy is set to leave the Gimnasio Nacional in La Sabana at 7:30 a.m. and reach the offices of the Regulatory Authority for Public Services (ARESEP) in Santa Ana around 8 a.m. Leave extra time, or check a live traffic app before you set out.

If you have a school bus, a work shuttle or a tour transfer booked this morning, it may run late. The Association of Special Transport Operators (ATRAE SOS), which organized the protest, has warned that student, worker and tourism transport could all be affected. The group says it represents about 16,000 operators. Their complaint is about new fees in the 2027 marchamo, the annual vehicle registration every owner in Costa Rica has to pay.

Special transport operators already pay a yearly fee to the Public Transport Council (CTP) for each vehicle. For 2027, ARESEP has added its own regulatory fee on top of that. The operators say this means they pay twice for the same van. ARESEP’s new fee for worker transport is 79,061 colones (about $176) for a microbus with up to 20 seats. It rises to 152,959 colones (about $340) for vehicles carrying 21 to 34 passengers, and 252,567 colones (about $561) for buses with 35 seats or more.

The CTP fee goes up with fleet size. A company with one vehicle pays 103,574 colones (about $230). Companies with more than nine pay 319,571 colones (about $710) per vehicle. That scale is what has angered independent drivers most. Many own a single van but work under a permit leased from a larger company, and the group says they end up billed at the big-fleet rate.

Marcos Chaves, vice president of ATRAE SOS, said it is unacceptable for an operator with one vehicle to pay as if they ran a large fleet. He said the fees ignore the sector’s economic reality and could put small and medium companies out of business. The group also argues that more vehicles doesn’t mean more income. Demand for private transport rises and falls, and a van can be booked solid one day and parked the next.

ATRAE SOS wants ARESEP and the CTP to cancel the fees, publish the technical studies behind them and open talks with each part of the industry. It says no studies were released and affected operators were never consulted. If the fees stand, the group warns, operators could pass the extra cost on to the families, schools and businesses that hire them.

ARESEP had not responded publicly as of early this morning. Whether the fees survive will affect what schools, employers and tour companies pay to move people around the country next year.

World.title: Have a US Visa Appointment Wednesday? The Embassy Will Be Closed
World.content:
The U.S. Embassy in San José will be closed all day Wednesday, Nov. 11. If you have a visa interview or any other in-person appointment that day, you’ll need a new plan. The closure covers the main embassy and the Consular Section, which handles visa applications and services for U.S. citizens. It’s for Veterans Day, a U.S. federal holiday honoring people who served in the American armed forces.

Both offices reopen Thursday, Nov. 12, on their regular schedule. If your appointment is on Wednesday, look for rescheduling instructions in your confirmation email or the embassy’s online visa appointment system. The embassy hasn’t said whether Wednesday appointments will be moved automatically.

U.S. citizens with a real emergency can still get help. The embassy says emergency cases are admitted case by case, and it asks citizens to give notice in advance by emailing ACSSanJose@state.gov. Two more dates matter if you have embassy business this month. The Consular Section closes for consular services on the last Wednesday of every month, which is Nov. 25. The embassy also closes on U.S. holidays, including Thanksgiving on Thursday, Nov. 26.

It closes on Costa Rican public holidays too, so check its online calendar before any visit. The embassy is in Pavas, west of downtown San José. Only people with scheduled appointments are let into the Consular Section, so turning up without one on a reopening day won’t get you in.

World.title: Costa Rica Paid $701 Million More for Fuel This Year as Diesel Soared
World.content:
Costa Rica paid about $701 million more for imported fuel in the first nine months of 2026 than in the same period last year, as higher international prices drove up the cost of every barrel, according to figures from the state fuel company, Recope. Fuel imports through September totaled $2,267 million, up 44.77% from $1,566 million a year earlier.

The volume imported grew only about 5.5%, from 18.81 million to 19.85 million barrels, so most of the increase came from higher prices. The average cost of a barrel rose 37.17%, from $83.27 to $114.22. Diesel was the largest single expense, at $961 million. Its average import price climbed from $90.79 to $135.82 per barrel, while jet fuel rose from $93.36 to $138.84. Karla Montero, Recope’s executive president, attributed the jump in diesel to attacks on Russian refineries.

The Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) projects in its Monetary Policy Report that the country’s oil bill will close 2026 at $3,086 million, compared with $1,976 million in 2025. Montero said higher import costs reach consumers gradually, through the monthly price adjustments approved by the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep). Diesel and regular gasoline currently sell for 808 colones per liter, about $1.80, or roughly $6.80 per gallon. Super gasoline sells for 806 colones per liter.

Diesel has historically been cheaper at the pump because it carries a lower single fuel tax, but international cost pressure has narrowed that gap. Diesel was up 17% in October’s inflation figures, as consumer prices rose for a second straight month. Alonso Alfaro, chief economist at the BCCR, said more expensive fuel adds inflationary pressure that could spread to other prices. He also said larger import payments increase demand for dollars and put pressure on the external deficit, although that demand has so far been met without instability.

The exchange rate has softened part of the blow. Recope said this year’s roughly 10% shift in the exchange rate has offset part of the increase in import costs, with the dollar now trading near 450 colones. Recope expects international prices to remain between $90 and $110 a barrel in the coming weeks. Pablo Guzmán, executive director of the Costa Rican Fuel Chamber, said Costa Rica is a price taker and that prices could ease or rise moderately in 2027.

Any relief next year depends on smoother oil shipments through the Middle East and a recovery in diesel supply. Recope said it has completed its annual tender for 2027 contracts, which fixes freight, insurance and supplier margins for the year.

World.title: Costa Rica Asks You to Cut Water Use as the El Niño Dry Season Begins
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national water utility is asking everyone to use less water as the dry season begins this week in Guanacaste and the Central Valley, with a strong El Niño expected to keep conditions drier and hotter than normal through January. The Costa Rican Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers (AyA) made the appeal on Monday. It is a request, not a restriction. AyA said it is not rationing water and has no plans to do so in the near future.

The reason is timing. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects the dry season to start this week in the North Pacific and Central Valley, during Nov. 16–22 in the Central Pacific and during Nov. 23–29 in the South Pacific. Once the rain stops, the sources that feed many water systems stop recharging. IMN director Bernard Stolz said in May that AyA is among the institutions hit hardest by El Niño because rain stops falling in the high parts of the mountains. Water saved now helps carry systems through the driest months of the year.

Here is what AyA is asking you to do at home.

Take shorter showers, and turn off the tap while you soap up or shampoo.

Fix leaks, and check faucets, pipes and toilets for water running when it shouldn’t be.

Don’t hose down sidewalks, patios or driveways.

Reuse water for household jobs that don’t need drinking water.

Collect rainwater for plants and outdoor cleaning, but don’t drink it.

Run the washing machine only with a full load.

One thing AyA does not want you to do is stockpile. Drinking water stored too far in advance can lose quality and become contaminated, so there is no need to fill containers unless your provider announces a cut. This year has already tested the supply. Water rationing reached dozens of Pacific communities, and in October authorities issued the country’s first red alert at sea.

The Central Valley is exposed too. A national El Niño contingency strategy drawn up by the National Emergency Commission (CNE) with AyA and other institutions projected lower output from the surface and underground sources that supply the Greater Metropolitan Area. That plan listed at least 120,579 AyA customers in San José districts, including Pavas, Tibás, Goicoechea, Moravia and La Uruca, as facing possible supply impacts. It also set out tanker-truck service for critical areas such as La Carpio.

If your water comes from a local ASADA rather than AyA, as it does in many Guanacaste beach towns and rural communities, that provider sets its own schedules. Check its notices or social media pages for any changes. AyA’s appeal did not single out specific regions or set a consumption target. If supply does tighten, service schedules would come from AyA or from local providers.

World.title: Spot an Injured Animal on Route 27? Don’t Touch It. Here’s Who to Call
World.content:
If you see an injured animal on Route 27, the toll highway between San José and the central Pacific coast, don’t pull over and try to pick it up. Slow down, keep your distance and call the highway’s 24-hour control center at 2588-4040. That is the advice from Route 27’s operator, Globalvia, and from specialists at Refugio Animal de Costa Rica, a wildlife refuge in Santa Ana. The highway has recorded 299 animal rescues since 2015, according to Globalvia.

The total includes 149 dogs, 58 cats and 92 wild animals. Among the wildlife were sloths, snakes, turtles, iguanas, birds, coatis and ocelots. An animal that has been hit by a car may be stunned, in shock or carrying a fracture you can’t see. Even one that looks calm can bite or lash out when you get close, and handling it the wrong way can make its injuries worse. Snakes and other potentially dangerous species add another layer of risk.

Stopping suddenly is a danger of its own on one of the country’s busiest highways. Brake gradually, don’t swerve, and give the drivers behind you time to react. Rodolfo Vargas, a biologist at the refuge, advises alerting other motorists without making sudden maneuvers. Don’t try to touch, capture or carry a wild animal yourself. Report it instead, so trained staff can deal with it safely.

The Route 27 control center answers 24 hours a day at 2588-4040. If the animal or the situation puts other drivers in immediate danger, call 911. For specialist advice on what to do, you can reach Refugio Animal de Costa Rica at 8828-0324. When you call, give your location as precisely as you can, ideally the nearest kilometer marker, along with your direction of travel. Say whether the animal looks injured and whether it is blocking a lane.

Route 27 recently trained 15 of its staff with specialists from the refuge. The course covered how to identify potentially dangerous species, how to recognize injuries and fractures, and how to handle animals safely. Montserrat Courrau, Route 27’s director of communications and corporate social responsibility, said every animal presents its own situation, which is why staff need to know how to handle each one correctly.

Globalvia says the highway has run its animal assistance and staff training program for more than a decade. The rescues are a small window onto a wider problem, as wildlife deaths on Costa Rica’s roads continue to mount and a new law requires wildlife crossings on public infrastructure.

World.title: SJCJC student Joseph Vernon sent to prison after failing to pay half of $10,000 in fines for illegal firearm and ammunition that led to arrest of 3 females, including 13-year-old
World.content:
SJCJC student Joseph Vernon sent to prison after failing to pay half of $10,000 in fines for illegal firearm and ammunition that led to arrest of 3 females, including 13-year-old

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 20-year-old St. John’s College Junior College (SJCJC) student has been fined a total of $10,000 after pleading guilty to possessing an unlicensed firearm and ammunition discovered in the ceiling of a Belize City home.

Joseph Anthony Christopher Vernon appeared before a magistrate in Court #5 on Monday, November 9, alongside three females, including a 13-year-old minor, who were initially charged jointly with him.

Police reported that around 10:00 p.m. on Sunday, November 8, officers searched a residence at the corner of Fabers Road and Avocado Lane, where they discovered a 9mm Glock pistol with a magazine containing 12 live rounds of ammunition concealed in the ceiling.

The residence belongs to 43-year-old Rachel Judith Ann Vernon, who was charged alongside Joseph, 24-year-old Julia Niecy Turton, and the minor.

During the arraignment, Joseph accepted responsibility for the firearm and ammunition and pleaded guilty to both charges. As a result, the prosecution withdrew the charges against the three females, allowing them to leave court.

In mitigation, Vernon expressed remorse, telling the court, “I made a mistake. I am a student. I see what my family is going through. I hope this mistake will not mess me up in my future criminology studies.”

The magistrate considered his early guilty plea and clean criminal record, opting to impose fines rather than an immediate custodial sentence. However, she warned that another conviction for a similar offense could result in imprisonment.

Vernon was fined $5,000 for keeping an unlicensed firearm and another $5,000 for keeping ammunition without a license.

He was ordered to pay $5,000 immediately, representing half of the total fines, with the remaining balance due by January 29, 2027.

Unable to make the initial payment, Vernon was escorted to the Belize Central Prison, where he will remain until the required payment is made.

He faces a default sentence of three years’ imprisonment on each count if the fines are not paid.

World.title: U.S. cites human trafficking concerns as Belize ends decades-old Cuban medical brigade agreement
World.content:
U.S. cites human trafficking concerns as Belize ends decades-old Cuban medical brigade agreement

By Zoila Palma: Recently, the Government of Belize informed that Belize and Cuba will not renew the agreement under which members of the Cuban Medical Brigade have served in Belize since 1990.

Through a new arrangement, the Government of Belize, through the Ministry of Health and Wellness, will sign individual contracts of employment with each Cuban professional that will allow them to remain and work in Belize.

US Ambassador Andre Bauer says that the U.S. welcomed this decision by Belize.

“Well, the US, a big thing for them is human trafficking. They want people to have control of their own identity and their own domain, and so, if another country is sending people out but keeping most of the money for the country and not actually compensating the people for doing their work and they have their passports, that’s important to our country and we want to make sure that people are treated fairly and right. So, that’s why they took this, the President and the Secretary of State. This was a big issue for them, to make sure that human trafficking, on any level, is unacceptable. So, we’re very pleased that Belize has worked with us on this, trying to resolve this issue, trying to give these people that are providing a service that we desperately need, that they are free in doing so,” Ambassador Bauer said.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca says that 22 Cuban medical professionals have signed contracts and more are signing in what he described as a win-win situation for Belize as the country retains the medical professionals.

World.title: Nail technician Shania Elliott charged with stealing over $1,200 in jewelry, watches and nail products
World.content:
Nail technician Shania Elliott charged with stealing over $1,200 in jewelry, watches and nail products

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 20-year-old Belize City nail technician has been charged with theft after allegedly stealing jewelry, watches, nail products and other personal belongings valued at $1,239 from another woman.

Shania Victoria Elliott, of Neal’s Pen Road, appeared before a magistrate in Court #5 on Monday, November 9, where she pleaded not guilty to a single charge of theft.

According to the allegations, Elliott stole several items belonging to another woman on October 13, 2026, on Freetown Road in Belize City.

The items reportedly included a gold chain valued at $160, two gold-plated bracelets valued at $40, a white Calvin Klein watch valued at $160, a brown Gregory Beanie watch valued at $180, another watch valued at $160, ten boxes of nail charms valued at $25, and a pair of black shoes valued at $46.

The total value of the stolen property was reported to the court as $1,239.

With no objection to bail from the prosecution, the magistrate granted Elliott bail of $600 plus one surety of the same amount. She was able to meet bail later that evening.

Elliott is scheduled to return to court on December 30, 2026.

World.title: Murder trial continues for two former police officers accused of killing San Pedro businessman Elvis Polanco
World.content:
Murder trial continues for two former police officers accused of killing San Pedro businessman Elvis Polanco

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The murder trial of two former police officers accused of killing San Pedro businessman Elvis Raul Polanco in 2022 continued in the High Court on Monday, November 9, with additional witness testimony and plans for a visit to the crime scene.

Winfield Mortis, 36, a former interdicted police officer, and Edward Moraga, 29, who was previously dismissed from the Belize Police Department, are standing trial before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim in proceedings without a jury.

The prosecution is being led by Crown Counsel Porsha Staine-Ferguson, assisted by Crown Counsel Maria Nembhard-Santana.

During Monday’s proceedings, two agreed witness statements were read into evidence, while two police witnesses testified. So far, the prosecution has called four witnesses and introduced approximately eight agreed statements.

Among those who have testified is Polanco’s common-law wife, Thomasa Velasco, who witnessed the November 19, 2022, shooting that claimed her husband’s life.

Polanco, 43, the owner of Jade Bar in San Pedro, was returning home with Velasco in a golf cart around 5:00 a.m. on Garifuna Settlement Day when they were ambushed near the entrance to the Escalante subdivision.

According to earlier reports, a masked gunman emerged from nearby bushes and opened fire, fatally wounding Polanco and injuring Velasco. Her purse, reportedly containing $12,000, was also stolen during the attack.

Mortis, who had reportedly worked as a security guard at Polanco’s business, and Moraga were formally charged with murder in January 2023 following directives from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Mortis is represented by attorney Dr. Lynden Jones, while Moraga is represented by attorney Simeon Sampson.

Before Monday’s adjournment, the prosecution informed the court that it intends to apply for a visit to the crime scene, known as a locus in quo. Velasco is among three witnesses expected to participate in the visit.

The prosecution also indicated that the Director of Public Prosecutions will personally join the team handling the case.

A date for the crime scene visit has not yet been established.

The trial, which commenced on November 3, is scheduled to continue on Tuesday, November 10, before Justice Pilgrim.

World.title: Sentencing postponed until February 2027 for Rupert Codd, convicted of raping woman outside KHMH
World.content:
Sentencing postponed until February 2027 for Rupert Codd, convicted of raping woman outside KHMH

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The sentencing of 25-year-old Rupert Codd, who was found guilty of raping a woman on a picnic table outside the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH), has been postponed until February 11, 2027.

Codd appeared before High Court Justice Derick F. Sylvester on Monday, November 9, expecting to be sentenced following his conviction on September 29, 2026. However, delays in the proceedings prompted the judge to adjourn the matter.

Justice Sylvester ordered both the Crown and defense to file their sentencing submissions at least two weeks before the February 11 hearing.

Codd was convicted following a trial by judge without jury for the rape of a 35-year-old woman who was walking to KHMH seeking medical attention in the early morning hours of April 2, 2023.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, the woman, who was ill and seeking medical help; was followed, physically assaulted and dragged onto a picnic table near the hospital, where she was raped around 3:00 a.m.

During the trial, Crown Prosecutor Maria Nembhard-Santana presented evidence from 11 witnesses, including surveillance footage that helped establish Codd’s presence in the area.

Codd denied raping the woman, claiming instead that she had stolen his wallet and cellphone while he was urinating nearby. However, Justice Sylvester rejected his explanation, finding that he had fabricated the account to explain his presence at the scene.

Codd faces a minimum prison sentence of eight years, although the penalty for rape under Belizean law can extend to life imprisonment.

He remains on remand at the Belize Central Prison pending sentencing in February.

World.title: Samuel Bolaños rejects 13-year prison sentence indication for manslaughter in 2024 shooting death of Mathew Moses, opts for murder trial instead
World.content:
Samuel Bolaños rejects 13-year prison sentence indication for manslaughter in 2024 shooting death of Mathew Moses, opts for murder trial instead

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Dangriga resident Samuel Bolaños has rejected a sentencing indication of 13 years in prison for manslaughter, choosing instead to stand trial for murder in connection with the November 2024 shooting death of 46-year-old Matthew Jonathan Moses on northern Ambergris Caye.

Bolaños appeared before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Monday, November 9, represented by attorney Dr. Lyndon Jones. He had previously sought a sentencing indication for the lesser offense of manslaughter after pleading not guilty to murder.

Justice Pilgrim indicated that Bolaños would face a 13-year prison term for manslaughter. However, Bolaños declined the indication, meaning his case will proceed to trial on the original murder charge.

The judge explained that Bolaños had the right to accept or reject the indication and that his decision could not be used against him during future proceedings.

The case stems from the fatal shooting of Moses on November 8, 2024, near Secret Beach on northern Ambergris Caye. Breaking Belize News reported at the time that the shooting allegedly followed an ongoing dispute between Moses and Bolaños, who was working as a caretaker.

Bolaños, who reportedly used a licensed nine-millimeter pistol, initially claimed he acted in self-defense. He was detained and subsequently released pending further investigation, but was formally charged with murder on March 7, 2025, following a review by the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Justice Pilgrim indicated that his court calendar could not accommodate the trial before the end of 2026 and scheduled proceedings to begin on February 8, 2027.

Bolaños remains remanded at the Belize Central Prison pending trial.

World.title: U.S. Ambassador commends BDF for professionalism during incident with Guatemalan Armed Forces
World.content:
U.S. Ambassador commends BDF for professionalism during incident with Guatemalan Armed Forces

By Zoila Palma: Following Saturday’s incident where the Guatemalan Armed Forces approached the BDF vessel in clear acts of aggression and intimidation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted that Belize would lodge a formal protest with the Guatemalan Government. The Ministry also commended the BDF for their professionalism during the incident.

U.S. Ambassador to Belize André Bauer joined in commending the BDF for their professionalism during the encounter.

During an interview with News 5, Ambassador Bauer said that we should all be grateful that the incident didn’t escalate.

“I wanna recognize that for a bunch of young people that are tasked with keeping this country safe, to not react is a big deal. For young people to conduct themselves and not respond back, but to keep themselves professional, I think we all, as Belizeans and people that live here as part of Belizean society, should be very thankful that that didn’t escalate,” Bauer said.

“My understanding is this happens often. And so, to have a demeanor, to have a professionalism to say, ‘Nope, we’re not gonna respond. We’re gonna wait and have our day in court,’” he added.

In addition, the U.S. Ambassador said that there is hope as the ICJ proceedings for 2027 could finally resolve the Belize-Guatemala territorial dispute.

“ I’m excited about what that will do for them, for how people feel about their country, to know that this is finally over, and they can move forward ’cause it’s gone on far too long,” Bauer said.

World.title: Belize City teen reported missing
World.content:
Belize City teen reported missing

By Zoila Palma: The family and friends of Belize City teen, Andrea Salguero,16, is concerned about her whereabouts.

Salguero was last seen on Friday November 6, 2026.

Since then, she hasn’t been seen or heard from.

Anyone with information on her whereabouts is urged to call Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 app, or report to the nearest police station.

World.title: Guilty after jury fury
World.content:
A photo of Andre Ruddock captured while he lay on the ground at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in St James on the night of October 17, 2021, after he cut the throat of fellow church member Taneka Gardner.

POLICE personnel were forced to rush in and restore order in the jury room at the Supreme Court on Monday after tensions boiled over following a split in their verdict during deliberations in the Andre Ruddock murder trial.

Eventually, after two hours of deliberations, the jury ultimately found Ruddock guilty of murder in the gruesome killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner, whose throat was cut at Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries in St James on October 17, 2021, in what was said to be a human sacrifice ritual.

Earlier, after trial judge Justice Leighton Pusey completed his summation, the jurors were sent off to deliberate at 12:46 pm.

At 1:25 pm police who were guarding the jury room indicated to the court registrar that the panel was ready to deliver the verdict. They were readmitted into the courtroom at 1:37 pm

— 51 minutes after retiring

— at which time the registrar asked the lead juror if they had arrived at a unanimous verdict. The lead juror indicated that they had not, pointing out that five among them believed Ruddock was guilty while two jurors weren’t satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that he had killed Gardner.

Justice Pusey informed the jurors that they would have to spend at least two hours in deliberations before they could return to the courtroom and deliver the verdict. They were subsequently sent back to the jury room by the judge.

At 1:49 pm the registrar again indicated that the jurors were ready to deliver their verdict, leaving everyone inside the courtroom to believe that they had arrived at a unanimous verdict. However, when they entered the jury box and the lead juror was asked if a unanimous verdict had been reached, she again said ‘No’, prompting the judge to explain to them that if the verdict was not unanimous, they would have to spend two hours or more deliberating. Pusey again sent them back to the jury room.

At approximately 2:09 pm, about five members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force were spotted rushing into the jury room where a heated argument was unfolding.

One juror was heard blurting out: “You want to be the boss of everything!” The police managed to cool the tension, then exited to give the jurors space to arrive at a final decision.

However, additional police personnel were called in to join the two who were already standing guard outside the door of the jury room.

At 2:52 pm, the jurors returned to the jury box where the lead juror indicated that there was a slight change in the decision, pointing out that six among them were convinced that Ruddock was guilty of killing Gardner and only one was not so convinced.

Judge Pusey then thanked the jurors for their service before dismissing them. The judge ordered that a social enquiry be done on Ruddock, with a report to be produced in the next six weeks.

Ruddock is to return for sentencing on January 22, 2027.

Lead prosecutor Latoya Bernard told the media that she would not be making any extensive comments on the matter following the verdict. All she offered was that, “The jury has spoken.”

Bernard was supported by prosecutor Carolyn Wright, while Venice Brown supported lead defence attorney Anthony Williams.

After the verdict, Williams breathed a sigh of relief saying, “Boy, the case is finally over.”

“The prosecution’s case essentially is that Mr Ruddock was the one who slashed the throat of Miss Taneka Gardner with a knife on instructions of Mr Kevin Smith. They also alleged that Mr Ruddock gave a caution statement as well as a question and answer document. We contend that, in the first place, it was Mr Kevin Smith who was the person who actually slit or cut Taneka Gardener’s throat.

“We denied it vehemently and that was the defence. We also say that the alleged caution statement and question and answer were, in fact, done under duress. He was forced and intimidated by a policeman in question who held him on the compound of the church. We made very, very heavy waters in this case. It was a very tough case. The jury retired once, it was a 5-2 verdict. They retired twice and in the end they came back with a 6-1 verdict of guilty,” the attorney pointed out.

Williams said the defence was proud of its performance and had given Ruddock the best possible representation in a very challenging case.

“We felt very optimistic of a not guilty verdict, and I say that because of the intensive cross-examination we did of the main witness in particular, as well as the other prosecution witnesses. They were discredited, undermined, and we think we made very good progress. At the end of the day, the jurors are the judges of the fact, and they have concluded that our expectation was not theirs,” Williams said.

Ruddock cut Gardner’s throat on the compound of Pathways International Kingdom Restoration Ministries allegedly on instructions from his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith. It was disclosed during the trial, through a witness, that Gardner’s name appeared on a piece of paper alongside other names. The witness said that Gardner was called onto the compound of the church and instructed by the pastor to write 999 beside her name.

The pastor then told her that she would have to die because her blood was unclean. He then proceeded to ask her if she believed that he could bring her back to life if her throat was to be cut. Gardner reportedly told the pastor “Yes” in response to his question. Smith then instructed a male member of the church to cut her throat. When that member hesitated, Ruddock took a knife from him and carried out the pastor’s order.

Pastor Smith died on October 25, 2021 in a motor vehicle crash on the Linstead bypass in St Catherine while being transported to Kingston by police to face charges.

Authorities reported that he died along with Constable Orlando Irons, who was among the lawmen transporting the cult pastor.

In May 2024 a coroner’s inquest found that the crash did not occur because of excess speed and as such the policemen, who were placed before the inquest, were credible witnesses.

The inquest found that Smith assaulted the cops who were transporting him, and the judge ruled that his actions were unlawful, dangerous, and caused the death of Constable Irons.

World.title: Merl Grove dispute boils over
World.content:
Merl Grove High teachers with placards on Constant Spring Road on Monday morning. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THE smouldering dispute at the all-girls Merl Grove High School in St Andrew boiled over into the public space on Monday, with scores of teachers taking to the streets to stage a silent protest.

Teachers at the school, who refused to speak to the media during their protest, left little doubt that they were opposed to the actions of Principal Dr Marjorie Fullerton who returned to the post in March following a Supreme Court ruling.

Fullerton was first appointed to the post in 2016 but was ousted by the school’s board — based on a recommendation of its Personnel Committee — in 2022 after she was suspended in September 2021.

The veteran educator took her dismissal to the courts which ordered her reinstatement on the basis that the board did not follow procedures of the Education Regulations.

The ruling marked a setback for the school board, the Ministry of Education and the Associated Gospel Assemblies Church, which owns the institution. All had upheld her dismissal following a dispute with staff over her leadership style.

Three months after returning as principal, Fullerton told the Jamaica Observer that the job remains challenging, given that she is still working with the same board that recommended her dismissal four years ago.

“It is not easy at all, because I thought that coming back after six years — and six successful years, and I’m saying successful because the school has moved in terms of ranking and academic performance. And coming back, I thought I was going to see a new board, but I’m facing the same school board, and there were teachers here before who are still here,” said Fullerton.

“It is very difficult if I’m not getting the support that I need. It’s not easy, but I have been through many fights, because I’m a breast cancer survivor, and during the time I was fighting for my job I was also fighting for my life. I believe that, even though it’s not the same thing, it’s still a fight,” she said then.

With the dispute simmering a meeting was organised last month with administrators at the institution and the education ministry’s Regional Educational Services, which mobilised an estimated 100 Merl Grove stakeholders and interested parties to the dispute.

According to Observer sources, the meeting was being spearheaded by the ministry not as a formal hearing, but to allow internal stakeholders to express their concerns and work towards achieving a more harmonious and conducive environment.

The ministry later indicated that it would be reviewing the outcome of the discussions for a follow-up meeting to be decided.

Some stakeholders said they were hopeful that the meeting would achieve a resolution but suggested that some of the issues were controversial and would require patience and a willingness to end the dispute.

When the Observer visited the institution on Monday, teachers were observed bearing placards calling for the resignation of Fullerton, but remained tight-lipped about what prompted the morning’s protest.

Efforts to speak with Fullerton were unsuccessful.

World.title: Resilience takes centre stage
World.content:
Protoje delivers a masterful set at the Treasure Beach Food, Rum and Reggae Festival at Breds Sports Park last weekend. (Photo: Brian Pitter)

If Friday night’s Dubwise session at Jack Sprat was the spark that ignited the 2026 Treasure Beach Food, Rum & Reggae Festival, then Saturday’s main stage concert at Breds Sports Park was a full-on fire.

Riding high on a wave of resilience, the Treasure Beach community pulled off a seamless post-Hurricane Melissa event, proving that a parish twice ravaged by back-to-back natural disasters simply refuses to lose its spark.

Through powerhouse performances from Lila Iké and Protoje the event transcended expectations. Song after song the concert became more than just another item on the annual entertainment calendar; it was a profound celebration of resilience, musical lineage, and cultural preservation.

Sporting her signature Afro, Lila Iké stepped into the spotlight, and the atmosphere inside the venue shifted instantly. Known for her remarkable ability to cater to a diverse cross section of fans, Lila Iké delivered a beautifully balanced set list that bridged the gap between sweet, vulnerable love songs and hard-hitting social commentary.

Opening her set with a soulful rendition of her powerful hit single Scatter, the artiste immediately captivated the crowd and established the tone for the rest of her performance. Building on that momentum with each successive track, the reggae songstress stamped her class on the evening. Songs such as Thy Will Be Done, Forget Me, Solitude, and Second Chance were well received by patrons, but it was her spirited performance of Where I’m Coming From that proved the highlight of her set.

As she introduced the track, she was met with screams of approval from the crowd. The single took on an added layer of purpose, resonating deeply with the St Elizabeth audience.

“Weh di people dem deh weh glad weh dem a come from dung a St Bess tonight? No disaster cyaan mash dis dung,” she said, sending the crowd into a frenzy.

“Yeah, St Bess, a we say resilience,” she continued before launching into the track.

Its lyrics, which speak to struggle, identity, resilience, and divine timing, struck a chord with the audience. The response was unmistakable, as Lila Iké’s set was punctuated by massive forwards and gun-fingers in the air from patrons who had connected deeply with her message.

By the time she brought her performance to a close the singer had further cemented her place among the leading voices of the modern reggae movement.

But the night’s musical treats didn’t end there. St Elizabeth was in for more, this time from one of its own, as Protoje took to the stage. As the headlining general of the In.Digg.Nation Collective, Protoje’s arrival was greeted by a thunderous roar that echoed across the sports park. With his signature effortless command, he delivered a structurally brilliant set, drawing heavily from his catalogue of “message music” and urgent social commentary, while seamlessly weaving in the relaxed, party-centric sounds that keep a festival crowd moving.

Protoje commanded the stage with precision, launching into conscious anthems such as Blood Money and Kingston Be Wise. The tracks, which highlight the socio-political issues affecting Jamaica, made quite an impact on the crowd. Chanting lyrics of resistance word for word, patrons transformed Breds Sports Park into a unified space of collective consciousness.

Recognising the assignment of a weekend festival fuelled by premium Jamaican rum, Protoje masterfully shifted gears into his lighter, feel-good catalogue. The weight of the socio-political commentary gave way to pure relaxation when the band struck up the infectious party anthem Big 45. The smooth, celebratory rhythms of Switch It Up and Who Knows continued to transform the atmosphere into one massive skanking party, allowing patrons to lose themselves in the sweet sounds of reggae.

But the true climax of Saturday night came when the catalogues of both main acts collided. The synergy between Protoje and Lila Iké was undeniable as the pair shared the stage. Bringing an entirely different level of artistic chemistry, the duo performed their collaboration All Over The World. Energy levels peaked as the two artistes traded verses with a seamless, almost familial rapport that spoke to their mutual artistic respect and the strength of their musical connection.

What’s more, patrons were treated to a little ‘brawta’ when Jesse Royal made a surprise appearance. The Small Axe artiste delivered a short but spicy set, joining Protoje for a performance of Sudden Flight, a collaboration the two entertainers recorded alongside Sevana more than a decade ago.

As the curtains closed on a successful staging of the St Elizabeth music festival, it became clear that the event was never just about entertainment. It was a declaration that the culture of the south coast cannot be washed away.

According to Gregory Wright, festival director, through the power of reggae’s finest contemporary voices, Treasure Beach didn’t just celebrate its recovery; it danced its way into a new chapter.

“Returning the festival to its home in St Elizabeth this year was especially meaningful for us, particularly after the parish was impacted by Hurricane Melissa last year. We are incredibly grateful for the opportunity to return and for the tremendous support and turnout we received, which exceeded our expectations,” he said. “The atmosphere throughout the festival was truly special, with the DJs delivering strong sets and the artistes putting on great performances, engaging with the audience and creating an experience that felt both celebratory and meaningful.

“We were also grateful for the artistes’ support beyond the stage, including our headliners, Lila Iké and Protoje, who took the time to interact with patrons and experience different aspects of the festival weekend,” he continued. “We are excited about what this means for the parish and look forward to building on this momentum in the years ahead.”

World.title: Chase credits Warrican for series win
World.content:
West Indies’ Jomel Warrican (centre) has been named Player of the Series after taking 16 wickets in the Caribbean side’s 1-0 series victory over Bangladesh. (Photo: AFP)

SYLHET, Bangladesh (CMC) — West Indies Test Captain Roston Chase has credited his deputy, Jomel Warrican, as one of the main reasons behind his side’s success in their just concluded two-match Test series against Bangladesh.

The West Indies won the series 1-0 after the second Test at the Sylhet International Cricket Stadium ended in a tame draw on Monday.

Left-arm spinner Warrican was named Player-of-the-Series after finishing with 16 wickets, the most of any player in the series.

He snared nine wickets and took home the Player-of-the-Match award in the opening Test in Dhaka, which the West Indies won by eight wickets, before returning to claim seven wickets in the final match.

Speaking in a post-match interview, Chase said Warrican’s variations were too much for the home side’s batters to handle.

“I thought Warrican bowled well in both games. He controlled his economy rate very well and I thought that he built a lot of pressure and put the balls in front of the batsmen for a long period of time, so I thought that was the hallmark of his bowling throughout the series along with straightening and spinning as well.

“I thought that he really kept us in this series and really won the series for us,” Chase said.

Speaking on the Windies’ victory, Chase said while they would have liked to win both matches, he was pleased with the team’s performance.

With the win, the regional team moved up to sixth in the ICC’s updated Test rankings, achieving a goal they set out to do from the start of the Test Championship cycle.

“I’m very happy obviously. Coming to Bangladesh is always a tough place to come and play cricket, so to beat them in their own back yard is always a pleasure.

“We wanted to win both games, but it didn’t happen. This game was a bit slower than the first one, especially with all the bad light taking time out of the game, but we still played well and kudos to the guys for winning the series,” Chase said.

“We had a tough year in the first year of the cycle and we sat down and we spoke about coming to dominate the second year in the cycle playing against Pakistan, Sri Lanka and also Bangladesh. We thought these were teams that were obviously closer to our skill level and closer to us in the rankings, so we wanted to challenge ourselves in terms of winning all three series.

“We won two out of three so I thought that it was a good year and also we went unbeaten in any series, which is something that hasn’t been done for a number of years. So, it just goes to show that when you sit down and plan and put in the hard work anything is achievable, so I think we’re going in the right direction as a unit,” the skipper added.

World.title: DIFFERENT BALL GAME!
World.content:
Demario Phillips (right) of Mount Pleasant moves in to close down LA Galaxy player Harbor Miller during both teams’ Concacaf Champions Cup match at the National Stadium on March 19, 2026. LA Galaxy won both legs by a 3-0 margin for a 6-0 aggregate score. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FORMER Reggae Boy Tyrone Marshall has noticed a challenge facing Jamaican clubs in continental football that goes beyond a lack of money and facilities. He said the way players are trained, prepared and taught to understand the game must also improve if local teams are to compete with clubs from Major League Soccer (MLS) and Liga MX.

Marshall, who has played more than 80 times for Jamaica, spent much of his playing career in MLS before moving into coaching in North America. His coaching experience includes roles as an assistant coach at Real Salt Lake and head coach of FC Cincinnati 2. He has also completed coaching certification at France’s Clairefontaine training centre.

His experience has given him an understanding of the differences between the professional environments in North America and Jamaica’s Legend Jamaica Premier League (JPL).

Marshall identifies the lack of an integrated sports science and recovery system as one of the biggest gaps affecting local players’ ability to maintain their performance over 90 minutes.

“In my experience in the professional game at the MLS level, it’s a different game compared to playing in the Jamaica Premier League,” Marshall told the Jamaica Observer.

“All the MLS and Liga MX teams have invested heavily in sports science — strengthening, conditioning, nutrition, physiotherapy, recovery technology, so on and so forth, to monitor the performance of their players so that they can maximise their efficiency when they get on the field.”

He said Jamaica has the talent and athletic ability, but players need consistent support with training, recovery and workload management. Without those systems, fatigue can affect more than their ability to run.

“When you have games and fatigue becomes a factor, the decision-making slows down, movement becomes less sharp, and the ability to maintain intensity begins to decline,” Marshall said.

His comments support concerns raised by Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL) Chief Executive Officer Owen Hill, who has identified gyms, recovery facilities and technical analysis as areas that need improvement across the 14 JPL clubs.

Hill, in a recent interview with the Observer, also mentioned what he sees as a shortage of specialised technical support.

“We don’t have super technical analysts that can scout a team, can tell you how the formation works, can give you all of that information to guide your own preparation,” Hill said in an Observer article on Sunday.

Marshall’s assessment shows why those resources matter on the field. Players need to recover properly and maintain their physical condition, particularly when they face demanding schedules and opponents who can sustain a high tempo.

However, Marshall said the problem is not only physical. He pointed to tactical awareness and decision-making under pressure as other areas where Jamaican players need to improve.

“Jamaican players have excellent athletic ability,” he said. “The creative technical abilities are there in the individual flair, which is God-given. However, when they step up and play international competition, the game does become much more demanding tactically. The opponents are better organised, the space gets closed down quicker, the players have much less time to make decisions.”

One area he identifies for particular attention is playing without the ball. Players must understand how to create space and passing options, when to press, how to maintain their defensive shape and how to anticipate what opponents will do next.

“It is not just about being talented when you have possession. You must understand how to influence the game when you don’t have the ball,” Marshall said.

Marshall also said players sometimes try to force passes or solve problems individually when better decisions could help their teams retain possession and control the game.

Hill identified a related issue in the way Jamaican football approaches matches.

“Tactically, we’re getting better, but in terms of our strategic approach to games, which, I think, goes deeper than the talent we have, it’s probably the resource gaps, ” he said.

Marshall’s comments provide a closer look at what that gap means for players and coaches, especially the need to improve how teams prepare for opponents and respond to different situations during matches.

Marshall said the standard of competition in the JPL must also improve to prepare players for the demands of international football.

“When you compete against teams regionally, in particular MLS and Liga MX, or other established professional leagues, the tempo is different,” he said. “The level is higher. Speed is faster. Players are stronger. When they press, they press with more coordination. The transitions happen much quicker.”

Marshall said players cannot be expected to maintain a high press and defensive shape against stronger opponents if those habits are not developed during regular training and league matches.

“You cannot expect a team to suddenly execute in a high press and maintain defensive shape if they don’t practise it — develop the habit where they can do this on a day-to-day basis — during training and during the league,” he said.

Squad depth and finances are also important, particularly when clubs have to manage injuries, travel and congested schedules. However, Marshall cautions against treating money as the only explanation for the gap.

He mentions coaching methods, tactical education, player recruitment and the overall training culture as equally important.

For clubs working with limited resources, Marshall recommends making youth development a priority. He wants clubs to establish a consistent playing philosophy from their academies through to their senior teams so young players understand the style of football expected of them as they progress.

He also calls for greater attention to coaching education and the use of performance analysts.

Marshall recalls his experience at Clairefontaine, where young players aged 14 and 15 studied match footage in the classroom as part of their development. They learned about different defensive systems, pressing, and how to analyse their own performances before putting those lessons into practice on the field.

He said Jamaican clubs must place greater emphasis on teaching players to understand the game from an early age.

“Ultimately I would not put all our resources into the physical conditioning alone because ultimately you don’t want to have a fit player and he can’t think for himself and don’t know how to pass the ball and all of that,” Marshall said.

“When you invest, you want to ensure you develop a fitter, smarter and more tactically adept player in a sustainable system.”

Marshall said clubs can improve their coaching standards and training environments without having the financial resources of MLS and Liga MX teams. But he warns against looking for quick solutions.

“We need to stop looking for quick fixes and start building environments that will produce better players year after year after year,” he said.

While there is agreement that a solution can be found, Hill did say that building a league capable of competing consistently at the highest regional level will take at least 10 to 15 years.

Cavalier were eliminated by Inter Miami by a 4-0 aggregate scoreline in 2025 after suffering 2-0 defeats in both legs while Mount Pleasant suffered a 6-0 aggregate defeat to LA Galaxy in this year after losing both legs 3-0 in the most recent clashes between JPL and MLS clubs in the Concacaf Champions Cup round of 16.

World.title: LuxBrides JA: BEYOND PARIS
World.content:
Model Nesrin Sanad stepped out in the Vine gown, a fitted silhouette with intricate botanical-inspired detailing and a statement slit. Alex Callejo

The Grand Entrance was inspired by the beauty, structure and transformation of flora, interpreted through the language of contemporary bridal couture.

I have always been fascinated by the delicate yet striking characteristics of botanical forms, from the intricate arrangement of petals to the dramatic beauty of a flower in full bloom.

I wanted to translate those elements into a collection that explored the relationship between softness and strength, romance and structure, and timeless bridal elegance and modern artistic expression.

The seven gowns were presented as a cohesive visual narrative, beginning with romantic silhouettes and gradually introducing more expressive structures, dimensional floral detailing, intricate embellishments and dramatic volume.

Each design has its own personality while contributing to the collection’s overarching story.

The Seven Looks



1. Sovereign — Romance with a Commanding Presence: A regal ballgown combining intricate lace, a structured bodice and a delicate high-neck overlay, establishing the collection’s romantic foundation.

2. Fleur — Where Romance Begins to Bloom: A striking sweetheart ballgown distinguished by cascading, petal-inspired layers that evoke the delicate unfolding of a flower.

3. Étoile — The Bloom Begins to Shine: An elegant statement gown featuring intricate floral embellishments, sculptural structure and a balance of romance and sophistication.

4. Vine — Romance Entwined with Radiance: A contemporary fitted silhouette with intricate botanical-inspired detailing and a statement slit, introducing modern elegance and fluidity.

5. Empress — Where Romance Blossoms into Royalty: A commanding ballgown featuring elaborate bodice detailing and flowing cape-inspired styling, embodying regal femininity.

6. Imperia — An Expression of Sculptural Grandeur: A dramatic off-the-shoulder creation combining dimensional floral embellishments, architectural structure and luxurious volume.

7. Eden — The Grand Finale: An extraordinary multi-tiered gown featuring sculptural layers, intricate detailing and dramatic proportions, representing the collection’s fullest expression of bloom.

Beyond Paris: The Next Chapter for LuxBrides JA



While Paris Fashion Week represents a defining milestone in our journey, I see it as the beginning of an exciting new chapter for LuxBrides JA.

My vision is to continue elevating the brand’s presence within the international luxury bridal industry while remaining proudly rooted in Jamaica. The experience has reinforced my commitment to creative excellence, innovation and developing a distinctive identity that resonates with brides both locally and internationally.

World.title: UPDATE: Police recover stolen courier vehicle, but money missing
World.content:
Stock image of armoured courier

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Police have recovered the courier vehicle stolen on Old Hope Road in St Andrew on Monday evening, but the money it was carrying remains missing.

Observer Online understands that vehicle was recovered in the vicinity of Blue Castle Drive, off Old Hope Road. A shotgun was reportedly also recovered. The value of the missing money is unclear at the moment.
