World.title: Thieves reportedly steal cash-loaded courier vehicle on Old Hope Road
World.content:
Stock photo of an armoured truck.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Thieves reportedly stole a cash-loaded courier vehicle belonging to a security company on Old Hope Road in St Andrew, the Jamaica Observer understands.

The vehicle reportedly went to pick up money from a popular fast food establishment when the heist occurred.

It is still to be officially confirmed, but it is alleged that armed guards exited the vehicle when it arrived at the popular fast food establishment on Old Hope Road to pick up the yield for the day.

While that was happening, the thieves hijacked the vehicle and made off with money that the couriers had previously picked up for the day from other establishments.

More details to follow.

World.title: L’Europe a besoin de Nvidia et il faudra plus qu’un scandale d’espionnage pour que ça change
World.content:
En réponse à une avalanche de questions sur l’entreprise, un porte-parole du gouvernement allemand a déclaré, lundi, que celui-ci “ne commentait pas les informations relayées par les médias” et que “nous respectons toujours les normes les plus strictes, y compris lors de la conclusion d’accords”. Un porte-parole de la Commission européenne n’a pas non plus souhaité s’exprimer sur le sujet.

Dans la Silicon Valley comme à Washington, les enquêteurs sont déjà à pied d’œuvre. Nvidia a ouvert une enquête interne visant à déterminer si son PDG avait été la cible d’une opération des services de renseignement chinois. Jensen Huang a entretenu une relation intime avec une femme d’affaires chinoise soupçonnée d’avoir tenté de transmettre à Pékin des informations confidentielles sur les puces électroniques américaines. Il a même reconnu publiquement avoir eu une liaison.

Le Congrès américain, en particulier ses membres les plus méfiantes envers la Chine, s’apprête également à prendre des mesures. “Les Etats-Unis devraient immédiatement suspendre les livraisons de puces d’IA de pointe à la Chine jusqu’à ce que nous ayons fait toute la lumière sur cet incident, et que nous nous soyons assurés que notre sécurité nationale n’est pas compromise”, a posté sur X Michael McCaul, représentant républicain du Texas et ancien président de la commission des Affaires étrangères de la Chambre basse.

A Bruxelles, le revers essuyé par le géant de la Silicon Valley pourrait sembler être une bonne nouvelle pour ceux qui mettent en garde contre la domination technologique américaine dans la course à l'IA. Mais, à l'instar des récents résultats des élections de mi-mandat, les difficultés rencontrées par Nvidia ne changent en rien la réalité européenne, car l'Union européenne dépend fortement des puces d'IA de cette entreprise.

“Nous n'avons pas d'autre choix, la conception [des puces] est presque entièrement américaine”, a souligné Bart Groothuis, eurodéputé néerlandais et l'un des négociateurs du dernier plan de l'UE en matière de fabrication de puces.

Bart Groothuis a dénoncé la “position monopolistique étrange” de Nvidia.

World.title: 5 ways Spain’s conservatives plan to put the country on a new course
World.content:
1. Clampdown on migration

The PP plans to harden Spain’s stance on immigration — a move that goes hand in hand with Vox.

The conservatives “will promote agreements to establish return centers in third countries,” following in the footsteps of other EU countries such as Denmark and Germany, which are already exploring this option. They will propose deportation as “the standard procedure” for migrants convicted of sexual, violent and repeated offenses.

The party will ban future mass regularizations such as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s move to grant legal status to 500,000 people — which Feijóo has fiercely criticized. The PP will also make it mandatory for foreign nationals who want to renew their temporary residence to sign an “integration agreement,” learn Spanish and become “familiar with the Constitution and the values of the EU.”

2. Not so green

As first reported in POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook, five nuclear plants would see their licenses extended. The PP will also relax climate rules, putting “an end to the imposition of unrealistic timelines,” based on three factors: “What is happening in the rest of the world, the technology that is available at the moment and changes in demand.”

On data centers, the manifesto calls for additional capacity on the electricity grid to meet Spain’s demand. On the fiscal side of energy, the document proposes to “immediately eliminate the 7% tax on electricity production and reduce fixed-rate energy contracts.”

3. All quiet on the foreign front

While Sánchez has been particularly vocal on foreign policy, criticizing Israel for its war in Gaza and the U.S. administration, at times diverging from most of his European partners, the PP will keep a lower profile.

World.title: Surge in EV demand blows past German government’s subsidy forecasts
World.content:
The budget allocation is being adjusted, but "without changing the overall size of the program."

According to government estimates, the funding is enough to subsidize around 800,000 vehicles. Buyers can receive government grants of up to €6,000 per vehicle.

In early October, Germany's BAFA export control agency, which administers the scheme, said it had already approved 100,000 applications and paid out more than €430 million.

If applications continue at the same pace, spending could reach €1 billion in 2026. The federal budget originally earmarked just €803 million for the scheme in 2027, but the government now expects to pay out €1.7 billion — draining the fund.

So far, the government has given no indication of whether it intends to put more cash into the program.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said in October that demand had exceeded all expectations. At the same time, he sought to reassure prospective buyers that there is enough money in the program to continue funding through 2027.

World.title: EU watchdog probes Commission’s AI pick over conflict of interest concerns
World.content:
The European Ombudsman in September launched a probe into the Commission over its failure to respond to the NGO concerns.

Now, it has gone one step further.

“You argue that the Commission did not properly identify, assess, and address actual or potential conflicts of interest,” Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho wrote in a letter to Corporate Europe Observatory. “Therefore you would like the Commission to revoke the appointment.”

“I have decided to open an inquiry into this complaint,” she wrote, adding that it was necessary for the watchdog to inspect Commission documents, and possibly meet with “relevant Commission staff members.”

Bram Vranken, Corporate Europe Observatory researcher and campaigner, said “it is clearly impossible for Mr Hagemann Snabe to navigate the potential conflicts of interest. He has direct financial interests in the data centre build-out and watering down rules on AI."

Snabe will serve in the unpaid role until the end of March 2027.

World.title: Iran denies role in cyberattacks on French supermarket refrigerators
World.content:
“We'll take all measures, including those we will not disclose publicly, which we ourselves consider proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks and punish those responsible for this unacceptable aggression,” he said.

Iran’s ambassador to France has been summoned to the foreign ministry after French prosecutors said that they were opening an investigation into the hacks.

According to French investigators, Iran’s cyber unit linked to the IRGC, Shahid Kaveh, carried out the destructive attacks.

The French investigation will focus on the unit’s head, the Paris prosecutor’s office said in a statement, adding that about 20 fires had been started because of the cyberattack.

“The attackers took remote control of the equipment via web interfaces to trigger abnormal defrost cycles of unlimited duration, while disabling the security alerts on the sensors that were supposed to activate once a certain temperature was exceeded,” it added.

On Monday, European Council President Kaja Kallas said that the topic of alleged Iranian hacks would be discussed at next week’s European foreign affairs council. If the attribution is confirmed, she said, “[Europe’s] response should be strong.”

World.title: EU needs only ‘very trusted partners’ on AI chips, tech chief says amid Nvidia crisis
World.content:
Virkkunen did not detail whether she considered Nvidia less trustworthy since news of the spy scandal broke. When asked who she considers trusted partners, she described the U.S. as the EU’s traditionally “closest partner when it comes to security and technology,” suggesting the bloc has no intention of blaming the U.S. but would prefer to collaborate to plug the security gap.

In “limited areas of technologies,” it is important to ensure that “we don’t have that kind of technological leakages,” the EU tech chief said. “We want to really keep the business secrets in Europe.”

Europe is heavily reliant on Nvidia chips, since it has little production or design capacity for AI chips of its own — something that the EU aims to correct for through an industrial policy push into chipmaking called the European Chips Act.

“It’s true that currently Europe is very dependent on AI chips on a few American companies and that's why it's important also that we are building up our own capacity to also design and also manufacture more advanced [chips] and also AI chips in the coming years," Virkkunen said.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Merz clashes with Fico over German bid to link EU budget and Ukraine loan
World.content:
The EU and partners are currently discussing a new €70 billion loan to support Ukraine in the next year against sustained Russian attacks. The EU plans to shoulder about €45 billion of the loan, while other allies like Britain, Canada and Japan are expected to stump up the remaining €25 billion.

Merz argued that he does not want to repeat last year’s approach, when a different €90 billion loan for Ukraine was agreed only with financial guarantees and liabilities from most EU countries, while three nations — Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia — secured an opt-out.

“In my view, continuing down this path is not a good option. We must fully incorporate Ukraine policy into the EU budget,” he said.

However, that view is not shared by Magyar, who came to Berlin with four ministers and a state secretary to discuss deeper cooperation, underlining the general rapprochement between Germany and Hungary after years of icy relations under Budapest’s previous leader Viktor Orbán.

“I would like to note here — diplomatically and with all due respect as the Hungarian prime minister — that I do not necessarily consider it the right approach for the European budget, which is actually intended for seven years and for Europe,” to be “linked to other matters,” Magyar said.

World.title: Europe and US agree to review postwar continental security as Ukraine talks begin
World.content:
Before the teams from Ukraine and Russia met, preparatory talks took place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday morning involving European powers, Ukraine and the U.S. team. Two officials familiar with these discussions, granted anonymity to discuss confidential matters, said these first talks were substantial and the mood was positive.

The topic of Europe’s future security architecture is acutely sensitive for European governments, who fear that President Donald Trump may be preparing to radically reduce U.S. support for security in their region, after years of bashing NATO allies.

Russia has been demanding a say over scaling back NATO’s efforts in Europe and has repeatedly insisted Ukraine should never join the alliance, something Kyiv and its closest allies have traditionally supported.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signs a guestbook in Berlin on Nov. 3, 2026. | Ralf Hirschberger/AFP via Getty Images

One critical question is sequencing. Will a deal on wider European security be part of a final Ukraine peace agreement or will it come later? Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and some of his strongest supporters have said in the past that there is no place for Russia to demand a wider European-NATO settlement as a condition for ending the war.

The Abu Dhabi talks mark the first time in nine months that negotiators from Ukraine and Russia have met with representatives from the U.S. for trilateral negotiations on peace. Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, and Witkoff are leading for the American side and pushing hard to expand the scope of the discussion to include Europe’s future security, and to get Europe a seat at the table.

Since Trump returned to the White House last year, his administration has publicly and privately criticized Europeans for not doing enough to take responsibility for their own defenses. Under American pressure, NATO allies agreed new targets to increase their spending on security and defense to 5% of GDP by 2035.

World.title: Democrats took the House, Senate and a good deal of Republican pride: So who are the real winners and losers?
World.content:
Two years ago, Hakeem Jeffries was a minority leader watching Republicans run the table in Washington. He is now the presumptive Speaker of the House, the most powerful member of Congress, and is expected to take the gavel in January.

 

By Tuesday, projections showed Democrats winning 254 seats to the Republicans’ 165, with 16 races still to be called. NBC News projects they will finish with 259, which would be the party's biggest majority in more than three decades.

A narrow one would have handed a dozen or so left-wing members a veto over his speakership and his agenda, and several incoming Democrats are still withholding their support. He can now afford at least three dozen defections.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks at a news conference in Washington, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) AP Photo

The same arithmetic works on legislation: he can lose his party's fringe on a bill and still pass it. Jeffries is set to become the first Black speaker in American history, and he inherits the two things this White House fears most from a Democratic House: control of spending and the power to subpoena.

Loser: Donald Trump

For two months, Donald Trump told voters to “pretend I'm on the ballot.” He took that message to Texas, Iowa and Kansas, states where his party should never have needed the help. Voters did as they were asked. Trump won Texas by 13.6 points in 2024. Democrat James Talarico won it by 12 last week. Kansas swung 21 points towards the Democrats, and South Carolina swung 22.

Mississippi, a state Trump won by 23 points, is still too close to call. About 24 hours after his last plea, the president posted that he “wasn't on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

The exit polls disagree. His approval among midterm voters stood at 37%. Many of his voters also appear to have stayed home: Trump voters made up 44% of last week's electorate, well short of the 49.8% of the vote he won in 2024. Trump has blamed weak candidates.

The trouble is most of them were his. He endorsed Ken Paxton over a sitting senator, handpicked Darline Graham and backed Michael Whatley. “It wasn't me” is a hard sell when your name is on every endorsement.

Winner: Moderate Democrats

If Democrats had a strategy, it was to be boring in all the right places. In Kansas, they ran Adam Hamilton, a first-time candidate who leads the largest United Methodist church in the US. In South Carolina, a paediatrician.

In North Carolina, a former two-term governor. In Iowa, a state lawmaker and four-time Paralympian who promised to work with Trump on border security. Independents were ready to punish Trump, and boring gave them a safe place to land.

Supporters cheer during an election night event for Iowa Democrats Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt) Supporters cheer during an election night event for Iowa Democrats Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)

Kamala Harris won independents by just three points in 2024. Last week, Democrats won them 58% to 38%, a 20-point margin. Roughly two-thirds of moderates backed Democrats for the House, up from about six in 10 for Harris.

Even Talarico, more liberal than most of the other seat-flippers, won Texas with a friendly, centrist pitch, taking about two-thirds of moderates, most independents and roughly one in 10 Republicans.

In Mississippi, District Attorney Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes, and that race is likely headed for a legal fight.

Losers: Ken Paxton and the MAGA picks

Trump's own advisers warned him that Ken Paxton carried too much baggage. He endorsed him anyway, calling the scandal-plagued attorney general “a true MAGA Warrior” and helping him push Senator John Cornyn out in the May runoff.

In October, Trump said he had no regrets because “Cornyn would have lost.” We will never know. We do know Paxton lost by 12 points in once-red Texas.

The pattern repeated across the map. Majorities of voters in Iowa and Ohio said their Republican candidates were “too supportive” of Trump, and most North Carolina voters said the same of Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman. Nationally, 6% of Republicans voted for Democrats.

That sounds small until you get to Texas, where about one in 10 crossed over. When your own voters walk across the aisle at that rate, the problem is not the ground game. It is the candidate and the message.

Winner: Progressive Democrats

The moderates won the map, but the progressive left won the primaries and a fair number of general elections too. Abdul El-Sayed, a Bernie Sanders ally, beat Mike Rogers in Michigan to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., center, poses for a photograph in his office with Sen.-elects Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Josh Turek, D-Iowa, Roy Cooper, D-N.C. AP Photo

Peggy Flanagan held Minnesota and Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins in Maine, both from the party's progressive wing. In 2010, a Tea Party wave swept into Washington, and its heirs went on to form the Freedom Caucus and make life miserable for Republican speakers.

The new progressive class could build the same kind of bloc and do the same to Jeffries. Majorities are easier to win than to manage.

Loser: The Graham name in South Carolina

For 23 years, Graham meant South Carolina's Senate seat. After Lindsey Graham unexpectedly died in July, his sister Darline took over as interim senator and became Trump's handpicked candidate to keep the seat in the family.

It did not go to plan. She flubbed a foreign policy question on the debate stage, and about two-thirds of voters said she lacked the right experience.

Even some Republicans hesitated. Others split their tickets, backing Republican Alan Wilson for governor but not Graham. Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since Fritz Hollings in 1998.

The family name carried a seat for two decades. It could not carry this campaign.

Winners: Kyiv and Brussels

The Kyiv Independent's headline said it plainly: “Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine.” A Democratic Congress holds the purse strings, and a Democratic Senate will be in no mood to wave through a deal that leaves Ukraine short.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he was optimistic both parties would now engage more with each other to boost backing for Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, hands over the Ukraine state award to European Council President Antonio Costa during a commemorative ceremony in Kyiv, AP Photo

Brussels will also note that tariffs proved a liability at the ballot box, with 66% of voters saying they hurt the US economy. Ukraine is one of the few places Trump could throw Democrats a bone, claim a bipartisan win and look like a dealmaker in the process. Whether he prioritises it over Israel and Iran is another matter.

Loser: JD Vance

JD Vance went into election day as a Republican front-runner for 2028. He comes out of it as vice president during a historic defeat. The morning after, he offered his own verdict: “The reason we lost is the war.”

It is a rare thing for a vice president to say about his own president's war in Iran, and Republican primary voters will read it either as courage or as a man reaching for the exit.

Some on the right have already chosen the second reading. A Washington Examiner op-ed called him “fundamentally unfit to lead the Republican Party".

It did not help that, asked a week before the election by a young Republican how her generation could afford to start a family, Vance opened with a joke about Jon Husted's backside. Husted lost Ohio. The seat he was defending was Vance's old one.

Vice President JD Vance starts to say a prayer for a person who required medical attention while he was speaking during a campaign rally at the D&N Event Center in North Platt AP Photo

Winners: James Talarico and Jon Ossoff

Every wave produces its stars, and this one produced two. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state lawmaker, ended a Democratic drought of more than 30 years in Texas statewide races and summed it up in five words: “We just took back Texas.”

Jon Ossoff, 39, did the harder thing in a wave year and made Georgia look easy. He beat Mike Collins by 18 points in a state Trump won two years ago, after raising $126 million more than his opponent.

Ossoff insists he has “zero interest in running for president.”

Washington has heard that before. Both men will spend the next two years fielding questions about 2028, and both will enjoy it more than they let on.

Loser: Trump's inner circle

Robert Garcia, who will chair the House Oversight Committee, summed up his plans in two words on election night: “Lawyer up.” His first target, he says, is “the Trump Crime Family.”

World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto company, tops that list, along with the Emirati royal nicknamed the “Spy Sheikh", who bought a $500 million stake in it.

Donald Trump Jr.'s venture firm, 1789 Capital, is next in the queue. Jamie Raskin, set to chair the Judiciary Committee, says Don Jr. “seems to have a clairvoyant sensibility of exactly who is going to get government contracts.”

Jared Kushner, Raskin says, “is a corporate executive that we absolutely will need to talk to.” Aides are on the list too.

Jared Kushner, center, and Steve Witkoff, right, U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, meet with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Mariinsky palace in Kyiv, Ukraine AP Photo

Garcia says Attorney General Todd Blanche could face a subpoena on “day one” and has promised quick action on alleged pay-to-play involving Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski. The White House can lean on executive privilege. The family businesses and their backers cannot.

Winners: Ad-makers, TV stations and, finally, viewers

OpenSecrets projects this will be the most expensive midterm in American history, at $11.9 billion, about a third more than in 2022. Ohio's Senate race topped $500 million on its own, more than $100 for every vote cast.

For the ad-makers, consultants and local TV stations of Ohio, Texas and Georgia, Christmas came in October.

The real winners, though, are viewers, who can now watch the evening news or a football game without being told someone's opponent wants to destroy America. Enjoy the quiet. The 2028 primaries start sooner than anyone would like.

Loser: Americans who want Washington to get something done

Voters sent Washington a to-do list last week. Washington is about to lose it. About eight in 10 registered voters told an AP-NORC poll last month that lowering the cost of living should be one of Congress' highest priorities, and roughly seven in 10 said the same of ending the war with Iran.

About half said the same about finding common ground between the parties. What they will get is a stand-off.

Trump has already told Fox News what happens next: “They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them.” Democrats are well short of the two-thirds needed to override him, and Senate Republicans still have the numbers to filibuster.

That leaves the executive order, even though 71% of voters told exit pollsters they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president. Add the investigations, and expect a lot of hearings and very few laws.

Three-quarters of voters already disapprove of Congress, according to the NBC News Exit Poll, and two years of gridlock will not change that. Prices, the war, the deficit and immigration will mostly be kicked down the road to 2028, by which point everyone will be campaigning again.

World.title: Costa seeks to reassure Merz after EU budget ultimatum
World.content:
European Council President António Costa has sought to reassure German Chancellor Friedrich Merz after he sent a letter laying down an ultimatum linking the EU budget to financing for Ukraine by all member states.

 

In a letter seen by Euronews, Costa said the discussion on the two issues will take place at the end of the month during a special summit in Brussels, once the European Commission has presented proposals to cover Ukraine's financial shorfall.

Merz, however, pushed to have the debate at this week's informal summit in Dublin.

"In light of ongoing developments, I will make time for a broad discussion on Ukraine at the upcoming informal European Council in Dublin," Costa says, leaving the door open for Merz to raise the issue with his peers.

The EU has promised to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's €70 billion gap, roughly €45 billion, through a yet-to-be-defined instrument. Given the massive scale of the needs, a new round of joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunner option.

Merz told Costa that a commitment to provide fresh aid for Ukraine was an "essential prerequisite" for approving the next EU budget. The move effectively ties two highly contentious issues, both of which require unanimity.

"Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support," Merz wrote.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have already pushed back against Merz's ultimatum, with Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico calling it "blackmail".

The four countries want to opt out from any future loan to Ukraine.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 10th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. World.title: Portugal on alert as storms Bruna and Charles raise sting jet risk of 160 km/h winds
World.content:
Portugal is on alert as the depressions Bruna and Charles pass over the country. For this Wednesday there is also the possibility of a phenomenon called sting jet, a rare meteorological event that can produce gusts with greater destructive power, as happened with Kristin at the beginning of the year, when it devastated several regions of the district of Leiria.

 

The Greater Lisbon area deserves particular attention because this phenomenon may occur there, especially between midday and late afternoon on Wednesday.

On Tuesday, during a precautionary press conference held by Civil Protection, IPMA acknowledged the possibility that a sting jet could form. "There are some signs that it may occur, but it is very hard to predict. That is what happened in storm Kristin and it is on the table," said Jorge Ponte of IPMA.

According to the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA), a sting jet is an air current that descends rapidly inside an extratropical depression and can hit the surface with great intensity. This phenomenon, which occurs in a relatively small and localised area, can produce very strong wind gusts, which may exceed 160 kilometres per hour, and cause significant damage.

Climate change specialist Duarte Costa, who turned to social media to explain the phenomenon and warn of the associated risks, describes it as "an extremely violent jet of wind that drops from the mid-levels of a storm down to the surface, suddenly and in a very localised way, as a result of a strong intensification when passing through a jet stream".

Simulations from the European ECMWF model show a hook-shaped pattern, "a dangerous similarity to the sting jet phenomenon", says Duarte Costa.

The big difference compared with Kristin is that this time the storm will be most intense during daytime, that is, when more people are on the streets and roads, which worsens the situation.

Duarte Costa warns that if the phenomenon coincides with rush hour, the period when travel is most intense, the risks could be heightened.

Preventive measures in place

The Portuguese government has declared a state of alert for this Wednesday across the entire mainland territory, in view of the approach of depression Charles.

The Minister for Internal Administration, Luís Neves, announced the closure of all schools (public and private) and non-essential public services, a ban on movement in parks, forests and gardens, and urged the population to stay at home, warning that there may be "very difficult moments of need for rescue", with particular concern about urban flooding, falling trees and interruptions to the power supply.

IPMA has placed eight districts under red warning: Beja, Évora, Faro, Leiria, Lisbon, Portalegre, Santarém and Setúbal, until 21:00 this Wednesday.

All tunnels and parks in the city of Lisbon, as well as some bridges, will be closed from midnight. The speed on the Vasco da Gama and 25 de Abril bridges, which connect the two banks of the river Tagus, has been limited to 60 km/h, and motorbike travel is discouraged.

Lisbon Metro and Fertagus expect to maintain public transport services. However, the Carris bus operation may be adjusted during the day, depending on the severity of the bad weather and safety conditions.

For its part, Rede Expressos has suspended services between 10:00 and midnight this Wednesday.

World.title: Italian government debates aid to Kyiv while Abu Dhabi holds talks on Ukraine's future
World.content:
On Tuesday 10 November the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine is presented to Copasir (Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic) by Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, but League Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti is biding his time over signing the new measure, as the procedure would require.

 

Within the governing majority, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Crosetto himself tend to play down the incident, citing the minister's absence, as on Monday he had been in Brussels for Ecofin. Tajani goes so far as to specify that, since the document is classified, it has to be signed in person and cannot be signed electronically.

Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has also spoken about Italian and European strategy for Ukraine, in an interview with the daily newspaper Repubblica (source in Italian). The Defence chief, who says he is convinced that Giorgetti will sign the aid package as soon as he returns from Brussels, has defended the need to continue supporting Kyiv.

He also stressed the need for Europe to maintain a common position, as requested by Meloni, and reiterated that "excluding a physical presence in Ukraine of European troops has always been our caveat". Sources at Palazzo Chigi reiterate the point even after the start of talks in Abu Dhabi: "Europe must speak with a single voice and equip itself with a clear and shared mandate".

The row has broken out, however, because Deputy Prime Minister and Infrastructure Minister Matteo Salvini has repeatedly voiced his reservations about military aid to Kyiv, despite Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has always remained firm (together with FI) on the need to continue supporting Kyiv "for as long as necessary".

A line that has become tighter after the League congress that reconfirmed him as secretary. League senator Claudio Borghi, in fact, steps up the pressure on X, calling the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine the "decree that does not exist (because an act that requires joint approval by several ministers does not exist until it has been signed by them)".

Without the signature of League minister Giorgetti, the decree cannot be published and the aid, not only military but also civilian, cannot be sent. This risks opening a delicate battle within the majority on this issue, which could turn into a clash whose consequences are still hard to make out.

What could be in the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine

On the list of measures in the decree (classified like all the previous ones) there will in fact not only be aid for Ukrainian civilians, such as generators, but probably also weapons for air defence. Since the Franco-Italian Samp-T battery has already been supplied in the past, there could therefore be a shipment of Aster missiles that arm the system.

Within the majority, many are convinced that in the end the minister will sign, also because otherwise the experience of the centre-right government would come dangerously close to the end of the line. A scenario that could prove catastrophic, not only for the European balance. The Italian government is in the middle of the budget session and a crisis at this point would risk sweeping away the budget plan as well.

Why the so-called framework decree introduced by Draghi is important

Moreover, the decree-law that serves as a "framework" for this mechanism, which then provides for the ministerial decree with the joint approval of Defence, Farnesina and the Economy and Finance Ministry, will also expire at the end of the year. This is a scheme introduced by the Draghi government in 2022 and already renewed four times with only a few small adjustments, regardless of the governing majority.

After being adopted in the Council of Ministers, those framework decrees were converted into law by the Houses of Parliament, allowing in four years the dispatch of twelve military aid packages through as many interministerial measures, for which only a briefing to the Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic is required.

The last aid package to Kyiv was sent at the end of 2025. A few days after Christmas last year, now eleven months ago, the government adopted a new "framework" decree that authorises the shipment of supplies, both military and civilian, to Ukraine for the whole of 2026.

World.title: Russia’s ‘unfriendly countries’ list now targets property, child custody and debts
World.content:
Russia's designation of "unfriendly countries" has expanded beyond foreign economic policy into domestic courts, family law, property rights and financial obligations, with a string of decrees and rulings extending its reach to individuals.

 

The list of states Moscow considers unfriendly was formalised as a form of retaliation in a government order in March 2022, weeks after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

It covers the US, the UK, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Ukraine, Australia, New Zealand and EU member states, all of which have pushed back against Russia's war of aggression.

This autumn, the Russian government nearly doubled import duties on spirits from unfriendly countries, raising the rate from 20% to 35%, primarily affecting European and North American producers.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the placement of foreign companies' Russian assets under temporary administration was directly linked to those companies' home countries being on the list.

The measure has affected the Russian operations of Nestlé, Auchan, FM Logistic, Leroy Merlin, Metro Cash & Carry, Tarkett, Japan Tobacco International (JTI) and others.

Russia's Supreme Court cited the unfriendly countries designation in a child custody dispute, ruling that returning a child to France could run counter to her interests in part because France appears on the list.

In March 2025, Russian citizen Alexei Ermakov took his daughter on a two-week holiday to Turkey and Slovakia with the consent of her mother, Ukrainian citizen Anna Tishkova, then brought the child to Russia in April.

He subsequently arranged Russian citizenship for the girl. Despite international agreements on returning children to their country of habitual residence, the court declined to order her return to France.

Property and vehicles under threat

A bill supported in the State Duma would allow vehicles stolen or illegally exported from unfriendly countries to be registered in Russia.

Supporters say it addresses legal gaps caused by the breakdown in cooperation with Western states; opponents say it would weaken property protections for owners in those countries.

In a separate case, the Supreme Court ordered the Interior Ministry to register a vehicle flagged in an international database at Canada's request, ruling that listing in an international stolen vehicles register is not in itself sufficient grounds to refuse registration in Russia.

Putin signed a decree this autumn under which individuals who cannot prove citizenship of Russia or a friendly state or produce a residency permit are automatically treated as persons from unfriendly countries.

A further decree allows Russian debtors to withhold payment from creditors in unfriendly countries, departing from the standard principle of equal treatment of parties to contracts.

Standard principles of private international law require courts to resolve contracts, custody matters and property disputes on their legal merits, regardless of the nationality or political status of the parties.

Russia’s application of a foreign-policy designation to those areas departs from norms in conventions it has ratified, among them the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, which obligates signatory states to return children removed across borders without consent.

World.title: Belgium: Prince Harry and Meghan visit EU Parliament for child safety event
World.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were photographed alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola after arriving at the institution. The couple also spent around ten minutes meeting families whose children had been affected by online abuse, before Harry took to the podium to address the gathering.

 

Footage shows the couple arriving together, posing for photographs with Metsola and Harry delivering his speech. The visit forms part of their public engagement with online child protection, an issue on which they have repeatedly sought to raise awareness.

The appearance comes just days after Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was charged over the alleged possession of child sexual abuse images. It marks the Duchess of Sussex's first public appearance since his arrest, bringing additional attention to an event focused on protecting children from online harm.

The Brussels event focused on the risks children face on digital platforms and the experiences of families affected by online abuse. By meeting those families and addressing the issue at the European Parliament, Harry and Meghan drew attention to the importance of child safety in an increasingly digital world.

World.title: DLR, NASA and CSA plan lunar greenhouse to grow vegetables for astronauts
World.content:
How can vegetables be grown in a place with no habitable atmosphere, no fertile soil and no freely available water?

 

This is exactly what the international Project Lunar Agriculture Module - Ground Test Demonstrator (LAM-GTD) (source in German) is about.

The German Aerospace Center (DLR) is working together with NASA and the Canadian Space Agency CSA on concepts for greenhouses on the Moon. These are initially intended to supply astronauts on future long-term missions with fresh food.

A greenhouse as life insurance in space

Temperatures on the Moon fluctuate extremely, its surface is almost airless, water is scarce and cosmic radiation poses a considerable danger. Simply putting plants into lunar soil is not an option. Controlled cultivation systems are needed that can operate independently of natural environmental conditions.

The idea is that a greenhouse module will be directly connected to a simulated living and working area for astronauts. This would allow researchers not only to study plant growth, but also to test how the greenhouse and habitat can supply each other.

The crew of the International Space Station ISS has already harvested two crops of different lettuce varieties. NASA

The planned demonstrator is to be built entirely on Earth to begin with. By 2032 at the latest the three partners want to decide whether and how it will actually be constructed.

NASA in particular has already carried out numerous experiments of this kind on the International Space Station ISS. Among other things, lettuce, Chinese cabbage and chilli peppers have been grown there.

NASA astronaut Peggy Whitson with cabbage plants in the ISS Veggie greenhouse during the harvest of the Veg-03 experiment. NASA/Peggy Whitson

The next step now moves on from small experimental setups on the ISS to much larger and more complex cultivation systems that could supply entire crews.

The German partner, DLR, can draw on experience from earlier projects, in particular the EDEN ISS greenhouse, which was operated in Antarctica for several years.

From 2018 to 2023 researchers ran a specially designed greenhouse in Antarctica, just a few hundred metres from the German research station Neumayer III. Under extreme conditions they grew fresh vegetables there without soil and without natural sunlight. LED lamps, artificial nutrient solutions and a sophisticated irrigation system made it possible to harvest lettuce, tomatoes, cucumbers, radishes and even strawberries. In total, around one tonne of fresh vegetables was produced.

A project built on international cooperation

Antarctica is not the Moon, but it offers an important similarity: supplies are difficult, environmental conditions are demanding and mistakes can quickly become a problem.

It is no coincidence that Germany, the United States and Canada are working together on LAM-GTD. DLR contributes its expertise from space research and previous greenhouse projects. NASA is working on the foundations for future lunar missions and a long-term human presence on the Moon. The Canadian Space Agency CSA adds its experience in space research and in technologies for crewed missions.

A small step for lettuce, a giant leap for humanity

The research is not only of interest to astronauts, because there are also places on Earth where growing food is difficult, such as arid desert regions or areas with limited water resources.

Technologies that can supply plants with as little water, energy and space as possible could also help in these regions. Controlled greenhouses could also contribute to producing food more precisely and with less use of pesticides.

Looking beyond Earth could therefore yield knowledge that helps us find new ways of growing food on our own planet.

World.title: ‘Monstrous injustice’: King Charles condemns slavery as UK agrees to talks
World.content:
In this episode of Spotlight on Africa, we talked to scholars from the continent and the Caribbean about slavery reparations – a key topic discussed at this year’s Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

Advertising

The Commonwealth is a 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies, 21 of them in Africa. King Charles III remains head of state in 15 of them, including the UK.

Its biennial Heads of Government Meeting took place from 1 to 4 November 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda.

In a final communiqué issued on Wednesday, the group said the time had come for “meaningful, truthful and respectful conversation towards forging a common future based on equity”.

Timetable of talks

While no timetable for talks was announced, the group welcomed the United Kingdom’s willingness to engage “in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms”.

In his opening speech, King Charles III, who is politically neutral, called the slave trade “a monstrous injustice” that filled him with “profound personal sorrow”, but stopped short of a formal apology.

UN backs resolution calling slave trade ‘gravest crime against humanity’

For his part, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.

Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also said it was “not feasible” for the country to pay reparations for slavery, but that “there are things we can work on co-operatively”.

According to reports, Britain could issue a formal apology next year, during its G20 presidency.

Britain played a pivotal role in the slave trade, which saw between 10 and 15 million enslaved Africans taken to the Americas over four centuries.

The country abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833. It paid financial compensation, but to plantation owners rather than to the enslaved people themselves.

UN resolution

In March this year, the United Nations adopted a resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade and the enslavement of Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity”, in a motion spearheaded by Ghana.

Ghana backs Jamaica’s petition to push UK for slavery reparations

For many countries, the time has come for formal apologies and concrete plans for slavery reparations.

To find out how these issues are being tackled on the African continent and in the Caribbean, RFI spoke to a panel of four guests:

Edem Adotey: professor at the Institute of African Studies in Accra, Ghana,

Joel Kibazo: Commonwealth spokesperson,

Matiangai Sirleaf: professor at the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law in the United States,

Verene A. Shepherd: Jamaican historian and one of three vice-chairs of the Caricom Reparations Commission.

This episode was mixed by Nicolas Doreau.

World.title: Turkey courts Egypt to tip the scales in eastern Mediterranean power game
World.content:
This week’s joint naval exercises between Turkey and Egypt in the eastern Mediterranean are the latest move in a burgeoning partnership, as Ankara intensifies its efforts to draw Cairo closer and loosen its bonds with Turkish rivals Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

Advertising

The "Sea of Friendship 2026" naval drills, held from 4-9 November off the coast of Alexandria, follow five years of rapprochement after nearly a decade of mistrust sparked by the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, a close ally of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

It is the second year in a row that Turkey and Egypt have held the joint drills, after a 13-year break.

“I think it's already a sign that the two countries are getting closer,” said Africa expert Elem Tepecikoglu of Ankara’s Social Sciences University. In her view, the naval exercises are part of an evolving partnership.

“This normalisation process started five years ago in the diplomatic realm,” she explained. “And then we see cooperation in the security domain as well. So this is why I say I'm optimistic that Egypt might come closer to the Turkish side.”

The strengthening alliance between Turkey and Egypt is stirring unease in Israel, at a time when Israeli-Turkish relations are already frayed by the war in Gaza and Ankara’s support for Hamas.

“Obviously, Israel does not see this as necessarily positive, because of the heightened tensions between Israel and Turkey,” warned Turkey analyst Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

She noted that Israel is growing ever more wary of Turkey’s expanding reach in the eastern Mediterranean. “There is concern that Turkey and Egypt can cooperate in ways that will squeeze Israel’s room to manoeuver, politically but also militarily.”

Lindenstrauss said she does not see this as a likely scenario, affirming that the 1979 peace agreement between Israel and Egypt is “still very much in place, despite many geopolitical turnovers”.

“But there was always a fear that the other countries surrounding it would unite and act against Israel,” the analyst added.

Lindenstrauss believes Egypt’s strong ties with Turkey’s rivals, Greece and Cyprus, allay fears of Israeli encirclement. “It is very important that this relationship keeps going ahead because it is a source of stability in the eastern Mediterranean,” she said.

Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff

Turkish leverage

Egypt, Greece, Cyprus and Israel are bound by a tightly knit strategic energy alliance centred on the Eastern Mediterranean Gas Forum, a regional organisation formed in 2020 that has its headquarters in Cairo.

Just last month, they stood united in condemning the Libyan parliament's ratification of a maritime deal with Turkey that encroached on Greek and Egyptian waters.

Still, Jalel Harchaoui, a regional expert at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank, observes that Turkey and Egypt are forging ever-closer collaboration on issues ranging from Libya to the Sudanese civil war to the Horn of Africa. Harchaoui suggests this growing cooperation is steadily boosting Ankara’s leverage over Cairo.

“I think observers should ask, can Egypt afford to do without Turkey? And the answer is probably no, and Turkey probably is aware of it,” he said.

Even so, Harchaoui doubts Cairo is ready to pivot fully toward Ankara. “If [Egypt] switches 180 degrees, it would be a disaster for the other side. I'm talking about Greece and Cyprus and Israel. So you could also ask yourself, can Egypt afford to anger its traditional friends?”

Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean

Egypt's balancing act

Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic courtship of Cairo, hoping to lure Egypt away from its longstanding partners.

But Turkish ambitions stumbled when Egypt declined to join the Mecca Defence Alliance with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. Analyst Lindenstrauss sees this as a clear sign of the boundaries in Turkish-Egyptian ties.

“Egypt has already moved closer to Turkey than was imaginable a few years ago,” she said. “However, at the end of the day, there are limits to how much it can accept greater Turkish influence. I think Turkey pretty much reached where Egypt is willing to agree to, and it will not give Turkey concessions in the eastern Mediterranean that will endanger its relationship with Greece and Cyprus, or its peace agreement with Israel.”

Lindenstrauss believes that despite diplomatic tensions with Israel over the war in Gaza, it still remains in Egypt’s interests to maintain ties with all sides. “Because of Egypt's importance in the region, I think it can definitely go ahead with this balancing act. It gives it all the gains and the risk is relatively low compared to having Egypt choose sides,” she added.

Ankara stands ready to ramp up its campaign to win over Cairo as the battle for influence in the eastern Mediterranean intensifies. In the unfolding rivalry between between Turkey on one hand and Greece, Cyprus and Israel on the other, Egypt is emerging as the pivotal player.

World.title: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support
World.content:
More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.

"We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

Unresolved issues of reparations have strained relations between Germany and Poland for decades Image: AP/picture alliance

While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."

Reparations offered to date seen as insufficient

The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews.

At 100, Auschwitz survivor recalls life during the Holocaust To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.

Tusk rejects €200 million as insufficient

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (front) has made no secret of the fact that he's waiting for a 'creative solution' from Germany Image: Kacper Pempel/REUTERS

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.

Germany's Greens still hope for 'humanitarian gesture'

Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

Green co-leader Franziska Brantner hasn't given up hope that Germany will still change its stance on Polish reparations Image: Michaela Küfner/DW

"Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.

Poland wants WWII reparations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German private donors support the victims' fund

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."

Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."

"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Iran denies role in fridge hack, France summons ambassador
World.content:
France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of IRGC involvement.

Iran on Tuesday dismissed French accusations that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets last month, as Paris summoned Tehran's ambassador to discuss the incident.

"Iran's Foreign Ministry categorically rejects the French government's baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France," the ministry said, adding that it "strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of leveling accusations against the Islamic Republic."

The alleged attack, which began overnight on October 11-12, raised the temperatures in supermarket refrigerators and freezer units, spoiling produce and even causing fires in isolated instances.

A series of similar incidents have since followed in Europe and beyond, even including a failed attack on cooling units at French blood banks this month, though it is not yet clear if these subsequent events are connected.

France summons ambassador, says it rules 'nothing' out in response

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that his government would "rule nothing out and will take all measures — including those we may not disclose publicly — that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks."

Barrot was speaking amid a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris that included discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the conflict with Iran.

Barrot even said that despite a change in tone from the Trump administration since the midterm election defeat in the US, the risk of a renewed escalation with Iran could not be ruled out, "otherwise, we would not have devoted so much time and energy over the past two days to addressing these issues with our American counterpart."

Barrot hosted G7 foreign ministers, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Paris this week Image: Brendan Smialowski/REUTERS

France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday and said it would be seeking European-level sanctions in response.

The EU said it would seek to provide a "swift and united response" pending discussion with member states.

"As the EU, we have consistently called on all states to refrain from malicious behavior in the cyberspace, and we will continue to address such malicious behavior, making use of all the tools that we have, also under the EU cyber diplomacy toolbox, including sanctions," spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.

Barrot said that the goal of any response would be "to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again."

Iran accuses French of 'projecting' its own failures

Tehran appeared to threaten retaliatory measures of its own if sanctions materialized, saying it would "not hesitate to take necessary and appropriate measures to safeguard its national interests and security in the face of unlawful foreign activities."

It accused France of "merely projecting its own governance failures" with its allegations.

"A government that cannot even manage the temperature of its own refrigerators now seeks to shift the blame onto foreign actors through these preposterous accusations," it said.

Around 700 supermarkets, of a total of roughly 10,000 across France, were affected by the alleged cyberattack Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

What did Paris prosecutors say about suspected Iranian involvement?

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that she had opened an investigation into leading members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit that is part of Iran's multi-force specialist military, the IRGC, that answers directly to its religious leadership.

She said her office had requested arrest warrants against two Shahid Kaveh officials and was investigating others.

She described the entity as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps."

French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit conducted "large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for the purpose of sabotage." It said it primarily targeted Israel and the US, but also France and other European countries.

Beccuau said that the attack targeted roughly 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets. It used web interfaces to "initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles," and also to disable automated alerts from sensors designed to go off when temperatures exceeded certain levels.

Sweden's Civil Defense Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin warned that more cyberattacks could be expected in the coming months, as AI tools make it easier to detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

He said that it was not yet possible to say if hacks targeted Swedish supermarkets last week were connected, not least because the type of sabotage would have "been easy to copy" after seeing the initial reports in October.

World.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
World.content:
Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial history. [Pictured: Cans of Zyklon B gas, Auschwitz-Birkenau, German Nazi concentration and extermination camp in Poland] Image: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposed to be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

From colonial brutality to Nazi rule

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust. Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

The extreme brutality of Fascist Italy's invasion of Ethiopia, including the use of chemical weapons, caused uproar around the world. [Pictured: The bombing of the Ethiopian village of Dessye by Italian planes] Image: Topfoto/United Archives International/IMAGO

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

One of the most notorious symbols of King Leopold II's rule was the amputation of hands, inflicted on men, women and children who failed to meet rubber production quotas. [Pictured: A Congolese child with an amputated hand, circa 1900] Image: United Archives/World History Archive/IMAGO

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met. Forced labor was central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

Racism, antisemitism and extermination

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

From 1904 to 1908, German colonial rule in present-day Namibia culminated in the genocide of the Herero and Nama, in which tens of thousands died. [Pictured: Concentration camp for Herero and Nama in German South West Africa in 1905] Image: Sam-Cohen-Bibliothek/Scientific Society Swakopmund

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The politics of historical comparison

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

After being deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1943, French artist David Olère depicted scenes he witnessed. Here, deportees arrive at a crematorium shortly before their murder. [Pictured: David Olère, 'Vers la mort' ('On the Way to Death'), Paris, 1945] Image: Mémorial de la Shoah/Coll. David Olère

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. In 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Rethinking Germany's culture of remembrance

Martinican intellectual Aimé Césaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. The exhibition opens amid renewed debates over settler colonialism, the definition of genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over German support for Israel during the war in Gaza. These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance. However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy. "I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

World.title: Poland: Krakow shooting suspect 'fascinated' by Norwegian mass murder Anders Breivik, says justice minister
World.content:
The 24-year old suspect was found to have read a significant amount of material about Breivik and other far-right figures. Speculation over his motives have prompted a bitter political feud in Warsaw.

Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek issued an update on Tuesday concerning the case of a mass shooting in Krakow over the weekend.

Accused gunman Michal Oksinski was deeply interested in international far-right movements, Zurek said.

"Authorities have accessed the terrorist's computer. It is clear that he visited websites concerning Anders Breivik," the Norwegian neo-Nazi who killed 77 people in July 2011, the minister added.

Zurek said a search of Oksinski's home turned up a Gadsen flag, a banner dating back to the US Civil War that is now associated with American white nationalists.

Police also gathered evidence that he had recently bought 10 magazines for a semi-automatic rifle and 500 bullets.

"It is clear that this individual was preparing to take action," the justice minister said.

Krakow shooting suspect 'fascinated by far right' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happened in the attack?

On Friday night, 24-year-old Oksinski is thought to have shot and killed his mother, father, sister and two family cats in the city of Ostrowiec.

The following day at around 3:00 p.m. local time, Oksinski is suspected of opening fire in Krakow's Main Market Square. Six people were killed — four Poles, one Austrian, and one UK national. Another 15 people were wounded.

After the attack in Krakow, authorities discovered the bodies of his family members in Ostrowiec.

Poland then observed two days of national mourning. Oksinski died of wounds sustained during his arrest at a local hospital on Monday.

Initial investigations have uncovered "very solid" evidence pointing to far-right radicalization and psychiatric issues as motives for the attacks, Zurek said.

However, Zurek and the centrist government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been accused by members of right-wing populist PiS party of lying about Oksinski's motives.

World.title: Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future
World.content:
Manuel Neuer's latest injury gives Jonas Urbig a run of games in Bayern's goal. Marc-André ter Stegen remains Germany’s No. 1, but Urbig now has a chance to strengthen his case for the future.

It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

What could Neuer's injury change?

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.
