Jonas Urbig replaced Manuel Neuer on Saturday and is expected to take over full time in the future Image: Jürgen Kessler/Kessler-Sportfotografie/dpa/picture alliance

The goalkeeper of the future

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

This article was adapted from German.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

World.title: Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China
World.content:
Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies.



The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed's mega rise

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

Megaspeed managed data centers for Chinese tech giant Alibaba Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

A brief history

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The relationship with Nvidia

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

China and the battle for chips

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Nvidia's chips are seen as the gold standard for AI applications Image: Kobe Li/ZUMAPRESS/picture alliance

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

World.title: Pope Leo vs. Javier Milei: How political is the pope?
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV's tour of South America has drawn huge crowds — and a measure of political controversy. Perceived criticism of Argentina's leader, and earlier rebukes of Donald Trump, offer a glimpse into papacy politics.

The 2.5 million people lining the streets of Buenos Aires to get a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV on Monday left little doubt as to his influence in Argentina and beyond.

"It's very important for Argentinians, for our unity and, above all, to reaffirm faith in the Catholic Church in this country. Argentina is a country of faith, it's always been so," one attendee told DW of the open air Mass.

"The mood from the public about his visit is overwhelmingly positive," Justin McLellan, Vatican correspondent for the National Catholic Reporter, told DW from Argentina's capital. "I think that people are big fans of Leo."

The previous day, Leo had made a series of remarks which many observers took to be criticism of Argentine President Javier Milei and his strict austerity measures, sweeping cuts to social services and the elimination of thousands of public sector jobs.

Afterward, there were suggestions from some of the president's supporters online that the pope, who is returning to duty just a month after cancer surgery, had overstepped his role.

Pope urges Argentina's president to put people first To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," said Leo, the first US-born pope, on Sunday. He also mentioned those who "despite hard work, nonetheless, struggle to meet their household's needs."

Leo doubled down on the message on a visit to a care home before Monday's Mass, where he preached to millions.

Pope Leo walks soft-power tightrope

"It's clearly targeting, without naming, the different policies that the president has put on recently," Jocelyne Cesari, a professor of religion and politics at the University of Birmingham in the UK, told DW, adding that Leo's words were "carefully calibrated."

Throughout its history, estimated by some at close to 2,000 years, the papacy has been a role with huge, and previously very direct, political power. Pope Innocent III, for example, was widely considered the most important man in the Europe in the late 11th and early 12th century. He wielded power over much of Europe and its monarchies, ensuring each territory was run according to Catholic doctrine.

An estimated 2.5 million people lined the streets to see the pope in Buenos Aires Image: REUTERS

But in the modern day, that power has softened, with 20th and 21st century popes tending to intervene in a broader sense away from direct party politics and policy.

Leo's commitment to walking that tightrope was tested early in his papacy by US President Donald Trump, an ally of Milei, who called him "WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy" in a social media post in April.

"I do not look at my role as being political, a politician," responded Leo. "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel, which is what I believe I am here to do, what the Church is here to do." It's a familiar stance, said Cesari.

"That's a line that all popes before him have walked. We tend to forget that the pope is the head of the state, is a diplomat and is a voice for more than 1 billion Catholics, so the role has always been political."

Can Pope Leo influence Argentina's election?

Both Cesari and McLellan agreed that Leo and his modern predecessors are keen to avoid party politics but instead offer guidance to the 1.4 billion Catholics in the world.

"The strategy of the pope is to position himself as a moral authority, his role is not just to say 'vote for X or Y.' His role is to say there are some moral teachings that can be applied to social life and communities, but people must make their personal decisions," said Cesari.

With Argentina a majority Catholic country, it stands to reason that the pope's word holds plenty of sway. But the longer-term question is whether Leo's perceived criticisms of Milei make a difference in Argentina's general election in October 2027.

Argentina loses 33 companies a day under Javier Milei To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"People want to be drawn close to him [Leo]. I think the visit to Argentina could have an influence in the election in that he's certainly given his support to the Argentine bishops who have been critical of Milei's austerity policies and his cuts to social programs," said McLellan.

"I think that that could have an impact in the election and that it will elevate and raise the voice of the Catholic Church in Argentina."

Milei's battle with Catholic Church

But Cesari is not so sure that being sympathetic to a speech transfers to action at the ballot box. "They may revere and respect the pope. But is not clear that that what he says has a direct impact on individual voters," she said.

"His voice will be heard. But from the studies we have, there is not a clear, direct impact on elections. We know that Catholics do not vote in a bloc and we know that lots of them voted for Milei in 2023, even after he called [Leo's predecessor Pope] Francis the representative of evil on Earth."

Milei, a right-wing libertarian and outspoken critic of the ruling class, has long clashed with the Catholic Church. He also called Pope Francis, a native of Argentina, an "imbecile" in 2020 and accused him of promoting communism. He did, however, find a more conciliatory tone on Monday when he called the late Francis an "exceptional figure" and the "most important Argentine in history."

Leo is, McLellan added, "diplomatic by nature." With Trump and Milei both having taken swipes at the Catholic Church in a time of ongoing geopolitical turmoil, that looks to be a critical papal quality.

World.title: Japan watches for signs of change in Trump's foreign policy priorities
World.content:
Tokyo fears the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm election may push him to pursue a diplomatic quick win at the expense of Washington's allies in the Indo-Pacific.

With just a week to go before the leaders of the United States, China and Russia are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Japan is closely watching for signs of any shift in Washington's policy toward the Indo-Pacific.

The APEC gathering, taking place this year in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, is scheduled for November 18-19.

Tokyo fears that the drubbing US President Donald Trump suffered in last week's midterm elections may push him to seek a diplomatic quick win, one he can point to as evidence of his statesmanship but that fails to take into account the interests of Washington's allies in the region.

Tokyo has moved swiftly to try to ascertain the mood in a White House that was left reeling by the results of the November 3 midterm election.

Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi held talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris on Monday.

Following their meeting, the Japanese Foreign Ministry released a statement saying that both sides agreed to "further advance security cooperation to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-US alliance."

They also vowed to "maintain close communication" on the situation in the Indo-Pacific, without providing further details.

Will Japan become the Indo-Pacific's most trusted power? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why is Japan worried?

"Japan's concern is that with Trump becoming a lame duck in domestic politics, he will use his presidential authorities to shift his focus to foreign policy," said Sebastian Maslow, a professor of politics at the University of Tokyo.

"A US deal with China may provide President Xi [Jinping] the ability to intensify pressure on Japan," he told DW. "With Sino-Japanese relations severely strained, this will put Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi in a difficult position and she will have to reassess how to navigate US-China relations."

Margarita Estévez-Abe, associate professor at Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and an expert on Japanese politics, said Japan fears "a transactional Trump who treats Taiwan as a bargaining chip."

She pointed out that after the May summit with Xi, Trump described US arms sales to Taiwan as "a good negotiating chip with China."

Tokyo is also "frustrated" that Trump has not come to its support over the rare earth export restrictions China imposed on Japan after Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last year, with the Trump administration treating the China-Japan feud as "Tokyo's problem," she said.

Efforts to preserve the geopolitical balance

Furthermore, Japan has concerns about Washington's foreign policy positions toward North Korea and Russia.

"Trump has not damaged the US-Japan alliance the way he has strained NATO, but his outreach to Moscow and Pyongyang worries Tokyo," said Estévez-Abe.

"The US relies on Japan as its main military base in the Indo-Pacific, so it is not in Washington's interest to embolden Russia and North Korea against Japan," she added. "But if American softness does raise the threat to Japan, Japanese trust in the alliance will erode. Japan can only hope that doesn't happen."

How China uses fishing boats for military power To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ultimately, Tokyo wants to preserve the geopolitical balance in the region and prevent already strained tensions from escalating further. But Japan is increasingly questioning the commitment of a security and trade partner that has stood by it since 1945.

"Japan's security strategy emphasizes preserving the status quo in terms of defending the liberal international order and containing China's role in the Indo-Pacific," said Maslow. "However, in order to achieve this, Japan has emphasized the role of the US alliance as a cornerstone of its foreign policy and security. The reality still is that Japan has no 'plan B' if the alliance unravels."

Diversifying security partnerships

Efforts to strengthen Japan's military are embedded within the framework of the US-Japan alliance, he pointed out. And while there have been calls for Japan to develop an autonomous defense capability, achieving that in the short term is unrealistic given the limitations of its defense industry and a lack of key resources, including critical intelligence.

Over the past decade, Tokyo has proactively diversified its security partnerships, stepping up defense cooperation with European Union member states and NATO, forging a quasi-alliance with Australia, and joining a range of minilateral frameworks across the Indo-Pacific, including with the Philippines.

This reflects Japan's desire to play a more proactive role in shaping regional and global security, Maslow said.

How Japan, South Korea and Taiwan hedge vs. US shifts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tokyo hopes no major clashes erupt in the region for the remaining two years of Trump's term and that Washington's resolve is not tested before a new and "strategically more amenable administration comes in," Estévez-Abe said.

Maslow stressed, however, that "hope is not a strategy" and that Tokyo needs to maintain efforts to protect the alliance and double down by demonstrating its own commitments to security with even greater defense spending and by safeguarding economic security.

World.title: David Broncano entona el ‘mea culpa’ por su entrevista con Abascal: “Estoy triste, me arrepiento de muchas cosas”
World.content:
La entrevista de este lunes de David Broncano al líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, en La revuelta ha despertado un alud de reacciones. Uno de los pocos que faltaban por opinar era el propio afectado, el codirector y presentador del programa. Este martes, cuando Broncano se dirigía a la grabación de la entrevista que se emitirá en el horario de máxima audiencia de La 1 a la candidata de Frente Amplio, Ada Colau, se ha parado a responder a las preguntas de varios periodistas.

“Estoy triste, sí, porque creo que no lo hice bien ayer”, ha expresado con gesto pesaroso. “Me equivoqué con varias cosas de cómo se hizo. Me arrepiento de muchas cosas. Posiblemente tenía que haber utilizado la comedia más, como hago siempre, pero es complicado. Mucha gente me decía que con políticos no hiciéramos bromas. No las hice especialmente en las entrevistas anteriores con Sánchez, Rufián y Montero, y ayer con Abascal mucha gente pensaba que no debía entrar a muchas bromas con él, y seguramente me equivoqué porque se podía utilizar la comedia”, reflexiona. Muchas de las críticas recibidas se dirigían precisamente al cambio de tono habitual del formato por uno mucho más serio. Broncano ha negado que ese cambio fuera algo impuesto desde Moncloa.

Otra de las cuestiones más polémicas de la participación de Abascal en La revuelta fue el hecho de que el programa accediera a que fuera Vox quien seleccionara el público que asistía al teatro en directo. Ese fue, para Broncano, el primer fallo cometido. “Abascal lo hizo bien, tanto él como la gente de comunicación del partido, a nivel estratégico lo han hecho bien. Porque nos pidieron venir con su público, y esa es la clave de todo. Aceptamos hacerlo con público seleccionado por Vox porque yo pensaba, y posiblemente fui demasiado ambicioso y posiblemente vanidoso, y me extralimité en mis capacidades, pero pensé que eso podía evitar que, si la entrevista no salía como querían, con nuestro público podrían excusarse en eso. Quería quitarles esa cosa que a veces hacen desde Vox, y me equivoqué”, explica Broncano.

Desde que comenzó la entrevista y el teatro recibió a Abascal al grito de “presidente, presidente”, se dio cuenta de que no había sido buena decisión. “Vi que era muy desigual y muy injusto, y para el público también: ¿por qué le están apludiendo cualquier cosa? Era muy complicado el hecho de que cualquier frase que dijese él fuera ovacionada y cualquier cosa que dijese yo, que a pesar de que estaba un poco descolocado con todo, dije cosas bastante razonables, y se recibía con un murmullo y como si hubiese dicho una barbaridad".

“Estuve incómodo conmigo mismo, me sacó un poco cuando me di cuenta de que había generado un ambiente raro y una situación que no merece un responsable político de cara a que esté tan sesgada la reacción del público. Yo mismo me tiré toda la entrevista pensando que la he cagado. Muchas veces, Santiago [Abascal] estaba hablando y yo estaba pensando por dentro: ‘Tío, eres tonto, lo has hecho mal, esto no tiene sentido’, y no me permitía responderle o rebatirle con la velocidad con la que habría que haberlo hecho”, ha explicado Broncano.

Sobre las críticas que ha recibido desde la propia RTVE y desde otros periodistas, Broncano asegura que en realidad no ha querido ni pedido hacer ninguna de las entrevistas a políticos. “Entiendo que haya periodistas a los que no les haga gracia, pero no he peleado yo por hacer estas entrevistas, es un buen marrón que me ha caído por estar en la televisión pública en el programa con más espectadores de la cadena y que he intentado hacer con responsabilidad y hacer un servicio público. Desde luego, ayer no fue el caso”, ha continuado.

Otra cuestión sobre la que se ha posicionado ha sido la idoneidad de que la televisión pública dé voz a la formación de ultraderecha Vox. “Ese debate es muy antiguo, y yo en el punto actual, que Vox es una fuerza que va a sacar un montón de escaños y es un partido parlamentario y democrático, me parece que tiene que venir al programa. La gente que dice que no hay que entrevistarles, puedo entenderlo, lo respeto, pero en 2026 creo que se puede entrevistar a alguien de Vox. Pero no lo hice de la forma adecuada”, defiende. “Siempre he pensado que podía entrevistar a políticos, sin la presión de un periodista profesional, pero podía hacerlo. Ayer, sin duda, fue un bache grande, pero asumo la responsabilidad”.

World.title: “Leer te hace más inteligente porque te hace elegir mejor”
World.content:
Paulo Cosín, director editorial de Ediciones Morata, especializada en educación, charla con Mar Buenhombre, estudiante de Bachillerato del IES La Senda de Getafe (Madrid), sobre el lugar que debe ocupar la lectura en los planes educativos

Cuestionado sobre qué hacer para enganchar a alguien a la lectura, Paulo Cosín, director editorial de Ediciones Morata, revela el secreto: “Debemos compartir con esa persona lo que a nosotros nos sucede cuando leemos. Seguro que querrá tener lo mismo que te sucede a ti”. La reflexión de un lector con el hábito tan arraigado como el suyo se complementa con una llamada a la acción, un consejo para cualquiera que desee iniciarse –o recuperar– la pasión por los libros. “Mañana ve a la biblioteca pública, le cuentas tus intereses al bibliotecario y le pides que, por favor, te recomiende un libro. Si no te gusta, lo devuelves y traes otro. Y así vas creando tus gustos literarios”, recomienda a su joven interlocutora, Mar Buenhombre, alumna de 1º de Bachillerato del IES La Senda de Getafe (Madrid), en el nuevo capítulo de Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación del futuro.

“La lectura es la gran herramienta para todas las situaciones de acoso que puedan ocurrir en la escuela”

En la conversación, ambos repasan en qué punto se encuentra la lectura en los planes educativos actuales, en un tiempo en el que las pantallas de los dispositivos móviles colman la atención del mundo. “¿Cuánto tiempo se dedica a la lectura, a las actividades artísticas, en la escuela?”, pregunta Cosín. A lo que la alumna responde: “Pues, según van pasando los cursos, cada vez menos”. Para Cosín, que dirige desde 2005 una editorial especializada en educación que se ha convertido en referencia para profesores y alumnos de toda España, esa verdad supone un grave problema: “La cuestión es si estamos dando a los jóvenes referencias suficientes para ayudarles en su desarrollo. A veces, para comprender las situaciones de sufrimiento ajeno”.

“Según pasan los cursos, creo que cada vez se le da menos importancia a la lectura”

Es ese, a juicio de Cosín, el valor diferencial que convierte a la lectura en una poderosa arma educativa: “Leer te hace más inteligente porque te hace elegir mejor. Es la gran herramienta para todas las situaciones de acoso y de malestar en la convivencia que pueda haber en la escuela”, resume.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

Paulo Cosín Director editorial de Ediciones Morata En 2005 tomó las riendas de una editorial que hoy es una referencia para la comunidad educativa hispanohablante. Firme defensor de devolver la lectura a un puesto privilegiado en los planes pedagógicos, imparte charlas para refrendar una idea: que leer vuelva a ser fundamental en la escuela Mar Buenhombre Alumna de Bachillerato del IES La Senda (Getafe, Madrid) A sus 17 años se confiesa una apasionada por la lectura que disfruta con el género de la novela policíaca. Para ella, es una forma de evadirse de la excesiva atención que su generación presta a las pantallas. Su pasión por los libros la ha llevado a participar en certámenes y concursos de escritura y lectura

World.title: Un viaje en tren por Georgia a bordo de modernos vagones y reliquias soviéticas
World.content:
Georgia está llevando a cabo una modernización de su sistema ferroviario. En la imagen, un tren en dirección a Bakuriani.

El país puede atravesarse en ferrocarril desde el mar Negro hasta el Cáucaso. Este es un recorrido con inicio en Batumi y final en Tiflis

Recorrer Georgia en tren puede ser un rápido y eficiente trayecto entre el mar Negro y Tiflis o una pintoresca reminiscencia de la época soviética, en vagones destartalados y hasta recónditos pueblos de montaña. Viajar en unos u otros dependerá de la prisa y de la antelación con que uno compre sus billetes, pero, en cualquier caso, podremos visitar de forma segura los puntos más atractivos del país, con vistas que nos mantendrán pegados a la ventana. Puntualmente, para ir a los lugares más apartados, no quedará más remedio que echar mano de una marshrutka, una de esas pequeñas furgonetas que se retuercen por donde no llegan el tren ni los autobuses, a velocidades capaces de infartar al más viajero más tranquilo.

Actualmente, Georgia está llevando a cabo una modernización integral de su sistema ferroviario, que este verano alcanzó el hito de reducir el trayecto entre Batumi y Tiflis a cuatro horas. Los billetes, a partir de 35 lari (unos 12 euros), se agotan rápido en verano, por lo que es conveniente reservarlos con hasta tres semanas de antelación por internet (la web más cómoda es tkt.ge), o tener en cuenta que en las estaciones solo se acepta efectivo. Con dos frecuencias diarias (y hasta cinco en verano), es el único tren de estas características, con paradas solo en Kutaisi, Ureki y Kobuleti. Así que el resto de trayectos nos ofrecerán más margen de improvisación y requerirán mucha más paciencia (y muy poco dinero).

En nuestra ruta desde la ciudad costera de Batumi hasta el pueblecito de Gardabani, en el extremo oriental de la línea, probaremos las dos modalidades, que tan bien reflejan esa Georgia moderna con miras europeas y otra mucho más rural, entregada al paisaje y al contacto humano. La duración del viaje dependerá del tiempo que dediquemos a cada una de las ciudades en las que paramos.

Antes de arrancar, Batumi

La historia georgiana parece escrita en vertical, por colonos otomanos y persas llegados desde el sur o rusos, venidos desde el norte. Aventuras que encontraban en la cordillera del Cáucaso, la más alta de Europa, el límite a sus ambiciones imperiales y el recipiente para un legado que, todavía hoy, hace de Georgia ese crisol del que solo pueden presumir las zonas de frontera.

Sin embargo, a finales del siglo XIX, los descubrimientos de petróleo en Azerbaiyán reformularon el mapa del viajero con el ferrocarril de Transcaucasia, que unía el mar Negro y el Caspio, de Batumi hasta Bakú. Una línea internacional que, por cierto, acaba de reabrir tras seis años cerrada, pero que todavía impide a los ciudadanos de la UE cruzar la frontera azerí (una medida que Azerbaiyán reevaluará a inicios de 2027). Esas mismas vías articulan Georgia en dirección oeste-este.

Una mujer en el andén de la ciudad georgiana de Borjomi. Ryhor Bruyeu ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Por eso, nuestra ruta empieza en el suroeste del país, junto al mar Negro y en la capital de la república de Adjara, Batumi. La segunda ciudad georgiana es una extraña mezcla de historia, naturaleza y consumo desatado. Aquí, el viajero tiene la sensación de asistir a una combinación aleatoria de elementos solo unidos por la exuberancia y el exceso. Por ejemplo, desde la monumental plaza de Europa sale la calle Memed Abashidze, con galerías, cafés y tiendas, pero si uno se deja llevar un poco, hasta la plaza Batumi, es posible que sienta haberse perdido por completo, dada la arquitectura kitsch de estilo veneciano.

Ya cerca del frente marítimo, dará con un Las Vegas caucásico donde nada existe si no es cubierto de neones, y el desconcierto aumenta ante una gigante estatua de Medea, una noria más grande todavía, una torre dedicada al alfabeto georgiano, acristalados hoteles, discotecas y una playa kilométrica. Un paraíso para rusos, turcos, armenios e israelíes que encuentran aquí lo que no les ofrecen sus países: sol, calor, alcohol asequible y casinos 24 horas.

Imagen aérea de Batumi, con la plaza de la Libertad en el centro. Vladimir Zapletin ( GETTY IMAGES )

Batumi-Samtredia

Nuestro primer trayecto en tren, hacia Samtredia (dos horas), transcurre en una lenta y ruidosa sauna metálica, que sirve para recrearnos en dos de las principales virtudes del país: un paisaje que no da tregua y una hospitalidad que siempre se traduce en ritual gastronómico; en este caso, té, jachapuri y galletas que nos ofrece la familia de nuestro compartimento. Desde Samtredia, tenemos dos opciones (ambas, a poco menos de dos horas, pero con frecuencias reducidas).

La primera es dejarnos llevar por la vegetación subtropical hacia la ciudad portuaria de Poti, base para visitar los humedales del parque natural de Kolkheti, cuya biodiversidad es reconocida como patrimonio mundial por la Unesco. De nuevo, las orillas tibias y turquesas del mar Negro, cercadas por una frondosidad selvática.

La segunda opción es otro tipo de naturaleza, más salvaje, como la que se encuentra en el extremo septentrional de la línea, en la pequeña Zugdidi. Ahí comienzan las estribaciones del Cáucaso y una de las mecas europeas para el senderismo: las montañas de Svaneti. Quien quiera caminar por ellas, deberá ir desde Zugdidi hasta Mestia, y hacerlo en marshrutka. Mucho más que la escalada, los trayectos de marshrutka, impenitente adelantadora, serán el verdadero deporte de riesgo en el Cáucaso.

Panorámica de la vía de ferrocarril frente a la costa de Batumi. Ryhor Bruyeu ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Comer en Imericia

Sin embargo, seguimos en nuestro tren abarrotado y lento hacia Kutaisi, cuna de los cólquidas, dos veces capital de Georgia en la Edad Media y actualmente la principal ciudad de la región de Imericia. Referencia arqueológica y del turismo de naturaleza, acaba siéndolo también a nivel gastronómico: el jachapuri imeruli (de Imericia) es el más popular del país y acompaña cada comida. Basta con entrar a cualquier restaurante o tasca y pedir la recomendación del día para comprobar que, aquí, comer es una religión con la que comulgamos. En el restaurante Palaty encontramos la mejor cena posible, con pjali (paté vegetal), berenjena rellena, khinkali (una especie de empanadillas) de cordero y vino saperavi, especialidad de la región.

Una excursión habitual en tren desde Kutaisi es a la zona rural de Sachkhere. El servicio, inactivo entre diciembre y marzo, es uno de los más vetustos, lentos y, a la vez, espectaculares, por cómo se adentra en las montañas hasta dejarnos en la no menos alucinante Chiatura (a casi tres horas), un espectro de la extinta minería de magnesio y conocida por su sistema de teleféricos.

Edificio abandonado en Tskaltubo. Vyacheslav Saltayev ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Algo similar encontraremos en Tskaltubo. Aunque la antigua conexión ferroviaria no opera, merece la pena subirse a otra marshrutka para visitar esta ciudad-balneario, hace décadas famosa por los baños en aguas de radón y ahora como destino de turismo urbex. Es difícil imaginar una definición gráfica más explícita del auge y caída de la Unión Soviética: la propia estación de tren abandonada, las decenas de sanatorios, hoteles y balnearios, construidos en un monumental clasicismo soviético, perecen ahora entre la vegetación como esqueletos de una civilización extinta hace no tanto tiempo, y a la espera de una restauración que no acaba de consumarse. Allí, el baño nº6, el único aún operativo, conserva como un tesoro la sauna personal de Stalin.

Stalin en Gori

La memoria histórica pega un giro aún más brusco cuando el tren nos deja en Gori, en el centro del país, y a unas dos horas y media desde Kutaisi. El propio nombre (montaña, en georgiano) da una pista sobre su orografía, con un aire fresco que ventila los abundantes parques y la colina en la que se asienta la muralla del siglo VII. No obstante, Gori se asocia mucho más con las cruentas —y todavía palpables— batallas de la guerra con Rusia en 2008 y, sobre todo, con la ciudad natal de Iósif Vissariónovich Dzhugashvili; o, para entendernos, Stalin. Su figura es todavía omnipresente, pone nombre a varios lugares de la ciudad y es homenajeada en el Museo Estatal de Stalin.

Un visitante frente a un retrato de Stalin, en el museo dedicado al dictador en su ciudad natal. George Gogua ( picture alliance / Getty Images)

Lejos de un centro documental que informe sobre la vida del dictador, este complejo exalta al que fue el habitante más ilustre de Gori con un estilo rococó de vidrieras, mármol, estatuas y alfombras que le dan el tratamiento de glorioso conquistador. Los guías (la mayor parte de las visitas son en georgiano y ruso) y la colección no escatiman en halagos para quien retratan como justiciero, bardo, revolucionario e indiscutido estadista. Quizá aún le agradezcan que el centro de Gori, pese a su modesto tamaño, posea una arquitectura más propia de una gran ciudad.

Tiflis, fin del trayecto

Apenas nos quedan 70 kilómetros hasta Tiflis, una ciudad que pide hacer un alto de varios días. Joven, multicultural, nocturna, creativa, inesperada, laberíntica, bulliciosa, alegre y reivindicativa, emana la historia y la vitalidad de una capital que trasciende a un país. En ella, se hacen evidentes la diáspora rusa, las tensiones políticas georgianas, la (de nuevo) comunión en torno a la gastronomía y la voluntad de encontrar nuevas vías de expresión. Como fue el tren lo que nos trajo hasta aquí, cabe decir que las estaciones de metro no desmerecen la reputación de otras antiguas capitales soviéticas. Pero, como de lo que se trataba era de cruzar el país, nos volvemos a subir a un viejo vagón para terminar el recorrido en Gardabani, a una hora al este de la Tiflis y ya rozando la frontera con Azerbaiyán.

El puente de la Paz, en el centro de Tiflis. Mirko Kuzmanovic ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Para quien prefiera emociones más fuertes, siempre quedan los viajes en marshrutka hacia Stepantsminda (la base para subir al monte Kazbegi) y la recóndita región vinícola de Kajetia, en la frontera con el Daguestán ruso.

World.title: Senators back plan to cultivate embryos for scientific research
World.content:
The Dutch senate has approved plans to allow specially grown embryos to be used for research into hereditary illnesses and infertility.

The bill, proposed by the liberal parties VVD and D66 during the last cabinet term while D66 was in opposition, achieved a narrow majority of 38 to 35 votes in the upper house.

The Christian parties ChristenUnie and SGP are opposed to cultivating embryos for scientific research because they see it as a violation of the sanctity of life.

The far-right PVV also voted against the plan, which party senator Ilse Bezaan called a “morally reprehensible” measure. “There are good alternatives, we shouldn’t open the door to a sliding scale,” she said.

Until now only embryos that are discarded during IVF treatment could be used for research purposes, but scientists say that using newly fertilised embryos would allow them to study the effect of treatments in the early stages of development.

World.title: Meat sector and government put profits before welfare: report
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch meat industry and the government are both failing to protect animal welfare, and put profits first as the laws are vague and hard to enforce.

“The system is failing to protect animal welfare: the government and the sector are falling short,” the committee, chaired by former transport inspectorate chief Jan van den Bos, said in its final report.

The agriculture ministry set up the panel in 2024 to review oversight of the meat chain. It found that food safety and animal health are well protected.

Welfare is harmed on a large scale even when companies follow the law, the committee said, because legal standards are vague and current production methods and costs are always the starting point when they are set.

Some 535 million animals are slaughtered in the Netherlands every year, more than 518 million of them chickens. Inspection figures cited in the report show that around 3 million birds arrive at slaughterhouses injured each year.

Two-thirds of 170 pig farms checked in 2023 and 2024 by the food and product safety watchdog NVWA were breaking welfare rules. The watchdog spends just 8% of its capacity on animal welfare.

The committee said the agriculture minister gives the sector too little direction and repeatedly delays decisions.

World.title: “Very dangerous”: Rights group condemns Kristallnacht speech
World.content:
The Kristallnacht remembrance service in Amsterdam’s Portuguese Synagogue has stirred controversy after the keynote speaker condemned the Red Line protests and said labelling the Gaza war a genocide was rooted in anti-Semitism.

In a highly political speech, Chanan Hertzberger, chair of Jewish umbrella organisation CJO, denounced the “genocide lie” in front of a congregation containing senior cabinet members including the prime minister Rob Jetten, who also spoke.

Gerard Jonkman, director of Amsterdam-based Rights Forum, which campaigns on behalf of Palestinian rights, told Dutch News Hertzberger’s speech was “absolutely unacceptable”.

“This is also mixing the issue of anti-Semitism with criticism of Israel,” he said, “which is very, very, very dangerous.”

Hertzberger began his speech by thanking Jetten for not giving in to “the demands of the organisers of yesterday’s anti-Israel demonstration”, which he said amounted “directly or indirectly” to wiping Israel off the map.

“Who is being held responsible, in Arnhem, in Groningen and in Amsterdam for this so-called genocide?” he said. “We, the Jews. In our own own cities. In our streets. In our children’s classrooms. We are being ostracised and pushed to the margins of society.”

Only hours before, Jetten had spoken to RTL Nieuws saying it had been “impossible to miss” the protest and that he decided to stay away (having attended previous ones) because of his new role as PM, which he and his fellow cabinet member have used from the beginning to “increase pressure on Israel”.

“He embarrassed Jetten”

Jonkman said he thought Hertzberger had embarrassed Jetten and that the prime minister should now react to “these ridiculous accusations of hatred towards Israel.”

He said many Jewish people joined Sunday’s demonstration, among them Holocaust survivors and children of Holocaust survivors, and that many people he had spoken to were hurt by the speech.

Linking the protest to anti-Semitism in this way makes Jewish people in the Netherlands appear accountable for the policies of the Israeli government, he said.

Hertzberger said the “lie” that Israel was committing genocide now “marches weekly through our streets”, citing chants at Sunday’s protest, though he added that not all demonstrators were anti-Semites.

Zionism

He claimed that in fact the majority of Jewish people in the Netherlands are Zionists, that Zionism is the recognition of Israel’s right to exist as a “safe, independent Jewish state”, and that those things are now “more important than ever”.

He mentioned the numerous attacks on Jewish schools and synagogues in the Netherlands this year, and said that the images of Gaza left no one unmoved, including himself.

A United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejects.

The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. Both men have firmly denied the allegations.

Jonkman said many Jewish people joined Sunday’s Red Line demonstration, and that many people he had spoken to, among them Holocaust survivors and children of Holocaust survivors, were hurt by the speech.

The CJO has not yet replied for comment.

Jetten’s premiership has marked a downturn in Dutch-Israeli relations. Since the cabinet enacted a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories in September, Israel has responded by stripping Dutch diplomats of their status and removing Dutch officials from a US-backed Gaza ceasefire centre.

World.title: Village threatened by port expansion could be saved by new plan
World.content:
A village with 1,100 inhabitants that has been facing shutdown for the last year under plans to expand an industrial port in Noord-Brabant could be saved after the government came up with an alternative, smaller-scale development.

The municipal council in Moerdijk said a year ago that the entire village would have to be demolished to make room for the Powerport development, which needs 400 to 500 hectares of land.

The expansion of the port and industrial site includes high-voltage substations, transformer stations, and pipelines to support the transition to clean energy and supply power to homes and businesses in the coming decades.

But junior climate minister Jo-Annes de Bat said in a letter to parliament on Tuesday that “a new scenario has arisen” that would involve a smaller expansion of around 200 hectares, allowing Moerdijk to remain.

Pim Meijer, spokesman for community group Dorpstafel Moerdijk, gave a cautious welcome to the new plan, but said the uncertainty surrounding the village’s future had taken its toll.

“People have no perspective,” he told Dutch News. “They’re suffering from stress and physical ailments. This year 25 people have already signed up for the scheme that lets them sell their house to the council and that’s a direct result of the uncertainty.”

Quality of life

He said villagers wanted the council, the province and the municipality to set down clear parameters to guarantee the village’s future and quality of life.

“What people don’t want is to see the industrial zone constantly encroaching on the village, which is what’s been going on for years. We want to draw a boundary and say: thus far and no further,” he said.

“If people with children leave that has an impact on our primary schools and our social clubs, and if no houses are built then new people can’t come to live in Moerdijk. But as long as people believe in a future for Moerdijk we will keep fighting for it.”

The government will continue to honour its financial commitments to Moerdijk, including a pledge to fully compensate villagers for their land and property and €25 million in community funding.

De Bat said the amount of space required for the development was less than previously estimated, partly because more efficient batteries were available and the government has downscaled its ambitions to develop hydrogen power.

“Residents of the village of Moerdijk and the surrounding region have rightly been asking for clarity for a long time,” he wrote.

World.title: Toolkit to help teachers spot suspected child abuse goes live
World.content:
Schools have started using a new digital support package to help teachers alert the authorities to cases of suspected domestic abuse and neglect.

The toolkit has been developed to try to increase the number of reports from schools, which is lower in the Netherlands than in neighbouring countries.

It is the product of two years of research that began when a series of cases came to light in which children had been systematically abused and tortured by their families. The children attended school but teachers were either unaware of the problems at home or unwilling to intervene.

Since 2019 teachers have been required to pass on details of children who they suspect of being abused to Veilig Thuis, the agency that specialises in domestic abuse and can compel parents to accept help.

The education minister at the time, Hugo de Jonge, said on average every classroom contained one child who was a victim of abuse or neglect at home.

The number of reports schools has almost doubled in the last seven years to around 4,000, while Veilig Thuis has advised in more than 9,500 other cases.

Need for training

But experts warn that teachers still lack the necessary expertise and are reluctant to contact the authorities because they fear repercussions from parents.

World.title: International student numbers rise as people leave US
World.content:
More international students are coming to study at Dutch universities, partly driven by people choosing to leave the US amid the current political climate, according to broadcaster NOS.

Around 17,600 first-year students this academic year come from abroad, up about 6% on last year, according to provisional figures from the university association UNL and the association of universities of applied sciences (VH), news agency ANP reported.

Universities had agreed to admit no more than 16,766 new international students a year, so that internationalisation would not come at the expense of Dutch students or undermine the Dutch language.

The universities say foreign students are “more often choosing to study in Europe because of developments in the United States”.

NOS linked this to president Donald Trump, who has tightened visa checks, clashed openly with several universities and interfered with academic freedom since returning to the White House.

UNL said the rise in foreign students was good news in itself, because they mainly study technical subjects in a sector short of staff. “We badly need international talent, particularly in priority sectors such as technology,” UNL chair Caspar van den Berg said, according to NOS.

“At the same time, universities have agreed to cap international intake. That is why we are taking targeted extra measures.”

Several universities will cut the number of places on English-taught psychology, economics, business administration and political science courses so that they stay below the agreed maximum next year. National student union ISO said it opposes caps on places and that every student should be free to choose their course.

World.title: Cabinet hopeful of securing majority for capital gains tax plan
World.content:
The cabinet’s plans to introduce a capital gains tax are on course to clear both houses of parliament after three right-wing opposition parties signalled they were prepared to back the measure.

Junior finance minister Eelco Eerenberg said in a debate on Monday that the trio of JA21, BBB and SGP would support the plan, overcoming objections from other opposition parties and criticism by the Council of State.

Coalition parties D66 and CDA also voiced reservations about the reform, with Henk-Jan Oosterhuis of D66 calling it a “rather creative explanation of the budget rules” and Christian Democrat Inge van Dijk admitting that it was “not pretty”.

Luc Stultiens, of the left-wing opposition party Pro, went further, accusing the coalition parties of writing “a blank cheque for €17 billion to the wealthy”, referring to the projected budget shortfall that will be created by the transition.

The three right-wing opposition parties would give the minority coalition a majority in the lower house, but the cabinet would still need to find support from one more party in the Senate.

€10 billion gap

The pensioners’ party 50Plus is seen as the most likely candidate, even though MP Corrie van Brenk said the “signal is red” during Monday’s debate. Oosterhuis pointed out that the latest revision is almost identical to a plan 50Plus tabled previously in the upper house.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen’s reform would replace the current system of taxing investments and savings annually, based on estimated rates of return, with a tax levied when assets are sold.

The finance ministry has estimated that the switch to capital gains tax will leave a €10 billion gap in the short term because investors will no longer pay tax on their assets every year.

The Box 3 levy was struck out in 2021 when the Supreme Court ruled that the use of fictional interest rates was deemed to breach European law.

The government introduced a stopgap measure allowing taxpayers to challenge their tax bill by submitting their actual financial results, but this is costing the treasury an estimated €3.5 billion a year.

The Council of State, which advises the cabinet on the legal implications of its bills, said Heinen’s plans to start charging tax on capital gains from 2028 were too hasty and would cause administrative problems at the tax office. Heinen compromised by shifting the start date for the new tax to 2029, which will increase the budget shortfall.

World.title: National weather warnings over thick fog, Friesland car crash
World.content:
Thick fog covered almost all of the Netherlands on Tuesday morning, cutting visibility to less than 20 metres in some places and causing long tailbacks and a head-on crash in Friesland.

The national weather service KNMI issued a code yellow warning for the whole country except Zeeland, the Wadden Islands, the IJsselmeer and Wadden Sea areas and parts of Limburg. The warning runs from 11.30pm on Monday until midday on Tuesday.

Around 6.50am, visibility in Flevoland had fallen below 20 metres, and 70 metres was recorded in Zuid-Holland, broadcaster NOS reported.

In Friesland, two cars collided on the N359 road between Koudum and Hemelum in dense fog, regional news site Omrop Fryslân reported. Ambulances were called to the scene in around 6.50am; how many were injured is not yet known.

The KNMI is advising drivers to slow down and leave more space. Front fog lights should go on when visibility is below 200 metres, and rear fog lights below 50 metres.

Fog may hang over the north all day and come back on Tuesday night. Rain is forecast for Wednesday morning’s rush hour in the centre and south.

World.title: Two Ukrainians charged with spying and sabotage for Russia in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia. The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych. ▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026 The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics. According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office. Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life. At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months. In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. ﻿ Main image credit: ABW (under CC BY-SA 4.0)

World.title: “Strong traces of right-wing extremism” in activity of Kraków terrorist, says justice minister
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, says that investigators have so far found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the activity of Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out Saturday’s mass terrorist shooting in Kraków that left six people dead. The perpetrator’s search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist who killed 77 people during two attacks in 2011. Żurek’s comments come amid intense debate and dispute in Poland over the beliefs and motives of Oksiński, who on Monday died from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police that brought his rampage to an end. W. Żurek ujawnia nowe ustalenia po zamachu w Krakowie. Tłumik w samochodzie sprawcy i ślady zainteresowania Breivikiemhttps://t.co/nd1XPBlmrI — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) November 10, 2026 On Tuesday, Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, spoke to local broadcaster Radio Kraków about the progress of the investigation into Oksiński. He confirmed that the perpetrator had not left behind any letter or other kind of message revealing his motives. “Those motives are being investigated,” said the minister. “There are very strong traces of right-wing extremism. I can already confirm some information because the services have access to the perpetrator’s computer. Indeed, visits to websites related to Anders Breivik are visible.” Żurek also pointed to the fact that, as prosecutors announced on Sunday, a so-called Gadsden flag (showing a snake above the words “Don’t tread on me”) had been found in Oksiński’s home. Prosecutors say a "Don't Tread on Me" flag was found hanging at the home of the perpetrator of the attack in Kraków They emphasise that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation and that they are still trying to determine the shooter's motives and beliefs pic.twitter.com/yoNfh7cHwU — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026 Although the National Prosecutor’s Office emphasised that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation, Żurek noted that it was displayed during the attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of Donald Trump in 2021. “We know well that during the attack on the Capitol, there were quite a few of these flags among far-right groups in the United States,” said the minister. “This flag [in Oksiński’s home] also sends a signal to the security services and the prosecutor’s office.” Żurek added that a search of the perpetrator’s workplace had also identified “symbolism there that could point to this thread [of right-wing extremism]”, but provided no further details. The minister noted, however, that investigators are also taking into account the potential for “mental disorders” playing a role in the actions of Oksiński, whose parents and sister were found shot dead in his home. Żurek’s remarks come following controversy in Poland over a statement by interior minister Marcin Kierwiński on Saturday, in the immediate aftermath of the attack, when he said that early indications suggest that Oksiński had held “very radical views”, including a “fascination with far-right ideologies”. Over the following two days, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence supporting those claims, and in a TV interview on Sunday evening said that he had simply been sharing “first hypotheses”. That led some right-wing opposition politicians and commentators to accuse Kierwiński of spreading false claims, either through incompetence or as a deliberate attempt to associate the attack with the right. However, speaking to Radio Kraków on Tuesday, Żurek said that “it seems that what Minister Kierwiński communicated in those first hours is confirmed by the evidence”. Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, is facing growing pressure to present evidence to back his claim that the Kraków shooter was driven by far-right ideologies, amid criticism from opposition parties that he is seeking to exploit the tragedy for political reasons. — Jakub Krupa (@JakubKrupa) November 9, 2026 On social media, many people have also been sharing alleged images of Oksiński’s past activities, both online and in real life, claiming that they show he held left-wing views. However, some of those images have proven to be false, such as one purporting to show him at a pro-refugee rally (the photograph is genuine, but the person in it was not Oksiński) and another purporting to show him shaking hands with Kierwiński (the image was AI-generated). Further alleged images from Oskiński’s social media accounts remain unverified and also depict posts that were made six or seven years ago. Another fake that is being widely shared. While the photo is genuine, the person highlighted is not the Kraków shooter. Other images from the event clearly show it isn't him, while fact-checkers @konkret24 actually tracked down the guy in the photo: https://t.co/4HeofUdOUm pic.twitter.com/pTfdkCZlAL — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026 On Monday, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told Polsat News that there had been an “enormous wave of disinformation” in the wake of Saturday’s tragedy. He criticised “pseudo-journalists and politicians” who had shared such content. “Digital platforms acted very responsibly, removing this content quickly,” said Gawkowski. However, he added that X, the social media service owned by Elon Musk, had been an exception and was “where the most radicalisation occurred”. Meanwhile, the interior ministry’s spokeswoman, Karolina Gałecka, announced on Monday that they would notify prosecutors about the creation and dissemination of the AI-generated image of Kierwiński shaking hands with Oksiński. She said it had been spread by social media accounts associated with right-wing broadcaster Republika.
