World.title: Pula Wins the Title of the Best 15-Minute City in the Region
World.content:
November the 10th, 06 – Pula has won the title of the best 15-minute city in the region, with around 60% of the people in this city getting from A to B within a quarter of an hour.

As many as 60% of Pula residents get from A to B within a quarter of an hour. In contrast, in Zagreb, more than 80% of citizens travel for much longer. There’s a coastal Croatian city in which one reaches their job, school, family obligations and more, all in the time it often takes a resident of Zagreb to leave a car park. Poslovni reports that this remains the case even as a city that receives hundreds of thousands of visitors from all over the world in summer. In spite of that, it has preserved what most European cities have long since lost – order and peace on the roads. That city didn’t win only in Croatia, as this Friendly City Index research spans 62 cities across 11 countries.

pula takes first place

The biggest city in Istria was victorious among 62 cities. This is because as many as 60 percent of surveyed Pula residents manage to reach most of their everyday destinations within 15 minutes. The research , which was carried out by Syno International in 62 cities across Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine, Bulgaria and Azerbaijan, show that Pula residents live the everyday life that many desire: one in which less time goes on travel, and more remains for and free time.

“Pula was packed with events this summer, and thousands of visitors from all over the world week after week filled the Pula Arena at concerts of the biggest music stars. Despite the hustle and bustle, tourists and the expected crowds of the peak summer season, the average Bolt ride lasted 11 minutes, and almost 80 percent of all rides finished in less than 15 minutes. Our mobility and user movement data thereby additionally confirm what Pula residents highlighted in the Friendly City Index research: Pula is indeed a 15-minute city,” said Sanja Babić. Such a city rhythm is not a coincidence. Short distances and roundabouts, which in Pula at many key intersections have replaced traffic lights and enable more fluid traffic without long waiting, make Pula an example of how urban mobility can be simple and efficient.

zagreb remains the croatian record holder… at the very bottom of the list

Zagreb failed the 15-minute city test, and rather catastrophically so. The majority of surveyed Zagreb residents consider that the capital is still far from the vision of a city within a quarter of an hour’s reach, so it found itself at the bottom of the ranking, in 50th place, with a result of 18 percent. A surprise also came in the form of Zadar, which last year led the regional ranking with approximately 54 percent of respondents, and this year fell to ninth place, with 46 percent. This year’s analysis was also expanded to Pula and Dubrovnik, whereby the number of covered Croatian cities was increased from five to seven. In addition to first-placed Pula, Split occupies fourth and Osijek fifth place, both with a result of 50 percent. They were followed by Zadar, Rijeka in 16th place with 38 percent, Dubrovnik in 38th place with 23 percent, and Zagreb as the last among Croatian cities.

pula beats bucharest

The Friendly City Index research, in which residents of 62 cities in 11 countries assessed whether they reach their everyday destinations within 15 minutes, showed that at the opposite end of the ranking from the winner Pula is Romanian Bucharest, which took last place in the research. In Bucharest only six percent of residents reach destinations within a quarter of an hour, which means that that share in Pula is as much as ten times higher than in the Romanian capital. Among the capital cities Bratislava fared the best, but even it with a result of 26 percent occupies only 30th place in the overall ranking.

what is the Friendly City Index?

The Friendly City Index is an international research that compares the quality of life in cities of Central and Eastern Europe as the residents themselves see it: how much time they need to work, educational, health and sports facilities or the shop, how close green areas are to them, what the cycling and traffic infrastructure is like. The research was conducted on Bolt’s initiative by the company Syno International, and this year’s edition covers 62 cities in 11 countries: Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine, Bulgaria and Azerbaijan. The ranking of 15-minute cities is based on the share of respondents who reach most everyday destinations within a quarter of an hour.

People who still want to live in cities move into them primarily because of practicality, but the accelerated growth and development of cities can make everyday life much more challenging. That’s why the concept of the 15-minute city is a good check of what the real situation is. It shows where cities succeed, and where there is room for improvement. The recipe for success is almost universal – fewer crowds, better public transport and more available alternatives to the private car. If people daily spend more time travelling, that indicates the negative consequences of urban planning that ultimately reflect on the quality of life, from the household budget to health.

World.title: Possible Tax Increase Looms for Croatian Private Landlords
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – A possible tax increase is looming for Croatian private landlords in yet another strike to their pockets. This goes alongside all of the other changes coming next year.

Croatian private landlords are facing a slew of changes in the way of registration and recording at the Tax Administration next year. As if all of what has previously been announced wasn’t enough, there’s also a possible increase in the annual lump-sum tax on the cards. Index reports that the government is now proposing automatic registration and de-registration of taxpayers who earn income from renting out their tourist accommodation, as well as an increase in the lowest tax amounts in the most tourism-developed cities and municipalities.

The final proposal of amendments to the Income Tax Act was sent by the government to the Croatian Parliament on the 5th of November, as part of the tax changes planned for 2027. One of the novelties relates to the establishment of automated data exchange between the competent institutions and the Tax Administration. On the basis of data from official records the Tax Administration could in the future independently carry out the registration and de-registration of those who earn income from tourist rentals.

official records and data should be better aligned

Until now, people starting to rent out accommodation and earn income from that activity had the obligation to report the start of performing the activity and register in the register of taxpayers. With the proposed solution part of that procedure would be taken over by the competent institutions, whereby administrative obligations should be simplified, and data in official records better aligned. Nevertheless, from the government’s proposal it does not follow that landlords would be freed from all obligations of reporting changes or submitting documentation. The scope of their future obligations will depend on the final legal solution and the rules of its implementation.

an increase in lump-sum tax…

In addition to changes in the recording of taxpayers, the government is also proposing an increase in the minimum amounts of the annual lump-sum income tax from tourist accommodation. These are amounts that are calculated per bed, or corresponding accommodation unit. For cities and municipalities in the first category of tourist development the legal minimum would increase from 100 to 150 euros per bed. In the second category an increase from 70 to 100 euros is planned. This, however, does not mean that the tax will rise by the same amount for all landlords. Local units still determine the amount of the lump-sum tax within the limits prescribed by law, so the concrete effect will depend on how much is currently paid in an individual city or municipality.

For example, a landlord who has six beds in a local self-government unit of the first category, and in which the legal minimum of 100 euros is currently applied, pays 600 euros in tax annually. According to the proposed amendments that amount would rise to 900 euros, which is 300 euros more. On the other hand, where local authorities already apply a lump sum of 150 euros or more per bed, the increase in the legal minimum does not necessarily mean an additional rise in the tax obligation.

there’s no way to avoid these tax hikes

The government’s proposal also covers the amounts that are applied in the event that city or municipal representative bodies do not make a decision on the amount of the lump-sum tax. In units of the first category of tourist development that amount would increase from the previous 200 to 225 euros per bed or corresponding accommodation unit. For the second category an increase from 135 to 150 euros is planned. In practice, this would mean that a landlord with six beds in the first category, in the case of application of that legal amount, would instead of the previous 1,200 euros pay 1,350 euros annually. These are amounts provided for in the draft law, and not already determined tax obligations for individual private landlords.

World.title: Research: Vučić Falling is More Important Than Price Increases and Protests for Croatia
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Research has discovered that Aleksandar Vučić falling in Serbia is more important than the price increases and protests within Croatia.

The defeat of Aleksandar Vučić in the elections over in Serbia was the most important topic for Croatians in the past month, ahead of inflation and price increases, shows the new CRO Demoskop. Index reports that the defeat of Aleksandar Vučić in the parliamentary elections in Serbia was declared the most important topic of the past month by 21.9 percent of respondents. Inflation and price increases took second place with 14.3 percent, while street protests in several European cities were singled out by 12.4 percent of citizens.

The death of Goran Bare and Mišo Kovač was an important topic for 11.9 percent of respondents. The Nazi rampage by part of Torcida fans, arrests and threats to journalists was singled out by 9.9 percent. Problems with the remediation of illegal waste in Gospić and protests against the incineration of waste in Koromačno received 4.7 and 4.4 percent respectively.

If elections had been held at the beginning of November, HDZ would have won 24.9 percent of the votes, and SDP 17.5 percent. HDZ fell by 0.1 percentage points compared to October, while SDP lost two points and recorded the lowest support in the current term. In the last year support for HDZ has fallen by five, and for SDP by six percentage points.

This is at the same time HDZ’s weakest result since Andrej Plenković began his third premiership in April 2024. Among the four leading parties support in one month fell by a total of 2.7 percentage points, and around three quarters of that drop falls on SDP. Možemo is in third place with 13.6 percent, and Most in fourth with 9.4 percent. Those parties also recorded a slight drop, by 0.2 and 0.4 percentage points respectively. Undecided voters stand at 18.8 percent, compared to 15.6 percent in October. The research was conducted by the agency Promocija plus on a sample of 1,000 respondents. The sampling error for party ratings is ±3.53 percentage points, with a confidence level of 95 percent. The data source is CRO Demoskop for RTL.

World.title: Will New Dawn in Serbia Result in a Change of Relations With Croatia?
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Will the new dawn in Serbia after the removal of Aleksandar Vučić finally result in a long-awaited change of relations with Croatia?

The fact that a new group of people with fresh policies will finally lead Serbia does not necessarily mean that it will totally abandon its old, poisonous national priorities. Zlatko Crncec reports for Novi list that the new political ruling elite in Serbia is encouragingly announcing a radical break with the foreign policy of Aleksandar Vučić. However, as in everything else, much, if not almost everything, remains rather unclear.

Both when it comes to who will make up the future Serbian Government, and what exact policy they will pursue. Because the fact that a new team is coming to the head of Serbia does not necessarily mean that it could abandon old national priorities. Between good-neighbourly relations, the protection of Serbs in the region, the constitutional issue of Kosovo and the attitude towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, space opens up for serious political uncertainties.

It is still not clear whether the victory of the Student List “Students are Winning” also means a real change in Serbia’s attitude towards neighbouring countries. Or will only the way in which the previous national and foreign policy goals are presented to the public change?

neighbourly relations…

This is especially important for Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Kosovo. These are the countries towards which Aleksandar Vučić’s policy, in various forms and intensities, has for years been burdened by unresolved issues from the past, national pretensions, the instrumentalisation of the position of Serbian communities and occasional political crises. The programme of the list and the public appearances of its leader Ilija Srdanović point to several important conclusions. First, the new political structure wants to distance itself from the personalised foreign policy of Aleksandar Vučić. Second, it does not intend to abandon traditional Serbian state priorities, especially when it comes to Republika Srpska and Kosovo. Third, it is trying to find a language that would simultaneously satisfy pro-European oriented citizens, the nationally sensitive part of the electorate and international partners. Precisely in that combination lies the greatest unknown of the new policy.

For Croatia the most important message is the one that the leader of the Student List Ilija Srdanović expressed immediately after the election victory. He announced that relations between the two countries will be based on good-neighbourliness, and not on a policy of confrontation. “Croatia will not be in any other status there except good-neighbourly relations,” Srdanović emphasised. In doing so he attributed responsibility for the deterioration of relations to the previous Serbian president. He spoke about the policy of one man who “set two peoples against each other”, emphasising that foreign policy should in the future be conducted by the government of Serbia, and not by an individual. Namely, in Serbia the government has greater powers than the president, but it is allowed that he can be a member of a party.

Vučić, at least for the largest part of his mandate, was also the president of the ruling SNS and in that way was able through party discipline to be at the same time the strongest political figure in Serbia. Therefore what Srdanović stated can still mean some progress. Vučić’s Serbia often used the Croatian state as a foreign policy opponent, and Croatian authorities as a convenient argument in domestic political showdowns.

Accusations about Croatian influence on the Serbian opposition, alleged interference in internal affairs and acting against Serbian national interests were part of everyday political life. Srdanović’s message suggests that such a practice could be abandoned. However, it is important to pay attention to his statement about Croatia, and for now much clearer regarding mere political tone than when it comes to concrete moves. Besides, at this moment it is still not clear whether Srdanović, although he was first on the list, will even be a member of the new Serbian Government. If he will be, it isn’t clear which portfolio he could take over.

minority rights

The more extensive Student List programme shows that a good-neighbourly policy does not mean abandoning issues that have traditionally burdened relations between Belgrade and Zagreb. In the part of the programme that relates to the position of Serbs in the region, the list particularly emphasises the rights of Serbs in Croatia, the preservation of their national, cultural and linguistic identity, the position of returnees, what it calls the selective application of law in certain court proceedings, and the conditions for the dignified marking of grave sites.

In doing so it invokes United Nations Security Council Resolution 1120, the Erdut Agreement and the bilateral agreement from 2004 on the protection of the rights of the Croatian minority in Serbia, and of the Serbian and Montenegrin minorities in Croatia. That part of the programme deserves a certain amount of attention. It shows that the Student List does not intend to abandon an active policy of protecting the Serbian minority outside the borders of Serbia. That in itself, of course, is not at all disputable. The protection of minority rights is a legitimate obligation of every democratic state, and Serbia and Croatia have bilateral agreements precisely so that those rights would be protected. However, a problem arises if minority issues are turned into an instrument of political pressure on a neighbouring state. Which Vučić abundantly used. Therefore for Croatia it will be important how Belgrade will concretise its demands.

Will it be a matter of institutional cooperation, exchange of information, solving the problems of returnees, protection of cultural heritage and equal treatment by judicial bodies, or will space again be opened for political accusations and unilateral interpretations of history? Particularly interesting is that the programme at the same time mentions the rights of the Croatian minority in Serbia. Which are far from what the Serbian minority has in Croatia.

However many shortcomings the model of electing three Serbian deputies in a special electoral unit has, the fact that Croatia nevertheless applies it speaks of the fact that it wants transparent and good relations. On the other hand, in Serbia there is no mechanism that would guarantee that Croats have their guaranteed representative in the National Assembly. The announcement that the Student List could work on that gives the possibility for a different and better model of mutual relations, instead of constant political competition around the position of Serbs in Croatia. If Belgrade is going to advocate for the rights of Serbs in Croatia, it should at the same time show readiness to protect the rights of Croats in Serbia without political calculations, including their cultural autonomy, representation and the possibility of participating in public life.

war crimes

The second major issue remains the wartime past and open questions from the 1990s. Srdanović has in previous appearances emphasised that the new generation does not want to be burdened by responsibility for events from a time in which its members did not participate. Such a position is politically understandable, but it is not sufficient for things to move from a standstill. In that sense more important than statements about a new beginning will be whether the new authorities will open space for a more serious attitude towards the missing, war crimes, archival material and compensation for victims. In the political confusion that currently reigns in Serbia, it is impossible to extract anything more than these genuinely encouraging wishes that Srdanović expressed in the above-mentioned and in several other public appearances.

the attitude towards srebrenica…

Bosnia and Herzegovina is perhaps the politically most sensitive issue in the entire regional agenda of the Student List. In an interview for Radio Free Europe Srdanović very clearly said that the new authorities will continue cooperation with Republika Srpska. “The continuation of cooperation with Republika Srpska is in the interest of the citizens of Serbia and the citizens of Republika Srpska,” Srdanović said.

To the question of whether Belgrade will encourage the authorities of Republika Srpska to solve problems with the institutions of the central government in Sarajevo, he answered that they will advocate for open dialogue and finding common solutions for all citizens of BiH and Republika Srpska.

Whatever that means.

The Student List does not question the special relationship of Serbia and Republika Srpska. It does not announce its reduction, redefinition or the withdrawal of Belgrade from political and institutional relations with Banja Luka. Another possibility is a change in the way that relationship is realised. Srdanović speaks of dialogue, common solutions and the interests of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which can be read as a distancing from the policy of constant conflicts between Republika Srpska and the state institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the programme does not give a precise answer to the question of how the Student List imagines the relationship of Belgrade towards the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Serbia has special ties with Republika Srpska, which also stems from its constitutional and political framework, but at the same time has the obligation to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The new authorities will have to show whether they can reconcile those two facts without creating additional tensions. Particularly indicative is Srdanović’s answer about Srebrenica. To the question of what position the new authorities will take, he said that the issue of Srebrenica is defined by court decisions, and he mentioned the documents that the Serbian Assembly adopted back in 2010.

World.title: Zadar Airport Smashes Previous Records in 2026
World.content:
November the 9th, 2026 – Zadar Airport has smashed its previous records in 2026 despite having a somewhat weaker October than usual. A brand new route from Zadar to German will also operate next summer.

In the first ten months of this year, almost 80,000 more passengers were recorded by Zadar Airport than in the same period last year. For summer 2027, a brand new Ryanair line to Friedrichshafen has also been announced. as eZadar reports, Zadar Airport has already by the end of October surpassed the number of passengers achieved during the whole of last year. According to official statistics, in the first ten months of 2026 1,714,335 passengers were recorded, or 74,734 more than in the entire record year of 2025. Compared to the same ten-month period last year, traffic rose by 4.89 percent, or by 79,947 passengers. The new annual record was thus set while two months still remain until the end of the year.

8,000 fewer passengers in october

October itself, however, finished in a weaker way than October last year. 95,956 passengers passed through Zadar Airport, while in October 2025 there were 103,829. That is a drop of 7.58 percent, or 7,873 fewer passengers. The number of aircraft in the official records was also reduced: from last year’s 532 to this year’s 499, which represents a drop of 6.20 percent. The October result is thereby the first monthly drop in the number of passengers this year compared to 2025. All previous nine months recorded growth.

a new line for summer 2027

In addition to the traffic results, the question of the director’s mandate is currently topical at Zadar Airport. Josip Klišmanić, who has been at the head of the company since October 2017, had his existing mandate, according to data available at the Commission for Deciding on Conflict of Interest, expire on the 14th of October 2026. The government has proposed his temporary appointment for a maximum of six months, until the appointment of a director through a public tender.

This period of the year is always quieter at Zadar Airport. The direct international connection is reduced to Munich, on Mondays and Fridays. Domestic connections are maintained via Pula and Zagreb. For the next summer season an expansion of the destination network has also been announced. The Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair in the summer flight schedule 2027 will connect German Friedrichshafen with Zadar, whereby Zadar Airport gains yet another direct connection with the German market.

World.title: 'Alien' rockers Henge to bring Cosmic Dross to Tallinn in 2027
World.content:
British act Henge, who perform as extraterrestrials spreading peace through a genre they call Cosmic Dross, are to appear in Estonia next year.

The band, from Manchester, are to play the Paavli Culture Factory a little over a year from now, on November 16, 2027, as part of a 75-concert world tour behind their fifth album "Humans", due out early next year.

Henge, sometimes styled HENGE, performs as four fictional characters: Zpor on vocals and guitar, Goo on bass, Sol on synthesizers and Nom on drums. According to their own story, they arrived from distant galaxies to spread peace and prepare humanity for life beyond its home planet.

Their music combines progressive rock, psychedelia and rave culture. Live, the group pairs instrumental passages and electronic rhythms with costumes and a visual language borrowed from science fiction films.

Beyond the stage, they have expanded their fictional world into a comic series made with artists including Boo Cook, an illustrator who has worked on the British cult comic 2000 AD.

Founded in 2015, their albums so far are "Attention Earth!" (2018), "ExoKosm" (2020), "Alpha Test 4" (2023) and "Journey to Voltus B" (2025), a concept album about a planet whose inhabitants are on the brink of discovering nuclear power. The vinyl B-side carries two parallel grooves leading to two different endings — one where the civilization uses nuclear fusion peacefully, one where nuclear winter arrives.

Henge won Live Act of the Year at the 2018 Independent Festival Awards and took silver for Best Music Video at the 2022 Tokyo Film Awards.

Henge appear at the Paavli Culture Factory (Paavli kultuurivabrik) in Tallinn on Tuesday, November 16, 2027.

World.title: Estonian mardipäev, kadripäev traditions await UNESCO decision
World.content:
Estonia's centuries-old mardipäev and kadripäev customs were nominated for inclusion on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. A decision is expected in early December.

Monday was St. Martin's Eve, or mardilaupäev, in Estonia, and to help hype up the nomination, a group of dressed up mardid went door to door in Tallinn's Old Town that evening.

The mardid even visited the Estonian government on Toompea Hill, entering Stenbock House to sing, do cartwheels in front of the prime minister, tell riddles and perform other traditional antics — including bless Prime Minister Kristen Michal with good luck.

"He's a good lad who needs strength and energy, and could use a switch as well," said one mart, adding that the bundle of birch twigs was a health-boosting switch.

Whether the Estonian tradition makes it onto UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity will be decided at a committee meeting in China in early December.

The Estonian Folklore Council (EFN) is leading the nomination.

"We're hopeful," said another mart, asking why shouldn't these centuries-old traditions be included on the list, like the smoke sauna. "We've submitted our application, and we're still making a little noise today, and then we'll be on our way there."

'It's a two-way dialogue'

Laura Liinat, a Cultural Heritage Department adviser at the Ministry of Culture, said the chances look good, though she stopped short of calling the outcome.

She said the tradition's value lies not only in the mardid and kadrid keeping alive the custom of dressing up and going door to door, but also in the interaction between the costumed visitors and the people who welcome them into their homes.

"It's a two-way dialogue, and the hosts who receive the mardid and kadrid play just an important role," Liinat explained. "The way we welcome them may be a reflection of how we treat one another."

St. Martin's Day falls on November 10, and much like Halloween, or All Hallow's Eve, dressed up marts traditionally make their rounds the night before, on St. Martin's Eve.

Kadrid follow suit on kadrilaupäev, or St. Catherine's Eve, on November 24.

World.title: Rapla student discovers a different Estonia as Kihnu exchange student
World.content:
While many students go abroad on exchange, one young Rapla student chose a different adventure: two weeks at a tiny island school in Kihnu.

Rosmary, known as Roosi on the island of Kihnu, is a student at Rapla Vesiroosi School. While she initially had her sights set on an exchange to the U.S., Roosi did some research and realized she'd fall behind on school back home.

Instead, she wanted to experience what it was like to learn in a much smaller class setting.

"My own school is really big, with around 20 students in each class," Roosi said. "Here, there are only 20 students in the whole school. I thought it'd be really interesting to see how that works."

Before the exchange, Roosi had never even visited Kihnu, a small island in the Gulf of Riga covering less than 17 square kilometers.

Now she is just the second student in her class at Kihnu School, and she loves how closely students from first through ninth grade are connected.

"It's basically one big family," she said. "That's so sweet."

'They've been so helpful'

During her two-week stay, Roosi also has to keep up with assignments from her school back home. She was initially worried about falling behind on her work, but said Kihnu's teachers have gone out of their way to help her stay on track.

"They've been so helpful and have made time to help me keep up with my other schoolwork too," she added.

Asked about what she misses from life on the mainland, Roosi admitted she misses shopping, her family and her dog. Her host family at Kolde Farm has its own dog too, however, along with some 200 farm animals, from horses to highland cattle.

World.title: Estonian kickboxer ahead of WBC fight: More girls than boys in the gym now
World.content:
Estonian kickboxer Astrid Johanna Grents is fighting for a WBC international title on Saturday, saying girls now sometimes outnumber boys in the training hall.

Grents, who won European Games gold in 2023, says Saturday's fight, at the Tondiraba Ice Hall against Italy's Ludovica Ciarpaglini, is the most important of her life — win it and she can challenge for a world title.

One inspiration is the number of women and girls training nowadays, compared with when she started over a decade ago.

"When I started out, there were very few girls doing boxing. Now you see that sometimes there are even more girls than boys in the gym, and you see they even have more discipline about coming to training every day than the boys," she told "Terevisioon," adding the sport has grown hugely in Estonia.

Grents, fights under the name Asteroid, took up kickboxing 12 years ago looking for a new hobby. She has also trained in classical boxing and kickboxing, but her main style is Muay Thai.

"I have the ability to defend myself and I think that makes you very confident. It has become such a part of my life that I can't imagine not going to training today."

She said the sport clears her head and is a great workout. "During a boxing session you can't think about anything, you have to be in the moment." She contrasted that with gym training, where people tend to scroll on their phones between sets: in kickboxing you get three minutes of work and a minute's rest, with no time to think about anything except getting your breath back.

World.title: Binturong breakout means Tallinn Zoo without a single Nicobar pigeon left alive
World.content:
Tallinn Zoo has lost its entire collection of an exotic species of pigeon after being killed by two escaped binturongs, Eesti Ekspress reported .

The pair of binturongs, also known as bearcats and native to southeast Asia, had absconded from their enclosure, and the Nicobar pigeons, found in the islands of the same name and further east, proved easy prey: Two if the three birds were killed outright and the third having to be put down after an injury inflicted by the arboreal viverrids turned necrotic.

The binturongs, who after a competition were named by the public Maimu and Maru, live in a rainforest house that opened at the zoo a few years ago, and their escape bids in recent months had become somewhat of a regular feature.

However, this time it went further than mischief – while they may appear "cute," a binturong's soft muzzle hides 36 to 40 sharp teeth; in their natural habitat, Nicobar pigeons have few predators, and roost in large flocks at night.

Their iridescent green-blue feathers also make them stand out.

The binturongs have reportedly climbed out of their enclosure at the zoo four times since August this year — the first during the Ironman event in Rocca al Mare, when noise from a nearby stage is thought to have driven them to seek somewhere quieter — and, after a mesh-covered enclosure failed to confined them, in October. They now await relocation, something which the zoo had planned anyway. Initially they were both thought to be female, but it later turned out one of the binturongs is a male.

World.title: Pensioners' party founder: Estonia must find more money, not take it away
World.content:
The founder of a new political party representing older people in Estonia wants to give that demographic a voice, and to fund a rise in pensions by boosting the economy and industry.

Ago Kokser heads up the newly founded party, Generations (Põlvkonnad), which he says will appeal to all age groups.

As we know, a political party must have 500 members [to legally register]. You held the founding meeting of your party on Saturday. What exactly is its status? Could it already be referred to a political party?

We wanted to set up a political party, and the founding meeting has taken place. We formed a provisional board, and now we have time to recruit members. I believe we will reach the required 500 members within the next week. Interest has been very high. We have already received 390 expressions of interest, and we have officially registered more than 50 members in just one day. When I have met people, everyone has been full of praise and said it was high time this was done.

So there are already around 390 people interested?

People who have indicated that they are willing to join us. We have an email address, but we did not have a party membership application form ready. It had not been available on the website. Now it is on the website, and people can immediately sign up and join the party there. We are also working directly with people. I give you my word that we will get this done.

This is by no means your first time as a member of a political party. You have been in the Center Party and the Reform Party. Those parties are still active, and there are other parties with strong ratings and very good prospects of entering the Riigikogu. Why did you feel that none of the existing parties offered a way to put your ideas into practice?

Initially, I had no such ambition at all. I was also involved with pensioners and pensioners' organizations, and we had a very large network across Estonia, with more than 24,000 members. But in recent years, the government's position has been that organizations do not need operating subsidies. That they should figure out for themselves how to manage and find money. But funding is only available for projects, not for keeping organizations alive.

We approached members of the Riigikogu, the chair of the Social Affairs Committee and the prime minister to ask whether a solution could be found. Promises were made, but a year passed, and nobody wanted to answer the phone or reply to emails anymore.

We called together the extended board to decide what to do. Should we disband or continue operating? We decided it was too early to disband because we still have ideas. And we could continue operating, since the network is already there.

So why shouldn't pensioners have their own representation? At the same time, people have asked me about the various attempts to establish pensioners' associations years ago. But political parties absorbed this interest group, and those organizations eventually disappeared. Now we felt it was the right time to come forward again because there is interest.

Politicians think that if they raise pensions a little, pensioners will be satisfied. They get their money and keep quiet. But there are more than 310,000 pensioners now. People want to have a say, not just be sitting at home. Communication is important.

In fact, whenever we are portrayed pictorially, we are depicted either with a walking stick or in a wheelchair. But we do not all use walking sticks; I did not come to this interview in a wheelchair or with a walking stick.

In our consideration, older people are those aged 55 and over, right through to end-of-life. We still have some capabilities. We have knowledge, skills and life experience.

And we decided this is not simply a party for older people. We need to involve everyone, the different generations. Young people also have many of their own problems, young families have problems, working-age people have their problems. And everyone of working age will eventually reach retirement age, so they should be able to prepare for that period of their lives.

The idea is certainly good, and the name Põlvkonnad [Generations] is very good, but from a marketing perspective, things seem to have gone a little wrong for you. You said from 55 to the end of life. I think a 55-year-old might be very offended to be referred to as "elderly."

But why would they be offended? When our media says that people aged 55 and over have a particular difficulty finding jobs. They are not accepted, and employers do not want to hire them.

I remember when I was younger, when the Estonian state was restored. Back then, people said that anyone over 30 could be written off; that there was nothing to be done with them.

We welcome all who want to join us. We do not set an age limit, but welcome people who have a good character, want to have a say and believe they have something to contribute.

Because at present when all these laws are being drafted, we are only sometimes involved. We are asked to give our opinions when everything has already been decided. In reality, only cosmetic changes can be made by that stage. And we are not involved in the decision-making process.

But we have the ability to contribute, we could have a say, but for some reason nobody wants to listen to us. So, now we have decided to try and see whether we can make ourselves heard.

You have major designs on taking part in next year's Riigikogu elections. Older people have always been very active voters, so you also have a strong base of support. What would be your main promises and issues, pensions aside, going into the elections?

There are actually many things. We wondered whether our little group had the right to put together the entire program. We will draft it, and everyone else gets to vote on it when we assemble the party's program. We still have a little time at the moment.

But you must have some ideas. You surely discussed these issues on Saturday. What are they then?

There is the care reform, how people can live out the final years of their lives with dignity and on their pensions. Pensions, the size of pensions, as although indexation exists, it does not guarantee that people's quality of life will be maintained, since prices are rising faster than pensions can keep up.

Are you pledging to hike pensions?

Of course, the entire system needs an overhaul. Everyone says we have no money for pensions and cannot do anything.

But if we change the system now, and 20-year-olds start approaching things differently, they will reach retirement age in 50 years. The decisions we make now will have an impact 50 years from now.

We also have to think about that, not just about what we do today and assume that in five years everything will be new and functioning. It will not.

You have been involved in pensioners' organizations. What changes could be made to Estonia's pension system?

There could be many changes. Perhaps we should review indexation, how the money comes in and how it is handled.

Should people, how should I put it, have to live on the edge of subsistence when they become pensioners? Or should they be able to live a dignified life?

Where the money would come from, I cannot say. Cutting or saving money is the easiest approach. But the goal of a society is to live well.

One political party once promised that in five years we would be among the five richest countries. That is what we should be striving for.

The purpose of politics is to stimulate the economy. If we do not stimulate the economy, we will get nowhere. We will simply decline.

What is your idea for stimulating the economy? I would still like to get to the question of where to find the money to raise pensions.

We have some very capable specialists who have retired. We can bring them together and form working groups.

Of course, there are many issues, as I said, including care reform, access to healthcare and mobility.

Just an hour ago, we were talking about how the main problem with Estonia's healthcare system is that there is too little money.

Yes, there is too little money. But everyone keeps saying õõ there is never enough money, while at the same time we hear in the news that a million goes here, another million goes there, and ten million goes on something else.

As I understand it, we do have money. The question is whether it is being directed to the right places and used properly. That is another matter.

Then I have a very good opportunity to ask you: if you had to take money away from somewhere, where would you take it from? Where is too much money being allocated at the moment?

I would not immediately say where money should be taken away from. I would find more of it.

In the near future, we need to find where additional money can come from. We need to focus on that and direct all our energy toward it, rather than looking for ways to take money out of somebody else's pocket.

So where would the additional money come from?

From the economy, from production. That means not just the soft-sector jobs we have here, but we need to work intensively on industry and encourage the development of manufacturing and industry.

That is where the money will come from.

World.title: Tallinn's 2027 budget prioritizes education and crisis preparedness
World.content:
The Tallinn city government approved its draft 2027 budget on Tuesday. The budget totals €1.3 billion, including €168 million in investments.

Education, transportation and social welfare account for the largest share of the city's operating expenditures.

Operating expenditures are projected at €1.1 billion, while total revenue is expected to reach €1.2 billion. Tallinn's net debt burden is projected to remain within the limits set out in the city's budget strategy by the end of 2027.

The city will continue to waive kindergarten fees, provide support payments for parents caring for children at home and support the transition to Estonian-language education.

In 2027, construction of the new Kullo youth center and Tallinn Helen School building will be completed, while work will continue on an extension to Jakob Westholm High School.

Investments in education and youth programs are budgeted at €70.8 million.

Tallinn city bus and tram. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Transport vehicles will get upgrades

Public transportation will remain free for Tallinn residents in 2027.

The budget allocates €31 million for transportation investments, including €29.5 million for road construction and repairs. Planned projects include work on Pärnu maantee, Peterburi tee and Rahumäe tee.

AS Tallinna Linnatransport also plans to replace 60 aging diesel buses and continue upgrading tram and trolleybus infrastructure.

The city will continue funding care services for children with extensive support needs and 24-hour general care services for older residents.

Funding for personal assistant services will also increase to support the independent living of people with disabilities.

Social welfare operating expenditures are budgeted at €145.4 million, with an additional €13.6 million allocated for investments.

In health care, the city will continue supporting the family doctor on-call service and mental health prevention programs for children and young people.

The budget allocates €1.5 million to improve crisis preparedness in apartment buildings.

In total, nearly €3.1 million is earmarked for crime prevention and public safety initiatives.

The city plans to expand shelter capacity, improve the readiness of designated emergency kindergartens and organize practical crisis preparedness training for residents.

The Tallinn City Council building. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Cultural institutions and sports facilities to be upgraded

Major projects planned for next year include the renovation of Kadriorg Stadium, upgrades to the A. H. Tammsaare Museum and further development of the library network.

Investments in culture and heritage preservation are budgeted at €11.9 million, while €14.4 million is allocated to sports and recreational activities.

Tallinn will continue preparing its new comprehensive plan, aimed at improving access to services close to home and guiding the city's long-term development.

The city also plans to simplify procedures allowing apartment associations to use city-owned land for parking spaces and waste collection facilities.

Operating expenditures for circular economy initiatives are budgeted at €4.9 million. The city will continue preparations for waste management reform and promote the separate collection of waste.

Maintenance of parks, green spaces and other public areas, as well as protection of the natural environment, will also continue.

The 2027 budget allocates €4.7 million to business development.

Through the Test in Tallinn program, the city will continue cooperating with companies to pilot new products and services in the urban environment.

The city government will now submit the draft budget to the Tallinn City Council for consideration.

World.title: Kaire Sepper: There are debts you can legally refuse to pay
World.content:
Debts are meant to be repaid. At least in an ideal world. Yet there are debts that people can legally refuse to pay, but thousands still do so, writes Kaire Sepper.

I have spent years working with debt collection, first in a bailiff's office and now as an attorney helping clients. Debts should be repaid. But should all debts? The answer is no.

The issue is also a hot topic at the national level. This summer, the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs circulated a proposal to amend the Code of Enforcement Procedure, under which debtors would be allowed to keep more of their wages in an effort to reduce envelope wages. In January, the Supreme Court clarified the rules governing the publication of time-barred debts. Estonians also lost €21 million to scammers in the first nine months of this year.

All three issues raise the same question: when does a debt stop being a debt that must be paid? The answer is more often than many people think. Here are three examples.

Time-barred claims in enforcement proceedings

I will begin with my favorite topic: enforcement proceedings. If enforcement of a claim has become time-barred, the debtor may refuse to pay it. The debt technically still exists, but a bailiff can no longer collect it through compulsory enforcement. The general rule is simple: enforcement of a claim arising from a court judgment becomes time-barred after 10 years.

There are 75,000 debtors in Estonia who are subject to more than 400,000 ongoing enforcement proceedings. A large share of proceedings initiated before 2016 involve collection of time-barred claims, and proceedings launched in 2016 are reaching the limitation period now. I am referring to private claims, such as apartment association debts and lender claims. Fines and tax debts expire under different rules and generally much sooner. Of course, there are exceptions, such as child support claims or proceedings that have been suspended for some reason, but the general rule remains the same.

Debtors must take the initiative and submit an application asserting that the claim is time-barred. Enforcement will not stop automatically. When withdrawals from the second pension pillar were made in 2021, an estimated €70 million went toward debt repayment. Many debtors unknowingly repaid claims that had long since become time-barred. Every day, employers transfer money from employees' wages to bailiffs to cover debts that could no longer legally be enforced.

"Many debtors unknowingly repaid claims that had long since become time-barred."

For creditors, however, the message is that it is time to review enforcement proceedings involving their debtors and obtain an overview from bailiffs. The principle of "first come, first served" applies in enforcement proceedings, and it is unwise to wait and hope a debtor will eventually start paying voluntarily. There are more options than many people realize: enforcement proceedings can be initiated in another country, Revolut and Wise accounts can be seized, and debtors' movable property and inheritances can also be attached.

Time-barred debt collection claims

The second category consists of debts pursued by collection agencies that are, in fact, already time-barred. In many cases, the collection agency's only leverage is the threat of adding a person to a payment default register.

In a January 30, 2026 ruling, the Supreme Court stated very clearly that publishing information about a time-barred debt in a payment default register is permitted only in exceptional circumstances. A time-barred claim does not necessarily reflect a person's creditworthiness because a time-barred obligation may legally be left unpaid.

An even more important conclusion followed. If an individual challenges publication of the debt, the registry operator must demonstrate a compelling reason for publication that outweighs the debtor's interests, regardless of whether the debt is time-barred or not. The logic of "we will keep publishing it until you pay" no longer applies.

Therefore, before paying a collection agency, individuals should determine whether the claim is valid in the first place. If they are added to a payment default register, they should consider whether there is a sufficient legal basis for doing so.

Loans taken out by scammers

Every day, media outlets report cases where scammers have emptied the bank accounts of individuals and companies through fraudulent schemes. In more serious cases, scammers have also taken out loans in their victims' names. Several Estonian court rulings have found that lenders do not have the right to recover such loans from fraud victims.

People should therefore not feel embarrassed or rush to repay loans taken out by scammers. The recommended first step is to consult a legal adviser, who can assess the situation and suggest the best course of action. Legal proceedings are not always necessary.

That is why fraud victims should preserve all evidence rather than begin deleting it. Save all correspondence, call logs and other relevant material. Victims should also notify the police, their bank and the lender. After that, they should contact a legal adviser.

The law does not help passive parties

In summary, not every debt must be repaid. If a creditor has not been proactive in recovering the money owed, debtors have the right to use the options provided by law: seek recognition that a claim is time-barred, refuse payment of a time-barred claim and challenge an unjustified payment default listing.

The same principle applies in both directions. Creditors who fail to take active steps to recover debts cannot be surprised when claims become time-barred. Debtors who do not know their rights may end up paying debts they do not actually owe. The law does not help passive parties, whether creditor or debtor. Both sides must take active steps to achieve the best outcome for themselves.

World.title: Explosive remnants of war kill 4 children in Syria in less than a week: Save the Children
World.content:
LONDON: Four children have been killed by landmines and unexploded ordnance in Syria in less than a week, Save the Children said on Tuesday, warning that explosive remnants of war are endangering families returning home after years of displacement.

Three children aged 8 to 12 were killed on Monday when unexploded ordnance detonated as they herded sheep near Palmyra, according to local news reports.

Their deaths followed a landmine explosion at a school in Hasakah last week that killed a child and injured 14 people, including children and teachers.

Save the Children said in a statement received by Arab News that four deaths were double the weekly average of children killed by landmines from July through September.

Jeremy Stoner, the organization’s acting country director in Syria, said children face danger whether they are attending school, working to support their families or playing.

“Children in Syria are playing a deadly game of stepping stones where one misstep will end their life,” Stoner said. “In Syria, when a child leaves their home, their parents often fear for their life.”

“Schools, which are protected under international law, are no longer safe, as we saw in Hasakah last week,” he added.

“Meanwhile children who have been forced out of school and into work just to support their families do so at their own peril. Others who seek a brief respite through play pick up what they think is a toy or something to kick around, only to have their life shattered.”

The UN said in September that landmines and unexploded ordnance had killed 269 children and injured 1,616 since December 2024, as displaced families began returning to their homes.

Meanwhile, the UN Children’s Fund, UNICEF, estimates that 5 million children live in areas contaminated with landmines and explosive remnants of war. More than two-thirds of recorded incidents have occurred on agricultural and grazing land, putting farmers, herders and children tending livestock at particular risk.

State-run Syrian media recently reported estimates that more than half a million mines contaminate Palmyra.

In another incident on Nov. 2, a child and an adult were killed, and another child and adult were injured, in a grazing area in Deir Ezzor.

The toll extends beyond those killed. Survivors can face lasting disabilities, costly treatment and the loss of income their families depend on.

Yaser, 15, lost a little finger and suffered an eye injury when an object he picked up exploded weeks ago in Deir Ezzor, one of Syria’s most heavily contaminated areas, according to Save the Children.

“I saw something that looked like a pen. I didn’t know what it was. I lifted it and it exploded,” he told the organization. “I didn’t feel pain at the beginning, but I then looked at my hand and saw my pinkie finger wasn’t there. I then started screaming and running.”

Yaser said his eye hurts and his vision is blurred. He fears losing his sight as his family waits to learn the cost of surgery.

No longer in school, he had been earning about $15 a week at an aluminum workshop to help support his family. His injuries have left him unable to work.

“Now that I can’t work for a long time, my brother alone cannot support the whole family and pay for my treatment and surgery,” he said.

The Syrian government has made mine clearance a priority and established a national mine action center led by the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management.

However, Save the Children said funding and equipment remain far below what is needed to clear contaminated areas, support survivors and teach communities how to recognize explosive hazards.

The organization urged Syrian authorities to accelerate clearance efforts and called on international donors to provide more funding and equipment to identify, mark and remove mines and unexploded ordnance.

“Any child killed is one too many,” Stoner said. “But the fact that hundreds have lost their lives to landmines in less than two years should be shaking up the world to intervene and support clearance and recovery.

“We need to see a huge shift — it is the only way to support children and families to be safe and to recover from a conflict that has already taken so much from them.”

World.title: UK police say member of US Army arrested under National Security Act
World.content:
LONDON: British police said on Tuesday that a member of the ‌US ‌Army had ‌been arrested under the National Security Act over allegations he was ‌assisting Russia.

A ‌41-year-old man ‌was ‌arrested near the city of ‌Gloucester on Tuesday and remains in custody at a London police station, police said.

World.title: Rwandan genocide suspect deported by the US to face charges
World.content:
KIGALI, Rwanda: A Rwandan man suspected of participating in the country’s 1994 genocide has been deported from the United States and will stand trial for his alleged crimes, according to local authorities.

Jean Léonard Teganya, who arrived in the East African nation on Monday, faces charges related to genocide, said Justin Nkusi, a spokesperson for the prosecution.

Teganya is currently being interrogated by police before prosecutors receive his file, Nkusi said.

Teganya, 55, was indicted in 2014 over his alleged involvement in genocidal crimes in several areas in the district of Huye, in Rwanda’s south. Rwandan authorities say he allegedly committed some of his crimes at a university campus and a medical school in Huye.

The 2014 indictment triggered an investigation into Teganya’s presence in the US, with Rwanda seeking his deportation. At the time, Teganya denied playing a part in the genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed by extremist Hutus.

Teganya fled Rwanda in July 1994 and later sought asylum in Canada. According to the US Justice Department, he evaded a Canadian deportation order and crossed into the US in 2014. In 2019, a federal jury in Boston found that Teganya had committed immigration fraud and perjury after seeking asylum in the US

One survivor of the genocide told The Associated Press in Kigali, the Rwandan capital, that she welcomed the decision to send Teganya home to face justice.

“Genocide crime and crimes against humanity are never time-barred and perpetrators will be hunted, arrested, deported and prosecuted,” said Yolande Mukakasana. “As survivors, we remain hopeful that justice will be done no matter how much time has passed.”

World.title: British comedian and children’s author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct
World.content:
LONDON: British children’s author and comedian David Walliams used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex, two British news outlets reported on Tuesday.

ITV News and the Guardian newspaper said their joint investigation featured interviews with multiple women who gave firsthand accounts of Walliams’ conduct. One woman alleged she was sexually assaulted by Walliams at his London home when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens.

Walliams, 55, denied the allegations. He unsuccessfully sought a court injunction to bar the news outlets from identifying him, claiming that publication of sexual misconduct allegations would lead him to take his own life.

The court fight delayed publication for months, but a judge rejected his injunction request last week and the protection of his identity expired late Monday.

“I am not a sexual predator,” Walliams said in a letter to the news organizations. “I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger toward me.”

“Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely, and it is something that I never did,” he added.

Walliams is best known for comedy sketches on “Little Britain,” a hugely popular British TV show in the 2000s, but he’s also a celebrated children’s book author with some 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website.

Several of them, including “Gangsta Granny,” have been adapted into BBC comedy dramas and stage productions.

Walliams was dropped last year by publisher HarperCollins after allegations were made of inappropriate behavior. Few details were published at the time, but the Guardian reported Tuesday that there were concerns about his behavior for years, including an allegation that he had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee.

He was also a judge for a decade on “Britain’s Got Talent,” though he stepped down in 2022 after apologizing for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants.

The BBC said Tuesday it was removing some programs, including “Little Britain,” while it carried out a review of “all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms.”

The literary agency Independent Talent Group also said it was dropping Walliams following the new allegations.

The court fight, in which Walliams was identified in news reports as a “famous man,” drew widespread attention in Britain because it highlighted questions over public figures’ right to privacy and what media can report on the basis of public interest.

Walliams’ lawyer, Sara Mansoori, told the High Court that he had made a suicide attempt when he received letters from ITN and Guardian News and Media seeking his response to the allegations. He later made another attempt, she said, and he was recently admitted to the hospital for psychiatric care.

Attorney Gavin Millar, representing the media companies, has said that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a strong public interest in publishing them.

Millar told the court that the investigation involved speaking to more than 100 people, and alleged that over a period of years Walliams “used his status and influence as a well-known public figure to establish contact with young women, some considerably younger than him, and that he engaged or sought to engage in seriously inappropriate conduct,” according to a summary of the court judgment.

Some of the alleged conduct could amount to criminal offenses if proven, a summary of the court judgment said.

The Metropolitan Police in London contacted the news organizations Tuesday to make sure any possible victims knew how to report criminal allegations.

In dismissing the injunction bid, Justice Matthew Nicklin said such a legal measure would mean “an exceptionally serious interference” with the rights of the media companies.

He noted that Walliams had a “serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability” which must be taken seriously, and said a decision allowing the allegations to be published would substantially increase his risk of suicide. However, he added that the evidence did not “establish that suicide is inevitable.”

World.title: Greta Thunberg arrives at UN climate talks saying ‘everything we love is at stake’
World.content:
ANTALYA: Prominent climate change activist Greta Thunberg arrived Tuesday at the UN climate meeting, where she emphasized the need to protect people and the planet over profits and power.

This year’s meeting — called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes after a year of climate-induced heat waves and other disasters.

As she arrived at the meeting venue in Antalya, Turkiye, Thunberg said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”

“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.

Thunberg is attending her first UN climate summit since she participated in the 2021 COP in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah.”

In 2024, Thunberg participated in a protest rally in Georgia against Azerbaijan hosting that year’s climate talks. Thunberg accused Azerbaijan of using that summit to “greenwash their crimes and human rights abuses.”

Thunberg is expected to join this year’s talks for a few days. She said structural changes are needed across the world to deal with the climate crisis because current political and economic systems “have become incompatible with human nature.”
