World.title: Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019239/Postscript: China Opens School Dedicated to Ancient Chinese Writing
World.content:
China has opened its first school dedicated to declining and obscure fields of study, with a focus on ancient and classical Chinese texts.

The School for Rare and Endangered Disciplines was inaugurated in Beijing on Nov. 6 under the University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (UCASS). At the opening, the university also announced the launch of a national alliance of more than 80 universities, museums, and cultural and research institutions to share resources, conduct collaborative research, and cultivate talent in related fields.

The school comes as the number of scholars studying ancient Chinese scripts dwindles. Nationwide, only about 500 people work in ancient Chinese writing studies, and of the roughly 4,500 known oracle bone characters — the oldest known fully developed form of Chinese writing and widely used for divination purposes during the Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) — nearly two-thirds remain undeciphered, underlining the need for further research.

The initiative also builds on previous attempts by UCASS to preserve such fields, such as establishing an institute for rare and endangered studies in 2024 to train future talent in fields such as bamboo and silk studies, which examines script on the two materials, as well as classical studies, Turkic studies, and Assyriology, or studies of the Ancient Near East.

Each student of the new school’s bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degree courses will be mentored by two members of the school’s more than 140 faculty members. UCASS has also built dedicated laboratories for the school’s use.

Students may pursue research in oracle bone studies, bamboo and silk studies, and classical studies. They may also train in over 10 ancient ethnic scripts, including Turkic, Tangut, Khitan, Jurchen, Manchu, Old Tibetan, Old Yi, Phags-pa, Naxi Dongba, and Zhuang.

“Ancient scripts like oracle bone script are on the verge of being lost, and some frontier history research relies on the survival of the country’s cultural roots and its long-term development,” Huang Dekuan, director of the Research and Conservation Center for Unearthed Texts at Tsinghua University, told state broadcaster CCTV.

Such disciplines are also hampered by scattered resources and research institutions working in isolation — key obstacles to research and transmission, according to CCTV.

China has called for increased focus on cultural heritage preservation in recent years. At an October press conference on cultural heritage protection, government officials called for advancing cultural heritage as a discipline, cultivating interdisciplinary talent in the field, and encouraging qualified universities to establish cultural heritage schools.

In a Nov. 7 commentary, domestic media outlet The Beijing News wrote that by emphasizing rare and endangered disciplines, the new school offers a lesson to other universities: schools should develop their own distinctive majors, resist the urge to offer only popular fields, and actively strengthen less mainstream majors.

“Only then can a university truly serve education,” it stated.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.title: Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019245/Fallback to First Choice: Why Chinese Parents Are Rethinking Vocational Schools
World.content:
Coming from a Shanghai family with a strong academic background, Yang Fan had always felt studying at university was his destiny. The only problem was, he was flunking middle school.

“He’d make the same mistake with a character the entire semester. I just couldn’t get him to do it right,” says his mother, Zhao Xuan, who could only look on in frustration as Yang struggled with his homework night after night. “Given how much it was taking for him to get through middle school, I felt high school would crush him.”

Last summer, with the conventional academic pathway looking a bad fit for their 15-year-old son, Zhao and her husband began to consider China’s integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program. Launched as a 2014 pilot in Shanghai, the initiative sees students spend up to three years at a vocational school before transitioning to a partner university to complete a related four-year bachelor’s degree program.

Over the past 12 years, the number of participating educational institutions has rapidly expanded, now covering at least seven provincial regions, and applications have soared.

Shanghai alone has established 91 majors across 38 vocational schools and 18 universities, enrolling about 20,000 students and producing six cohorts of graduates. Planned enrollment this year was 2,756, up from just 120 in 2014 and a 17.5% increase from 2025.

Programs cover diverse fields including robotics, accounting, digital media arts, big data engineering, logistics, environmental design, hospitality management, cultural heritage restoration, smart manufacturing, performing arts, sound recording, information security, and materials science.

The trend reflects a sea change in attitudes toward vocational education in China. Technical skills training has long been stigmatized as “low status” and a “fallback option,” but as the country’s workforce undergoes a massive restructuring driven by an aging population, advancements in artificial intelligence, and an economic slowdown, more people feel it now makes students more employable compared to those with purely academic backgrounds.

In real terms, most students in the integrated program say their experiences are far less stressful than those of their peers at traditional Chinese high schools, and that they are encouraged to focus more on their personal strengths rather than sticking to a one-size-fits-all curriculum.

However, because most applicants are only in their mid-teens, it’s often parents who make the final decision, with research suggesting that more-passive children have only a vague idea of, or interest in, what might lie ahead.

The path less traveled

It was only when Zhao learned that the prestigious Shanghai Maritime University (SMU) would join the integrated secondary vocational-to-undergraduate articulation program in 2026 that she was sure the pathway was a “realistic match” for Yang.

Soon, Zhao and her husband, who holds a Ph.D., had researched the job prospects of various degree holders and consulted with their son, who was willing to give vocational school a try. For him, it was an opportunity to follow his growing interest in mechanics and spend time on activities he’d been forced to drop in middle school, such as table tennis and learning to play guitar.

In the 2026 zhongkao, the national high school entrance exam, Yang scored highly enough to earn a place this fall in the mechanical design, manufacturing, and automation major run jointly by Shanghai Harbour School and SMU.

With the increase in applications, programs have been setting higher admission thresholds. More than 80% increased their cut-off in 2026, and over half by 20 to 30 points. To secure a place in either of the two majors run in partnership with SMU, students must score at least 690 points out of a maximum 750.

In the final year of middle school, “we really pushed ourselves to the limit,” says Zhao, though she dismisses the idea that her son’s zhongkao score was a reflection of any academic acumen. “We got lucky. The exam was on the easy side.”

Kuang Ying, a professor specializing in vocational education at Shanghai’s East China Normal University, points out that students and parents today have far more information about the integrated program compared to when it started.

“People weren’t familiar with these programs, and many working-class families lacked the information they needed to make a reasoned decision back then,” she says.

Pan Yuxiao, who grew up in Shanghai’s northern Chongming District, was among the first students to enroll in the pilot in 2014. He’d wanted to continue his studies at a high school closer to the city center, but his zhongkao score was too low.

By chance, he came across a brochure about the integrated program. “There was hardly any information back then. The teachers didn’t know about it, and neither did the parents,” recalls Pan, who eventually enrolled in the mechanical engineering major offered by Shanghai Industrial Technology School and Shanghai Polytechnic University (SSPU).

Kuang believes that not only has awareness of such courses substantially improved since the inaugural cohort but parents’ priorities have also changed. “Now people are looking for a more certain future,” she explains. Families are no longer solely fixated on school rankings and prestige; they are taking a more honest look at their child’s academic standing relative to their peers and what they can realistically achieve. This allows them to make more informed, pragmatic choices tailored to a child’s abilities and circumstances, she adds.

The reason many have chosen the integrated program over a standard high school, then and now, is simple: It virtually guarantees a spot on a bachelor’s degree course. However, for some, mental health is another major factor.

Wu Yulu, a sophomore student at SSPU, scored 640 in the 2022 zhongkao, enough to get into a selective local high school in Shanghai. But she doubts she would ever have made it to college through the traditional route. “I just wouldn’t have had the stamina for it,” she says.

The pressure of middle school took its toll on Wu. In her first year, she would work on her homework late into the night and often woke up at her desk. When her grades began to drop, she took a leave of absence due to stress.

A 2022 report by the China Youth and Children Research Center based on interviews of 24,758 students in 10 provinces found that 23% of middle school students were at risk of depression, while 31% showed signs of anxiety.

When Wu returned to middle school the following fall, she had lots of material to catch up on but had learned to “let myself off the hook.” It was around then that she heard about the integrated vocational-to-undergraduate major in taxation that led to a bachelor’s from SSUP.

For Wu and her parents, it seemed a fitting path forward. “I wouldn’t have to wear myself out,” she says. As the program was still relatively unknown in 2022, she was one of only two students in her class who applied.

Same but different

As in Yang’s case, Jia Xinyi’s parents first suggested she join an integrated program, recommending she study early years education. This was 2017, and China had just relaxed its one-child policy. Her family predicted a baby boom and reasoned that Jia could land a stable job at a kindergarten, yet she had little interest in the subject.

When it came time to decide, Jia was torn. “No one could guarantee how things would turn out, but the integrated pathway offered a clearer route,” she says. She eventually settled on a major in materials science and engineering because a relative already worked in the field.

Once enrolled at Shanghai Material Engineering School, Jia found the daily schedule fairly typical: four morning classes, another four after lunch, and 30- to 90-minute study sessions in the evening. Chinese, mathematics, and English formed a core part of the curriculum for all three years, with students using standard textbooks. However, she feels the homework was far more manageable than at regular high schools.

Wu agrees. She says the learning atmosphere at her vocational school was relatively relaxed; she was no longer plagued by the workload-induced sleep deprivation she’d experienced in middle school.

However, on top of core academic subjects, vocational school students also take practical classes in their chosen field.

While preparing for a vocational qualification exam, Jia learned to conduct chemical analyses of construction materials, received skills training in cement production, and was given a factory tour. Pan says his teachers at Shanghai Industrial Technology School introduced him to 3D printing technologies and a five-axis machine center, an advanced cutting tool.

Professional skills competitions also offer a different dimension. Wu took the opportunity to enter contests in intelligent finance and taxation, and won awards for several videos she made after teaching herself how to use editing software. These achievements helped her come to terms with her tough middle school years and showed her that she could shine through her strengths.

In most provinces, students on the integrated pathway take a transition exam after three years.

Wu recalls that the test was undemanding. For the academic section, the pass mark was 180 points out of 300, while the only vocational requirement was that candidates reach 70% of the class average. “The pass rate was very high,” she notes, adding that only one student in her year had failed.

Parental guidance

Twelve years in, the integrated program is still a work in progress. Local education officials commonly visit participating schools to solicit student feedback on the teaching quality and the curriculum. Jia recalls that some of her classmates called for more class hours in physics and chemistry, as well as better-qualified teachers.

However, for her, the major challenge was what came next. While studying for her bachelor’s at the Shanghai Institute of Technology, Jia discovered that she needed to take the kaoyan, China’s national postgraduate entrance exam, to progress to one of the university’s master’s programs. To prepare, she had to start from scratch in several foundational academic subjects because her vocational school had devoted so little time to them. She believes this has since been addressed in training plans for subsequent cohorts.

Meanwhile, education experts are concerned by the fact that it’s typically parents pushing their children to choose the integrated program, rather than driven by personal interest.

According to an education industry magazine article written this June by a finance tutor at Shanghai Economic Management School, surveys show that roughly 80% of students on the integrated program had primarily followed their parents’ wishes in applying, “placing themselves in a passive stance” and leading to a “lack of initiative.”

Pan notes that several of his vocational school classmates had “no interest in their major and felt that their potential was being wasted.” Whenever Jia posted about her studies on social media, she also noticed that the vast majority of comments and questions were from parents.

Kuang believes few adolescents have the ability to think clearly about decisions with such far-reaching consequences. “Middle school students are often bewildered when it comes to making choices. Even high school graduates are,” she says, adding that China’s education system doesn’t provide children with enough formal career guidance or expose them to different professions early.

It’s been five years since Pan’s inaugural 40-strong cohort graduated from university. He estimates that only 25% to 33% of his classmates work in fields related to their majors. He initially found a job working with machinery after graduation but has since switched to the medical industry.

Jia is completing a postgraduate internship in environmental, health, and safety management, far removed from her academic focus of materials science. She believes it’s highly unlikely she’ll end up working in her field of study.

Switching track

As China’s real economy develops and the central government places greater emphasis on skilled professionals, Kuang says the integrated program’s growing popularity is inevitable. “Technical skills will become one of the major pathways to success,” she predicts.

Since 2014, the public has gained a better understanding of how the integrated program differs from conventional vocational education. Schools are committing quality resources and assigning their most capable teachers. “These positives give Chinese parents greater confidence in choosing this once-stigmatized pathway,” Kuang adds.

In Pan’s view, much of what students learn in high school is irrelevant to real life, while those who choose the integrated route are making a conscious decision to use their time and energy wisely.

Jia adds that parents are having to consider alternatives because the days when graduating from a prestigious university guaranteed a secure job are gone. However, she still worries that some see the integrated vocational route as a “back door” to a bachelor’s degree.

Yang started at Shanghai Harbour School this fall and hopes to take part in many extracurricular activities and competitions. On registration day, the incoming cohort was encouraged to pursue independent learning, which Zhao was glad to hear.

“We don’t want our child spending his time in a passive learning environment, simply being dragged along by others,” she says. “Choosing the integrated pathway doesn’t mean taking the easy way out. It means stepping onto a different track, one that still demands hard work but puts my son in the driver’s seat.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Yang Fan, Zhao Xuan, Pan Yuxiao, and Jia Xinyi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Chen Lei, Wang Zhaoxue, and Zhang Zhenyao.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Students during a practical training class at Shanghai Information Technology School, Aug. 13, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.title: More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019236/More Chinese Regions to Require Autumn and Spring School Breaks
World.content:
More Chinese regions are implementing autumn and spring breaks in compulsory education, expanding a decadelong national initiative. Some have also waived fees for students on break and rolled out support measures to help parents take leave at the same time as their children.

Spring and autumn holidays across all compulsory education schools have been rolled out provincewide in at least 15 provinces, as well as numerous cities in other provinces, such as the southern megacity of Shenzhen, domestic media reported last week. In China, compulsory education lasts nine years, encompassing primary and middle school. Breaks will occur in November and April for four to five days each.

The reform dates back to 2004, when Hangzhou, capital of the eastern province of Zhejiang, piloted the breaks. In 2013, the initiative expanded nationally when the State Council issued an announcement encouraging local governments to adopt it, and the rollout accelerated again in 2025 when central authorities urged more schools to implement the holidays.

Chu Zhaohui, a researcher at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, told domestic media outlet Red Star News that the holidays actually boost learning.

“Learning isn’t confined to schools or taught only by teachers and parents,” Chu said, adding that the holidays give students space for self-exploration.

At the same time as introducing spring and autumn holiday policies, many cities have also added supporting measures so parents can sync their leave. In October, Longnan city in the northwestern Gansu province encouraged employers to implement paid leave and prioritize compensatory rest for employees with school-age children, aligning staff leave with school holidays.

Foshan, a city in the southern Guangdong province, also issued a proposal on Nov. 3 calling on employers to prioritize arranging leave for employees with children during the autumn holiday. The city’s five-day autumn break begins Nov. 11.

Many tourist spots are also waiving entrance fees for children during the upcoming fall break. In the eastern city of Wuxi, a theme park dropped entry fees for students 16 and under throughout November; 15 top tourism sites in Huangshan in the eastern Anhui province, a city known for its mountain of the same name, are now entry-free for children under 18; and the Dujiangyan scenic area in the southwestern Sichuan province waived fees for primary and middle school students between Nov. 12 and 16.

The breaks have significantly boosted travel demand, according to online travel booking platform Qunar. Data from Qunar revealed that in November, air ticket bookings for children 12 and under increased 1.6 times year on year, while parent bookings rose by 50%.

Wang Qiyan, director of the Leisure Economy Research Center at Renmin University, told Red Star News that spring and autumn breaks “enable off-peak travel, avoiding the packed scenic spots of winter and summer vacations.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Tourists take photos of St. Sophia Square during the autumn break in Harbin, Heilongjiang province, Nov. 4, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.title: A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019228/A Bad Review, a Suicide, and a Debate Over Cyberbullying in China
World.content:
On Oct. 6, 2026, a female customer posted complaints on multiple social media platforms about a fried skewer stall in Gao County, Yibin, in southwestern China’s Sichuan province. “Avoid XX Copper Pot Potatoes. The owner can’t take the heat,” she wrote. She had bought a 10-yuan ($1.40) fried food combo from the stall, run by a 33-year-old woman surnamed Hu, but was dissatisfied with the portion of potatoes. “She just refused to add potatoes afterward,” the customer added. Her location-tagged posts quickly spread, and negative comments about Hu and her stall flooded the comment sections.

Hu responded to the criticism, writing, “I stand behind my portions.” Three days later, on Oct. 9, she jumped into a river and died by suicide.

Hu had run the stall for more than four years, sleeping less than six hours a night. In her suicide note, she described the enormous pressures she faced in life. She had hoped to watch her child grow up, she wrote, but the video telling people to avoid her stall had been the straw that broke the camel’s back.

She also wrote: “These past two days I have experienced what I consider cyberbullying. One person complained about no potatoes in her order, and then the comments came flooding in about bad service and poor-tasting food.”

This was not the first tragedy of its kind. In August 2025, a 57-year-old obstetrician-gynecologist surnamed Shao in Zhoukou, central China’s Henan province, jumped to her death. According to her family, she had endured more than seven months of cyberbullying over a medical dispute. In 2023, after a primary school student in Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, was killed in a traffic accident on campus, his mother was subjected to online attacks and later jumped to her death. In cases like these, public opinion often attributes the tragedies to cyberbullying.

But in Hu’s case, labeling the entire incident “cyberbullying” and placing the blame on the customer who posted the negative review would exaggerate the power of a single act of expression.

The customer maintained that she was simply describing a genuine experience, with “no malice, incitement, or falsehood.” She did not insult or personally attack anyone, disclose private information, or call for coordinated attacks online or offline. Her criticism may have been harsh, subjective, or exaggerated, but based on the content of her posts alone, it is difficult to characterize it as cyberbullying.

Many negative comments about the stall owner appeared beneath the posts, but there is currently no evidence that they were all malicious. Public criticism can be harsh, but legal liability must rest on provable facts.

In July 2026, China released a draft Anti-Online Violence Law for public comment. It defines online violence as “concentrated or sustained” acts involving “insult and abuse, rumor-mongering and defamation, incitement of hatred,” and similar behavior. A negative review based on a genuine transaction cannot automatically be classified as cyberbullying because it has harmful consequences. Moreover, the draft has not yet become law.

A common misconception is that anything posted online will inevitably spread and attract attention. That is simply not true. People publish vast amounts of content every day, but only a tiny fraction attracts widespread attention.

Consider Dr. Shao’s case. Following an investigation, the platform disclosed that her account had received more than 10,900 comments, about 60 of which were suspected of containing attacks or other inappropriate content. The rest were classified as normal or neutral interactions. Although the platform’s findings should not be treated as a definitive record of every offensive interaction, they serve as a reminder that not every comment should be regarded as a malicious attack.

None of this excuses genuine cyberbullying. In 2018, a female doctor surnamed An in Deyang, Sichuan, became involved in a dispute with a boy at a swimming pool. The boy’s family posted edited surveillance footage online accompanied by inflammatory text. After enduring sustained online attacks, An died by suicide. In 2021, a court sentenced three defendants to prison for criminal insult.

The law is not powerless against cyberbullying. Precisely because it has the power to punish such behavior, however, we must distinguish criminal incitement and insults from harsh criticism.

Tragedies often result from a combination of factors. We cannot draw a direct causal line from a single negative review and the comments that followed to a person’s suicide. The negative review was one link in a chain of events, but it was neither the sole cause nor something that made the outcome inevitable.

Hu’s final message makes clear the immense pressures she faced in her personal life and as a small business owner. Her psychological state and the support available to her at the time also deserve attention.

The platform’s decision to promote the post to nearby users is just how online reviews work. Positive and negative reviews must be visible to help consumers distinguish good businesses from bad ones. But regulating them presents a dilemma.

Any screening system risks two types of errors: false positives, in which legitimate criticism is flagged as malicious, and false negatives, in which malicious comments go undetected. Tightening controls reduces false negatives but increases false positives, while relaxing them has the opposite effect. Platforms must therefore balance the costs of both.

For platforms such as the consumer review service Dianping and the short-video app Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, determining a post’s motives is difficult, and predicting its consequences even harder. Siding with businesses risks suppressing legitimate criticism, while siding with consumers risks allowing malicious attacks. There is no one-size-fits-all solution.

Anyone who has maintained a blog or public social media account knows how pervasive online negativity can be, with abusive comments and private messages a common occurrence. We cannot expect everyone to tolerate such abuse, but where should we draw the line in regulating it?

Cyberbullying typically involves a series of acts including verbal abuse, defamation, and insults. Such behavior may constitute a civil infringement and, in serious cases, give rise to criminal liability. But the definition of cyberbullying must not become so broad that it exaggerates the harm caused by ordinary expression.

The “clear and present danger” standard in U.S. legal history offers a useful reminder that speech should not be restricted merely because it causes discomfort. However, that standard arose in a specific legal context and cannot be directly applied as a general principle of Chinese law.

If we endlessly magnify the psychological harm that speech can cause and attribute tragic outcomes solely to what people say, the argument that “speech can be harmful” risks becoming a blanket justification for restricting expression.

If we blame every tragedy on the criticism that preceded it, consumers may hesitate to post negative reviews, and others may begin to self-censor. Free expression would suffer, potentially undermining market competition.

Such a focus on cyberbullying also overlooks two critical issues: the pressures facing small business owners and the need for better mental health support. Long hours, unstable incomes, and the stresses of running a business can make a single bad review feel overwhelming. China’s national mental health hotline, 12356, also has an important role in identifying and responding to people in crisis.

We must confront genuine cyberbullying without silencing legitimate criticism, while also addressing gaps in mental health care and support for small businesses. Blaming a single review may offer a convenient explanation for Hu’s death, but it brings us no closer to understanding the tragedy or preventing the next one.

Translator: Gabriel Kwan.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.title: China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019225/China’s Sea Goddess Has a New Job: AI Weather Forecasting
World.content:
As it expands its weather-warning systems across the Global South, China has handed over equipment for a customized version of MAZU — an AI-powered weather prediction tool created by the China Meteorological Administration — to Sri Lanka, one of eight countries where the platform has been deployed.

The device, described by domestic media as a rectangular black box roughly the size of a portable toolbox, was presented to Sri Lanka’s meteorological department on Nov. 1. It will form part of a system designed to warn of heavy rain, strong winds, and cyclones, and is expected to enter service by the end of the year.

Launched in July 2025, MAZU takes its name from a Chinese sea goddess revered as a protector of sailors. It combines AI forecasting models developed by Chinese research institutions with data from the country’s weather satellites.

Conventional weather forecasting relies on supercomputers to calculate how the atmosphere will change using equations based on physical laws. AI models, by contrast, learn from years of weather data.

“Chatbots familiar to the public learn patterns in language, while AI weather models learn how the atmosphere evolves,” Niu Zeyi, an assistant researcher at the Shanghai Typhoon Institute who led the development of a forecasting model used in MAZU, told Sixth Tone. “By training on years of meteorological data, these models can predict future weather conditions based on current variables such as wind, air pressure, temperature, and humidity.”

Once trained, AI models can produce forecasts faster and more cheaply than conventional methods. One model can generate a 24-hour global forecast in 1.4 seconds, about 10,000 times faster than traditional numerical methods. For forecasts covering 15 to 60 days, AI models can reduce computing costs to one-thousandth of those of conventional methods.

But most of the savings come from running routine forecasts, Niu said. Training models, building datasets, and maintaining systems still require investment — resources many countries in the Global South lack.

MAZU’s cloud-based services are being tested by 58 countries, according to domestic media, and China plans to deploy the system in 30 countries over the next five years.

In Pakistan, the system has reportedly incorporated local radar and satellite data to develop warnings for heavy rainfall and glacial lake outburst floods. In Djibouti, the model developed by Niu’s team helps provide tailored weather warnings for the East African country’s port.

Studies show AI models can be less accurate than conventional methods when predicting record-breaking extremes, for which there is little historical data. Local weather in complex terrain also remains difficult to forecast, and it is not always clear how AI models arrive at their predictions.

The models also need to be adapted to local conditions, Niu said. “Our approach is to work with local meteorological agencies to improve datasets, conduct independent evaluations, and make local adjustments.”

Even with AI, he added, “human forecasters must still combine observations, AI predictions, and their own judgment before authorities issue warnings.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: The weather warning system Mazu at the China Meteorological Administration booth during 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. VCG）

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.title: China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019218/China’s Traditional Colors Are Trending. But What Are We Missing?
World.content:
Traditional Chinese colors have become a popular topic on Chinese social media, with posts sporting catchy headlines such as “Our Ancestors Had the Ultimate Eye for Beauty” and “Out-of-This-World Color Combinations in ‘Dream of the Red Chamber.’” Open one of these posts, and you’ll often find neatly arranged color swatches labeled with evocative traditional names such as tianqing, “celestial blue”; yuebai, “moon white”; qiuxiang, “autumn fragrance”; and yanzhi, “rouge.”

In my opinion, this enthusiasm is undoubtedly a good thing. Traditional colors deserve greater attention and should be made more accessible. Color swatches can also be useful for showcasing the colors of historical artifacts and help modern audiences connect with the past. But this kind of simplification is a double-edged sword. In making something rich and complex easier to understand, it can also reduce it to a crude, one-dimensional representation. What makes information easier to communicate can also obscure or distort its meaning.

In fact, color swatches have significant limitations when it comes to representing and explaining traditional colors. They can only scratch the surface of a much richer cultural history.

Modern color charts emerged from Western industrial and commercial systems designed to control production quality and reproduce specific colors. But this standardized, scientific approach often falls short when applied to traditional Chinese colors. Anyone who has visited an exhibition of antique clothing or textiles and tried to photograph it may have experienced this firsthand. What appears to the naked eye as a beautiful pine green might look mustard yellow on a smartphone screen. Or the various golds and yellows of an imperial dragon robe might lose their distinctiveness entirely. If even digital cameras equipped with sophisticated image-processing algorithms struggle to capture these colors, what chance does a simple color swatch have?

So why do modern industrial color charts fall short in representing traditional Chinese colors?

First, color swatches are designed to standardize colors within specific product categories, whereas traditional Chinese color names developed within particular craft traditions. As these traditions evolved, a color’s name could refer to subtly different hues in different periods.

Several factors contributed to these variations. In the age of traditional handicrafts, differences in materials and craftsmanship could produce markedly different hues. Local production conditions also gave products from different regions their own distinctive characteristics. Fashions changed over time, altering the shades associated with particular color names. Even on a single garment, colors could appear different depending on the lighting, viewing angle, or direction of the weave.

Traditional indigo dyeing offers a good example. Indigo must first be fermented in vats and chemically reduced before it can be used to dye fabric. A single dip produces a pale blue, and the color deepens after each subsequent immersion. As a result, even fabrics dyed in the same vat can emerge in countless different shades.

Second, modern industrial color standards demand precision, assigning each color a numerical value. Traditional color names, however, did not follow this quantitative model. Rather than corresponding to a single fixed value, they generally described a natural range of hues.

Take xinghuang, or “apricot yellow,” for example. The yellowish-red of a ripe apricot is not a precisely defined hue. Yet despite natural variations in its color, people can still recognize the familiar shade of a ripe apricot.

Finally, the meanings and appearances of colors have changed considerably throughout Chinese history. These changes reflected rulers’ preferences, interpretations of cultural doctrines, shifts in folk customs, the rise and decline of craft techniques, and the movement of goods through domestic and overseas trade.

Consider qing, a color term widely used in ancient China. Depending on the context, it could describe the blue of the sky, the green of plants, or even the black of someone’s hair or eyes. By the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing (1644–1911) dynasties, it still encompassed a broad range of hues. People wore qing-colored robes, but their exact shades varied. Although the “Da Ming Huidian,” or “Collected Statutes of the Ming Dynasty,” prescribed shiqing for officials’ outer robes, surviving examples range from reddish tones to bluish-green and darker, more somber shades. Meanwhile, the robe the emperor wore during rituals at the imperial tombs was yuanqing, a shade that appeared almost black.

Another example is zi, or “purple.” Examining the cloud and wave motifs on Qing imperial dragon robes reveals how the color evolved over successive reigns, from dark brownish shades early in the dynasty to mauve hues in the middle period and brighter purples in the late Qing.

Furthermore, in ancient China, color was not simply something to admire or enjoy. It also symbolized divine authority and helped define ritual conventions and social hierarchies, distinguishing the central government from local authorities and the nobility from ordinary people.

Ancient China developed a five-color system associated with concepts such as the five directions and five elements. Qing, chi (vermilion), yellow, white, and black were the five primary colors, while green, red, bi (jade), purple, and liuhuang (“flowing yellow”) were the five auxiliary colors. Successive rulers used these distinctions between primary and auxiliary colors to reinforce social hierarchies.

During the Qing dynasty, for example, the emperor’s ceremonial attire followed a four-color system from the middle of the dynasty onward. He wore tianqing, “celestial blue,” when performing sacrifices to Heaven; minghuang, “bright yellow,” for sacrifices to Earth; dahong, “deep red,” for sacrifices to the Sun; and yuebai, “moon white,” for sacrifices to the Moon.

The Qing imperial court also expanded the use of yellow in imperial dress, a practice dating back to the Sui (581–618) and Tang (618–907) dynasties. Strict rules determined who could wear particular shades. Minghuang, “bright yellow,” was reserved for the emperor, empress dowager, empress, and imperial noble consort. Xinghuang, “apricot yellow,” was restricted to the crown prince and crown princess, while jinhuang, “golden yellow,” was worn by princes, noble consorts, and consorts. Xiangse, “fragrant yellow,” was designated for imperial concubines and various ranks of princesses and princely consorts.

Clearly, color swatches alone cannot convey such rich cultural meanings and historical details. But the problem goes beyond how we reconstruct traditional colors. It also concerns how we understand history itself.

Modern industrial products are generally designed for mass consumption, often favoring simplicity and practicality. By contrast, many of the objects that have survived from ancient China belonged to emperors, empresses, and other powerful figures. The differences between their world and ours, in social context, cultural values, and everyday life, mean that interpreting these objects through a modern lens can easily lead to superficial conclusions or misunderstandings.

This brings us back to today’s enthusiasm for traditional colors on social media. China’s color traditions never formed a fixed, unchanging system, and preserving a tradition involves more than simply reproducing the past. It is a process of critically engaging with what came before, deciding what to discard, what to preserve, and what to adapt or develop further.

But meaningful preservation must begin with an understanding of the historical traditions themselves. That means looking beyond individual colors to examine the contexts in which they emerged, how their meanings and uses changed over time, and the cultural, social, and material relationships that shaped them.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Palace Museum, reedited by Fu Xiaofan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: How Sara Duterte witness is linked to auditor of Mans Carpio’s firms
World.content:
WITNESS. Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan takes the witness stand on Day 41 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 10, 2026.

Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team brought Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan as their second witness for her trial. She testified on Tuesday, November 10, a day after Davao City assessor Jaime Adalin.

But coming from Davao City is not the only common denominator between the two officials. They were also both flagged by the impeachment court for failing to recall things connected — either directly or indirectly — to their job.

Both the senator-judges and the prosecution grilled Bajan over her ties to the Elises and Ciudadano accounting firm (formerly known as Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano and Co.) Prosecutor Mae Divinagracia showed documents supposedly showing Bajan’s involvement with the firm.

At one point, Divinagracia showed a copy of amended articles of general partnership that supposedly removed the accountant’s name from the firm in 2015, but Bajan said she could not recall anything.

“Hindi ko na maalala (I could no longer remember),” said the accountant. “Hindi ko po ma-remember, your honor (I could not remember). Sorry.”

Bajan later confirmed that she’s no longer part of the firm but still insisted that she no longer remembers the document being presented to her.

“Miss Evan, parte kayo ng accounting firm, hindi ‘nyo maalala kung kailan kayo umalis o kung finile po ‘yan? Nasa harap ‘nyo na po ‘yong dokumento?” presiding officer Chiz Escudero asked. (Miss Evan, you are part of the accounting firm, you cannot remember when you left or if that document was filed? Even if the document is already in front of you?)

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo then interjected and said he fears for Bajan because of her failure to answer the questions directed at her.

“Kung ngayon pa nga lang, sa signature pa nga lang, hindi mo na kayang sagutin, ‘yon pa kayang mahihirap na katanungan later on? Baka ma-contempt ka,” warned Tulfo. (If we’re only talking about signatures and you cannot answer already, what more with the harder questions later on? You might be held in contempt.)

“Sign ko po ito (This is my signature), your honor,” said Bajan later on.

After establishing Bajan’s link to the firm, the prosecution proceeded to the point of its cross-examination — to cast doubt on the witness’ credibility.

Divinagracia pressed Bajan to confirm whether the auditing firm she previously worked for was the same firm that served as external auditor of the companies connected to Mans Carpio, the Vice President’s husband.

As it appeared, the firm had a working relationship with Gencorp Industries and Metro City Chow Foods, among others.

Again, the witness said she did not know.

Play Video

“‘Yong external auditor po ng Gencorp is Elises, Ciudadano, from 2019 onwards. And ‘yong Metro City Chow, from 2020 onwards, sila rin po ang external auditor. Pero napansin ko rin po dito po sa external auditor ni Attorney Manases at ni Vice President Sara ay Elises, Ciudadano rin,” said Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.

“So, para sa akin…parang nagkakaroon ng koneksiyon ‘yong partnership sa Elises, Ciudadano…. Parang may koneksiyon sa inyo itong external auditing firm,” he added.

(Gencorp’s external auditor from 2019 onwards is Elises, Ciudadano. And from 2020 onwards, it is also Metro City Chow’s external auditor. But I also noticed that Elises, Ciudadano is also the external auditor of Attorney Mans and Vice President Sara. So, for me, there’s a connection in the partnership with Elises, Ciudadano. It seems the external auditing firm has a connection to you.)

“Hindi ko po alam ‘yon (I don’t know that), your honor,” said Bajan. – Rappler.com

World.title: Esperon, 4 other Duterte officials improperly spent P1.96M for ASEAN 2017
World.content:
Auditors earlier found that part of the funds meant for security and emergency preparedness and response went instead to the purchase of two vehicles, worth P980,000 each, reportedly used to transport personnel during ASEAN-related activities

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) junked the petition of former national security adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr. and four National Security Council (NSC) officials that sought to recall a 2020 notice of disallowance involving improper spending of funds meant for the country’s hosting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2017.

In March 2017, the Duterte-era Department of the Interior and Local Government then transferred P6.85 million to the NSC for the Philippines’ chairmanship and hosting of the ASEAN, which also commemorated the regional bloc’s 50th anniversary.

However, an audit showed that part of the funds meant for security and emergency preparedness and response during ASEAN went instead to the purchase of two Isuzu Crosswind XT vehicles worth P980,000 each, totaling P1.96 million. The vehicles were reportedly used to transport personnel during ASEAN-related activities.

Without authority from the Office of the President, the purchase was considered irregular, and the commission issued the notice of disallowance in 2020.

But Esperon and NSC officials Vicente Agdamag, Ruperta Salvanera, Edwin Servigon, and Maria Purificacion Sison filed their petition challenging the notice of disallowance way beyond the allowed period of 180 days, which was 1,012 days after the notice was received.

Both the notice of finality of decision and the COA order of execution had since been issued in 2022.

“This Commission finds the present petition without merit as it was filed after the ND has already become final and executory. Moreover, the petitioners are cognizant of their failure to secure authorization from the OP,” the COA en banc said in its August 13 decision released recently.

“Rules of procedure must be faithfully complied with and should not be discarded by the mere expediency of claiming substantial merit,” state auditors said, citing the Supreme Court as having ruled that “the right to appeal is neither a natural right nor a component of due process.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Davao accountant can’t confirm own signature, tests senator-judges’ patience
World.content:
WITNESS. Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan during Day 41 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 10, 2026.

The soft-spoken Vingelin Bajan elicits warnings of contempt as she evades questions on her former affiliation with the auditing firm that has among its clients Sara Duterte-linked companies, the Vice President, and husband Mans Carpio

At the resumption of Vice President Sara Duterte‘s impeachment trial on Monday, November 9, senator-judges had to contend with what the prosecution called a “rude awakening” in the person of Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin, the defense witness who initially lied about a trip to China.

With that incident still fresh on the minds of senator-judges, two of them, Vicente “Tito” Sotto III and Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, on Tuesday, November 10, asked the impeachment court to remind witnesses of the penalties they face if they lie under oath. It was fair warning for all other witnesses of the trial, which Escudero would repeat every time a new witness took the stand.

Play Video

Engineer John Kenneth Enumerables, city assessor of the Island Garden City of Samal, seemed to have heeded the reminder, and his testimony did not elicit any contempt warning. But then came the third defense witness, Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan.

At one point, the usually jovial presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero expressed frustration and said in a stern tone that his patience was “wearing thin” over Bajan’s “evasive” responses to the prosecution’s questions.

“My patience is wearing thin, forgive me,” Escudero told Bajan, as she directed her to respond to questions.

What was Bajan being evasive about? In challenging her credibility, House private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia asked the city accountant about her previous employment as a partner of the Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano, and Co. accounting firm.

Bajan repeatedly said she could not remember working as a partner of the firm. Confronted with documents bearing her own signatures, Bajan appeared confused, saying the Articles of Partnership and Amended Articles of Partnership, indeed, contained her tax account number and signatures similar to hers, but still could not recall signing them.

She was also seen looking at the defense team as she thought of what to say, which Divinagracia called out.

“I can’t recall all of these documents…. But this is my tax account number and signatures,” Bajan said.

Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano, and Co. — now Elises & Cuidadano — served as the external auditor of Gencorp Industries Incorporated and Metro City Chow Foods Inc., two companies linked to Duterte. Senator-judge Win Gatchalian said in his interjection later in the trial that the company is also the external auditor of the Vice President and her husband, Manases Carpio.

Frustration among the senator-judges was so strong that even Senator-judge Lito Lapid stood up to manifest what he thought about her testimony as well, saying: “Naawa na ako sa inyo. Kaming dalawa ni Sen Lacson…. Sa haba-haba nang halos maghapon na tanong ng mga senator-judge, halos hindi ‘nyo nasasagot.”

(I pity you. Both of us, Senator Lacson and I…. The senator-judges have been asking for hours and you hardly gave any answers.)

Bajan’s answers triggered senator-judges, who were already impatient following their experience with another Davao City official — Adalin — the past day.

“Yesterday, the witness was laughing and today, this witness is being evasive. Should we cite them in contempt to respect the impeachment court? Because as I see it, they have no respect for us,” said Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo.

“Maybe, it’s about that time we provide them as an example,” Tulfo added.

After being pressed by senator-judges, the city accountant admitted to being part of the firm. She likewise said she had forgotten leaving the firm in 2015.

However, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva countered her statement, emphasizing that the Amended Articles of Partnership included her signed affidavit of withdrawal.

“We’re practicing utmost patience with you. I hope you’ll help us help you,” said Villanueva.

The Senate impeachment court has repeatedly reminded witnesses against dodging questions during the trial.

Earlier in the day, Senator-judge Sotto inquired about the possible sanctions for witnesses lying under oath, with Senator-judge Lacson citing Senate Resolution No. 39, establishing the court’s contempt powers.

“Yesterday was not a good day for the impeachment court, Mr. President, Mr. Presiding Officer, simply because we had a witness who smirked, who laughed, almost made a mockery of the impeachment trial,” Lacson said.

“We don’t want to have a repeat of that kind of testimony,” he added.

Will the other witnesses finally heed the warning? – Rappler.com

World.title: [Local Vote] Voter registration for 2028: Answers to your common questions
World.content:
REGISTRATION. Cebu residents flock to the Commission on Elections office in Cebu City on November 10, 2026, as voter registration resumes for the 2028 national and local elections.

The registration will run until July 30, 2027, Tuesdays to Fridays, 8 am to 5 pm

The presidential, national, and local elections of 2028 are 18 months away, and prospective candidates will be filing their certificates in 11 months yet, but the poll season has technically started in the Philippines.

On Tuesday, November 10, the Commission on Elections (Comelec) resumed the registration of voters for the 2028 exercise.

So I guess I will also have to resume this early my Local Vote series, which I usually write only during campaign periods.

And for this edition, I have put together answers to your most common questions on voter registration. The answers are from various and relevant documents and information from the Comelec.

I will be updating this Q&A if and when there are new information you should know. In the meantime, you can also download Rappler’s MUNI app — for free — and join the Voter Hotline channel. There, we post updates about voter issues, while Comelec personnel and representatives of election watchdogs also address voter concerns.

Until when is the voter registration for the 2028 elections?

The voter registration, which reopened on November 10, 2026, will close by end of day on July 30, 2027.

That’s a good eight months and 20 days, so I hope we can avoid any last-minute rush and, with it, the usually unfair criticism against the Comelec and its processes.

What is the schedule during the voter registration period?

Registration days are from Tuesday to Friday, 8 am to 5 pm.

There will be Saturdays and holidays when the Comelec or its local offices can and will schedule registrations. Remember: not all Saturdays and holidays.

To know on which Saturdays and holidays registrations will be conducted, follow the Comelec’s official social media account or check with the election office in your city or municipality. Rappler’s Voter Hotline channel will also post advisories as they come in.

Where can I register as a voter?

Local Comelec offices. They will accommodate you during office hours.

Comelec-approved satellite registration sites. These are usually malls or schools in key cities across the country. I will upload lists here once available.

Special Register Anytime/Anywhere Program (SRAP) sites. These are select areas where Comelec makes one-time deployments. For example: On November 10, the opening day of the voter registration period, a SRAP team was at the Mabini Hall in Luneta in Manila; it will be stationed there until Thursday, November. 12. It is open to the general public from 8 am to 6 pm. On November 19, SRAP will be at WalterMart Makati. It will also be open to the general public from 8 am to 5 pm. On November 24, a Comelec team will be at the Far Eastern University’s (FEU) Manila campus. The registration will be for FEU students only, from 8 am to 5 pm. You can check future SRAP locations and dates here.



EARLY. Cebu City residents take advantage of the first voter registration day for the 2028 elections. Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

Who can register as a voter?

Filipino citizen

At least 18 years old by election day (May 8, 2028)

For at least one year before election day, a resident of the Philippines

For at least six months before election day, a resident of the locality where he/she intends to vote

Who cannot register as a voter?

Sentenced to prison for at least one year, unless pardoned or granted amnesty A person automatically reacquires his/her right to vote five years after serving his/her sentence. Reacquisition can happen earlier if his/her full civil and political rights are restored through plenary pardon or amnesty.

Convicted of rebellion, sedition, violation of the firearms laws, or any crime against national security A person automatically reacquires his/her right to vote five years after serving his/her sentence. Reacquisition can happen earlier if his/her full civil and political rights are restored in accordance with law.

Declared by a competent authority to be insane or incompetent, unless a proper authority declares the person is no longer suffering from such condition.

What are the different kinds of voter registrants?

First-time voters

Voters who want to reactivate their records (after failing to vote for two consecutive elections)

Voters who want to transfer their registration within the locality (for example: from one barangay to another, or from one municipality to another)

Voters who want to correct certain entries in their records, or want to reflect changes in their names (for example: now carrying a spouse’s surname or marriage has been annulled)

Voters who want to transfer their records from a foreign service post to a local registration site

Persons with disabilities, senior citizens, members of Indigenous Peoples or Indigenous Cultural Communities, and other vulnerable sectors who need to update their records

Voters who will be abroad on election day. (These registrants can submit application forms online here, but they have to go to the Philippine embassy or consulate for the biometrics capturing. Once registered, they can only vote for national positions.)

REGISTER ANYWHERE. First-time voters line up at the Comelec’s special registration site in Luneta Park in Manila on November 10, 2026 to register for the 2028 national and local elections. The registration period will run until July 30, 2027. Rappler photo

How do I check the status or record of my voter registration?

As of September 4, 2026, these are the deactivated voters. The Comelec has uploaded lists for every city and municipality. In every list, it is indicated whether the person failed to vote in two consecutive regular elections (totally deactivated and must register again) or has transferred and therefore has an active record in another city or municipality (so decide if you want to transfer to your old locality).

If your name is not on the list of deactivated voters, it means your registration is intact. So if you need to transfer or make changes to your record, go to your local Comelec office or to satellite registration sites.

What are the requirements for voter registration?

Accomplished application form

Any of the following identification documents: National ID from PhilSys Postal ID card PWD ID Card Senior citizen’s ID card Student’s ID card or library card, signed by the school authority Driver’s license or student permit from the Land Transportation Office National Bureau of Investigation clearance Philippine passport Social Security System (SSS) or Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) or other Unified Multi-Purpose ID card Integrated Bar of the Philippines ID card License issued by the Professional Regulatory Commission Certificate of Confirmation issued by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples Barangay Identification or certification with photo Any other government-issued valid IDs



If the applicant doesn’t have any of these IDs, in the absence of any of the above-mentioned identification documents, he/she can submit a sworn affidavit by any fourth-degree relative.

How do I get a voter ID?

You don’t. The Comelec stopped issuing voter ID cards starting December 2017. This was after the House of Representative approved the bill seeking to establish a national identification system, under which a single ID would be issued to every citizen for all their government transactions.

(Republic Act 1105 or the Philippine Identification System Act was signed into law on August 6, 2018. We all know what happened to the national ID applications and issuance — many Filipinos are still waiting for their cards after years — but that’s a column for another day.)

Here’s a detail many people overlook: Submitting an application for registration doesn’t automatically make you a registered voter. Applications will be vetted and approved by an election registration board in every city and municipality. So far, these boards meet only once every 3 months, so they deliberate on the list per quarter — an incentive for you to register early. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Martin Romualdez over plunder case
World.content:
ARRAIGNMENT. Former House speaker Martin Romualdez during his arraignment on September 16, 2026.

'The court issued a resolution ordering the suspension pendente lite of former speaker Ferdinand Martin Gomez Romualdez for a period of 90 days from receipt of the resolution,' says the Sandiganbayan 3rd Division

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan 3rd Division ordered the suspension of former speaker Martin Romualdez due to his plunder case related to the flood control scandal.

“The court issued a resolution ordering the suspension pendente lite of former speaker Ferdinand Martin Gomez Romualdez for a period of 90 days from receipt of the resolution. The resolution orders the former speaker to cease and desist from the functions of his office or any other office,” 3rd Division Executive Clerk Dennis Pulma said on Tuesday, November 10.

Play Video

Romualdez is facing plunder, a non-bailable offense, due to alleged P7.44-billion in kickbacks from government projects.

The Office of the Ombudsman filed the plunder charge against him with the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan on September 7. On the same day, the 3rd Division issued a warrant of arrest against Romualdez and ordered his detention.

The lawmaker, a first cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., has been detained in the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September 14.

Under Section 5 of Republic Act No. 7080 or the Plunder Law, any public officer charged with the case “whatever stage of execution and mode of participation, is pending in court, shall be suspended from office.”

Romualdez is Leyte 1st District representative – Rappler.com

World.title: [Kasalikasan] Here we go again: Climate talks kick off in Turkey
World.content:
'The world has been addressing climate change together for over three decades, yet the numbers are still alarming'

Hello!

The annual United Nations Climate Change Conference opened Monday, November 9, in Antalya, Turkey — now the 31st session (COP31) since talks started in Berlin, Germany, in 1995.

The world has been addressing climate change together for over three decades, yet the numbers are still alarming. According to the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) State of the Climate Update released also Monday:

2026 will be one of four warmest years on record.

With the “off the charts” Super El Niño underway, temperatures are likely to rise further. “It is different from any El Niño that we have monitored,” warned WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, urging countries to prepare for an even warmer 2027. In the Philippines, senators are urging President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in Super El Niño-hit areas.

Ocean heat is the highest on record for the 10th consecutive year. Sea level has also reached a record high, increasing risks for 900 million people living along low-lying coasts.

Saulo said during a COP31 briefing that the world is “supercharging our weather…. Heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for. The human and economic cost is unacceptably high.”

Lest we forget, we’re starting this year’s climate talks after a disappointing COP30 outcome that promised to triple adaptation finance by 2035 but omitted any mention of the fossil fuels that drive climate change in the first place. No wonder former leaders and climate experts had two years ago criticized the annual climate talks as “no longer fit for purpose” and needing reform. (WATCH: What happened at COP30?)

But I’ve covered these talks closely for the last five years, and no matter how disappointing each conference ends, tens of thousands still participate because it remains the only platform for the world to negotiate climate change solutions. And as long as countries keep showing up, the hope continues.

For instance, the Philippines is finally coming to Antalya with an updated nationally determined contribution, incomplete it may be.

This year’s COP is also putting the spotlight on the world’s oceans — fitting, considering how the ocean absorbs 90% of the excess heat trapped in the Earth’s climate system by excess greenhouse gases. And aside from world leaders, communities that are oceans apart come together at COPs to share best practices and solutions, especially those that face similar challenges.

“No COP is a silver bullet,” said UN climate chief Simon Stiell in his opening remarks on Monday. “No single conference can bridge the chasm between science and reality. We must deal with the world as it is, not as we might wish it to be. Every recent COP has delivered strides forward. This one must too.”

Let’s get to work.

We’re doing things differently this year: follow Rappler’s coverage of COP31 high-level events in the Environment and Science chat room of our MUNI app. Here’s what happened on Day 1. For more stories, bookmark this page.

Till the Tuesday after next!

World.title: More room to improve budget transparency, steps were taken – solons
World.content:
Several leaders of the House attending the formal turnover of the National Expenditure Program on Aug. 11, 2026. —Photo from the House of Representatives

MANILA, Philippines — While admitting there is room for improvement regarding budget transparency, Bataan Rep. Albert Garcia has maintained that the House has been working on existing and new reforms to ensure a clear process in crafting the appropriations plan.

In a press briefing on Monday, Garcia, vice chair of the House committee on appropriations, which prepares the General Appropriations Bill (GAB), reminded the public that they have continued the reforms initiated in 2025 for the 2026 budget cycle, and are looking toward initiating more measures to boost transparency.

Among the existing reforms Garcia referred to are the Budget Amendments Review Sub-committee (BARSc), which replaced the small committee and addresses amendments before the budget bill’s passage on final reading, and the livestreaming of the bicameral conference committee hearings.

Article continues after this 

READ: Solon says House only amended P115B in 2027 budget bill

“Let us acknowledge the fact that we have made earth-shaking reforms with regard to the budget,” Garcia said. “These are new reforms that have never happened before. And we’re learning as we go along.”

“Are we happy with the reforms? Are we complete with the reforms? Is it perfect already? No. Far from it,” Garcia said. “We welcome the critique of the media and our civil society, the church. And we try to improve as we go along.”

READ: Farm-to-market road errors ‘blown out of proportion’ – House rep

One of the reforms, Garcia said, was the creation of an online portal which civil society organizations and budget watchdogs can use to monitor allocations.

Article continues after this 

Garcia also noted that this is a directive from the House leadership led by Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III and Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander Marcos.

“With regard to the ghost project, the Speaker said, ‘Not on my watch,’” Garcia said.

Article continues after this 

Several lawmakers have also supported calls for greater transparency and the portal, which will also prompt representatives to explain the allocations provided to their districts.

No objection

Camarines Sur Rep. Arnie Fuentebella said that his party, the Nationalist People’s Coalition, has no objection to making information on projects and allocations in individual districts available to the public.

“Wala po kaming problema na ipakita kung ano ’yung mga proyekto sa kanya-kanyang distrito,” Fuentebella said at a press conference. “We want to be very transparent. And makikita naman po talaga ito.

(We have no problem showing what the projects in our districts are. We want to be very transparent. And we can clearly see this.)

Negros Oriental Rep. Janice Degamo of Lakas-CMD and Davao del Norte Rep. JM Lagdameo of Partido Federal ng Pilipinas shared their fellow lawmakers’ sentiments.

“Every member of the party is open to show the budget,” Degamo said. “Walang tinatago po ang mga kasama natin in the party.”

(No one in our party is hiding anything.)

“On behalf of PFP, we share the same sentiment as Honorable Fuentebella and Honorable Degamo on the point of transparency for our budget and the budget process. We’re okay to have it open, as well as the portal being available also as a method or a means of transparency,” Lagdameo added.

Similarly, Surigao del Sur Rep. Romeo Momo Sr. said the Nacionalista Party has no qualms about the portal and the disclosure of district allocations.

“Wala hong problema ang Nacionalista Party in terms of allocations,” Momo said.

(The Nacionalista Party does not see any problem in terms of allocations.)

“We believe that there is no equal allocation in each district. Wala hong equal talaga,” he added. “May malalaking distrito, may mga distrito ang dinadaanan ng bagyo, may mga distrito maraming river systems, mayroon mga distrito na laging prone to typhoons and earthquakes.”

(We believe that there is no equal allocation in each district. Nothing is equal there. There are big districts, then there are those hit by typhoons, there are districts with many river systems, then some are prone to typhoons and earthquakes.)

The House has been facing several questions regarding the proposed 2027 national budget, as contained in the General Appropriations Bill, for having issues involving allegedly inserted projects, wrong coordinates for projects, and the return of flood control projects.

Blown out of proportion

Fuentebella and other lawmakers have previously pointed out that the errors in the coordinates of projects, like farm-to-market roads (FMRs), have been blown out of proportion, as only a minimal number of items are affected.

The Department of Agriculture (DA) confirmed this during a hearing held by the House committee on agriculture and food.

“There are just eight lang (only), out of [more than] 1,600. It seems to be blown out of proportion. Like the whole budget or coordinates of the farm-to-market roads were wrong,” Fuentebella said in a mix of Filipino and English.

READ: House adds clause to correct budget bill’s tech errors, wrong project details

DA Assistant Secretary for Operations U-Nichols Manalo confirmed that eight projects had errors and clarified that all 1,669 FMR projects were included in the National Expenditure Program, or the proposed budget submitted by the executive branch to Congress.

The errors were carried over when the House approved its version of the 2027 proposed budget.

World.title: Take better care of elderly, PWDs amid Super El Niño
World.content:
Photo by Leah D. Agonoy

MANILA, Philippines — Quezon City councilor Alfred Vargas on Tuesday called for special care for senior citizens and persons with disabilities (PWDs) amid the effects of the Super El Niño, particularly the drought expected to hit Metro Manila by January.

Vargas issued the call as he urged Quezon City residents and barangay officials to prepare their households early for the effects of El Niño.

According to Vargas, families and caregivers should ensure that seniors and PWDs are in well-ventilated spaces and hydrated at all times.

Article continues after this 

READ: No need yet to declare state of calamity over El Niño – Palace

He also told them to consult doctors on how heat may affect maintenance medicines.

“Tandaan po nating alagaan at bantayan nang mas mabuti ang ating mga lolo, lola, at PWD. Lalo na po ang mga bedridden o hirap magsabi ng nararamdaman na mas kailangan ang tulong natin sa mga panahong ito,” Vargas said in a statement.

(Let’s remember to take better care of and watch over our grandparents, and PWDs, especially those who are bedridden or have difficulty expressing their feelings need our help more during these times.)

He then assured residents that the Quezon City government is ready to provide support when needed, with the QC Heat Action Team under Mayor Joy Belmonte designating 32 public libraries as cooling centers, and integrated Hotline 122 into a round-the-clock emergency response network.

Article continues after this 

“Nasa QC na ang mga sistema, manpower, at ang diwa ng bayanihan. Ang kailangan natin ngayon ay maging maagap, magtulungan, at alagaan ang bawat miyembro ng ating pamilya. Kakayanin natin ito basta sama-sama,” Vargas said.

(QC has the systems, manpower, and the spirit of communal unity. What we need now is to be proactive, work together, and take care of each member of our family. We can do it together.)

Article continues after this 

He then advised residents of all ages to drink water often, wear light clothing, use an umbrella or a hat outdoors, and avoid heavy physical activity during peak heat hours.

Families should also store enough drinking water in case of service interruptions, avoid panic buying, and prevent overloading outlets as electricity demand is expected to rise.

Projections from the United Nations as well as the state weather bureau show that drought will expand across Luzon, including Metro Manila in the coming months.

World.title: Over 1,000 Negros residents apply as voter registration resumes
World.content:
Inquirer files

BACOLOD CITY, NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines — A total of 1,544 voter applications were processed across the Negros Island Region (NIR) on Tuesday, Nov. 10, as the Commission on Elections (Comelec) officially reopened nationwide voter registration for the 2028 national and local elections.

The Comelec NIR reported that Negros Occidental processed the highest number with 856 applications, comprising 423 males and 433 females.

Negros Oriental followed with 651 total applications consisting of 301 males and 350 females, while Siquijor registered 37 applications made up of 23 males and 14 females.

Article continues after this 

READ: Comelec opens voter registration for 2028 polls from Nov. 10 to July 30

Overall, female applicants outnumbered male applicants across the region, with 797 females compared to 747 males.

Seven applications were processed under the Register Anywhere Program (RAP) in Bacolod City, composed of four male and three female registrants.

READ: Comelec surprised by ‘overwhelming’ turnout as voter registration reopens

Ian Lee Ananoria, Negros Occidental Provincial Election Supervisor and concurrent Bacolod Election Officer, said the nationwide registration period will run through July 30, 2027.

Article continues after this 

Local election offices and designated satellite registration sites are currently accepting new voter registrations, transfers of registration records, reactivations, and corrections of entries.

To spare applicants from the heat, Ananoria said registration in Bacolod is being held from Tuesday to Saturday at SM City Bacolod this week, while next week’s registration will be at Robinsons Place Bacolod.

Article continues after this
