World.title: Two people killed in crash in Melbourne's south-east
World.content:
Two people have died in a collision between a motorcycle and a car in Melbourne's south-east.

Emergency services were called to Cranbourne Road in Narre Warren shortly after 6pm yesterday.

Both the motorcycle rider and driver of the car died at the scene.

The driver of the car died at the scene. (ABC News)

Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the collision.

Cranbourne Road was closed between Centre and Golf Links roads, with traffic diversions in place.

Police have asked anyone with information or dash cam footage to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Workers at notorious youth justice centre compensated $7m for violence
World.content:
Justin White had been working at a youth justice centre unit in Victoria for a matter of weeks when he was violently assaulted by a group of inmates armed with a plastic cricket bat.

He said the life-altering attack at Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre in October 2019 happened on a day when the mood had been "deteriorating quickly".

"I clearly was the target and then that descended into what became a gang assault, which I'm still living with today," Mr White said.

"I genuinely thought I wasn't going to come out of it. It's only because of the actions of others that I did."

A CCTV image shows the plastic cricket bat used as a weapon during the 2019 assault. (Supplied: Bendigo Magistrates Court)

Mr White is still unable to work due to severe PTSD.

"I hope one day for it to be further in my memory, but at the moment it still feels like it happened yesterday," he said.

Mr White sustained spinal fractures, as well as a traumatic head injury that has affected his cognitive functioning.

He continues to battle post-concussion syndrome.

Three of his colleagues received bravery awards for trying to intervene and stop the attack.

The inmates, two aged 18 and the other 19 at the time, were charged and moved to an adult prison.

Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre re-opened this year. (ABC News)

The assault is one of hundreds that took place at the notorious youth justice centre in central Victoria before it closed in December 2023, following riots and escapes.

Twelve weeks before it closed, seven staff members were held hostage during a riot where a worker's keys were stolen and used to unlock parts of the prison.

Data released to the ABC by the Department of Justice under freedom of information laws shows almost $7 million in compensation was paid to workers at the centre for occupational violence incidents that happened in the three years before it closed.

An occupational violence incident was logged every 2.6 days on average between January 2020 and December 2023.

There were 326 physical assaults reported, 114 verbal assaults, 21 assaults with biological material and 95 exposures to aggression or violence.

Of the incidents, 60 resulted in WorkCover claims by staff members.

150 staff for 22 inmates

The Victorian government reopened Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre in April, initially announcing 30 beds would be recommissioned, before adding a further 45.

Ros Spence says operations at the centre are being scaled up in stages. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Youth Justice Minister Ros Spence told Nationals Member for Northern Victoria Gaelle Broad that 22 young people were at the centre, with more than 150 staff employed as of September 9.

Ms Broad told the ABC the figures reflected an "extraordinary" amount of waste.

Gaelle Broad is concerned about the centre's value for taxpayer money. (Supplied: Gaelle Broad)

"It seemed crazy to me. The government spent millions on it, then closed it, and then they were going to do something else with the land, and then they announced it's reopening," she said.

"The staff didn't see it coming, and then trying to recruit and find people, and incentives to get people to come back."

In her statement, Ms Spence said operations were being ramped up in stages to allow time to recruit and train staff and "stress test operating processes".

She said the Malmsbury site had been maintained "in a reasonable condition" during its closure so it could be reopened if required.

That was despite a group of residents workshopping ideas for a new, alternative use of the site with a belief the community would be consulted.

The capital works to reopen Malmsbury this year were budgeted at $17.6 million, according to the department's annual report.

Ahead of the state election, Labor has pledged to introduce rehabilitation detention for low- and mid-level youth offenders, including at Malmsbury.

Legal costs may climb

Law firm Grainger Legal said it had seen the "life-changing" damage sustained by some youth justice workers from working at Malmsbury.

Lawyers Caroline Grainger and Laura Paterson said it was not uncommon for payouts to be in the six figures if a worker was seriously injured and could establish negligence.

Caroline Grainger has represented Malmsbury Youth Justice workers in compensation claims. (Supplied: Grainger Legal)

"The workers we've assisted have experienced injuries including concussions, lacerations and broken limbs, and psychiatric injuries such as PTSD, major depressive disorder, insomnia, stress and anxiety," the lawyers said.

They said the reopening of Malmsbury brought concerns about staff safety, "having seen physical and psychological injuries occur in high numbers".

"In the past we have heard complaints including insufficient staffing, reliance on casual or agency staff to fill gaps, and staff feeling under-trained, unsafe or unsupported," they said.

"Our hope would be that these issues had been addressed prior to the centre re-opening."

Government data shows Victoria's youth justice facilities were at 63.5 per cent capacity combined as of November 2, with about 224 detainees across three precincts.

Life-altering violence

Mr White said he was concerned to hear about the reopening of Malmsbury "for the people who have to step back into that environment".

Justin White is still living with the effects of the 2019 assault. (ABC News: Anna McGuinness)

He is calling for more support for corrections and youth justice workers, particularly in dealing with occupational violence.

"Seeing the supports that other frontline staff have and what we don't have, I'm not saying it's perfect in any role, but you'd like to see more for what people navigate every day," he said.

" It's quite lonely and hard to fight a big system or issue on your own. "

World.title: Breaking: UK arrests US Army member suspected of helping Russia
World.content:
British police say a ‌senior member of the US Army ‌has been arrested over allegations that he was assisting Russian intelligence.

A ‌41-year-old man was ‌arrested under ‌the National Security ‌Act near the ‌city of ‌Gloucester, west England, on Tuesday.

He remains in custody at a police station in London, police said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, added: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

World.title: Australia considering world-first criminal charges for AI companies
World.content:
Australia could become the first country to prosecute AI companies for failing to take reasonable steps to prevent harmful conduct by their models.

The federal government has announced it would consider a new criminal offence for tech companies over AI harm and an AI safety watchdog empowered to issue significant fines, as part of its response to September's OpenAI Medicare statistics hack.

"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast-changing world," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters yesterday.

AI companies Anthropic, Google and Meta, which were not given a substantial forewarning of the government's response, did not respond to requests for comment.

An OpenAI spokesperson told the ABC that the company was reviewing the government's proposals.

OpenAI hack not being criminally investigated

When Mr Albanese disclosed the Medicare hack in September, he said the government would seek urgent advice on whether any offence had occurred and whether the incident should be referred to the Australian Federal Police (AFP).

Yesterday, he did not answer questions about whether he believed OpenAI had committed a crime.

In a letter released last week, the AFP told a parliamentary inquiry it had received no formal report of a crime and had begun no criminal investigation or prosecution over the incident.

No other country has created a criminal offence that centres on AI companies needing to take reasonable steps to prevent harm. (AP: Michael Dwyer/File)

Mr Albanese said the government had accepted all the recommendations of the review into the incident.

One of those was to consider "options to reform the criminal law to improve AI safety".

An option to be considered is the creation of a "failure to prevent" offence for AI companies behind models that engage in harmful conduct and do not take reasonable steps to prevent the harm.

The other was to consider criminal penalties for egregious breaches of AI safety standards.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the OpenAI hack prompted the government to clarify the law around criminal liability.

"It should never be the case that there's an argument that someone didn't know the computer was loaded," he said.

What would criminal charges add?

Monash University associate professor Michael Duffy said both criminal liability and civil remedies were "important" in dealing with harm from AI.

"It is good to see the government now trying to grapple with the issue of potential harm from AI, which could be quite significant," he said.

Dr Duffy said both routes could deter harmful conduct, and civil remedies could also compensate victims.

"The area will not be without difficulty, however, in terms of problems of proof, working out if harms were foreseeable and proving fault," he said.

Ed Santow says the criminal offence could prove an effective deterrence alongside other penalties. (Supplied: UTS)

University of Technology Sydney industry professor Ed Santow said he saw the merit of a criminal provision as part of a suite of options.

"I think what will be much more useful is the civil one," he said.

He said the measures would give the government more tools for dealing with companies that do not meet their safety obligations.

Professor Santow drew a parallel with workplace safety and said unreasonable conduct might warrant a civil penalty, while more serious conduct, such as acting recklessly with disregard for someone's safety, could warrant criminal charges.

Australia's push to lead on AI regulation

The Albanese government has signposted its desire to lead the world on regulating AI, with the prime minister describing it as a "first mover in this space".

While other countries have pursued distinct criminal offences for AI harm, one centring on a failure to take reasonable steps to prevent harm would be the first of its kind at a national level.

Italy recently introduced a criminal offence for high-risk AI uses that do not have required technical safeguards or human oversight where a failure would be a serious threat to people or national security.

No company or individual has been prosecuted under the law to date.

It remains unclear whether Australia's OpenAI incident would reach the threshold of harmful conduct, but Mr Albanese yesterday described it as "minor in terms of direct implications".

World.title: SA Labor slammed 'basketball stadium' to fix ramping but the crisis is far from over
World.content:
"I'm choosing to scrap the basketball stadium and invest in our health system."

That was how then SA Opposition Leader Peter Malinauskas announced a key part of his election campaign on social media back in June 2021.

The campaign — focused on "fixing the ramping crisis" — helped Labor storm back to power after just one term in opposition.

A large plank of the campaign was not going ahead with the Marshall government's plan to spend more than $600 million building a multi-purpose city arena.

It would have sat on the banks of the Torrens, with a capacity of 15,000, and the capacity to host conventions, concerts and basketball and netball games.

At least some of the cost would have been offset by a planned sale of the Adelaide Entertainment Centre in Hindmarsh to developers.

The then-Liberal government proposed the Riverbank Arena in 2021. (Supplied)

When it was first announced, Mr Malinauskas appeared open to the idea.

But just a few months later, he came out strongly against it, saying with a health system in crisis, it wasn't the right time to build the Riverbank Arena — which Labor from then on referred to exclusively as a "basketball stadium".

The price tag was high, and in a campaign focused overwhelmingly on health, it was an easy target.

Why revisit that ancient history?

More than one electoral cycle later, the Malinauskas government holds on to power with an even bigger margin.

And while ramping remains at near record levels, the government isn't shy about investing in new sporting facilities and major events.

An artist's impression of the temporary pit building for the planned $96 million MotoGP racing circuit. (Supplied: SA Government)

You've got a couple of controversial parklands developments — $45 million to redevelop and expand the North Adelaide Golf Course, and $96 million to prepare the eastern parklands for the MotoGP.

Then there's $92 million to build a new netball stadium, $100 million for a gymnastics stadium and a $20 million dollar contribution to the Barossa Park football grounds to upgrade them for Gather Round.

There's also a number of events where the taxpayer contribution hasn't been disclosed for "commercial in confidence" reasons.

That list includes the AFL's Gather Round, the now failed LIV Golf competition, golf's Australian Open tournament, the Super Netball grand final, and the Beach Volleyball World Championships.

Despite those expenses, the government has made major investments in the health system.

It's poured more than a billion dollars trying to fix ramping, including hiring more health workers and increasing hospital beds.

A little-known office, $55k contracts and a growing political problem The Malinauskas government has made a virtue of its willingness to take risks and do things differently, but could that strategy be about to become unstuck?

But that has not made the picture look much better.

Last month 4,759 hours were lost to ramping — not the highest ever but still significantly higher than the peak of 2,867 during the Marshall government's time in office.

A major factor in those numbers — the hundreds of people in hospital beds, waiting for a place in the aged care system.

This week Labor held crisis talks with unions, industry and advocacy bodies, even giving the "empty chair" treatment to federal aged care minister Sam Rae, who did not attend.

Never mind that the aged care system and the NDIS were both known to be major factors of bed block before the 2022 election, they just weren't factors Labor chose to highlight at the time.

One could argue that, if you followed the logic of the basketball stadium campaign, all the money spent on fun events, should instead be funnelled into a health system in crisis.

But of course, governments should spend money on cultural events and facilities.

While each should be assessed on its merits, the argument that it's a waste of money ignores the importance of a cultural life to a community.

And there's the argument that these investments return to the state and then some, toput attracting visitors who spend money while they're here.

The Malinauskas government has readily put money towards new sports facilities and major events. (ABC News: Che Chorley.)

But while the government argues its investment in facilities and events will have a net benefit to the South Australian economy, the Marshall government could have made the same argument about its arena plans back in 2021.

Possibly that was a failure of the Marshall government, which didn't do a great job rebuffing the "basketball stadium" allegations.

During the 2022 election campaign, after two years tackling the COVID pandemic, it appeared the Liberal government had run out of momentum.

In reviewing the loss, even then new Opposition Leader David Speirs said "I don't think we actually ran a campaign, in some definitions of the word."

Apart from the cost, one of the most controversial elements of Marshall's stadium proposal — it was going to be built on the parklands.

The plan was to build it on Helen Mayo Park, next to Morphett Street, with a tunnel connecting it to the Convention Centre.

Then-Labor candidate Lucy Hood gave a speech against a new stadium proposed by the Marshall government. (ABC News)

It sparked protests, including at least one where then Labor candidate Lucy Hood gave a speech.

"It begs the question, why is the Liberal Marshall government undertaking the largest land grab that we have ever seen? There is a reason are voted Australia's most livable city and it's because of vistas like this," she said while gesturing across the park to the river.

A far cry from today's parkland rallies, where Lucy Hood — or anyone from the current Labor government — is unlikely to receive a warm welcome to put it lightly.

World.title: Consumers bear the cost as India's sugar farmers struggle
World.content:
From crop to crystal, making sugar is thirsty work.

On the outskirts of Mysuru in India's south, sugarcane is cut, bound, and thrown onto carts headed for nearby factories.

Phailwan Venkatesh watches his workers hack at the cane under a baking sun.

The stalks should be fatter, the 63-year-old says, and should not snap so easily.

"There is hardly anything in this sugarcane crop," he says.

"It's all dry."

A sugarcane farm in Karnataka, just outside of Mysuru. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

India is the world's second-largest sugar producer and its biggest consumer. But this year, a record-setting El Niño weather system has sent warm ocean conditions across the Pacific, weakening the monsoon season.

The lack of rainfall in July and August meant Phailwan's sugarcane crop struggled to grow.

It compounded an already perilous situation for the farmer, who has had to fork out more for fertiliser due to global conflicts.

Farmers are trying to make the best of a tough season amid rising prices. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Sugar squeeze hits global markets

Bhargabi Bharadwaj, an expert in food system risks at Chatham House, says India's sugar production has not crashed, but uncertainty is adding to a general strain.

"The immediate impact of a climate disruption is often just a price shock rather than a physical shortage, but rising prices can quickly threaten food affordability and economic stability," she explained.

According to the latest figures from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation, global sugar prices rose by 6.6 per cent in October — the fourth consecutive monthly rise, hitting the highest level since April last year.

Sugarcane brought to the mills has less juice than last year due to a weak monsoon during the planting season. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Analysis by ANZ Bank found the sugar squeeze, coupled with higher cocoa prices, has made chocolate and lollies more expensive to manufacture and could see retail prices jump.

Australian sugarcane growers have been far less affected by dry conditions and may even benefit from cane with higher sugar content, lifting overall output, according to a report by the US Department of Agriculture.

In India, prices increased more than 30 per cent in August compared to July, according to India's Department of Consumer Affairs.

This year's El Niño comes on the heels of an already difficult year for the country's sugar industry, which was hit by excess rain in 2025, leading to pests and crop diseases.

One of India's biggest sugar factories, Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar, reported an almost 11 per cent drop in sugar production last financial year.

Kodihalli Chandrashekar says farmers are facing another difficult season. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Kurubar Shanta Kumar, president of the Karnataka State Sugarcane Growers Association, says that so far this year, sugarcane yield has dropped by 9 million tonnes compared to last year.

"We are completely dependent on Mother Nature," he said.

"We can't grow sugarcane on computers; we can't cultivate crops on computers."

Tariffs lifted to boost supply

Karnataka's state government is providing about $50 million in financial support to farmers, and an extra $1.70 for every tonne of sugarcane supplied to mills.

To boost supply and bring down prices ahead of the Hindu festival season, India's federal government has lifted tariffs on sugar, allowing up to 1 million tonnes to be imported duty-free until the end of the year.

It has also banned sugar from being used to produce ethanol.

Even so, the price hike has begun to hit businesses.

Dasappa has been forced to increase the cost of his sugarcane juice as prices rise.

Dasappa has owned a sugarcane juice cart for 15 years. Last year he sold a cup for about 10 rupees; now he charges 25.

"If customers bargain, I charge them 20 rupees," the 45-year-old said.

"The price has increased [for me]. Sugarcane costs 80 rupees per kilogram; it used to be 40 rupees per kilogram."

Others, like sweet shop owner Thejaswini Suhas, have tried to absorb the cost. Her shop in Mysuru's busy city centre is packed every afternoon with customers buying the popular South Indian sweet Mysore Pak, made with chickpea flour, ghee and sugar.

"[Higher prices are] affecting our business, but we don't want to lose customers [by putting prices up]," she said.

"If this situation continues, we won't have any other option; we will have to increase the price."

Consumers of sweet foods could soon feel the pinch of the poor season. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

That could prove inevitable. This year's El Niño has a long tail and may not peak until December.

Forecasters from the World Meteorological Organization have warned the weather event will persist until at least February 2027, and increase the risk of extreme heat, droughts and flooding worldwide.

For India's sugarcane growers, it could spell disaster. Higher fertiliser, labour, and fuel costs mean farmers have struggled to sell their crop to mills for a profit despite higher sugar prices.

"We are struggling to buy food," Phailwan said.

"We used to grow our own paddy [rice] and other grains; now that is also scarce.

"Our earnings are very low; we could have managed if the [sugar] yield was good and had recovered our returns on our investment. We have borrowed money and invested in crops which have backfired, and we are unable to repay the loans."

World.title: DFAT investigates reports of another Australian killed fighting for Ukraine
World.content:
Australian authorities are investigating reports that another Australian has died while fighting for Ukraine.

Last week, numerous Russian-aligned social media channels began reporting the death of Jeremie Robert Munso, claiming he had been killed in late August.

The posts claim he was killed in the same incident as another Australian, Shane "Mozzie" Bagley, who died while fighting with the Ukrainian International Legion's Med Team Alpha.

Reports former ADF soldier killed The soldier, known by the nickname "Mozzie", was serving as a combat medic with Ukraine's 1st Foreign Legion Squadron.

Officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) are working with Ukrainian authorities to try to confirm Mr Munso's death, and support is being provided to his family.

Confirmation of deaths in Ukraine can take significant time, and Australian consular assistance is limited due to the ongoing war.

It is understood Mr Munso is from Melbourne.

Ukraine's International Legion advertises online for foreigners to join, offering pay of up to $14,600 a month for soldiers engaged in "assault missions".

An unknown number of Australians have taken up the opportunity, but Ukrainian authorities have previously suggested as many as 16,000 foreigners have served from more than 72 countries.

Australia's travel advice for Ukraine remains at "do not travel" due to the ongoing war.

The ABC yesterday revealed that Daryl Fladung, a Queensland security guard, is missing and feared dead after leaving Australia to fight for Russia.

Reported death used for 'propaganda'

Australian fighting for Russia feared dead Daryl "Dundee" Fladung was recruited to fight for Russia while playing video games at home in outback Queensland. Ten days after posting about joining the front line, he went missing.

Russian-aligned social media channels have sought to highlight the deaths of foreigners serving in Ukraine's foreign legions.

Last week, numerous channels across various social media platforms, including Instagram, X and Telegram, began posting about the death of Mr Munso and other foreigners.

Associate professor Matthew Sussex, an expert on Russia from the Australian National University, said the Russian state tried to use unofficial social media accounts to give its message a wider reach than what it could achieve with more obvious propaganda tools.

"Russia wants to create distance between official state media channels and unofficial ones, which are more likely to be believed than Russia Today or than things from the Kremlin," Dr Sussex said.

Matthew Sussex says Russia uses unofficial social media accounts to give its message a wider reach. (Supplied: ANU)

"So it's created a sort of social media ecosystem that it uses, and it uses a variety of platforms from Telegram all the way through to Twitter, X and Facebook."

Russian-aligned Telegram channels have sought to try to identify foreigners serving in Ukrainian units, particularly when they are killed.

Dr Sussex said the channels aimed to deter others from joining.

"Sometimes it's speculation, but sometimes it is accurate," he said.

"But that's not really the job of [these channels].

"The job then gets passed down through the chain to those who will put a spin on it to say: 'Don't come and fight for Ukraine, otherwise you will die."

World.title: Would you push a neighbour into unemployment to reduce inflation?
World.content:
The Reserve Bank has acknowledged that more people are losing faith in its ability to control inflation in the next 12 months.

It says it is taking the matter seriously because "trust" plays an important role in the bank's ability to manage people's inflation expectations, which feed back into the bank's ability to control inflation.

RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser talked about it in a speech last week.

Trust in Reserve Bank is under strain, deputy governor warns Trust in the RBA is under strain "just as we need it most", RBA deputy governor warns.

The ABC covered the speech here, with a focus on its main message.

But it is worth revisiting elements of the speech where Mr Hauser talked about the RBA's "values" and "full employment", for more interrogation.

Because they begged a question: do Australians know what the bank actually means when it talks about "full employment"?

And does the bank's modern usage of the term make people have more, or less, trust in its inflation-fighting approach and its ability to hit its inflation target?

When do we experience full employment?

Mr Hauser said the full impact of a rate hike depends on whether people "trust" the bank to do what is necessary to meet its inflation target.

Getting by but 'not much fun' in wake of rates decision Discretionary spending parties will be over following rates decision.

By that he meant, if people believe the RBA will keep lifting rates until inflation comes down, that "belief" will influence their spending decisions, which will ultimately help the bank to control inflation.

"In simple terms, do they expect us to return the economy to balance, with on-target inflation and full employment, in the long run?" he asked.

But in the Q&A portion of his speech, Hauser was asked a fascinating question from the audience about the link between trust, accountability, and full employment:

"Trust needs something people can check you against," the audience member said. "With inflation, that's the [RBA's] target band. [But] with full employment, there isn't an observable one. "And when your estimate of [full employment] changes … that can look like [you're] moving the goalposts. "So how can people hold you to account on that side of your mandate other than waiting to see what inflation does?"

It was a penetrating question, because what is full employment these days?

In email correspondence with the ABC, one of the complaints readers often have is about the modern meaning of the term.

Millions of older Australians remember when full employment was associated with an unemployment rate of roughly 2 per cent, when the labour market was overwhelmingly comprised of full-time jobs, when jobs were relatively abundant, and when loyalty to an employer was typically rewarded with predictable career progression and regular pay increases.

People 'furious' with RBA Some of the main drivers of high inflation are supply issues caused by the US-Iran war and American tech giants spending huge amounts on AI, which are not problems a rate hike will solve.

Today, full employment means something very different.

Today, it refers to the level of unemployment (and assorted other 'indicators') that coincides with a situation in which the total level of demand and supply in the economy is in "equilibrium", and where wage growth is steady enough that inflation is low and manageable and is not accelerating.

But depending on the state of the world, that could mean the economy is in full employment when the unemployment rate is around 5 per cent, or 6 per cent, or 7 per cent, or higher.

That is not what full employment used to mean.

What's in a word?

Mr Hauser was delivering the annual Sir Leslie Melville Lecture. Melville (1902-2002) was a titan of Australian economics in the 20th century.

Andrew Hauser says "trust" is essential for monetary policy to work properly. (ABC News: Adam Wyatt)

Hauser reminded his audience that Melville helped to shape the intellectual foundations for clause 8 of the Commonwealth Bank Act 1945, which set the bank's dual mandate of price stability (originally, stability of the currency) and "the maintenance of full employment."

"That mission remains fundamentally unchanged. It shapes everything we do," Hauser said in his speech.

But is that literally true, what Hauser said?

'Pressures bearing down' on rates Why is Australia stuck in an inflation problem that has sent interest rates to 15-year highs?

The meaning of "full employment" today is fundamentally different from its original meaning.

The phrase is a relic from the post-World War II era when Australia's economic, institutional, and cultural context was thoroughly different. It comes from a time when politicians were ashamed if unemployment increased.

Australia's policymakers waved goodbye to "full employment" in the mid-1970s.

They then cycled through various models of economic management before stumbling upon inflation-targeting in the early 1990s.

And when they adopted inflation-targeting, they had to develop an updated definition of "full employment" to fit their new method of economic management, which would allow the bank to keep meeting its full employment mandate.

So, the words "full employment" have remained in the RBA's mandate, but their insides have changed; it is like removing a kilogram of gold from your backpack and replacing it with a kilogram of sand.

Measuring modern full employment

The point the audience member (at Hauser's speech) was making about the link between trust, accountability and full employment was therefore insightful.

Since full employment is not observable anymore, how do people know if the RBA is delivering that part of its mandate?

Hauser said the RBA tries to draw together a range of measures of what it "feels like" when you're at full employment to give a sense of how close we may be to it.

See the graphic below:

The RBA says there has been some easing in labour market conditions in recent months. (Source: Reserve Bank of Australia, Statement on Monetary Policy (November 2026), page. 49)

At the moment, according to those measures, the RBA says a majority of labour market indicators still appear close to, or slightly tighter than, their estimated trend levels.

That means the RBA thinks employment is still a bit too "full" at the moment and it needs to get less full to slow inflation down.

The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent, but the bank is forecasting the unemployment rate will need to rise to 5.1 per cent by December 2028 to secure the necessary disinflation.

Unemployment for thee, less inflation for me?

Now, on the question of whether there is an alternative to managing inflation, instead of using the unemployed and mortgage-holders as shock absorbers, that debate is getting livelier as each year passes.

But in his Q&A, Hauser made an observation relevant to that debate.

He said the RBA made the decision in 2022 and 2023 to raise rates by a little less than some other countries, knowing it would mean that inflation would take a little longer to come down in Australia, to preserve as many of the gains in employment as possible that Australia made in the aftermath of COVID.

The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy RBA officials argue the hit to borrowers' income isn't the main way rate rises lower inflation. But they often omit a key fact.

But looking back, given the anger people feel about inflation now, was that the right decision?

"Inflation is experienced by everyone, and unemployment, sadly, is only experienced by those who are unemployed or … in some cases, indirectly attached to it," Hauser said.

"So that has been a very live issue.

"We have tried to explain that, but obviously one person's benefit — 'Thanks very much, I'm still in a job' — may be another person's, 'Wow, you've let inflation remain pretty high for a long period of time,'" he said.

Hauser was making an uncomfortable point about human psychology.

High inflation hits you and your neighbour (not equally, mind you), but if you could lower inflation for everyone by pushing your neighbour into unemployment, would you do it?

Some people who seem like they would relish that choice have been giving the RBA a lot of free advice in recent years about the need to crank interest rates higher and faster than the bank has felt comfortable doing.

World.title: The boss says it’s ‘a wonderful place to be’. Staff call it an embarrassing place to work
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland councils The boss says it’s ‘a wonderful place to be’. Staff call it an embarrassing place to work Julius Dennis November 11, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Redlands councillor has lashed out at claims the council is a “wonderful place to be”, following the resignation of its mayor, who alleged a culture of bullying and intimidation. In an interview with this masthead, councillor Wendy Boglary said the council’s longstanding cultural issues had only worsened in recent times. Redlands led the state in complaints to the Office of the Independent Assessor last year. Matt Dennien “Staff feel that if they are making a presentation to council – which is based on data and research and they are qualified – they can be ridiculed and even laughed at,” she said. “Their reports are heavily criticised, maybe even with expletives.



“I know over the years we have lost staff because they just don’t feel they are valued.” Councillor Wendy Boglary. Redland City Council Boglary has served on the council for 18 years, and was an ally of now former mayor Jos Mitchell. She said the culture at the council was distressing, and she felt she had borne the brunt of inappropriate behaviour, which she said, “can be 24/7”. Boglary said a 2025 state government decision to remove bad councillor conduct as an offence to be investigated by the Office of the Independent Assessor had only made matters worse.



“People who like to use intimidation and belittling of others … The floodgate has opened now for them to go for it,” she said. Boglary raised the issue at a public state government inquiry into councillor conduct laws last month, and said the issue was not contained to Redlands, which often led the state in such complaints. Mitchell previously said she had been the subject of about 70 complaints to the OIA, which she claimed was used as a political weapon to overwhelm her with related paperwork. At a press conference following Mitchell’s resignation, Redlands chief executive Louise Rusan rejected claims of a culture problem at the council. “I believe we have a very good culture,” she said.



“We have wonderful officers, and if you look at our general meetings, you can see that we’re making quality decisions by the councillors. I would say we’re a very good organisation.” Politics in the bayside council have long been heated. Dan Peled But Boglary’s claims were supported by a Redland City Council worker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to freely discuss internal matters. “I’m embarrassed to say I work at Redland City Council,” the worker said. They said quality staff had either left or been pushed out of the council, and many more were looking for an exit.



For example, since the 2024 election, five members of the respected ethics and integrity unit has left the council in one way or another. Related Article Updated

Queensland councils ‘Up until two seconds ago, I had not had contact’: In bizarre presser, council claims mayor had not resigned The worker said remarks about council having a positive culture were met with cynicism by staff. “Most people would see the culture at Redland City Council as dysfunctional. They see concerns raised by staff about how the council is operating are ignored,” they said. “There is a perception – or it certainly looks like – there is a cabal at the top of the organisation that is a collusive block between certain councillors and senior executives.”



The worker said it was clear that Mitchell had been excluded by certain staff. “Everyone could see it, it was obvious to staff that the mayor was being iced out.” They said staff members were fearful of raising issues, and those who did were treated as if they were the issue. “It’s a culture of inequity, of the senior levels of the organisation looking after themselves and in the interest of certain councillors, and that comes at the expense of the staff that are working hard to make this work on a day-to-day basis.” A byelection for a new Redlands mayor is under way, with the postal vote closing on December 12. World.title: ASX set to fall as Wall Street slumps on inflation report; Anthropic targets $2 trillion valuation
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall as Wall Street slumps on inflation report; Anthropic targets $2 trillion valuation Stan Choe November 11, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. US stocks are falling after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected. The S&P 500 fell 0.8 per cent and gave back some of its big rally from the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 291 points, or 0.6 per cent, in early afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.3 per cent lower. Higher-than-expected inflation could push the Federal Reserve to hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in December and beyond. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 4.56am AEDT pointing to a fall of 61 points or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped 1.1 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was weaker at US68.54¢. Pressure from the bond market undercut stocks following the discouraging report on inflation. People had to pay prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living that were even higher last month than economists expected. That could push the Federal Reserve to hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in December and beyond.



Higher interest rates can help rein in inflation, but they do so by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and by slowing the overall economy. Higher rates also make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Opinion

AI Nvidia CEO’s fling will be an affair to remember for AI, and for Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist One Fed official even hinted the central bank may increase the federal funds rate by double the typical amount next month because of how high inflation has remained for years. Speaking in London before the inflation report was released, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said “a stronger policy move may be needed” if the report showed an important underlying measure of inflation rose by 0.3 per cent from September. In that case, he said the Fed should consider hiking the federal funds rate by half a percentage point rather than the typical quarter point. Moving by only the usual amount could “put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.”



Shortly afterward, Tuesday’s inflation report showed that the underlying measure of inflation Waller was worried about was exactly 0.3 per cent, the threshold he had set. It’s the Fed’s job to keep inflation under control, along with keeping the job market strong. That sent yields jumping in the bond market as traders upped their forecasts for coming hikes to rates by the Fed. The yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.02 per cent from 4.88 per cent late Monday. It’s a notable move for the bond market, and the yield helps set where rates are for mortgages and other loans going to US households and businesses. The 10-year Treasury yield had been dropping since early October, when it topped 5.30 per cent as worries spiked about high inflation, higher interest rates, the US government’s big debt and other concerns. Tuesday’s jump in yields came even though oil prices fell again. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 0.7 per cent to $US91.91. President Donald Trump said late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.”



Brent’s price has been falling from more than $US112 at the start of the month amid uncertainty about what will happen with the war with Iran. Jumps in Treasury yields push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and they can particularly hurt companies in the real-estate business. Higher mortgage rates can keep potential customers away from homebuilders, for example, and Lennar fell 4.8 per cent for one of the sharper losses in the S&P 500. Rival homebuilders also fell, including drops of 3.9 per cent for D.R. Horton and 3.8 per cent for PulteGroup. Builders FirstSource, which sells crown mouldings, cabinets and other products to homebuilders, sank 3.8 per cent. The single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 was Nvidia, which fell 6.3 per cent. It’s been under pressure since its board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, who admitted to a relationship with a woman who, according to The New York Times, US intelligence determined was gathering information for China.



It’s also been swinging amid broader worries that have knocked the artificial-intelligence industry around recently. Democratic victories in statehouses across the country last week raised concerns about possible restrictions on construction of AI data centres. That built on top of already longstanding worries that AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble. Related Article David Jones collapse Stressed and out of pocket: David Jones’ great-great-great grandson is owed money, too Other stocks in the AI industry also slipped. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 6.2 per cent. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, fell 3.7 per cent after flipping between gains and losses earlier in the morning. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 2.2 per cent. Advanced Micro Devices held up better and was mostly unchanged. The recent shakiness for AI-related stocks had raised questions about whether Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, may delay its initial public offering of stock.



But Anthropic said in a filing with US regulators that it’s looking to sell its stock at a price that values the company at roughly $US1.4 trillion ($2 trillion). That would make it one of the most valuable companies on Wall Street, worth more than Walmart, JPMorgan Chase, ExxonMobil or Coca-Cola. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 4.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains on strength for its two tech giants that have benefited from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. World.title: The untouched block of land that is key to a $100 million arm wrestle with the Victorian government
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing The untouched block of land that is key to a $100 million arm wrestle with the Victorian government Danny Russell November 11, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The state’s harness racing industry claims it was shortchanged $100 million in a state government land deal on the outskirts of Melbourne that threatens the sport’s survival. Harness Racing Victoria was forced to sign over ownership of 93 hectares of Melton real estate to the government in 2024 to settle an $86 million debt, but the land has since been valued at up to $200 million. Harness Racing Victoria wants to get its hands on land Melton Entertainment Park to help secure its future. The Western Highway property sits near two trains stations – Melton and Cobblebank – and a new hospital site, and is ideally situated for commercial or housing development in a fast-growing area of the western suburbs. But a potential boon for the Melton community sits untouched, stuck in the middle of an ongoing tug-of-war, despite repeated interest from at least one developer.



Harness racing was delivered a stark wake-up call in 2023. Related Article Harness racing ‘Losing millions a year’: The $610 million racing code on the precipice The government severed the sport’s financial umbilical cord and Racing Minister Anthony Carbines ordered the industry to start living within its means. The future looked grim. At the end of the 2024 financial year, HRV announced a $34 million operating deficit. As a result, it axed 40 per cent of its staff (cutting the workforce from 120 to 70) and slashed $14 million in prizemoney.



This financial year, HRV posted an EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) of almost $1 million. But while the financial haemorrhaging was stopped, the industry suffers in other ways. Traditional wagering revenues remain under pressure and following three years of savage cuts, key stakeholders fear a mass walkout of breeders, owners and trainers – an exodus that would bring the sport to its knees – because they can no longer make ends meet. “There is no incentive to stay,” said one insider, who was not authorised to speak on behalf of the industry. HRV chairman Bernard Saundry told this masthead the sport needed control of the Melton land because the sport could not “cut our way to permanent sustainability”.



“Harness racing needs new sources of income beyond traditional wagering revenue, and we have an asset capable of helping create them,” he said. “We are not wanting a handout. We are asking for the opportunity to use the value created by our own asset to build a sustainable future, stand on our own two feet and ultimately reduce our reliance on government. Racing Minister Anthony Carbines told harness racing to stand on its own feet. Eddie Jim “Harness racing contributes more than $623 million to Victoria each year, with almost two-thirds of that contribution in regional Victoria. “There are communities, livelihoods and a 170-year sporting tradition behind these numbers.



“We think that’s a fair proposition: let harness racing use the value of its own asset to help secure its own future.” Harness Racing Victoria bought the land for $5 million in 2007 and began racing at Melton Entertainment Park in 2009 after relocating from Moonee Valley. But it lost independent control of the land in 2019 following changes to state legislation under then premier Daniel Andrews. HRV is a statutory body, answerable to the government, and the new law meant proceeds from any land sale would go straight to the Treasury. At the time, HRV was also swimming in debt. It had borrowed $42 million from the state government to prop up prizemoney, and still owed $44 million on its Melton track facilities.



Harness Racing Victoria chairman Bernard Saundry. Angela Milne The government agreed to wipe the debt in 2024 in exchange for the land. Former HRV chairman Adam Kilgour and his board agreed to the deal. Meanwhile, the land surrounding the harness racing track remains unloved. This masthead reported in October 2024 that a developer offered $90 million for a 30-hectare parcel of land at the Melton site, but it went unanswered. Experienced estate agent Mark Shelly, who is managing director of Stockdale & Lego at Bacchus Marsh, said he was “dumbfounded” the land was going to waste.



“It is mind-boggling that the land is sitting there doing nothing,” Shelly said. “It is this sort of hamster wheel, just spinning around, and nobody seems to be able to make a decision on what can or can’t happen with it.” A state government spokesperson said that “harness racing has a long and storied history in Victoria, and we’re backing the sport, local clubs and the jobs its supports”. “We’ve provided substantial support to Harness Racing Victoria to help clear its debt and implement a new sustainable business model,” the government spokesperson said. Melton City Council mayor Lara Carli declined to comment when approached by this masthead and asked about the potential benefits of developing the Melton land for the local community.



Harness Racing Victoria abandoned plans earlier this year to return to Moonee Valley as part of the thoroughbred racing venue’s mega rebuild because of the prohibitive costs. Related Article Harness racing A $90m land offer could save harness racing. Instead, it is gathering dust But it engaged a consultant last year to come up with three fundraising scenarios should it be able to wrestle back ownership of the Melton land. In all cases, it would continue to race at Melton. The first was a part-sell, part-development agreement, which would return $136 million to the industry over 60 months. The second was an all-out development agreement in which HRV retained ownership but would work with a partner to develop the land. The return was $190 million over 80 months.



The third was a staged acquisition, which returned $130 million over a 50-month period – HRV would receive $14 million every six months, starting month 24. In all cases, HRV would have to renegotiate the initial $86 million debt absorbed by the government in exchange for the Melton land. Other changes are happening in a structural sense. HRV will transition from a statutory authority to a company limited by guarantee on July 1, 2028, after the government changed the Racing Act. Had such a move been made in 2024, HRV would have had the power to retain its land. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: I’ve been renting my house for two years. Will I have to pay tax when I sell?
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingAsk an expert Opinion I’ve been renting my house for two years. Will I have to pay tax when I sell? Noel Whittaker Money columnist November 11, 2026 — 5:01am

November 11, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I am 72, single and planning to sell my former home, which I bought in 2007 for $860,000 following my divorce. It was my principal residence until two years ago, when I moved out and rented it. The property is going to auction in February, and the agent estimates it is now worth $1.5 million. I intend to move permanently into my beach house and give some of the sale proceeds to my children. Will I have to pay capital gains tax because the property has been rented for the past two years? Also, if I contribute about $200,000 of the proceeds to superannuation, will I have to pay the 15 per cent contributions tax, or could it qualify as a downsizer contribution? My current superannuation balance is $1.4 million. If you’re planning to offload a house you’ve been renting out, you might be able to avoid paying CGT. Simon Letch The good news is that the six-year capital gains tax rule allows you to continue treating a former home as your main residence for up to six years after moving out, even if you rent it to tenants. This means that, provided you do not treat another property as your main residence for tax purposes during those two years, you should be able to sell the property without paying capital gains tax. You could certainly take advantage of the downsizer-contribution provisions, but as you are under 75 and your superannuation balance is below $2.1 million, you could also contribute the $200,000 directly to superannuation as a non-concessional contribution, using the bring-forward provisions if eligible.



No 15 per cent contributions tax applies to non-concessional contributions. This would preserve the downsizer contribution option in case you need to downsize again in the future. There are no upper age limits or total superannuation balance limits on downsizer contributions, although other eligibility conditions apply. A hypothetical for you: our group of six are all pensioners and members of a local club that we regularly visit for meals and a chat. The club holds regular “Badge Nights”, at which a member’s membership number is drawn to win a cash prize that can be as high as $60,000. Before each draw, we have agreed that if one of us is lucky enough to win, the prize will be shared equally among all six of us. My question is whether distributing $6000 to each of the other members would be considered “gifting” by Centrelink, potentially leaving the winner with an additional $20,000 counted as part of their assessable assets for the next five years. The bigger decision is whether you really need a $3 million home as you approach retirement. That’s a fascinating question. If you won $60,000 and gave $6000 to each of the other five members, you would be distributing $30,000. Centrelink allows pensioners to give away $10,000 in a financial year, subject to a maximum of $30,000 over five financial years, without affecting their pension.



Assuming you had made no other gifts, the remaining funds would normally continue to be counted as an asset for five years and would also be subject to deeming under the income test. However, there is another possibility. If you have a genuine agreement in place before the draw that any winnings will be shared, the payments may not be gifts at all, but distributions of money to which the other members are entitled. I would suggest getting Centrelink’s view on the arrangement before the next draw. It could make a significant difference. My partner and I are both 62. There is $255,000 left on the mortgage for our family home, which is worth about $3 million. The variable interest rate on our mortgage is currently 6.8 per cent. I earn $115,000 a year and my partner earns $85,000 a year. I have $530,000 in super and my partner has $400,000. Currently, neither of us is salary sacrificing. I am happy to work until retirement age, but my partner would like to start reducing his working days over the next few years. We keep procrastinating over whether we should sell the family home and buy something cheaper. If we decide to keep the family home, should we draw down on our super to repay the mortgage? You are in a strong financial position, with a home worth about $3 million, combined superannuation of $930,000 and a relatively modest mortgage of $255,000. My first suggestion would be to take full advantage of the tax benefits available through superannuation while you are both working.



Assuming your salaries are exclusive of superannuation, your employer’s compulsory 12 per cent contribution would be $13,800 a year, while your partner’s would be $10,200. With the concessional contributions cap now $32,500 each, you could salary sacrifice an additional $18,700 a year and your partner $22,300. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’ve just retired with $650k in super. Should I spend it faster? Paul Benson Money contributor That’s an extra $41,000 a year going into superannuation between you, taxed at just 15 per cent instead of your marginal tax rates. These are full-year figures, so if you start salary sacrificing part way through the financial year, you will need to check how much your employers have already contributed and how much room remains under your individual caps. Your partner may also be eligible to use unused concessional contribution caps carried forward from previous years, given his superannuation balance is below $500,000. This could provide an opportunity to contribute even more at concessional tax rates, provided he has sufficient taxable income to make it worthwhile. As for the mortgage, at 6.8 per cent it is costing you about $17,340 a year in interest if the full $255,000 remains outstanding. Paying it off would give you a guaranteed, tax-free saving at that rate, which is certainly attractive.



However, I would be reluctant to start withdrawing large amounts from superannuation while you are still working and building your retirement savings. Although you are both over 60, unrestricted access to super generally requires retirement or ceasing an employment arrangement after turning 60, unless you have already met another condition of release. Your partner could also investigate a transition-to-retirement pension, which may allow him to reduce his working hours while supplementing his income from super. If you maximised your superannuation contributions over the next three years, you would be adding an extra $55,250 a year to super. That would amount to $165,750 in additional contributions before investment earnings. Assuming a return of around 7 per cent a year, this would give your retirement savings a substantial boost. Combined with your existing superannuation balances, it should put you in a strong position to retire debt-free. The bigger decision is whether you really need a $3 million home as you approach retirement. Selling and buying something more modest could eliminate the mortgage altogether and release substantial capital to fund a very comfortable retirement.



But there is no need to rush that decision. My preference would be to maximise your tax-effective super contributions while you are both working, review your mortgage repayments and then consider downsizing when you have a clearer idea of your retirement plans. Editor's pick Opinion

Household debt Six months ago, Australians were optimistic. Now, we’re cutting back on toothpaste Victoria Devine Money columnist At your ages, the aim should be to enter retirement with as little debt as possible, adequate accessible savings and the freedom to enjoy the years ahead. My daughter and her partner took out a $265,000 mortgage with Suncorp in 2009 to buy a three-bedroom house in Brisbane. It was a 30-year loan, with the interest rate fixed for three years at a time. They currently pay $375 a week and still owe $160,000. They have always tried to make extra repayments when possible, but the bank seems to discourage this. Is there a better way for them to pay off their mortgage faster? Based on what you have told me, they should have well over 20 per cent equity in their home, which means they should be able to refinance without paying lenders mortgage insurance when their current fixed-rate term expires.



I suggest they talk to a mortgage broker, as lending policies and interest rates vary between banks. A good broker should be able to find a competitive loan that suits their circumstances and allows them to make extra repayments without penalty. They could also consider a split loan, with part fixed and part variable, giving them some interest rate certainty while retaining the flexibility to make additional repayments on the variable portion. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: I overheard two execs making fun of employees’ accents and weight. What do I do?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I overheard two execs making fun of employees’ accents and weight. What do I do? Kirstin Ferguson November 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: an overheard conversation, setting boundaries during pregnancy and a confusing job application. Responsibility for the cruel comments you heard must lay with the people who said it, writes Dr Kirstin Ferguson. Dionne Gain I joined an online meeting early and no one noticed. I heard two senior executives ridiculing several employees, joking about one person’s accent, another’s weight and a third employee’s mental health leave. Should I expose them, even if doing so may also reveal that I stayed silent? These executives are showing contempt for people they lead and, especially in the case of someone on mental health leave, a breach of individual privacy. Unfortunately, it is not something you can easily ignore. I don’t think it matters that you stayed silent when you heard what was said; that is a normal reaction. I do think you should say something – you can use a whistleblower or speak-up line if you have one – so make sure you keep an accurate record of what was said, when and by whom.



Related Article Got a Minute? Is it unethical to look for a new job while I’m trying for a baby? If you don’t have a formal way of reporting this sort of behaviour, report it to someone with authority and is outside these executives’ reporting line if possible, like a board member or HR leader. Also be sure to keep what you heard confidential from your other work colleagues. These comments shouldn’t become office gossip. Ultimately, responsibility for the outcomes of what you heard must lie with the people who said it. I am a senior leader, and since falling pregnant, I feel sick and exhausted. I am usually a workhorse, regularly operating at 150 per cent and getting good results, and have done this for years without complaint. But now, I just don’t want to work that way any more.



Unfortunately, my colleagues seem to be reacting badly to the sudden shift. Now that I’m setting boundaries and doing what is reasonable rather than constantly pushing myself, I’m sensing disappointment and resentment. How do I handle this without feeling guilty or damaging my reputation as a leader? Is it reasonable to expect people to adjust to my new way of working, even temporarily? Is it possible you are hyper-sensitive to your own sense of working “less”, and what you are sensing are your fears of what they may be thinking rather than what actually exists? If you have years of hard work behind you, it would only be a true a---hole who would think less of you for slowing down a little while you are pregnant. Related Article Got a Minute? I have a very personal health condition. How much do I need to share at work? There is no doubt others would have loved when you worked at 150 per cent, and I am sure you have picked up the slack for others for years. However, any disappointment they might feel from the fact you are now setting boundaries and managing your work and life in a healthier way is theirs to manage. I don’t think you are damaging your reputation, and if anything, you are a role model to those you lead about how to work effectively, sustainably and reasonably. Regardless of the reason you have felt the desire to slow down, you have chosen the healthier option. Ultimately, anyone who works at 150 per cent for years on end is going to need to set boundaries or burnout will do that for them. My encouragement to you is not to think of this as a temporary shift, but one that you will be able to incorporate into your life from here on. Your career, your health, those you lead, and your family will be thankful for it.



I recently spotted two government jobs I was keen to apply for. Both ads seemed interested in finding candidates with significant transferable skills to bring to the job, but when I investigated more closely, they wanted someone who has done the same job before. In your opinion, is it worth applying for jobs that seem to have been written for an incumbent? Before spending too much time on an application, I would call the person running the process and find out whether your assumption is correct. It may just be that the  has been written poorly, in which case it would be worth finding out whether your experience would be considered transferable. If you do apply, make sure you mention your skill set using their language – you want to make sure that the transferability of what you know is as obvious to others as it is to you. If you find out during the call that they are looking for someone who has done the exact role before, you will save yourself the time of writing an application. You can also ask whether other openings often come up, which your skills may be useful for. To submit a question about work, careers or leadership, visit kirstinferguson.com/ask. The hotel Six Senses Fiji, Malolo Island Check-in Six Senses’ fast-tracked check-in process is swift, pain-free and greatly appreciated by this toddler parent. After a 45-minute private speedboat from Port Denarau, we arrive at the island of Malolo (in Fiji’s Mamanuca archipelago) to the gentle strums of a ukulele woven into the salty breeze. We are greeted by Claude, the resort manager, in an open-air lounge setting and introduced to Pana, our “GEM” (guest experience maker), aka personal butler, who will be at our service during our stay. There are no desks or lengthy waits. Within 10 minutes we are in Pana’s golf buggy on our way to our room. The to-do list.



The look 



A beachfront room with everything you could possibly want. Food + drink Like all luxury hotels responding to the longevity boom, Six Senses’ wellbeing ethos extends to the cuisine. The menus at the four on-site restaurants make a point of using organic ingredients sourced from local farmers and fisherman. At the waterfront restaurant Tovolea, house-fermented kombuchas are on offer at breakfast alongside lighter alternatives such as homemade granola presented inside a whole papaya. RaRa Restaurant & Bar focuses on South East Asian fare, while TeiTei Pizzeria is a low-key eatery in an outdoor setting where pizzas are topped with fresh herbs and vegetables from the adjoining garden. Free gelato for the kids can be found at the on-site ice-creamery. Hatha yoga at sunrise feels decidedly achievable here. Out + about



Excursions to the surrounding Mamanucas by air or boat provide a welcome change in programming to resort life, but take note of the weather. Too much wind on our scheduled snorkelling day meant our excursion was cancelled. If you’re desperate to get out on the reef, I suggest booking earlier in your stay to allow for rescheduling. The verdict Honeymooners and kid-free travellers will enjoy the romantic and grown-up vibe (the Kids Club is strategically located some distance from the main restaurant and lobby area). Parents with young kids (under six) may be more suited to a resort with a livelier atmosphere. Zero decision fatigue at Six Senses Fiji. Essentials



Beachfront Pool Villas start from $2235 a night. Vunabaka Bay, Malolo Island, Mamanuca Islands, Fiji. Phone: +679 666 5028. See sixsenses.com Our score out of five ★★★★ Highlight Having a dedicated personal butler (GEM) is a game-changer not just for a seamless check-in/check-out experience but for restaurant and activity bookings and general logistics. Hello, lighter mental load.



Lowlight All guests have a golf buggy at their disposal (driven by your GEM), which feels luxe to begin with. But the lack of guests on foot makes the resort feel unusually quiet. World.title: I’ve been a principal for decades. Here’s how to choose a school for your child (it’s not the one you think)
World.content:
NationalSchools Opinion I’ve been a principal for decades. Here’s how to choose a school for your child (it’s not the one you think) Adam Voigt CEO and former principal November 11, 2026 — 5:00am

November 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every year, parents of year 6 children sit at kitchen tables attempting to answer an inconvenient question. Is our local school good enough for my child? I’ve spent 32 years as a teacher, principal and system leader. I’ve sat with hundreds of families nervously weighing this decision. And there’s something those parents deserve to know that isn’t in the brochures they’re clutching. Wellbeing is an important factor in choosing a high school for your child. There’s zero wrong with the parental instinct they’re in the grips of – every good parent asks questions like this. But this particular question has been engineered, over decades, to point parents in a particular direction. It leads towards waiting lists and unmanageable fees. It coaxes parents towards the school that feels like a utopian promise.



I don’t blame those families for a moment. But they’re making one of the most consequential decisions of their child’s life in a system that has been deliberately tilted against the option they’re walking past. Related Article Education The fast-growing private schools offering an alternative to mainstream education Let me tell you what the research says makes a school good. It isn’t the uniforms or the facilities. Nor is it the student cohort’s socio-economic, religious or ethnic composition. It’s definitely not their latest capital works project or even their median ATAR. The consistent predictors of good life outcomes for children are a relational culture where students feel known and safe; teacher quality and stability; leadership that fosters deep belonging; and a community with a shared sense of purpose. None of these are owned by a sector and none appear in any fee schedule. Visit a prospective school in person. Not on the open day when everything is window dressed, but on an ordinary Tuesday. Walk the grounds and observe how teachers talk to students in the corridor. Notice whether the principal knows kids by name. That’s how to choose a school.



Talk to parents whose children already attend – just choose them carefully. The loudest voices in the toxic WhatsApp group are rarely the most reliable narrators. Find a parent whose child is similar to yours and ask them honestly: does your kid feel known here? Check the MySchool website data too if you feel so compelled. Just remember that a school’s improvement trend over time tells you far more about teaching quality than a raw year 7 NAPLAN score ever will. Related Article School funding Victorian public school students get nation’s least funding from government What the research also tells us is that belonging is no soft extra – it is the engine of learning. Children who feel they belong learn more, persist longer and flourish further. Australia’s PISA results show that 30 per cent of our students don’t feel they belong at school. The problem sorting children by the financial means of their parents is that belonging is harder to build in a school that begins from a position of competitive self-selection. You don’t engineer community from the top down. You find it when everyone is welcome.



In recent weeks, the Victorian and federal governments announced a deal to fully fund Victorian public schools. It was trumpeted as the biggest investment in public schools ever. Sounds awesome, eh? What went less celebrated by the pollies is when that full funding arrives: 2034. A child starting year 7 today will have finished school before the money arrives. Victoria is currently the lowest-funded public school system in the country. Yet, just the promise to fix it depends on the result of a state election weeks away that the current government seems unlikely to win. Related Article Education Australian students’ reading and maths results plunge in global rankings In NSW, government schools also won’t be fully funded until 2034. The underfunding that has made parents anxious about public schools was not a verdict on their quality. It was a policy choice. Decades of funding decisions directed more public money, per student, to private schools than was required to meet their minimum schooling requirements as set out in the Gonski reforms. Meanwhile, public schools absorbed proportionally 2.4 times the number of disadvantaged students, 2.7 times the number of First Nations students and higher numbers of students from non-English-speaking backgrounds.



The perception gap between sectors worrying parents at kitchen tables wasn’t discovered by them. It was constructed. Mark Morris and John Bush, co-convenors of Schools For All Australia, put it succinctly: “By continuing to under-resource public schools we have, as a nation, pushed parents to feel like better-resourced schools are a better choice. In many ways this is a false narrative. Related Article Opinion

Education Our kids are segregated in every way imaginable. We should look to Canada for a solution Jane Caro Novelist, author and commentator When you choose your local public school, you’re also doing something that goes beyond your own child’s benefit. You are keeping that school strong for the kid next door whose parents don’t have the same options you do. Every family that leaves makes that school harder for the ones who stay. Every family that stays makes it stronger for everyone. That isn’t a guilt trip. That’s called citizenship. Canada – our peer in prosperity and stability – sends 92 per cent of its children to public schools without suffering for it. What it has built, over generations, is a school system that functions as a piece of civil infrastructure, like a road or a hospital, but not a market.



Public schools are one of the few institutions left in Australian life where a child from a professional family sits next to a child from a working family, where differences aren’t filtered before these students connect. Related Article Opinion

Education Male politicians blame female teachers for our angry boys. They’re right about one thing Adam Voigt CEO and former principal This mixing isn’t a consolation prize of public education. It’s the point. A school sorted by wealth teaches children, day after day, that the world is made of people like them. The public school down the road teaches them the truth - and navigating that truth is what prepares a young person for adult life. What’s a better question to ask when choosing a school? Not just: is this school good enough for my child? But: what kind of adult do I want my child to become – and which school is built for that? The evidence suggests the answer, more often than the marketing implies, is the school at the end of your street.



Adam Voigt is a former principal, the founder and CEO of Real Schools and the author of new book The Truth About Student Behaviour. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘The talent is there’: Western Sydney collectives claim Powerhouse’s rooftop
World.content:
CultureMusicCity life ‘The talent is there’: Western Sydney collectives claim Powerhouse’s rooftop Kayla Olaya November 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
