World.title: Starc's 'opinion hasn't changed' as he disputes Khawaja ball-tampering revelations
World.content:
Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc has rejected Usman Khawaja's claim the 2018 sandpaper ball-tampering plot was known by all members of the team.

Speaking at Fox Cricket's season launch, Starc became the first current player to respond to the revelations in Khawaja's new book, Sabr.

In the book, released today, Khawaja says the plan to use sandpaper on the ball in the Cape Town Test was common knowledge among the team, and his pleas to have the entire squad take the blame fell on deaf ears.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

David Warner, who, along with Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, was among the only men punished for the scandal, said today that Khawaja's claims were "100 per cent accurate".

But Starc insisted he did not know a substance was being taken onto the field in Cape Town.

"Obviously there are differing opinions of eight years ago," Starc said.

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since. I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"We weren't aware anything was taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town."

In 2021, Starc joined fellow bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in releasing a statement disputing any suggestion they had wider knowledge of the ball-tampering plans.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," the 2021 statement said.

Starc said his stance had not changed since that statement was released but that "clearly there are differing versions from differing people".

Starc also said he knew nothing about Khawaja's claim sandpaper had been used to tamper with the ball in the Test before Cape Town.

Mitchell Starc bowls during the second Test of the 2018 series at St. George's Park. (AP: Michael Sheehan)

Earlier today, Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg said there were no plans to reopen the investigation in light of Khawaja's assertions.

"There are specific details in his book that contradict the versions that have been provided by others," Greenberg said.

"It's important to know that back at that time, players were urged to come forward, and they had the opportunity to do so over these past eight years, and that remains the case.

"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received.

"That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that.

"We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that."

Starc said he had not spoken to Khawaja in recent days. He said he had not read the new book and "probably won't read it".

World.title: Ahead of the World Cup final, Jamayne Isaako can't miss
World.content:
As New Zealand's Jamayne Isaako lined up his conversion attempts in the World Cup semifinal against Tonga, he did so in the middle of a hurricane while it was raining sideways.

The Kiwi winger is one of rugby league's best goal-kickers, but even he admits the horrific weather took things away from him in Newcastle.

"I had no idea where I was aiming the ball," Isaako said.

But despite the conditions, Isaako kept slotting them — into the wind in the first half and bending them through like a boomerang in the second because right now, Jamayne Isaako can't miss.

Loading Instagram content

His last kick from the sideline, when he hung the ball miles outside the right upright only for it to turn harder than even legendary New Zealand spin bowler Daniel Vettori ever managed, and go through with all his teammates there to celebrate, was his favourite, as the Kiwis stormed into the World Cup final with a 34-10 victory.

"I knew if I aimed it right, the shape would bring it back around, but I had no idea where they were going," Isaako said.

"I have a massive hook in my kick, so I aim a bit more right than most kickers, but I was just happy I got them.

"Particularly the last one, with all the boys behind me."

With the rugby league year ending after Sunday night's World Cup final, Isaako is about to finish one of the greatest-scoring seasons in the game's history.

Isaako's kicking, in atrocious conditions, was typically excellent in the semifinal win over Tonga. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

He was the NRL's top scorer in 2026, becoming just the fourth player ever to pass 300 points with his final total of 310 the third-highest single-season mark in league history.

Throw in a prolific and accurate World Cup campaign, in which he's kicked 36 goals from 38 attempts and scored personal hauls of 38 points against the Cook Islands and 26 against Fiji, and his total stat line for the season is 30 games, 26 tries and 145 goals at an 86.3 per cent success rate for a total of 394 points.

With New Zealand needing every edge they can find against Australia if they're to claim their second World Cup, Isaako's kicking form could prove crucial.

Between Cameron Munster, Reece Walsh and Kotoni Staggs, the Kangaroos have no shortage of kicking options for the final, but none of them are in Isaako's class.

Isaako's kicking could provide an edge for New Zealand in the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Staggs and Walsh have never spent a club season as a primary goal-kicker, while Munster, who took the tee in the semifinal win over Samoa and kicked six from eight, has a career success rate of 58.02 per cent.

Isaako, by contrast, has long been one of the NRL's elite boots and is in the kicking form of his life.

"This year has probably been the best for kicking for me," Isaako said.

"I've worked on it a lot, the last two years especially. The game is only getting quicker and if there's more tries, the two points add up quickly.

"It's something I pride myself on."

Isaako has worked closely with the legendary Daryl Halligan in the Kiwis camp each of the past four seasons, and the kicking guru likens his hook on the ball to Johnathan Thurston's.

Isaako was the NRL's leading pointscorer in 2026 for the third time in his career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Like everyone else of a black-and-white persuasion, Halligan enjoyed Isaako's circus kicks to finish the semifinal but nominated his two strikes in the opening stanza, which gave New Zealand a crucial 12-10 half-time lead after running into the gale, as his most impressive.

"His first two kicks into the breeze in the first half were his best and he could have a bit of fun with the ones at the end when there was a bit less pressure," Halligan said.

"Jamayne is pretty similar to JT in a way with that curve. He's a buoyant guy like JT, even if he doesn't have the laugh."

Isaako credits Halligan with simplifying his kicking approach and while Halligan is quick to direct credit back to the Melbourne-bound winger, he isn't surprised to see the 30-year-old's accuracy improved as he's aged.

Australia's old power conquers the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times, but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semifinal was a reminder of Goliath's power.

"There's not a lot of hard coaching this time of year, you're not going to change much and there's not much that needs to be changed," Halligan said.

"But goal-kickers get better as they get older. Why wouldn't they? They've ironed out the things they can do better.

"He makes good contact and puts a lot of work into his details. He knows where he's heading with it.

"The wind can play a factor if you want it to, but it won't change what he wants because he knows where it has to go."

History could beckon for Isaako on Sunday night in more ways than one.

He's currently level with Shaun Johnson on 225 points as New Zealand's all-time highest Test pointscorer and is all but certain to take outright possession of the record in the World Cup final.

Why the RLWC is New Zealand's to lose It took all their power and all of Kalyn Ponga's brilliance and toughness, but after getting past Tonga in Newcastle, the World Cup is within New Zealand's grasp.

But Isaako would give every one of them back in a second if it would mean a Kiwi victory.

The Christchurch man is of Samoan descent and played one Test for the Toa in 2019 but has represented New Zealand ever since because of how the country changed his family's life, a debt he feels he can never repay.

"New Zealand is where I was born and raised, and I choose the black jersey because New Zealand gave my family an opportunity, like a lot of the Pacific Island boys in this team," Isaako said.

"To win a World Cup would be a dream come true. We know what it meant to the old boys who were there in 2008, we've been fortunate enough to have a few of them come into camp and tell us their story.

"Whenever we're able to represent the black jersey, it's an honour and a privilege and for a lot of us, it's the pinnacle.

"It would be huge for us as players to win, but more for our country."

World.title: Clive Palmer says dilapidated luxury resort will reopen after decade in mothballs
World.content:
Billionaire Clive Palmer has begun revamping his luxury resort on the Sunshine Coast, with a new pledge to reopen the rundown site after a decade in mothballs.

The Queensland businessman purchased the five-star Hyatt Regency resort in Coolum in 2011 before shutting it four years later.

Mr Palmer announced a $100 million redevelopment in 2021 that would include replicas of famous landmarks, such as Rome's Trevi Fountain.

Clive Palmer erected a large Tyrannosaurus rex called Jeff at his resort in 2012, before the dinosaur burnt down in 2015. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

The work was due for completion in 2022 but has faced repeated delays.

Several job vacancies at the resort have been advertised recently, including skilled labourers, painters, security guards, electricians and plumbers.

A spokesman for Mr Palmer confirmed to the ABC the resort would reopen mid-next year.

Workers can be seen on site and renovations are underway.

Workers were seen clearing gutters at the Palmer Coolum resort on Tuesday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In its prime, the precinct employed 700 people and featured more than 300 luxury rooms and villas, a day spa and a popular village green.

The site still features an active 18-hole golf course, which used to host the Australian PGA Championship for 11 years from 2002 until 2012.

Mr Palmer rebranded the resort in his own name following a legal dispute with Hyatt in 2012, before closing the facility in 2015.

In 2023, dozens of tradesmen were among 125 employees sacked amid accusations of theft and fraud, with the Fair Work Commission later finding some dismissals were unfair.

Greg Norman plays a shot on the 13th fairway during the Australian PGA Championship at the Hyatt Regency Coolum in 2011. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Residents hopeful but sceptical

Many Coolum residents have fond memories of the old resort and hope it can be restored to its former glory.

"It would be extraordinary … everyone would support it," Coolum Business and Tourism vice-president Casey O'Hare said.

"It was absolutely gorgeous in its day … it was such an amazing asset for the Sunshine Coast.

"If Clive Palmer could rebuild and get it back on the market as a hotel and resort, it would be such a boon for the coast."

But Ms O'Hare said locals were sceptical given the repeated broken promises to reopen the premises.

Clive Palmer's resort in Coolum has been shut since 2015 but work has now begun to revamp it. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

"I'll believe it when I see it, because of the fact that this has happened before where it's been mooted as reopening," she said.

Retired builder Mark Hatfull helped construct the original resort back in the 1980s and said the "world-class" facility transformed the region.

"It took it from a backwater to where we are today … It was an absolute godsend," he said.

Residents like Mark Hatfull are hopeful the resort can be restored to its former glory. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

"The gym and the spa was something to die for … It was like something out of a dream.

"Obviously, Clive has got his business and then he makes a decision and one day a place is open, the next day it's closed."

'Devil in the detail': councillor

Local councillor Taylor Bunnag said he grew up around the resort where his father was a greenkeeper.

He said it would be "a wonderful thing" if it reopened, but he understood the scepticism.

"If you actually look at the site … there's a lot of existing infrastructure that's quite run down," Cr Bunnag said.

"I think the devil is in the detail with all these sorts of proposals.

A swimming pool area in disarray at the Palmer Coolum Resort in December 2017. (Supplied: Maree Frecklington)

"We've been told that Palmer Resort was going to reopen at certain times and that hasn't eventuated."

Cr Bunnag said a renovated facility would be "extremely welcome" in fixing the region's accommodation shortage ahead of the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

"We need thousands of extra hotel rooms added to our region by 2032 to cater for the demand," he said.

"It's hard to speculate about what further approvals they'll need because I'm not sure what product they're delivering.

Cr Bunnag said he had not seen any formal proposals for Mr Palmer's original plan of building replicas of famous landmarks such as Rome's Trevi Fountain.

A tradesman working on a building at the Palmer Coolum Resort on Tuesday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

"I'd only be speculating but my assumption is that they'll be renovating certain parts of the resort and some might open, some might not," he said.

A Sunshine Coast Council spokesperson said the site held existing approval for a resort and residential community facility.

"Provided the development continues to operate in accordance with the conditions of that approval, no further development approvals are required from council," they said.

World.title: 2027 Netball World Cup the 'next defining moment in women's sport'
World.content:
The 2015 Netball World Cup final was the stuff of legend.

A good old-fashioned trans-Tasman clash, it was decided by just three goals, 58-55.

The Australians managed to survive a desperate comeback by New Zealand and send retiring players Julie Corletto, Kim Green and Bec Bulley out on a high. Gutsy Corletto famously played through the game with a broken foot, needing painkillers injected at half-time.

Being there in person to witness it is something netball fans love to reminisce about.

A world-record crowd watched the Diamonds hold on against the Silver Ferns in 2015. (AAP: Paul Miller)

The contest was enthralling of course, but it's the atmosphere they remember most.

As the 16,752-strong crowd at Sydney SuperDome cheered an octave higher than at other major sporting events, they set a world record attendance for the sport that is yet to be broken.

Now, 12 years later, the 2027 tournament heads back to the same venue and organisers are hoping that nostalgia will help them break the record again.

Can they break the crowd record?

They have boldly set a target of 200,000 attendees across 64 matches from August 25 to September 5 and would love to fill the venue's 18,000-seat capacity for the finals.

The first batch of tickets goes on sale on today.

Chief executive Jane Fernandez said it would be the next defining moment in women's sport.

Netballers from Australia, Uganda, Jamaica and England pose with administrators at a Netball World Cup event. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

"There's a connection to place that is still front of mind," Fernandez told ABC Sport.

"For the netball community, this is a huge opportunity to be part of another World Cup on home soil, and I've met with a lot of people who talk so fondly of 2015.

"I think it's going to take netball into the next stratosphere."

The introduction of new silverware

The impact of that 2015 World Cup was undeniable.

Two years later, Super Netball was born. The modern era of the elite competition has revolutionised the game and offered players a professional wage for the first time.

It also allows unlimited imports, opening up full-time contracts in high-performance environments to players all over the globe. This has helped opposition nations grow stronger.

Australia has had a rough patch of form, recently losing the Constellation Cup 3-1. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

If the Diamonds found it hard to win back then, imagine the immense pressure on the current crop of players.

Following its lowest-ever finish at a Commonwealth Games, the Australian team conceded the Constellation Cup and is on the verge of losing its number one ranking.

Twenty-four internationals have been signed for the next Super Netball season and most of them will occupy starting positions across the eight teams, so it's only going to get tougher.

No matter what happens at this World Cup, the impact will be felt by generations to come and greater competition for the host team should help with ticket sales, according to Fernandez.

As will the introduction of a new piece of silverware.

Australia will be hoping to defend the 2023 Netball World Cup title it won in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

"It's going to be absolutely fierce," Fernandez said.

"It changes the energy of a tournament when you've got strong competition, so I do think it's great for the World Cup.

"This is anyone's to win and for the first time, teams can also play for the plate.

"After the first four days, the teams will be split and the top eight will continue to play for the World Cup trophy, while the bottom eight continue to play for the plate.

"All participating teams will have something to play for, which is a great opportunity for fans to keep cheering their side on until the very end."

Learning from other sports

The Matildas celebrate victory after a penalty shootout in their quarterfinal against France in 2023. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Fernandez is best known for leading Australia and New Zealand's 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup bid and eventual tournament, which captured the hearts and minds of the nation.

A key marketing strategy from that event was the storytelling of teams and players. They rebranded the Matildas and built the profiles of the athletes over several years.

Momentum built and it paid off with enormous crowds and TV ratings.

Crowds celebrate the Matildas' win over France in the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup. (AAP Image)

"We already know they are unbelievable athletes, and we knew that with the Matildas," Fernandez said.

"Our job is to make sure everyone knows the players by the time we get to the tournament.

"I mean the moment Sam Kerr started backflipping, which was around the time we were bidding, we were like, 'This is awesome.'

"We saw with the FIFA tournament that FOMO kicked in, and everyone wanted to be part of it."

Jane Fernandez (far right) poses with key figures at a 2023 FIFA World Cup event. (Getty Images: FIFA)

For this World Cup, Fernandez was hired once Netball Australia had won the hosting rights.

With less time up her sleeve, the aim is to leverage off the back of the Super Netball season, which culminates 25 days before the World Cup, and generate hype around the international players already at their disposal in the domestic competition.

The Super Netball grand final will be held at Sydney SuperDome on July 31, cementing the stadium as the home of netball next year, after the NSW government bought the hosting rights.

Melissa King was the CEO of the successful 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup at the same venue. It recorded the highest attendance across the event in the tournament's history.

Lauren Jackson was chaired off after playing her final game for the Opals at the 2022 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Sydney. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

King met with Netball Australia at the end of that year to share her lessons from the event.

One of basketball's main strategies was also to tap into the story behind the athlete.

Legend Lauren Jackson came out of retirement to play for the Opals, so they leaned hard into that narrative with clever marketing strategies.

King said it was just as integral for organisers to engage the multicultural community in Australia linked to the travelling teams.

The 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup captured the attention of the Chinese community. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

"The United States and China were in the final and we had former NBA player Yao Ming here watching with FIBA," King told ABC Sport.

"The Chinese community really got into it, so it's important to keep promoting and telling people about who's coming to Sydney.

"We had a situation where Lauren Jackson had a birthday during the tournament, so we created a ticket promotion around her birthday number.

"Of course, an Australian team being there on the final day creates a powerful connection too, but that's out of your control and just a bonus, not a strategy."

What are the challenges?

Although the entire event happening in one place is easier logistically, it does create challenges.

Loading Instagram content

It can make it harder to draw attention across the country. There is risk that activation outside the arena could start to feel stale for returning fans, and Homebush isn't the easiest place to get to in the city.

Aside from that, there could also be crossover in timing with the NRL and AFL finals.

Fernandez said transport would be included with each ticket and there would be a considerable uplift in bus and train services.

She is confident about their position in the sporting calendar, placing a higher value on international competition and its appeal to a different audience.

"You can't compare a World Cup to a week-in, week-out national sporting league," she said.

"Our promotion is focused on it being the pinnacle of netball and that's what sets us apart."

Three types of tickets will be available to subscribers at NWC2027.com from today.

Vouchers will be available for Christmas gifts in December, while single-match tickets will go on sale in February.

World.title: Aloisi sacked from Chinese club after losing final five games in title choke
World.content:
John Aloisi has paid the price for Chengdu Rongcheng's catastrophic title choke, with the Chinese club sacking the Socceroos great.

Chengdu had appeared a lock to win the Chinese Super League for weeks, on top all season and leading the competition by 14 points with five rounds remaining.

But they lost all five games and, after slipping to a 3-2 defeat to Shandong Taishan on the final day, handed the title to Dalian Yingbo, where former Western Sydney Wanderers coach Mark Rudan is an assistant.

While Chengdu had a superior goal difference, the Chinese Super League prioritises head-to-head records between teams, and Dalian had won both meetings between the sides.

Aloisi had been hoping to become the next Australian to guide a team in China's top league to a championship after Kevin Muscat led Shanghai Port to glory in 2024 and 2025.

Instead, the former Western United championship winner will have to continue his journey elsewhere after Chengdu parted ways with Aloisi and his staff on Tuesday.

"Mr John Aloisi will no longer serve as head coach of Chengdu Rongcheng Football Club. Members of his coaching staff will also depart," the Chinese club said in a statement.

Aloisi had apologised to Chengdu fans after the capitulation.

"We are indeed very disappointed not to have won the championship. We are in a very despairing state. There is nothing else to say," Aloisi told local media via a Chinese translator.

"I want to say sorry to everyone. We certainly know that our fans have travelled a long way to fight alongside us and support us.

"Right now, my only feeling is one of great dejection and disappointment, because we could see the trophy right in front of us, but could not get it."

Meanwhile, John's older brother Ross Aloisi departed Zhejiang FC after just one season when they finished ninth.

AAP

Tech.title: One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you’re tired of filament jams and clogged nozzles, perhaps it’s time for a new 3D printer. Through December 1st, the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, currently one of the best models that’s easy to use, is discounted. It’s $649 at Best Buy, as well as directly from Bambu Lab. That’s $100 off the list price for the bundle, which includes the Bambu P2S printer and the AMS 2 Pro multi-filament handler for multicolor prints.

My colleague Sean Hollister praised the P2S printer for its consistency and hands-off approach to 3D printing. Automatic bed leveling, including a warning if you forget to reinstall the plate, and a bevy of sensors helps ensure every print goes smoothly. There’s a live camera feed, too, so you can check in on your prints or share a timelapse. On its own, the P2S printer is usually $549, but is also currently $100 off.

The AMS 2 Pro’s filament handler’s fully enclosed setup saves your filament from absorbing moisture and clogging the nozzle or tubes. As a result, you can go weeks between prints and fire one off from your computer without checking on colors or manually swapping filaments. The AMS 2 Pro itself is typically $299, but is currently on sale for $229, and the P2S printer supports up to four AMS 2 Pro units simultaneously.

Tech.title: ChatGPT is getting verified AI ‘Business Agents’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

ChatGPT is going to let you chat with verified “Business Agents” that represent a brand to help you with things like comparison shopping. The feature, available first to “eligible” e-commerce and online service businesses in the US, is launching as part of a suite of business-focused features in ChatGPT being announced today in beta.

You can start talking with a Business Agent if a business that has created one appears in a response from ChatGPT. While chatting with a custom agent, you can ask about a business’s offerings and ask follow-up questions, like asking about differences between two different products. Businesses can specify a Business Agent’s instructions and provide business context so that the agent knows how to respond.

Image: OpenAI

Chats with Business Agents will be clearly labeled and separate from your main ChatGPT conversation, OpenAI says. To help people know that they’re talking with an agent that actually represents the business, companies will be able to claim their organization and get verified through a feature called Business Hub. (OpenAI isn’t sharing specifics about its verification methods because there are different methods for different businesses, VP of monetization Benji Shomair said in a press briefing.) Business Hub will also let companies see insights such as mentions in ChatGPT responses and top “discovery topics” where their business pops up.

“Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT,” OpenAI says in a blog post. “We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights and conversations that help people make informed decisions.” As things evolve, “we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers — directly or through agents and in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.”

Tech.title: Ableton Live 13 announced with a step sequencer, new drum synth, and more
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Today, Ableton announced Live 13, which is expected to arrive in early 2027 with a slew of new features. Most of the changes are seemingly minor on paper, but when combined, they make for the biggest update to the digital audio workstation (DAW) in years.

The feature most likely to draw attention is the addition of a proper step sequencer. While Ableton’s Push controller had a dedicated step sequencer, and you could effectively use the piano roll as one, the desktop app never included one. Ableton didn’t phone this feature in either — it’s a powerful sequencer. You can change velocity, timing, chance, length, and repeats for each step in the grid. Each track can have its own length, playback rate, and direction, letting you create something complex and evolving.

The addition of ARA plugin support will also likely excite pro producers and vocalists. This means compatible plugins can now be used directly on audio in the DAW. For example, pitch correction and time-stretching tool Melodyne previously required you to import audio from Ableton into Melodyne, then render it back out to a track in your DAW. Now it can clean up messy vocal takes directly in Live’s UI.

Ableton has also added a new mixer view that lets you see all the loaded devices on a track in a compact vertical view. Here you can drag and drop them between tracks, or copy and paste them. It also makes it much easier to navigate a sprawling 30-track session quickly at a glance.

My personal favorite new addition is Looplet, an experimental looping instrument with four playheads and a ton of options for manipulating your audio. It offers granular processing, filtering, pitch and speed control, and each playhead can be routed to individual tracks for additional processing. It’s a powerful tool for ambient and soundtrack work.

The full list of new features is sprawling, so here are just a few more highlights:

A new drum synth with more than 20 different models across nine categories spanning classic drum machines and experimental abstract percussion.

Capture now includes not just MIDI notes but automation as well.

Contextual browsing lets you swap instruments and presets directly in the device view, reducing the need to open the main browser.

Multiband racks for processing different frequencies through different effect chains.

A bread-and-butter transient shaper for tightening up drum sounds.

Envelope clips on return tracks for automating effects.

Racks can now have up to 32 macros and custom mapping curves.

Custom layouts on Push 3 for combining mixers, note grids, step sequencers, and more.

Tech.title: The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.”

According to the jurors’ statement, while this year’s IGF entries have been “incredible,” there has been “a significant increase” in the number of games “developed with generative AI tools,” leading to “fairly intense discussion and disagreement” with no “universal consensus.” The statement includes a list of beliefs, including that generative AI has “negative effects,” that AI-generated code is “not an exception to these harms,” and that use of AI tools is “not a forgone conclusion in our industry.”

IGF jurors that signed include Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow and Celeste composer Lena Raine. The jurors say that the statement doesn’t speak for IGF as an organization or for all IGF jury members, noting that some voiced concern about being able to safely sign “without professional blowback.”

One contentious title was apparently Big Walk, the co-op adventure game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. In a statement to Aftermath and posted on its website, House House said that “In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.”

House House said its “primary use case” of LLMs was “to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code,” including fixing an issue with shadows by modifying LLM-suggested code. House House noted it turned to the “LLM chatbot” after researching the problem “extensively” and even speaking to an engineer at Unity.

The studio said it disclosed its AI usage as part of its IGF submission, though it has not disclosed AI usage on Big Walk’s Steam page because “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.”

“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House said. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable’. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”

House House didn’t have an AI policy in place when it developed Big Walk, which it described as a “failure,” and said it will “work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.”

Tech.title: Google Fi is bringing back multiple cell network support for better coverage
Tech.content:
“Previously Fi’s switching was single-SIM switching which could only connect to one network at a time, so your phone had to wait until service dropped completely before performing a slow SIM profile swap into another network without knowing if coverage was actually better there. Fi also tried dual-SIM iterations that required both a physical SIM and eSIM which could be slower to transition.

Now we are back with added networks domestically. We have rebuilt the experience from the ground up for the modern era. With our new switching on newer Pixel devices, your phone keeps two eSIM network profiles on standby at the same time (via MEP technology) and uses the Android OS to monitor live connection quality. It also lets your phone transition faster and more fluidly with minimal battery impact—knowing a better connection is available before it switches.”

Tech.title: Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For years, Anthropic has been known for its focus on enterprise and coding tools that attract high-flying corporate clients, inspiring competing frontier labs — like OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and Meta — to copy its strategies. Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle. And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint to other knowledge workers with an AI-powered suite of office tools.

At an event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Anthropic unveiled new tools for non-technical workers who spend a lot of time attending meetings, brainstorming new ideas, and analyzing metrics: Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards. The tools allow for Claude to join a meeting, take notes, lay out ideas on a shared whiteboard, edit spreadsheets alongside employees, or turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video. The new “Artifacts,” or Anthropic’s version of graphical UI, come two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted, and join existing tools like Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion.

Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Meetings are all now available in beta, with the first two available to all paid plans and Meetings available for Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also announced that Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards when it was introduced in beta in October) is now generally available to all paid plans.

Image: Anthropic

Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge in a pre-briefing that Claude Code “changed how engineers work a year ago” — and now, the company is looking to knowledge workers as “the gap we’re hoping to close.”

“I think there’s still a lot of friction when it comes to adopting AI for non-developers,” he said.

The company also unveiled new interactive connectors that allow for users to open apps from partnered companies, such as HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian, inside Claude. The company launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago, and its marketplace of tools has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options; now, Lin says, the company is looking to make those connections a lot deeper, so that users don’t have to switch tabs to access the services they use every day and instead just embed them into Claude. For example, with the new tools, people can access a native Adobe PDF editor or a HubSpot marketing campaign tracker inside Claude itself.

Image: Anthropic

The tools follow other AI companies’ offerings in recent years: Google’s Gemini can join meetings and take live notes, and so can OpenAI’s ChatGPT, in some cases, via its “record” feature. Gemini is also well-versed in creating spreadsheets (thanks to Google Sheets), and Google has a lot of different “interactive connectors” for its suite of office tools. At OpenAI’s DevDay last month, OpenAI leaned even further into integrated apps and connectors in order to make its new Dots agents more useful. Anthropic is following in some of their footsteps, plus trying to gain new ground in the AI agent race.

The company is under a lot of pressure to generate more revenue and drive more product engagement ahead of its IPO, as it’s slated to potentially make the most valuable public debut of all time. And although that will turn heads, it also translates to a lot of pressure from investors, who want to see a viable path to profit at Anthropic.

The tools Anthropic debuted on Tuesday are some of the company’s first native products for non-technical knowledge workers. Lin said that although Claude Cowork, one of the company’s other tools for non-engineers, is essentially a wrapper for Claude Code, that tool was aimed at the “technical parts of [Anthropic’s] non-technical audience,” Lin said.

“Now we want to expand that reach toward everybody else.”

Tech.title: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, from browsing on the platform — the latest speed bump in the AI agent race.

A reader tells The Verge that for several weeks he’s had his Muse agent browse and curate a daily digest of watches for sale on platforms like eBay, including a link to listings, price, shipping details, and relevant notes about condition or style. This weekend, though, Muse was unable to pull any links or details from eBay, with Muse saying it was blocked from the site. The Verge was able to re-create the experience using other search requests, and in some cases we found that Muse instead directed users to outside sites that mirrored eBay listings.

Shopping is frequently invoked as one area where AI agents can augment or improve the human-driven experience. Technology companies tout the use of agents to book travel, find deals, and even purchase goods and services on behalf of humans. But AI agents are regularly getting blocked from accessing retailers’ sites, calling into question how useful they can really be.

eBay previously updated its user agreement to ban the use of tools like “buy-for-me agents” and “LLM-driven bots” that place orders without human review. Until recently, though, agents like Muse were able to browse the site and pull listings for users.

AI is becoming embedded throughout the platform for the discovery, personalization, and selling process, eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand told The Verge in an email. St. Arromand declined to directly answer whether eBay recently imposed new limits on AI agents.

“As it pertains to third-parties, we take a selective approach to how they access and interact with our marketplace. We have restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on our data,” St. Arromand said. “We have ongoing discussions with potential partners and are evaluating ways third-party agents could help new customers discover eBay’s unmatched inventory, and our focus is on preserving the trusted end-to-end experience that buyers and sellers expect from eBay.”

Meta declined to comment.

Retailers and service providers who’ve enthusiastically added AI features to their platforms have shown varying levels of comfort with third-party agents accessing their sites. On one end of the spectrum is Amazon, which is blocking external agents entirely from browsing or shopping. Some retailers like Target have restrictions in place that allow agents to successfully browse in some instances but get blocked in others. Shopify, meanwhile, has opened its catalog of a billion listings so that shoppers can set up their agents to purchase items on their behalf.

Throwing agents into the e-commerce mix has the potential to upend how people shop online, partly because retail sites are largely assuming they’re selling to humans, with human limitations, and not swarms of bots. For example, The Verge discovered in October that someone could use Muse to effectively hold product listings hostage on The RealReal, a secondhand designer consignment site, by having an agent continually add the product to the user’s cart. The RealReal updated its bot system after The Verge’s reporting.

But as retailers tweak their sites in real time to handle bots, it remains unclear how widespread agentic commerce is. In fact, there are signs that most people are not using AI this way. Uber said it fulfilled only four rides via third-party agents in Q3 and only around 500 Uber Eats orders during the week of Halloween. DoorDash similarly said it fulfilled only “several hundred” orders placed via third-party agents. It reported 993 million total orders last quarter.

Tech.title: The Verge’s 2026 holiday gift guide for moms
Tech.content:
Given everything moms do for us, it feels good to give back during the holidays. But where to start? How do you come up with a physical representation of how you feel about such a key and influential figure in your life? The possibilities seem as endless as they are daunting, but fear not, we’ve done the hard work for you.

To help you make the mother figure in your life feel truly appreciated, we’ve created a sprawling list of intriguing, lovingly curated gift ideas. Tech.title: OpenAI rolls out new business profiles, making ChatGPT just a little bit more like Google
Tech.content:
In an effort to make ChatGPT an even better consumer discovery engine, OpenAI is launching a host of new features designed to help companies control how users interact with their businesses.

On Tuesday, the company rolled out a Business Hub that will serve as a place where companies can create business profiles that — in a feature that greatly resembles the kind of profiles that Google and other search engines already offer — allow enterprises to verify and update information about their products and services. The feature is currently in beta.

Eligible companies will also be able to create and launch a specialized business agent, which gives ChatGPT users the ability to ask questions about the business and its products.

“As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI,” the company said on Tuesday. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT.”

In a move that calls to mind Google’s Analytics, the Business Hub will also give users access to limited business insights. These insights will reveal how ChatGPT users interact with their products — including profile views, business mentions, website clicks, and other metrics.

Businesses will have to verify their profiles through a formal process, although the company did not share specifics of what that process would entail. Benji Shomair, VP of Monetization, told journalists on Monday that there are “multiple verification methods that we use for different types of business in different markets.”

Image Credits:OpenAI

OpenAI previously tried to position ChatGPT as an e-commerce hub by which users could buy products directly. This effort — which used a commission fee system — was viewed as a potentially huge source of revenue and a way to make ChatGPT a more direct Amazon competitor. However, that project ultimately failed to take off and, in March, the company retired the effort, which had even included a “checkout cart” feature.

With the integration of business profiles and intelligence, ChatGPT seems to be attempting to become more like Google, which — since the advent of the internet — has been the place where web users go to understand the companies they want to shop at. It remains to be seen whether this initiative will bear better results than the one that sought to make ChatGPT a direct e-commerce hub.

Tech.title: Pixel Tag, Google’s $30 Android-ready answer to Apple’s AirTag, is now available
Tech.content:
Google’s answer to Apple’s AirTag, the Google Pixel Tag, goes on sale starting Tuesday, allowing Android users to track items like their keys, wallet, or bag using their smartphone’s built-in Find Hub.

First announced in August, the $29.99 device takes cues from the AirTag and other lost-item finders by offering connectivity via Bluetooth and ultra-wideband for precision finding. This lets Android device owners, including Pixel Watch wearers, locate their missing items using a combination of visual distance and directional guidance.

Image Credits:Google

Plus, the tag has a built-in speaker to play a chime that helps you locate your item if nearby. (Or, if you’ve lost your phone, you can press the button on the Pixel Tag twice to ring it, too.) You can choose between three different levels of loudness in the settings within the Find Hub, with the maximum volume around 80 decibels.

Though the Pixel Tag serves the same purpose as an AirTag, Google has opted for a different design. Instead of a small, round device, like Apple’s, the Pixel Tag is slimmer and more elongated.

Image Credits:Google

Spec-by-spec, the Pixel Tag is 1.1-inches wide, compared to the AirTag’s 1.26 inches. As the Pixel Tag is oval-shaped, it’s 1.8-inches high from top to bottom. Thickness-wise, the Pixel Tag clocks in at a depth of 0.2 inches, compared with the AirTag’s 0.31 inches (which Apple calls its height). The slimness of the device might make it more appealing for some, particularly if they’re adding the tag to a small item, like a keychain.

The device weighs just 0.4 oz, with the battery included.

Unlike Apple, Google opted for a physical button you can press on the tag, which makes it more obvious how it’s meant to work.

However, the Pixel Tag doesn’t include NFC, which Apple’s AirTag uses to aid the people who find lost items, as they can tap the side of the tag to launch a webpage that displays the owner’s contact information.

Instead, for lost items that are not nearby, the Pixel Tag relies on Google’s crowdsourced network of over a billion Android devices globally. The network, similar to competitive offerings from Apple and Tile, taps into the connectivity provided by other Android devices, which can identify and share the location of the lost item back to its owner. This location information is displayed on a map inside the Find Hub app.

Image Credits:Google

While the person who found the item can’t tap it, as with NFC-enabled devices, Pixel Tags that are put into “Lost” mode will be able to share the owner’s email, number, and a short message so the person who finds the tag can contact you. When the tag comes back into range of the user’s phone, the item is automatically marked as found.

The Pixel Tag’s location can also be shared with up to 10 people in the Find Hub app, which could be useful for shared items like the family car keys, which multiple people might rely on.

Like AirTag, the Pixel Tag is also powered by a user-replaceable coin cell battery (the CR2032), which makes the device reusable for the long term. (Google claims the device has up to one year of battery life to start.)

Meanwhile, the device itself is made from stainless steel and features IP67 water and dust resistance (maximum depth of 1 meter up to 30 minutes). It pairs with devices running Android 9 or newer via Fast Pair technology.

The Pixel Tag comes in two shades: silver and a pale green, and can be bought individually or in a four-pack for $99.99.

Alongside the launch, the company Bellroy is debuting its own keychain cases in a variety of colors and styles, which will also be sold on the Google Store.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches Claude Meetings to turn workplace discussions into plans and tasks
Tech.content:
Anthropic announced new workplace features on Tuesday, including Claude Meetings, which brings Claude into video calls to begin working on tasks while participants are still talking. The company also unveiled Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets.

The launch of Anthropic’s new productivity-focused features comes just a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled a series of workplace tools that allow users to collaborate with ChatGPT to do things like visualize company information and create presentations, as both companies compete to turn their products into office suites of sorts to take on Microsoft and Google. Meta is also joining the competition with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks.

With Claude Meetings, teams can add Claude to a video call as a visible participant. Claude then follows the conversation and gets to work on tasks in real time. As participants talk, it can draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline on a whiteboard, answer questions in the meeting chat, and access connected work apps to retrieve information, such as last year’s figures. After the call, the meeting notes, action items, and other materials Claude created are available in claude.ai.

The work that comes out of a meeting usually starts after everyone hangs up, but with this new feature, teams can turn discussions into actions in real time, Anthropic says.

Claude identifies itself as a meeting participant and posts a notice in the meeting chat. It won’t join calls with external guests unless authorized by an admin, and will automatically leave if an external guest joins.

Claude Meetings is launching in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. At launch, it works with Google Meet, with support for additional plans expected to follow.

Image Credits:Anthropic /

As for Claude Whiteboards, Anthropic describes the feature as a collaborative board where teams can talk through a plan and have Claude turn it into an organized visual workspace with timelines and deadlines.

The company notes that many people already brainstorm with Claude, but that in order to share their results with others, they would have to copy-paste them somewhere else. Now, a team can work directly with Claude on the same board in real time.

When the brainstorm is done, Claude can turn the board into a doc or a slide deck. Additionally, Whiteboards also work inside Claude Meetings, so the board builds while people talk, Anthropic says.

Claude Whiteboards is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop, and mobile.

The company also launched Claude Sheets, which lets teams create and collaboratively edit spreadsheets with Claude. A team can ask it to build a campaign tracker or hiring budget, and Claude will then generate a working spreadsheet.

Image Credits:Anthropic /

Anthropic says Claude handles the initial setup of trackers and budgets, while allowing teams to continue refining and updating the same spreadsheet. Each spreadsheet can include multiple tabs, formulas, formatting, and dropdown menus. Claude also makes edits directly in cells alongside the team, and outlines each change so users can see what it did.

Claude Sheets is available in beta on paid plans, on web, desktop and mobile.

Anthropic also announced that Claude Data, formerly known as Claude Dashboards, is now generally available. The feature connects Claude to systems that companies use to keep their numbers, like a data warehouse or CRM. Users can ask questions, and Claude responds with dashboards, written data stories, or narrated videos.

Additionally, the company announced interactive connectors that open the full version of apps like Adobe, Atlassian, and HubSpot inside Claude. Anthropic notes that teams can now open these apps directly alongside their Claude conversations and ask the assistant to work within them, essentially bringing existing workflows into the same workspace.

Tech.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy: a timeline
Tech.content:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.

United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.

As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.

November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements

The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.

November 9 -10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became a Nvidia preferred cloud partner giving it priority access to chips, the Information reported. The Info reported that Shanghai Century Litong. facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 US government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.

In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.

November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”

On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.

“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.

When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”

November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia Board of Directors begins investigation

Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.

November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy

U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.

A Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers which warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.

Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO, but does not take action

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship to Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.

The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.

October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.

Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, a Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

Tech.title: Sundrop turns your endless baby photos into recaps, time lapses, and more — without AI
Tech.content:
New parents take a lot of pictures of their children, but those photos often end up languishing in photo galleries, never to be seen again after the initial snap and share.

A new app, Sundrop, aims to make those pictures more useful by turning them into weekly recaps, highlights, time-lapses of the child growing up, and other cute scenes, like putting the child’s photo on a magazine cover or a rookie card.

While Google Photos and Apple Photos already provide extensive tools to organize and manage photos, Sundrop is taking aim at a particular niche: Parents with a new baby (usually their first!) who take an overwhelming number of photos and want to do more with those pictures.

Image Credits:Sundrop

The app was developed over the past few months by the same team behind the read-it-later app, Matter: Ben Springwater, Sky Lan, and Rob Mackenzie (all dads themselves).

Notably, Sundrop claims it is designed to be private, and processes all photos locally on the device it is installed on. To make this possible, Sundrop taps into Apple’s Vision framework and on-device Core ML (machine learning) models instead of uploading photos to a cloud server or some other hosted AI service.

Both of the child’s parents can use Sundrop together by linking their accounts, which allows the app to sync their shared photos via Apple’s iCloud service. This feature, the company says, means the pictures aren’t sent to any external servers it runs.

Image Credits:Sundrop

In addition, the team notes that no generative AI is used in the creation of its scenes or highlights.

This differentiates it from many photo editing apps on the market, including Google’s, which are increasingly tapping generative AI to create new versions of your photos.

Image Credits:Sundrop

To find highlights and recaps, Sundrop scans pictures in the parents’ respective Camera Rolls on their iPhones, skipping things like screenshots or duplicates. It then creates highlights or fun scenes, which it calls “drops.”

One of these is a recap of the week every Sunday, announced as a Lock Screen notification. Others can put two siblings side-by-side at the same age, generate a time-lapse series of photos or a video of a kid growing up, or cut out a photo of the child and place it into a layered template.

Image Credits:Sundrop

Parents can also manually edit the photos Sundrop uses to make its creations, or use the app to automatically organize the best photos into galleries with other similar shots.

The app costs $39.99 per year, and offers a week-long free trial. The annual plan also includes Family Sharing, so only one parent needs to purchase it.

Tech.title: Apple TV makes sign language interpretation a built-in accessibility feature
Tech.content:
Apple TV is making its content more accessible to Deaf audiences with the launch of a new Sign Language Interpretation feature, the company announced on Tuesday. The feature will initially be available across a limited set of titles, starting this Friday with the release of “Being Heumann,” a biopic about disability rights activist Judy Heumann.

American Sign Language (ASL) and British Sign Language (BSL) will also be made available for Apple’s hit movie “F1.” Later this year, other titles will follow, including “Way of the Warrior Kid” and “Greyhound.”

What makes Apple’s offering different from other platforms is that the sign language version of the film is not a separate product — that is, it’s not a separate film designed just for Deaf viewers. Instead, Apple’s support for sign language is just a setting you enable that’s integrated with the main title, similar to how you could turn on or off closed captions.

When a title with the sign language option is playing, an interpreter appears in the bottom right of the screen, translating the spoken words into signs. Apple says it has partnered with a group of DASLs (Directors of Artistic Sign Language) to ensure that the interpreter for each film fits the tone of the film. Notably, the company is not using any AI-generated interpreters, as Apple says that’s not what the Deaf community has said it needs.

The feature is shipping in the latest release of iOS 27.2, and can be turned on through a new sign language option in Settings. After being enabled, a new button will appear in the supported Apple Original titles on Apple TV indicating that sign language is available.

These titles are labeled with a sign language icon that appears on the title page alongside other features like closed captions or audio descriptions. There’s also a new section under languages that will list the specific sign languages that are available with the given title.

To make the titles more discoverable, Apple TV will highlight which titles include the sign language option in a “Movies & Shows with American Sign Language” editorial collection. Meanwhile, users can easily surface supported titles via search by typing in keywords like “with ASL,” for example.

The new feature builds on Apple’s other investments in accessibility features, which it builds itself.

“At Apple, we believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” said Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, in a statement about the launch. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences. Accessibility is a core value at Apple, and we’re proud to continue creating experiences that allow more people to enjoy the content they love,” she added.

Tech.title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips
Tech.content:
Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house-developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads.

The new units, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the company’s eighth generation of chips introduced in April this year, and build on what those chips offered, which was more inference capacity and support for large training requirements.

TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post. The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote.

The chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can be used to distill and train small models on the fly. That ability, according to Google, could prove useful for cases where a company might want to train a model on its proprietary data without having to move the data between devices.

Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries.

The chip launch comes as hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, and even AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own lines of AI-specific semiconductors and accompanying software in order to reduce their reliance on the dominance of Nvidia.

The news also comes at a particularly vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend admitted to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Tech.title: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes dozens of zero-day bugs
Tech.content:
In Brief

Remote access company N-able has confirmed it took down its cloud-hosted offering to fix a slew of security vulnerabilities that were published online this week, giving the company no advance notice to fix them.

In a status update on its website, the company said its hosted N-Central offering for customers is now offline “while we take the necessary actions to secure the environments and implement appropriate remediation.” The company also urged customers to take down their own self-hosted deployments of N-Central, fearing that attackers could use the publicly disclosed exploits to hack into customer networks.

N-able said during this time customers will not be able to use their N-Central service, which allows corporate customers to remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network. Remote access technologies are a frequent target of hackers, as these systems can grant vast access to a company’s network and internal data.

Security researcher Ben Bales released the “zero-day” bugs on GitHub on Sunday. In a post on X, Bales dubbed the bugs Able2Shell, describing them as a mix of vulnerabilities capable of stealing credentials, creating new administrative accounts, and gaining root access to affected N-able systems.

Bales told Bleeping Computer that he publicly released the bugs as the company allegedly failed to patch the flaws reported in a different product.

N-able said that it has no evidence of successful exploitation against any of its customer environments. A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment about whether it has the ability to check, such as server logs, or if it has no way to check.

Tech.title: ‘We Have to Take Over’: Far-Right Extremists Want to Seize Control of the GOP
Tech.content:
On Election Day last week, white nationalist Nick Fuentes urged his supporters on X to “get out and vote Democrat today.” The post racked up over 12 million views. Hours later, in the wake of the Democratic sweep, Fuentes took credit for the victory. “We did it again” he wrote on Telegram, later calling the phenomenon “the Groyper Effect,” a reference to the nickname given to his followers.

In recent days, Fuentes has claimed the election results are an opportunity for him and his allies on the far-right.

“Let the Democrats rule, see how that goes,” Fuentes said during a livestream last week. “There will come a time when the far left will terrorize people, and they're going to push all of them into the arms of the right. Who's going to fight the far left? Only the far-right. This is why we have to take over the right wing now.”

In another livestream last week, Fuentes added a warning to the GOP leadership: “It’s our party now … You need to cooperate with us… Groypers are open for business. It has [to] be America First—and if it's not, we'll do it again for the enemy.”

A WIRED review of comments from white supremacist, Christian nationalist, and other far-right groups in the wake of the midterm results shows much of the same. While the groups are uniformly attacking Trump’s failure to prioritize white, Christian American values, they also believe that this sudden shift to the left will result in a backlash that will see more people embrace far-right groups and ideologies.

Tech.title: Kitchen Gear From Our Place Is Steeply Discounted
Tech.content:
I’ll sing the praises of Our Place to anyone who will listen. I’ve tried most of its kitchenware, and I have yet to use a product I disliked. Not only do they perform well, but they’re all thoughtfully designed and look great in my kitchen. The only downside is that it can be spendy. Right now, Shop is offering 15 to 30 percent off a huge variety of Our Place kitchenware, and you can get an extra $60 off when you spend $100 or more. This is an excellent way to save on a gift for yourself or someone else.

For more home and kitchen deals, check our stories on the Best Black Friday Espresso and Coffee Maker Deals and this great Mustard Made home storage sale.

Tech.title: Rocco’s Mini Mini Fridge Is Here (2026)
Tech.content:
If you've always coveted Rocco’s vintage-inspired beverage fridges but haven't been able to swing the $1,999-plus price tag, here's some news you might like: Today, the brand released the Mini Mini, a desktop version of its legendary mini fridge. It comes in Green, Graphite, Cream, and new Stainless Steel. (Only Stainless Steel is available right now.)

Courtesy of Rocco

Courtesy of Rocco Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rocco Mini Mini Fridge $295 Rocco

We haven't tested it yet or even seen it in person, but Rocco says the Mini Mini can hold 12 standard 12-ounce cans and gets down to 41 degrees Fahrenheit. If you've ever tried other fridges of this size, you'll know this is an impressive stat. (Sorry, mini Frigidaire—you're cute but warm.) Rocco calls the Mini Mini “the first countertop fridge with real fridge standards.” It's got 360-degree ventilation with the refrigeration mechanics underneath the unit. That means it can sit flush against a wall, wherever that might be.

The only note is that, unlike the larger fridges, like the Classic and the Essential, this Rocco does not have a smart-beverage recognition feature—it's just for looks and performance only.

It's available for $295, and while it’s not currently on sale, unlike the brand's larger fridges, you can get it for $50 off when you buy a full-sized Rocco Classic or Essential.
