Tech.title: 4DX Movies Are Entering Their Thirsty Romance Era
Tech.content:
Following the temporary collapse of the fan fiction website A03, extremely horny millennial women are on the hunt for other ways to get their rocks off—and Regal Cinemas execs are more than happy to help.

On Tuesday, the movie theater chain announced that for one night only, on November 16, it will be screening 4DX versions of episodes 5 and 6 of Heated Rivalry, the smash-hit gay hockey show adapted from the bestselling novels by Rachel Reid that first aired on the Canadian network Crave but blasted into the mainstream when it came to HBO Max. The screenings will be at 59 theaters across the US, as well as a handful of theaters in Canada and the United Kingdom.

The screenings are intended to give fans the opportunity “to go to the cottage and really experience” Hollanov all over again, says Jack Grimes, senior director of alternative business development at Regal.

The 4DX screenings are upping the ante for the fan-favorite Heated Rivalry screenings, which have been selling out in movie theaters across the US for the past month. Though the series is widely available to stream, fans have flocked to theaters to shout along to t.a.T.u’s “All the Things She Said” during the club scene in episode four and post photos of the Heated Rivalry–themed popcorn buckets featuring stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams in a sweaty, shirtless embrace. Thus far, such public displays of down bad-ness have been incredibly lucrative: as of November 8, Regal has earned $1.4 million from its limited theatrical release, per Variety’s reporting.

Still, Heated Rivalry isn’t an obvious candidate for a 4DX release. Originating in South Korea in 2009, 4DX technology provides an immersive experience for the viewer, such as motion-enabled chairs; environmental effects like wind, snow, and rain; or even scents, such as the smell of gunpowder or explosives during battle scenes. It’s mostly been used for big-budget action-adventure movies and thrillers such as The Odyssey and Avatar: The Way of Water.

Recently, however, there’s been increasing demand for 4DX big-screen releases for not just conventional action movies but also straightforward dramas, comedies, and even romances. Put another way, there’s evidence that a not-insubstantial number of the filmgoing public would like nothing more than a two-hour license to hump their seats.

For instance, as the result of what was essentially an extremely online in-joke, last month the film distributor Black Bear hosted 4DX screenings of the romantic black comedy Wicker, starring Olivia Colman as a woman who falls in love with a straw-plaited man (Alexander Skarsgaard). The screening featured such immersive special effects as water splashing in the audience’s faces when Colman’s character empties out her chamber pot, as well as synchronized motion-activated “thrusts” in the audience’s seats during sex scenes.

Tech.title: This New Linux-Based Desktop Operating System Is Built for AI Nerds
Tech.content:
Kirt McMaster knows that his new operating system—Kora—won’t be for everyone, and he’s fine with that.

Kora, announced on Tuesday, is designed as a desktop alternative to Windows or macOS for “the AI native, not mass market,” he says. McMaster, the company’s CEO and cofounder—who also cofounded Boost Mobile—likens his strategy to how Steve Jobs targeted creators when overhauling desktop publishing with the Mac.

This “next-generation” desktop OS can integrate context from user interactions across multiple AI tools. Targeted to creators and developers, Kora’s central idea is to bring AI models together at the system level and help power users interact more seamlessly with multiple providers, rather than siloing everything off into desktop apps and browser tabs. It’s scheduled to launch sometime in 2027.

Tech.title: Ring’s Indoor Drone Camera Is Back—and Now Powered by AI
Tech.content:
This isn't the company's first at-home drone camera. CEO and founder Jamie Siminoff says he had the idea for a flying sentry in 2016 before Amazon bought Ring. The company previously announced an indoor security drone in 2020—the Ring Always Home Cam—and nearly launched it last year. But Siminoff says the team kept running into edge cases that forced them to add more sensors. Those additions required more computing resources and made the drone more power- and battery-hungry, which made it harder to fly. The solution? Move the intelligence off the vehicle and into the cloud.

The Drone Cam has enough smarts to land if it loses internet connectivity, but the rest of its intelligence now sits entirely in the cloud; the drone sends video straight to Ring’s servers, where a custom AI Pilot agent tells it where to go. That lets the drone be lightweight and nimble.

It will avoid people and objects, and if you accidentally stick a finger into the propellers, Siminoff says, you will feel it, but “you'll be fine.” If your cat manages to swat it out of the air, however, that's a different story. A Ring spokesperson tells WIRED customers shouldn't “fly it” if it's damaged and should contact support for help (no word on repairability). The Drone Cam runs a motor health check before take-off every time and won't fly if it detects a problem.

Users can't manually control the drone but can also set up custom flight routes and patrol schedules. It can automatically respond to alerts from security sensors you may have set up in the home, like motion, door, or window sensors. It will not leave your home, as it needs a Wi-Fi network to operate and uses the Alexa Home Map you may have created with existing Echo devices to help it navigate. It can fly five to eight minutes per charge. (The final production model will be black, not white like in the photos.)

“There are times when you do want to just be able to see everywhere around the home, but you don't necessarily want a [fixed] camera," Siminoff says. “That's why we invented Ring Robotics.”

Tech.title: The Grindr 1 Percent Is Getting Its Own Gated Community
Tech.content:
In a reddit AMA on Friday, in between jokes about gay bears and JD Vance’s potential username being CushionCasanova, Grindr CEO George Arison answered a question about the economy. He didn’t hold back.

“Inflation is terrible, and there’s a massive affordability crisis in this country that our government has ignored since at least 2020,” he wrote in the r/wallstreetbets subreddit, where, following the release of the company’s quarterly earnings report, he took questions from users.

It was a startling admission from the man whose company is about to release a subscription offering intended to price out most Grindr users. On November 17, Edge, a “premium tier” with some AI-powered features costing $120 a month, will be available to members worldwide, according to the report. Early access opened today.

The document suggests that Edge will help users find connections “with less effort” and will include a personalized recommendation feature, Insights, to “understand compatibility and the likelihood of a reply,” as well as Reconnect, which “brings past connections back into view.” The app will have an entirely new design, interface, and icon intended to create a vastly different experience for users willing to foot the high price tag.

But even if you can afford it, you may not get in. As with Raya, an invite-only app where some people have been on the wait list for as long as seven years, the company is planning to turn Edge into a digital gated community of sorts: Sign-ups will be limited to 1 percent of global monthly users.

Tech.title: Louis Rossmann Wants More People to Care About the Right to Repair
Tech.content:
Do you mind telling us a little bit about what Section 1201 of the DMCA is and how it ties into this conversation and makes it a little bit more fraught to do that unlocking?

Section 1201 of the DMCA makes it illegal to bypass a technical protection measure, otherwise known as a digital lock, to gain access to a protected work, even if it’s for the purpose of repair. It was put in place to try and stop piracy, and it was put together in one of the most corrupt ways possible.

Congress repeatedly said no to this law. No, this is way too restrictive. So the architect of it, Bruce Lehman, decided to try and get it negotiated into an international treaty. Then he came back to the United States and said, “Look, we signed this treaty, so now you have to pass this law. We’re going to be out of step with our obligations to the international community.” So he’s potentially sidestepped Congress in order to get this law passed that says that you cannot bypass a digital lock, even if it’s on something that you own.

Now, I can’t go to your house and break into your home. That’s illegal. I should not be allowed to do that. But if I spend $600,000 on a house, and I notice that there’s a locked closet in the house, once I’ve paid $600,000 for the house, I should be able to break that lock to get into that closet, because I own the house.

The problem with this law is that it allows companies to lock you out of things that you have already paid for. And the way that you see this being abused now is when you see companies taking away features from you or sending out firmware updates that stop features from working on the device after the company has gone bankrupt and they figure out, “Oh, wait, we need more money.”

I’ve had companies that failed before, and I really wish I had the ability to say, “You know what? I realize that I sold it at a price that’s a little too low. I’m gonna need to take $5 from every customer I had in the past year.” I’m not allowed to do that. I can’t stop my customers’ products from working.

But because I was selling a physical good that did not have any sort of firmware on it that connects to the internet, I’m not able to do that. Section 1201 of the DMCA is a law that came out in the late 1990s. This was before most normal people even had the internet, much less had their washing machine, their television, their dryer attached to the internet like they are now.

That law was, in my opinion, horribly put together for the world of the mid- to late-1990s, and it is way worse built for today. The architect of the law also said that the purpose of it was to try and fight piracy, and he admitted in 2007 and 2013 when he was looking back on it that it didn’t do that at all.

It’s very easy right now. I was able to show my 79-year-old father how to pirate television, movies, music, and it took me less than 10 minutes to show him how to use something like SoulSeek or Usenet to be able to get whatever he wants. These laws fundamentally have not worked, but what they’ve done a very good job of is making it much more difficult for people who wanna follow the law to be able to use their media.

Right.

If I want to rip my legally purchased Blu-ray and be able to play it on my legally purchased phone, I have to break the digital lock inside the Blu-ray disc to do that, which is illegal. What I’m actually supposed to do is I’m supposed to buy another version of it that’s only gonna work on here, and it makes it much more difficult for people who actually want to obey the law.

I think people are now waking up to this, but software is copyrightable. So when you buy a book on Amazon Kindle, say, and you have a Kindle book, what you’re actually doing is you’re signing an end-user licensing agreement that gives you the right to access that book.

You don’t own that book in a technical way, even though it feels like you should and feels like you do. So we’ve had cases where Amazon has actually removed books from Kindles after you bought them, and there’s no recourse for that. I think the idea of ownership in the digital age is informed by so much of Section 1201 and the way that we approach copyright and software.

Do you see any progress towards changing that?

Instead of every single year going back and asking for an exemption, what we’d really like to do is we’d like to pass durable legislation that doesn’t require that we ask for an exemption. We’re starting with the area that is the most reasonable, which is repair. If you want to be able to fix what you bought and paid for, that should not be a crime.

You should be able to repair what you own, and you should be able to show other people how to repair what they own without that being considered a copyright crime. We’re not even saying, “Can I please rip my legally purchased Blu-ray so that I could watch it on my legally purchased portable media player?” Right now, we’re simply saying, “I would like to fix what I bought and paid for.”

The problem that I’ve experienced throughout this process is there’s always an issue that people find more exciting, that’s more accessible, because you can only focus on so many things at once. If people are concerned about the economy, culture-war issues, if somebody’s concerned about immigration or Covid or policing—there’re so many issues that resonate far more with the voting public than this. The right to repair is this really abstract issue, and when you start talking about digital locks—my job, as I see it, is to get ordinary people to understand why this acronym and set of numbers directly ties into your thermostat saying it’s not gonna work anymore unless you give them $10 a month.

I don’t think that I’ve done a good enough job of that over the past 12 years to get it on par with all these other issues that people face every day. Admittedly, if you’re paying like $5, $6 a gallon for gas, you’re probably gonna care about that before you care about this.

So we’re talking not long after the midterms, and Democrats have won control over the Senate and the House. You do have a couple of politicians who actually have been speaking out about the right to repair who are in office now: Josh Turek in Iowa; Jake Johnson in Minnesota looks like he’s gonna get a seat. Is it encouraging that it’s even an issue people are talking about, or is that still not enough?

It’s encouraging to see that they’re talking about it, but I also realize that, especially going into this next Congress, there is going to be so much work and so many things that they’re going to want to do. I remember somebody asking me, “Like, no offense Louis, but I’d rather see them spend time on, I don't know, getting rid of Pete Hegseth.” I never tell people my issue is more important than your issue, and everybody votes according to what is important to them.

But there’s so many things that I imagine this Congress is going to want to do when they get elected that my job is gonna be making sure that there’s enough of a base of support and showing that there’s enough people that care about this, that if you spend the 20 minutes to do something about this, that it will actually work in your favor.

And that’s part of what we’ve been trying to do with the FULU [Freedom from Unethical Limitations on Users] Own Your Shit tour over the past few months. We’ve traveled around the country to 13 different cities, and in every one of these cities, we are trying to bring people together.

We had one of the ex-FTC commissioners show up, which was really cool. He gave an inspiring speech in San Jose. We’re also inviting their congresspeople to say, “Yeah, this is an issue that I will actually be more likely to vote for. This is as important to me as the other issues.” And our job is showing the people that are elected that we care about this. Because what’s their job? Their job is to represent us. If people are not talking about this issue or it's only being talked about on a couple of subreddits or on the fringes of the internet, I almost don't blame the representative for not prioritizing it. But our job is to show them that if they prioritize it, they'll be rewarded for it.

So I am happy to see that there are people talking about it. I remember when right to repair was put into an executive order by Biden in summer of 2021. I was excited, but there wasn’t a lot that came from it. I’m hoping for something different here.

So FULU is your organization that supports right to repair. You also have bounties that you pay out for people who can disable these digital locks. How is that going? Have you successfully paid out bounties yet? Can you talk about that program a little bit and why you're sort of taking matters into your own hands here?

That program came out about 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning. I was doing a video on Futurehome after somebody who works there, or used to work there, sent me information on what they were doing. He was talking about this thermostat that when it got a firmware update after the company went bankrupt, it stopped you from being able to use some of the features you could use before.

I did the video going over it, and I’m just sitting there at, like, 2 am editing this and thinking, “This is not enough.” And I said, “I'll give $5,000 or $10,000 to whoever makes this thing work again.” I was thinking back to what I was doing when I was doing all these repair videos showing the schematics.

Now you have hundreds of people doing repair videos that are way better than mine every single day on YouTube, and I love it. But back in 2013 and 2014, I didn’t see anything like that, and that’s because at the bottom right corner of the screen, it has this little message on the schematic. It says, “Proprietary property of Apple Inc. Keep confidential. Do not share.” Most people don’t like getting sued or having their livelihoods destroyed. For me, that’s like a Tuesday. I find it fun. I enjoy going to court. I encourage my employees to go to court.

Got it.

So I was thinking, “How do I get more people to start poking at these things? How do I get more people to start saying, ‘No, this is not enough. You can’t do that.’” So we came up with this bounty, and you could see in that video that most of it was done during the day, and the part with the bounty was done at 3:00 in the morning in some corner of my house when I’m dead tired.

I said, “5,000 bucks to whoever makes this work again.” And there was an employee that emailed me with a solution shortly thereafter, and he said, “Louis, I appreciate this. I would’ve done this for free, but here I made a Home Assistant integration,” and people were able to use the thermostat again.

So what we’re trying to do with the bounty program is we’re trying to show people that, A, this is a problem, and B, we’re trying to incentivize people to start making things work again so that we can point to how bad this law is. We can also point to things that tangibly work again. The reason that the right-to-repair stuff with Apple that I was doing was successful is because I wasn’t just saying, “Here’s why you should care about this.”

Millions of people probably have working MacBooks again because of those videos that I was doing back in the day. So when somebody personally saves $1,000, when they personally get their data back, they are now invested in my cause in a way that no Twitter hashtag and no bumper sticker is ever gonna make happen.

What’s a gateway drug into right to repair? If you want to get into repairing your own stuff, what is an easy thing? Is it an iPhone battery replacement or a trackpad upgrade? What do you point people to and say, “This is something that you can actually do. This is something you can manage. It’s gonna make your life better. It’s gonna make your experience better”?

I don't have a very well-packaged answer for that. For me, it it has to be something fun. It has to be, It's 103 degrees in Texas this week, and my asshole air conditioning technician has stiffed me three times. Let me open it up and, oh, I just used compressed air on the contactor and I blew out the fire ants, so now it works again. That’s what’s gonna get people excited about this. I get excited about repair not because of the repair that’s being done, and admittedly not even the money, it’s the story that’s involved in it.

So anytime you’re fixing something because I need this to work right now, or I don't have the money to make this work again, anytime there’s some sort of story attached to it, it’s going to be something that gets you excited.

Some people may feel incredibly excited about replacing the battery in their phone. Some people are really just gonna hate it. But I think there has to be some sort of story behind it that makes it worth it. I actually don’t find repair fun. I don't think that putting 96 solder balls back onto a chip that's the size of my pinky fingernail is fun.

I don’t do it for that. I do it for the hug that the customer gives you when you get back all their baby pictures, or when you do this for the police and they're able to catch the murderer because of it. I don’t find taking a battery out of a phone, using a heat gun, and using a little spudger to get all this off, but not breaking the screen—that’s not fun.

It’s fun if you can’t afford a new one. That makes it a lot of fun. It’s fun if you’re doing it to get something back. But there has to be a story. There has to be a reason that makes that particular repair exciting to you, and that's gonna be different for everybody, and it’s usually gonna be based on whatever your circumstances are at the time.

Tech.title: Live Now! The iPhone Duo Has Been Folded 385,000 Times and Counting in Our Custom Machine
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo wowed us, but it’s time to test out how its first-gen hinge holds up. We’re now testing Apple’s $1,999 foldable phone using our custom-made folding machine, the Fold-a-Phone, which has been diligently opening and closing the phone since we bought the Duo on Oct. 23. We’ve already passed 385,000 folds. All this folding isn’t expected to stop until the Duo breaks.



CNET is livestreaming our iPhone Duo long-term folding test on our YouTube channel, which you can watch embedded above. Our robust in-house machine is opening and closing the foldable phone around 20,000 times per day to simulate years of wear and tear on the hinge. So far, it’s holding up pretty impressively. You can watch this testing on a livestream from our CNET Labs location in Louisville, Kentucky.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

The livestream isn’t just for watching a phone open and close — you’ll also be able to chat with CNET editors who will be available to answer your iPhone Duo questions live in the chat. Will Apple’s first foldable live up to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold? Will its neat opening animation remain slick over thousands of folds? Join us and find out.

The iPhone Duo has surpassed 385,000 folds in our custom Fold-A-Phone machine. Matthew Murray/CNET

This long-term test will join our iPhone Duo review, which provides a snapshot of what it’s like to be among the first to use Apple’s first foldable phone. If you’re sold on it, check out the best iPhone Duo deals. And if you want to compare even further, you can check out our roundup of the best foldable phones currently available if you want help deciding between the Duo and other folding and flip-style phones from Samsung, Motorola and Google.

Tech.title: Google Fi’s ‘Super Network’ Hops Networks to Keep Your Pixel Phone Connected
Tech.content:
Even in areas that seem abundant with overlapping cellular coverage, phones sometimes sputter when you’re looking up information or trying to get directions when your carrier’s signal gets weak. To avoid those annoying interruptions, Google Fi Wireless is rolling out what it’s calling a “super network” feature. It automatically switches your phone between two 5G networks to maintain the best connection.

The new capability works only on Google’s phones, starting with the Pixel 9 and newer Pixel models.

The super network is included free for existing Google Fi customers on all of its plans: Flexible, Unlimited Essentials, Unlimited Standard and Unlimited Premium.

More from CNET

Google says that it’s using “two top 5G networks,” but the company is refusing to reveal which networks those are in the US. Traditionally Google Fi runs on T-Mobile’s network.

The network switching also applies when you’re traveling internationally, and is included in the Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

According to a source at Google, the phone will use two eSIM slots to switch between networks, but it will appear to only use a single eSIM on the customer’s phone. A fine-print disclaimer notes that any other eSIMs on your device must be disabled, which is worth knowing for anyone that already uses multiple carriers on a single device.

In addition to the super network news, Google said its Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus feature is available in millions of more locations across the US. If the phone is in an area where cellular is spotty and a compatible Wi-Fi network is nearby, it automatically makes an encrypted connection if the Wi-Fi network is stronger.

Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus is available on Pixel phones, but is also becoming available on Samsung phones running One UI 9 or later and “select modern Motorola phones.”

Tech.title: Xbox Game Pass Subscribers Can Play Football Manager, Warhammer Survivors and More Now
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, Microsoft announced the games it’s adding to its Xbox Game Pass service in the first half of November. However, Rockstar Games is preparing to release Grand Theft Auto 6 on Nov. 19, so that game will likely take up a lot of your playtime from then on. That still leaves plenty of time to give these upcoming Game Pass titles a shot. I’m particularly excited about Warhammer Survivors. I really enjoyed Vampire Survivors, and can’t wait to play as Fo’Baran, the chaplain of my beloved Salamanders from Warhammer 40K.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award winner, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 per month. With a higher-tier Game Pass Ultimate subscription ($23 per month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones on release day, each month.

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass soon.

More from CNET

Escape Academy 2: Back 2 School

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Class is back in session in this puzzle game. This sequel to the award-winning Escape Academy brings you more puzzles to solve and a series-first open-world format. That makes the campus one big puzzle room filled with secrets, traps and more. If you get stuck, you can always chill with your friends and enjoy student life away from the classroom. The choice is yours.

Warhammer Survivors

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Poncle, the creator of the indie hit Vampire Survivors, teamed up with Auroch Digital to let you bring your favorite Warhammer primarchs and champions into bullet-heaven action. Each character has their own special ability to help you defeat waves of enemies. Every stage is a new arena full of enemies and secrets to uncover. So grab your chainsword and whirlwind axes, because there are pixelated enemies to destroy.

Football Manager 2027 Console

Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

Get ready for the most immersive matchday experience yet in the latest installment of the long-running Football Manager series. You’ll shape your club and define your team’s style, and you can get lost in the wider football universe thanks to smart news and events that mirror the drama of the football calendar.

These other games are also coming to Xbox Game Pass

In addition to the titles above, Xbox is also adding these games to Game Pass soon:

Xbox Game Pass Essential gets new games too

Game Pass Essential costs $10 a month and offers access to a relatively small library of games compared with Game Pass Premium and Ultimate. While Microsoft doesn’t regularly add many games to Essential’s library, it’s adding these eight titles to this Game Pass tier on Nov. 15.

Games leaving Xbox Game Pass on Nov. 15

While Microsoft is adding several games to Game Pass soon, it’s also removing over a dozen games on Nov. 15. So you’ll have to buy these games separately if you still need to complete your main campaign or any side quests after they’re removed.

For more, here’s our Xbox Game Pass review and other titles you can play on the service. You can also read our recent review of the Xbox Nano Controller.

Tech.title: Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: The AirTag for Android Fans
Tech.content:
When a company comes out with its own version of a product in an established market, there has to be a good reason. Maybe it’s created a design that sets the product apart, or it’s included features that none of the competition has.

If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google is releasing the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available starting Wednesday for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

More from CNET

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

I don’t trust taking keys anywhere without a smart tracker like the Google Pixel Tag. Jeff Carlson/CNET

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Nice in the hand when hands-on is necessary

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

The Pixel Tag at right is much slimmer than the second-generation AirTag at left. Jeff Carlson/CNET

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Google stretched the length of the Pixel Tag compared to the round puck design of the Apple AirTag. Jeff Carlson/CNET

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

Find Pixel Tags nearby

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

Finding a Pixel Tag: Using just Bluetooth (left); with Bluetooth and ultra-wideband (middle); and when close enough to point in the direction of the smart tracker (right). Screenshots by Jeff Carlson/CNET

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a couple of days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Privacy features

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

Tech.title: Apple TV Adds Sign Language Interpretation, Starting With Original Film ‘Being Heumann’
Tech.content:
Apple TV is adding sign language interpretation for a handful of supported streaming titles, beginning with the Apple original film Being Heumann, which premieres on Friday.

With iOS 27.2, you’ll find new options for American Sign Language and British Sign Language within Apple TV’s app settings. When you select one of these languages, a new button will appear on supported Apple original titles indicating sign language availability. You can also turn off or change your language selection directly within the player.

Titles that support sign language interpretation will have a sign language icon displaying an image of a hand. This icon appears on the title page of a show or movie, next to other accessibility options like closed captions and audio descriptions.

More from CNET

Being Heumann is an apt pick for debuting this accessibility feature. The film centers on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and her leadership in the historic 1977 protest that helped advance equal rights and protections for Americans with disabilities. Sign language support will also roll out to other Apple TV titles starting with F1 The Movie, followed by Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid (which debuts Nov. 25) later this year.

Apple TV is adding a dedicated collection called Movies & Shows with American Sign Language to make it easier to browse supported content. That collection will include movies where sign language is part of the story, such as 2021’s Oscar-winning film CODA. You can also look up “with ASL” in the app’s search bar to find relevant titles.

“We believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, said in a statement. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences.”

A rising tide of sign language support

Sign language interpretation can add more context and nuance than closed captions do. Apple TV

Apple TV joins a handful of other streaming platforms with sign language options, including HBO Max and Prime Video. Netflix also features sign language interpretation for dozens of kids and family titles through a partnership with SignUp Media, which built a Chrome extension that overlays an interpreter onto supported shows and movies. SignUp is also available on select Disney Plus and Peacock content.

While closed captioning can help some deaf and hard-of-hearing people better understand what’s happening on screen, many viewers prefer watching with sign language interpretation, which can better convey emotion and expression.

“For the deaf community, our first language is ASL,” Nakia Smith, a deaf storyteller and an interpreter for the HBO Max series It: Welcome to Derry, told me in an interview earlier this year.

Unlike closed captioning, which has become nearly ubiquitous across streaming and television, sign languages like ASL are slowly making their way into more entertainment spaces, from sports broadcasts to awards ceremonies and red carpets. But there’s still a long way to go.

The challenge is that sign language interpretation requires skilled human professionals who can capture context and nuances, which takes time and resources. More companies appear to be making the effort. And while some studios are exploring AI to automate captioning, the complexity and diversity of sign languages suggest this will remain a largely human-driven endeavor for the foreseeable future.

For its part, Apple worked closely with the deaf community, partnering with Directors of Artistic Sign Language to ensure they matched the tone of the films and maintained authentic representation.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and who directed the film’s sign language interpretation, said in a statement. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

Tech.title: Your November Stargazing Calendar: Meteors, Morning Planets and a Supermoon
Tech.content:
Looking to see some amazing sights in the autumn sky? You’re in luck. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time having ended on Nov. 1, the sun has been setting even earlier. That’s good news, since some of November’s best views come before sunrise.

Venus, Mercury, Mars and Jupiter all appear in the morning sky this month, with Mars and Jupiter drawing close together around Nov. 15–16. The Leonid meteor shower peaks a couple of nights later, and the hours after moonset on Nov. 17–18 offer the darkest window to catch it. Evenings have their own highlights, from Saturn after dusk to the Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24.

When to see each planet in November

Venus and Mercury are tough to spot at the start of November, but they’ll get easier to spot later on. Stellarium

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, when it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

Nov. 14-25: A four-planet alignment

The four planets should line up nicely just before dawn. Mars and Jupiter are also very close together. Stellarium

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Saturday, there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Saturday and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

Nov. 11-12: Northern Taurids peaks

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on Wednesday and Thursday morning. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Wednesday, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Nov. 16-17: Leonids peaks

The Leonids shoot meteors from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars. Stellarium

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It started on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41% illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

Nov. 23-24: Supermoon

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon. NASA/JPL-Caltech

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

Nov. 30: Another moon, Mars and Jupiter dance party

This is arguably the better meetup for this quartet, as they’ll all be much closer together than at the start of the month.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

All month: Constellations and asterisms

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

Tech.title: Spotify DJ Adds Nine New Voices and a Mute Option
Tech.content:
Music streaming service Spotify has unveiled new abilities for its popular AI-powered DJ feature, including new hosts — speaking in Spanish and English — and an on/off announcer toggle. The update rolls out to existing DJ markets starting Tuesday.

Also read: Best Music Streaming Services of 2026

The lineup includes seven new English voices with British, American, Irish, Australian and Indian accents, as well as two new Mexican-accented voices that speak in Spanish.

More from CNET

The personalities also differ by announcer, too — for instance, Spotify says American Tess is “direct but inviting, has a bit of an edge. In-the-know” while Australian Sam is “gregarious, fun, likes to keep things not-so-serious.”

You can also turn the announcer off, but it would then be hard to tell how a Spotify DJ mix differs from a random mix. The company says you’ll still hear a “brief acknowledgment” when you start the DJ or press the DJ button to switch modes.

Spotify’s DJ was introduced in 2023 and is a way to set up your own radio station with a dynamic announcer. In addition, Spotify is the most popular music streaming service, with over 100 million tracks and a plethora of features including audiobooks, podcasts and the end-of-year Spotify Wrapped. Subscriptions are available starting at $13 a month.

Tech.title: The New Adobe Firefly AI Is All About Video Editing
Tech.content:
Adobe has been on a journey for years to turn itself into an AI behemoth, and its latest round of Firefly AI updates brings its dreams one step closer to fruition. At Adobe Max on Tuesday, the company announced a slew of Firefly AI updates focused on building out its video-editing capabilities.

Firefly is getting an upgraded video editor. Like other creative AI companies, Adobe has been building up its AI video capabilities over the past year, with video models made both in-house and by third-party AI companies. Now, the new interface incorporates the Firefly AI assistant, which is in beta, in a bigger way. There’s a dedicated ideation panel and more ways to storyboard ideas.

It’s a more feature-packed alternative to beginner or everyday video editors like CapCut, without overloading creators with all the features of professional-grade Adobe Premiere. Part of that push is integrating agentic AI, or agents that can handle editing tasks for you autonomously. And there are a lot of AI agents coming to Adobe’s programs.

More from CNET

That beginner-to-intermediate design is, well, by design — Adobe is aiming to lure in folks without decades of video-editing know-how with its generative AI features. It fits with Adobe’s larger goals; it wants to build Firefly for video and image editors the same way it built Photoshop — to be the “career partner” for creators.

Firefly Design

Another new project is Firefly Design, an AI-heavy version of a graphic design program that incorporates print, motion graphics and 3D. The intelligence assistant is a big part of the interface, where you can use text prompts to come up with variations of different scenes.

There are a few new Firefly AI image tools, and their names describe their uses well: relight, retouch and edit object. These are more precise controls, keeping with Adobe’s goal of giving AI enthusiasts more ability to edit their video content. There are also new quick actions, or shortcuts, including a video thumbnail generator that’s based on your video.

In this example, you can see how each individual element (or node) is pulled together into the final product. Adobe

And if you remember Project Graph from last year’s Adobe Max, it’s back in a public preview as Firefly Graph. This is a node-based editing system, where you can create individual “nodes” and connect them to create an entire system, or ecosystem, of content. It won’t be for everyone, but it’s aimed at creative teams who want to visualize large workflows.
